steps.desc: Check for other reports of the same fake update lure and APK source domain.
steps.outcome: Campaign scope established.

ITID-11323.def: A smishing message linking to a malicious iOS configuration profile (or MDM enrollment profile) which, once installed, grants the attacker device-management-level control, certificate trust, or traffic-interception capability — an iOS-specific vector with no direct Android equivalent.
ITID-11323.purpose: Distinguishes smishing that lures an iOS target into installing a malicious configuration/management profile rather than an app.
scopeIncludes: Links leading to an iOS .mobileconfig profile install prompt outside legitimate enterprise MDM
scopeExcludes: Android APK sideload (a distinct leaf, ITID-11322)
Legitimate enterprise MDM enrollment spoofing targeting corporate device fleets specifically (a distinct leaf, ITID-11329, scoped to the enterprise-targeted variant)
ITID-11323.severity: High — a malicious configuration profile can grant persistent, privileged control over the device.
ITID-11323.priority: P1 if profile installation is confirmed.
ITID-11323.escalation: Escalate to mobile security immediately; remove the profile and assess for certificate/traffic-interception compromise.
indicators: iOS prompt to install a configuration profile following a smishing link
Unrecognized profile present in device settings
vectors: Smishing link directing to a hosted malicious .mobileconfig file
rootCauses: iOS's native support for user-installed configuration profiles outside enterprise MDM oversight
Lack of restriction on profile installation on personal/BYOD devices
controls: MDM supervision restricting profile installation
Mobile threat defense profile-scanning
User awareness training
ITID-11323.detection: MDM-supervised devices offer meaningful visibility into unauthorized profiles; unsupervised personal devices offer little.
ITID-11323.response: Remove the malicious profile, assess for traffic interception or certificate abuse, and reset affected credentials.
metrics: Count of confirmed malicious configuration-profile installs per quarter
ITID-11323.notes: iOS-specific vector; kept distinct from the enterprise MDM-enrollment-spoofing leaf (ITID-11329), which is scoped to the targeted corporate-fleet variant of this same general technique.

playbook.name: Response: Malicious Configuration Profile Smishing (iOS)
playbook.description: For a reported SMS linking to a malicious iOS configuration profile (MDM enrollment profile, VPN profile, or certificate) designed to intercept traffic or install a rogue root certificate.

steps.title: Preserve the message and confirm the device is iOS
steps.desc: Screenshot the message and sender number; confirm the target device is iOS/iPadOS, since this attack relies on Apple's configuration profile mechanism.
steps.outcome: Message and platform context preserved.

steps.title: Isolate the device from corporate resources
steps.desc: Revoke the device's corporate access via MDM/conditional access immediately if a rogue profile is confirmed, since traffic interception may already be underway.
steps.outcome: Device access suspended.

steps.title: Remove the malicious profile
steps.desc: Delete the rogue configuration profile via device Settings or MDM; if a rogue MDM enrollment cannot be removed by the user, escalate for a full device wipe/reset.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed free of the malicious profile.
steps.abort: If the rogue profile blocks removal or re-enrollment persists, escalate to full device wipe.

steps.title: Restore device access after compliance check
steps.desc: Re-enable corporate resource access once the device passes a fresh compliance check with no unauthorized profiles present.
steps.outcome: Device restored to normal, compliant status.

steps.title: Log the profile-based attack and update MDM restrictions if needed
steps.desc: Record findings; consider whether MDM policy should restrict manual profile installation on managed devices going forward.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; policy hardening considered.

steps.title: Determine whether the profile was downloaded and/or installed
steps.desc: Interview the user and check Settings > General > VPN & Device Management (or MDM inventory) for any unrecognized installed profile.
steps.guidance: A malicious profile may add a rogue root certificate, proxy/VPN configuration, or unauthorized MDM enrollment — all of which can intercept traffic.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether a malicious profile is installed.
steps.abort: If never installed, skip eradication and proceed to blocklisting only.

steps.title: Block the profile-hosting domain and report the sender
steps.desc: Add the hosting domain to the web/DNS blocklist and report the number to the carrier.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked; number reported.

steps.title: Check for evidence of intercepted traffic or captured credentials
steps.desc: If a rogue proxy/VPN or root certificate was installed, treat any credentials entered while the profile was active as potentially compromised and reset them.
steps.outcome: Exposure window identified; affected credentials reset.

steps.title: Assess campaign scope
steps.desc: Check for other reports of the same profile-installation lure and hosting domain.
steps.outcome: Campaign scope established.

ITID-11324.def: A smishing message claiming the target has a new voicemail or needs a media/codec player to view content, linking to a malicious app install rather than a system-update or security pretext.
ITID-11324.purpose: Distinguishes smishing that uses a fake voicemail or media-player app lure to deliver mobile malware.
scopeIncludes: Voicemail-notification or media-player-required lures leading to a malicious app install
scopeExcludes: Fake app-update pretext (a distinct leaf, ITID-11322)
Fake security/antivirus pretext (a distinct leaf, ITID-11326)
ITID-11324.severity: Medium-High — voicemail/media lures are a known distribution vector for mobile banking trojans.
ITID-11324.escalation: Escalate to mobile security if install is confirmed; isolate/wipe the device.
indicators: SMS referencing a missed voicemail with a link to 'listen'
Prompt to install a media/codec app to view an attachment
vectors: Malware distribution disguised as a voicemail-playback or media-viewer requirement
rootCauses: Users' familiarity with legitimate visual-voicemail apps lowers suspicion
controls: Mobile threat defense app-scanning
User awareness training
ITID-11324.detection: MTD tooling on managed devices provides partial coverage; otherwise relies on user reporting.
ITID-11324.response: Isolate/wipe the device if install confirmed; block distribution domain.
metrics: Count of voicemail/media-lure smishing incidents per quarter
ITID-11324.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves purely by lure theme (voicemail/media rather than update or security).

playbook.name: Response: Fake Voicemail / Media Player App Smishing
playbook.description: For a reported SMS claiming a voicemail or audio/video message is waiting and linking to a fake media-player app or codec download that is actually malware.

steps.title: Preserve the message and sender identifier
steps.desc: Screenshot the message and record the sender number and claimed voicemail/media source.
steps.outcome: Message preserved.

steps.title: Isolate the device from corporate resources if installation occurred
steps.desc: Revoke corporate email/VPN/SSO access via MDM/conditional access pending remediation.
steps.outcome: Device access suspended.

steps.title: Remove the malicious app and check for granted permissions
steps.desc: Uninstall the fake player app via MDM and check whether it was granted microphone, contacts, or SMS permissions that should be revoked or that indicate broader compromise.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed free of the malicious app.
steps.abort: If removal cannot be confirmed clean, escalate to device wipe.

steps.title: Restore device access after compliance check
steps.desc: Re-enable corporate access once the device passes a fresh compliance check.
steps.outcome: Device restored to normal, compliant status.

steps.title: Log the lure and app package identified
steps.desc: Record the lure content and any malicious app package name/hash for detection tuning.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine whether the fake player/app was downloaded or installed
steps.desc: Interview the user and check MDM for any unmanaged app install or permission grant since the message arrived.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether installation occurred.
steps.abort: If never installed, skip eradication and proceed to blocklisting only.

steps.title: Block the hosting domain and report the sender
steps.desc: Add the hosting domain to the web/DNS blocklist and report the number to the carrier.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked; number reported.

steps.title: Assess campaign scope
steps.desc: Check for other reports of the same fake voicemail/media lure.
steps.outcome: Campaign scope established.

ITID-11325.def: A smishing link that, upon being opened in the mobile browser, exploits a browser or OS vulnerability to compromise the device directly, without the victim needing to download, sideload, or install anything.
ITID-11325.purpose: Distinguishes smishing links that compromise the target's mobile device via a browser exploit (drive-by) with no explicit install step, from lures that require the user to download/install something.
scopeIncludes: Cases where compromise occurs purely from opening the link (drive-by), with no app/profile install step observed
scopeExcludes: Any lure requiring the victim to actively install an app, profile, or file (all other leaves in this Malware Links group)
ITID-11325.severity: High — drive-by compromise requires no victim error beyond clicking the link, and often indicates a zero-day or unpatched exploit in use.
ITID-11325.priority: P1 given the exploit-based, low-user-interaction nature.
ITID-11325.escalation: Escalate immediately to mobile security and threat intelligence; treat as a potential zero-day until the exploited vulnerability is identified and patched.
indicators: Device compromise/anomalous behavior immediately following a link click with no subsequent install prompt
Browser crash or unusual behavior upon visiting the link
vectors: Exploitation of an unpatched mobile browser or OS vulnerability via a malicious webpage
rootCauses: Delayed mobile OS/browser patching
Use of outdated or unsupported mobile browsers
controls: Mandatory mobile OS/browser patch compliance via MDM
Mobile threat defense exploit detection
ITID-11325.detection: Weak — exploit-based compromise with no install step is hard to detect without EDR/MTD behavioral monitoring.
ITID-11325.response: Treat as a potential zero-day incident: isolate the device, engage threat intelligence, and prioritize emergency patching once the vulnerability is known.
metrics: Count of confirmed drive-by mobile compromise incidents per year
Mean time to patch after exploited vulnerability identified
ITID-11325.notes: Distinguished from all other sibling leaves by the absence of any install step — compromise occurs purely from viewing the link.

playbook.name: Response: Mobile Browser Exploit / Drive-by Smishing
playbook.description: For a reported smishing link that attempts to exploit the mobile browser itself (drive-by compromise) without requiring the user to install anything, potentially achieving code execution just by visiting the page.

steps.title: Preserve the message and do not re-visit the link
steps.desc: Screenshot the message and sender number; explicitly instruct the user and responders not to open the link on any device, since visiting alone may trigger exploitation.
steps.guidance: If the link must be analyzed, only do so in an isolated sandbox environment, never on a live corporate device.
steps.outcome: Message preserved without further exposure.

steps.title: Isolate the device from corporate resources immediately
steps.desc: Revoke the device's access to corporate email, VPN, and SSO via MDM/conditional access pending forensic clearance.
steps.outcome: Device access suspended.

steps.title: Reimage or factory-reset the device if exploitation is confirmed or cannot be ruled out
steps.desc: Given the difficulty of reliably detecting browser-exploit persistence on mobile, factory-reset and reprovision the device rather than attempting selective cleanup.
steps.outcome: Device returned to a known-clean state.

steps.title: Restore device access after reprovisioning and compliance check
steps.desc: Re-enable corporate access once the reprovisioned device passes a compliance check.
steps.outcome: Device restored to normal, compliant status.

steps.title: Report the exploit chain and push urgent patching if a 0-day is suspected
steps.desc: Document the suspected vulnerability and browser/OS versions affected; if a zero-day is suspected, escalate urgently to the vulnerability management team and consider a fleet-wide emergency patch push.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; patch urgency escalated if warranted.

steps.title: Determine the browser version and whether the page was visited
steps.desc: Interview the user, and check the device's mobile OS/browser version against known vulnerable versions for the suspected exploit, and whether the link was opened.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exposure window and patch status.
steps.abort: If the device OS/browser was already fully patched against the known exploit and the link wasn't opened, downgrade priority and proceed to blocklisting only.

steps.title: Block the exploit-hosting domain and report the sender
steps.desc: Add the hosting domain to the web/DNS blocklist and report the number to the carrier.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked; number reported.

steps.title: Ensure the browser/OS is fully patched before reprovisioning
steps.desc: Confirm the latest OS and browser updates are applied before returning the device to service.
steps.outcome: Device patched to current version.

steps.title: Escalate for deeper forensic triage if the page was visited on a vulnerable browser
steps.desc: Engage the mobile forensics/incident response function to assess for signs of exploitation (unexpected crashes, battery drain, new processes, unexpected network connections).
steps.outcome: Forensic assessment initiated for potentially exploited devices.

ITID-11326.def: A smishing message claiming the target's device is infected or at risk, urging installation of a 'security' or 'antivirus' app that is in fact a malware trojan.
ITID-11326.purpose: Distinguishes smishing that uses a fake security/antivirus warning to lure the target into installing a trojan disguised as protective software.
scopeIncludes: Scareware-style lures ('your phone is infected') leading to a malicious app posing as security software
scopeExcludes: Fake app-update pretext (ITID-11322)
Fake voicemail/media pretext (ITID-11324)
ITID-11326.severity: High — victims often grant the fake app broad device permissions, believing it protective.
ITID-11326.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if broad device permissions were granted.
ITID-11326.escalation: Escalate to mobile security immediately; isolate/wipe the device.
indicators: SMS warning of infection with a link to install 'security' software
Fake antivirus app requesting excessive permissions (accessibility, SMS, contacts)
vectors: Scareware pretext exploiting fear of infection to justify broad permission grants
rootCauses: Users conditioned to trust security-branded apps
Excessive permission requests not scrutinized before granting
controls: Mobile threat defense app-scanning
MDM app-permission policy enforcement
User awareness training
ITID-11326.detection: MTD tooling provides meaningful coverage on managed devices given the fake app's often-flagged permission profile.
ITID-11326.response: Isolate/wipe the device; audit granted permissions for downstream data exposure.
metrics: Count of fake-security-app smishing incidents per quarter
ITID-11326.notes: Scoped to the scareware/security pretext specifically, distinct from update- or media-themed sibling leaves.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Security/Antivirus App Smishing
playbook.description: For a reported SMS urging installation of a fake 'security scan' or antivirus app claiming the device is infected, which is itself malware.

steps.title: Preserve the message and sender identifier
steps.desc: Screenshot the message and record the sender number and the fake security app's claimed name/branding.
steps.outcome: Message preserved.

steps.title: Isolate the device from corporate resources
steps.desc: Revoke the device's corporate access via MDM/conditional access pending removal of the fake app.
steps.outcome: Device access suspended.

steps.title: Remove the fake app and revoke any device-admin/accessibility grants
steps.desc: Uninstall the fake security app via MDM; if it was granted device-admin or accessibility rights that resist removal, wipe the device.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed free of the fake app and its elevated permissions.
steps.abort: If the app cannot be cleanly removed, escalate to device wipe.

steps.title: Restore device access after compliance check
steps.desc: Re-enable corporate access once the device passes a fresh compliance check.
steps.outcome: Device restored to normal, compliant status.

steps.title: Log the fake app package and lure
steps.desc: Record the app package name/hash and lure content for detection tuning and awareness content.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine whether the fake app was installed and what permissions it requested
steps.desc: Interview the user and check MDM for the app install and any requested permissions — fake security apps commonly request broad device-admin or accessibility access.
steps.outcome: Confirmed installation status and permissions granted.
steps.abort: If never installed, skip eradication and proceed to blocklisting only.

steps.title: Block the hosting domain and report the sender
steps.desc: Add the hosting domain to the web/DNS blocklist and report the number to the carrier.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked; number reported.

steps.title: Assess campaign scope
steps.desc: Check for other reports of the same fake security app lure.
steps.outcome: Campaign scope established.

ITID-11327.def: A smishing message delivering a malware-install link, sent immediately after or as part of a completed/attempted SIM swap, exploiting the hijacked number's inherited trust or the confusion window during the swap to push malware onto the victim or a related contact.
ITID-11327.purpose: Captures a malware-delivery smishing message sent to exploit the trust or compromise window created by a SIM swap — not the SIM swap itself.
scopeIncludes: Malware-delivery smishing sent from or referencing a recently swapped number
Follow-up malware smishing exploiting SIM-swap-driven urgency (e.g., 'your account was compromised, install this security app')
scopeExcludes: The SIM swap technique/attack itself, including its sub-methods (social-engineering-based, insider-assisted, self-service-portal) — tracked under the SIM Swapping ITID family (ITID-12641 and children)
Credential-harvesting (non-malware) links sent in a similar context (Credential Harvesting Links group, ITID-11315)
ITID-11327.severity: High — occurs in the context of an already-compromised phone number, compounding the incident.
ITID-11327.priority: P1 given the compounding SIM-swap context.
ITID-11327.escalation: Escalate immediately and coordinate with the SIM-swap incident response; do not treat as an isolated smishing event.
indicators: Malware-link smishing traced to a number recently subject to a SIM swap
Timing correlation between a reported SIM swap and a follow-up smishing message
vectors: Leveraging a hijacked number's contact trust to distribute malware links to the victim's contacts
Using the post-swap confusion window to push a 'security fix' malware link to the victim
rootCauses: SIM swap already granting the attacker control of the number/identity
Victims and contacts not yet aware the number has been compromised
controls: Carrier SIM-swap protection (PIN/port-freeze)
Rapid user notification upon detected SIM swap
Mobile threat defense
ITID-11327.detection: Weak on its own; detection typically comes from correlating with the underlying SIM-swap incident.
ITID-11327.response: Handle jointly with the SIM-swap incident: notify affected contacts, block the malware link, and secure the account.
metrics: Count of malware smishing incidents correlated with a SIM-swap event per quarter
ITID-11327.notes: Deliberately scoped to exclude the SIM swap technique itself, which is fully covered under the SIM Swapping ITID family (ITID-12641 and children) elsewhere in the taxonomy — this leaf exists only for the follow-on malware-delivery smishing message.

playbook.name: Response: SIM Swap Follow-up Malware Smishing
playbook.description: For a reported SMS malware link received shortly after a suspected or confirmed SIM swap, indicating the attacker already controls the number and is using it to push a follow-on malicious payload.

steps.title: Confirm whether a SIM swap has actually occurred
steps.desc: Check with the user for loss of cellular signal, unexpected carrier notifications, or check the carrier account directly for a recent SIM/eSIM change.
steps.guidance: This is the priority check — the malware link is secondary to establishing whether the attacker controls the number.
steps.outcome: SIM swap status confirmed.
steps.abort: If no SIM swap occurred and this is a standalone malware link, use the general SMS malware link playbook instead.

steps.title: Escalate to carrier for emergency SIM/number recovery
steps.desc: Have the user contact the carrier's fraud team directly (via a verified channel, not the compromised number) to reverse the SIM swap and lock the account.
steps.outcome: Number recovered and carrier account locked against further swaps.

steps.title: Remove any installed malware and confirm device is clean
steps.desc: Uninstall any malicious payload via MDM or wipe the device if removal cannot be confirmed reliable.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore number, accounts, and device access
steps.desc: Confirm the number is recovered, accounts are secured with new MFA, and the device is compliant before restoring full access.
steps.outcome: Full restoration confirmed.

steps.title: Document the full SIM-swap-to-malware chain
steps.desc: Record the attack chain end-to-end; recommend moving high-value accounts off SMS-based MFA org-wide if not already policy.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; policy recommendation raised if applicable.

steps.title: Preserve the malware message and identify what it delivers
steps.desc: Screenshot the message; determine via sandbox analysis what the link installs or harvests.
steps.outcome: Message and payload behavior documented.

steps.title: Lock down all accounts using this number for MFA
steps.desc: Force password resets and switch MFA off SMS to an authenticator app or hardware key for every account identified in the prior step.
steps.outcome: At-risk accounts secured and moved off SMS-based MFA.

steps.title: Identify all accounts relying on this number for SMS-based verification
steps.desc: Enumerate corporate and personal accounts using this phone number for SMS OTP/MFA or account recovery, since a confirmed SIM swap puts all of them at risk.
steps.outcome: Full list of at-risk accounts compiled.

steps.title: Isolate any device that received or acted on the malware link
steps.desc: Revoke corporate access via MDM/conditional access pending inspection.
steps.outcome: Device access suspended.

ITID-11328.def: A QR code (on a physical flyer, poster, or compromised screen) that, when scanned, opens or pre-fills an SMS conversation which then delivers a malware-installation link — classified here because the payload delivery occurs via the SMS channel, even though the initial lure is a QR code.
ITID-11328.purpose: Captures a multi-step attack chain where a physical or displayed QR code is the entry point but the actual malware payload is delivered via a subsequent SMS conversation.
scopeIncludes: QR codes that redirect into an SMS/text conversation carrying the malware link
Physical or digital QR-code lures where the SMS step is the payload-delivery mechanism
scopeExcludes: QR codes that link directly to a malicious webpage with no SMS step involved (a separate QR-code-phishing ITID elsewhere in the taxonomy, not a smishing leaf)
ITID-11328.severity: Medium-High — the physical/visual entry point can reach a broad, undefined population before narrowing to a targeted SMS exchange.
ITID-11328.escalation: Escalate to SOC and, if the QR code is physically posted on organization property, to physical security as well.
indicators: QR code discovered on organization property or in a phishing report leading to an SMS-based malware link
SMS conversation initiated via a pre-filled 'sms:' link from a scanned QR code
vectors: QR-code stickers placed over legitimate codes in public or organizational spaces, redirecting into a malicious SMS chain
rootCauses: QR codes provide no visual indication of their destination before scanning
Physical QR codes on organization property not regularly audited
controls: Periodic physical audit of organization-posted QR codes
Mobile threat defense URL scanning of QR-derived links
User awareness training on QR code risks
ITID-11328.detection: Weak — relies almost entirely on physical discovery or user reporting.
ITID-11328.response: Remove the malicious QR code if on organization property, block the SMS-delivered link, and alert anyone who may have scanned it.
metrics: Count of QR-to-SMS malware chain incidents per year
ITID-11328.notes: Classified under this Smishing branch specifically because the payload delivery step is SMS-based; a QR code linking directly to a malicious webpage with no SMS step belongs to a separate QR-phishing ITID, not this leaf.

playbook.name: Response: QR-to-SMS Malware Link Chain
playbook.description: For an incident where a scanned QR code (quishing) redirects into an SMS conversation or triggers an SMS containing a malware link, chaining two social-engineering channels together.

steps.title: Preserve both the originating QR code and the resulting SMS
steps.desc: Photograph/preserve the QR code source (poster, email, flyer, website) and screenshot the resulting SMS message and sender number.
steps.guidance: Understanding where the QR code was encountered is important for scoping — physical (poster/parking meter) vs digital (email/website) distribution.
steps.outcome: Full attack chain from QR source to SMS payload preserved.

steps.title: Isolate the device from corporate resources
steps.desc: Revoke corporate email/VPN/SSO access via MDM/conditional access pending remediation if installation occurred.
steps.outcome: Device access suspended.

steps.title: Remove any installed malware
steps.desc: Uninstall the malicious payload via MDM or wipe the device if removal cannot be confirmed reliable.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore device access after compliance check
steps.desc: Re-enable corporate access once the device passes a fresh compliance check.
steps.outcome: Device restored to normal, compliant status.

steps.title: Log the QR-to-SMS chain and warn about physical QR tampering if relevant
steps.desc: Record the full attack chain; if physical QR tampering was involved on organizational premises, alert facilities/security to check other QR-code signage.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; physical premises checked if applicable.

steps.title: Determine whether the malware link was opened and anything installed
steps.desc: Interview the user and check MDM for app installs or profile changes since the SMS was received.
steps.outcome: Confirmed installation status.
steps.abort: If not opened, skip eradication and proceed to blocklisting only.

steps.title: Block the SMS destination domain and report the sender
steps.desc: Add the malware-hosting domain to the web/DNS blocklist and report the number to the carrier.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked; number reported.

steps.title: Identify and physically remove the QR source if it is a physical asset under organizational control
steps.desc: If the QR code was a sticker placed over a legitimate one (e.g. on a physical sign or corporate poster) on organizational premises, locate and remove it.
steps.outcome: Physical QR source removed if applicable.

ITID-11329.def: A smishing message targeting an employee's corporate-owned or BYOD device, spoofing an internal MDM enrollment or device-compliance notification, to get the employee to enroll into an attacker-controlled MDM profile or install an attacker-controlled management agent.
ITID-11329.purpose: Distinguishes smishing that specifically targets corporate-owned or BYOD devices by spoofing an internal MDM enrollment or device-compliance message.
scopeIncludes: Messages impersonating the organization's own IT/MDM branding, targeting corporate or BYOD devices specifically
scopeExcludes: Generic (non-enterprise-targeted) malicious iOS configuration profile smishing (ITID-11323) — this leaf is scoped to the enterprise-targeted, MDM-branded variant specifically
Legitimate internal IT communication (not applicable — this is inherently a malicious pretext leaf)
ITID-11329.severity: High — successful enrollment can grant the attacker broad device-management control over a corporate asset.
ITID-11329.priority: P1 given the enterprise device-control implications.
ITID-11329.escalation: Escalate immediately to IT/MDM administrators; verify the organization's real MDM enrollment status for the targeted device.
indicators: Smishing message closely mimicking the organization's real MDM enrollment branding/process
Employee reporting an unexpected MDM enrollment prompt
vectors: Spoofing internal IT/MDM branding to trick an employee into enrolling a device into an attacker-controlled management profile
rootCauses: Employees not trained to verify MDM enrollment prompts against known IT communication channels
Lack of out-of-band verification for enrollment requests
controls: Out-of-band verification requirement for MDM enrollment communications
MDM enrollment restricted to on-network/verified processes
User awareness training targeted at IT-impersonation smishing
ITID-11329.detection: Moderate — the organization's real MDM console can confirm whether an unauthorized enrollment occurred.
ITID-11329.response: Verify against the real MDM console immediately; if a rogue enrollment is found, remove it and treat the device as potentially compromised.
metrics: Count of MDM-enrollment-spoofing smishing incidents per quarter
Count of confirmed rogue enrollments
ITID-11329.notes: Enterprise-targeted counterpart to ITID-11323's general iOS configuration-profile leaf; distinguished by the corporate/BYOD device target and IT/MDM-branded pretext.

playbook.name: Response: Enterprise MDM Enrollment Spoofing Smishing
playbook.description: For a reported SMS impersonating the organization's IT/MDM team, urging the user to enroll their device into a fake 'corporate MDM' profile that actually grants the attacker device management control.

steps.title: Preserve the message and confirm it did not originate from the real IT/MDM team
steps.desc: Screenshot the message and sender number, and confirm with the actual IT/MDM team that they did not send this enrollment request.
steps.outcome: Message confirmed illegitimate.
steps.abort: If IT confirms this was a legitimate but poorly-communicated enrollment request, close as a false positive and address the internal communication gap.

steps.title: Immediately isolate the device from all corporate resources
steps.desc: Revoke corporate email/VPN/SSO access via conditional access the moment rogue enrollment is confirmed, since the attacker may have management-level control.
steps.guidance: Treat this at the same urgency as a confirmed device compromise, not a routine phishing report.
steps.outcome: Device access suspended immediately.

steps.title: Remove the rogue MDM enrollment
steps.desc: Un-enroll the device from the rogue management profile; if it resists removal (a hallmark of malicious MDM control), escalate to a full factory reset before returning the device to service.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed free of rogue management control.
steps.abort: If un-enrollment fails or the profile blocks removal, escalate to factory reset.

steps.title: Re-enroll the device into the legitimate MDM and restore access
steps.desc: Enroll the device into the real corporate MDM and confirm compliance before restoring corporate resource access.
steps.outcome: Device restored under legitimate management with normal access.

steps.title: Document the rogue enrollment campaign and reinforce verification procedures
steps.desc: Record the full incident; reinforce in awareness training that enrollment/management requests must be verified via official IT channels, never via SMS links.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness content updated.

steps.title: Determine whether the device was enrolled into the rogue MDM
steps.desc: Check Settings > Device Management (iOS) or Device Admin apps (Android) for an unrecognized MDM/management profile, and interview the user.
steps.guidance: A successful rogue MDM enrollment gives the attacker significant control: app installation, configuration changes, and potentially remote wipe or data access.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether rogue enrollment occurred.
steps.abort: If never enrolled, skip eradication and proceed to blocklisting only.

steps.title: Block the rogue MDM enrollment domain and report the sender
steps.desc: Add the enrollment domain to the web/DNS blocklist and report the number to the carrier's fraud channel.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked; number reported.

steps.title: Audit for unauthorized configuration changes made during rogue enrollment
steps.desc: Check for unexpected apps, certificates, or policy changes pushed while the rogue MDM had control.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of changes made; all reverted.

steps.title: Assess campaign scope across the organization
steps.desc: Check whether other employees received the same fake enrollment message.
steps.outcome: Campaign scope established.

steps.title: Alert the wider organization if this is a targeted campaign against employees
steps.desc: Send an urgent notice reminding staff that IT will never request device enrollment via unsolicited SMS, with instructions to verify any such request through official channels.
steps.outcome: Employees warned before further enrollments occur.

ITID-11331.def: An SMS-based attempt to obtain, relay, or exploit a one-time-passcode or MFA-related code, logged before the specific tactic (fake code flood, real trigger+relay ask, spoofed sender, volume barrage, etc.) is confirmed.
ITID-11331.purpose: Catch-all for an SMS-based OTP/MFA fatigue or code-relay attempt that does not yet match a more specific leaf in this Tier-4 group.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific OTP/MFA fatigue tactic is confirmed
scopeExcludes: A tactic clearly matching a more specific sibling leaf
Push-notification-based MFA fatigue with no SMS/OTP component (a channel-agnostic ITID elsewhere, ITID-12621, MFA Fatigue)
Static credential-harvesting smishing with no OTP/code component (Credential Harvesting Links group, ITID-11311 family)
ITID-11331.severity: Medium-High; OTP/MFA-targeted activity is a strong precursor to account takeover.
ITID-11331.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IAM immediately regardless of confirmed success, given the account-takeover risk; reclassify once the tactic is confirmed.
indicators: User-reported unexpected OTP/MFA-related text
vectors: SMS message soliciting or exploiting an OTP/MFA code
rootCauses: Insufficient detail available at time of report
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/hardware keys)
User awareness training on OTP-relay scams
ITID-11331.detection: Relies primarily on user reporting; authentication logs may show correlated login attempts.
ITID-11331.response: Reset credentials/re-issue MFA regardless of confirmed relay; reclassify once the specific tactic is known.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
sops: MFA Fatigue/OTP Relay Incident Response SOP
ITID-11331.notes: Intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General SMS OTP/MFA Fatigue Attempt
playbook.description: For a reported pattern of unsolicited SMS one-time-passcodes or MFA prompts sent to a user's phone, intended to pressure or trick them into forwarding a code, not fitting a more specific sub-category.

steps.title: Preserve the OTP messages and confirm the user did not share any code
steps.desc: Screenshot the received OTP messages and interview the user to confirm no code was shared, entered elsewhere, or approved.
steps.outcome: Messages preserved; confirmed whether a code was disclosed.

steps.title: Force an immediate password reset and session revocation
steps.desc: Reset the account password and revoke all active sessions/tokens, since repeated OTP triggers indicate the attacker holds valid credentials.
steps.outcome: Account secured against further login attempts using the old password.

steps.title: Verify no MFA approval or code disclosure succeeded
steps.desc: Confirm via sign-in logs that no successful authentication occurred during the fatigue attempt window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no unauthorized access was achieved.
steps.abort: Escalate to account-takeover response if a successful login is found in the window.

steps.title: Restore account access with new credentials
steps.desc: Confirm the user can authenticate normally with the new password and existing MFA method.
steps.outcome: User has restored, confirmed-clean access.

steps.title: Log the fatigue attempt and reinforce 'never share an OTP' guidance
steps.desc: Record the pattern; reinforce with the user and, if widespread, the organization that OTP codes should never be shared or approved for a login they did not initiate.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness reinforced.

steps.title: Identify which account is generating the OTPs
steps.desc: Check identity provider/application sign-in logs to identify which account triggered the OTP requests and from what source IP/location.
steps.outcome: Source account and triggering login attempts identified.

steps.title: Block the source IP/range generating the login attempts
steps.desc: Add the identified source IP(s) to the conditional access/firewall blocklist.
steps.outcome: Attacker source blocked from further attempts.

steps.title: Determine whether this is an active credential-stuffing/brute-force attempt
steps.desc: Check for repeated failed login attempts or password-spray patterns against the account immediately preceding the OTP requests.
steps.guidance: MFA fatigue attacks are triggered by an attacker already possessing valid credentials and repeatedly attempting login to prompt the user.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the account's password is likely already compromised.

ITID-11332.def: A flood of SMS messages that look like OTP codes but are not tied to any real, backend-triggered authentication event; sent purely to desensitize, confuse, or bait the target into replying with information (or simply to erode trust in legitimate OTP messages).
ITID-11332.purpose: Distinguishes fake OTP codes sent purely as a social-engineering flood — not tied to any genuine backend authentication attempt.
scopeIncludes: Fake/spoofed-content OTP-style messages with no corresponding real login/reset attempt on the target's account
scopeExcludes: Cases where a real authentication attempt genuinely triggered the OTP message and the attacker separately asks the victim to relay it (ITID-11333)
A high-volume barrage of genuinely triggered OTPs across one account (ITID-11336) or across multiple accounts (ITID-11339)
ITID-11332.severity: Medium — no account is at immediate risk since no real auth attempt exists, but it may be reconnaissance or precede a real attempt.
ITID-11332.priority: P3 default, P2 if part of a coordinated campaign against multiple employees.
ITID-11332.escalation: Escalate to SOC for pattern tracking; verify with the relevant service that no real authentication attempt is occurring.
indicators: Multiple OTP-formatted texts with no corresponding account activity when checked against the real service
Codes that do not validate against any live session
vectors: Bulk-sent fake OTP-style texts to desensitize targets or bait a reply
rootCauses: Users unable to distinguish a genuine OTP from a fabricated one without checking account activity directly
controls: User awareness training to verify account activity independent of the SMS
Carrier SMS spam filtering
ITID-11332.detection: Weak — no backend authentication log correlates since no real attempt exists; relies on user reporting.
ITID-11332.response: Confirm with the real service that no authentication attempt occurred; advise the user not to reply or click.
metrics: Count of fake-OTP-flood reports per quarter
sops: MFA Fatigue/OTP Relay Incident Response SOP
ITID-11332.notes: Distinguished from siblings by the absence of any real, backend-triggered authentication event.

playbook.name: Response: Repeated Fake OTP Code Flood
playbook.description: For a reported flood of SMS messages containing fake one-time-passcode-style content (not tied to a real login attempt) intended to overwhelm/confuse the user or mask a genuine attack among the noise.

steps.title: Preserve a sample of the flood messages
steps.desc: Screenshot several representative messages, the sender numbers/short codes, and the approximate volume and time window.
steps.outcome: Sample messages and flood pattern documented.

steps.title: If a real attack is found within the flood, contain that account immediately
steps.desc: Force password reset and session revocation on any account with genuine suspicious activity uncovered during the flood window.
steps.outcome: Genuinely targeted account secured.

steps.title: Confirm the flood has stopped and accounts are clean
steps.desc: Confirm no further flood messages and no residual unauthorized account activity.
steps.outcome: Flood stopped; accounts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Log the flood as a possible distraction technique
steps.desc: Record the incident, noting whether it was used to mask another attack, for future correlation.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine whether any of the flooded codes correspond to a real authentication attempt
steps.desc: Cross-check the codes/timestamps against real identity provider sign-in logs to rule out that a genuine attack is hidden within the flood.
steps.guidance: SMS floods are sometimes used as a distraction technique to bury a real fraudulent transaction alert or login notification.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the flood is pure noise or masking a real event.

steps.title: Block the flooding sender numbers and report to carrier
steps.desc: Report the sending numbers/short codes to the carrier's SMS abuse channel; block on the device where possible.
steps.outcome: Flood source reported; further messages blocked at device level.

steps.title: Check for correlated account activity (financial, email) during the flood window
steps.desc: Review the user's financial and email accounts for suspicious activity occurring during or shortly after the flood, since floods are frequently paired with account takeover attempts elsewhere.
steps.outcome: Correlated malicious activity identified, if any.

ITID-11333.def: An attacker-initiated real login or password-reset attempt that causes a genuine OTP SMS to be sent to the victim, followed by a separate text message asking the victim to reply with or forward that code.
ITID-11333.purpose: Distinguishes the case where an attacker genuinely triggers a real OTP to be sent to the victim, then separately asks — via text — for the victim to relay that real code.
scopeIncludes: A confirmed real authentication attempt correlated with a subsequent SMS/text relay request for the resulting code
scopeExcludes: The equivalent relay ask delivered via a live phone call rather than text (a distinct Vishing-branch ITID, ITID-11218 Real-Time MFA/OTP Relay Vishing)
Fake OTP codes with no real underlying authentication attempt (ITID-11332)
ITID-11333.severity: High — a real authentication attempt is in progress; successful relay results in immediate account takeover.
ITID-11333.priority: P1 — treat as an active account-takeover attempt.
ITID-11333.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IAM immediately; lock the targeted account pending investigation regardless of whether the code was relayed.
indicators: Genuine OTP SMS correlated with a real login/reset attempt in authentication logs
Separate text message explicitly asking the victim to reply with the code just received
vectors: Attacker enters the victim's username on a real login/reset page to trigger a genuine OTP, then texts the victim posing as the service or IT asking for the code
rootCauses: OTP delivery via SMS with no binding to a verified request context
Users not trained to recognize that legitimate services never ask them to relay a received code
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/hardware keys) that cannot be relayed
User awareness training explicit on 'never share a received code'
ITID-11333.detection: Strong — authentication logs directly confirm the real triggering attempt, giving a genuine technical signal.
ITID-11333.response: Lock/reset the targeted account immediately, review authentication logs for the triggering attempt's source, and treat as a confirmed active attack.
metrics: Count of confirmed real-trigger relay-ask incidents per quarter
Count with confirmed successful relay/takeover
sops: MFA Fatigue/OTP Relay Incident Response SOP
detections: Authentication log correlation for OTP-triggering events
ITID-11333.notes: The SMS/text-channel counterpart to ITID-11218 (Real-Time MFA/OTP Relay Vishing); use this leaf when the relay ask is delivered by text rather than a live call.

playbook.name: Response: Real OTP Trigger + Relay Request Smishing
playbook.description: For an incident where an attacker deliberately triggers a real OTP to the victim's phone (having already obtained their password) and then contacts them, via a follow-up SMS or other channel, asking them to reply with or relay the code.

steps.title: Immediately confirm whether the code was shared
steps.desc: Urgently interview the user to determine whether the OTP code was relayed to the attacker, since this determines whether the login has already succeeded.
steps.guidance: This is time-critical — treat as active incident, not a retrospective report.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the code was disclosed.

steps.title: If the code was relayed, immediately lock the account regardless of login status
steps.desc: Force an emergency password reset and revoke all sessions/tokens immediately — do not wait to confirm a successful login first, since confirmation may lag real-time attacker activity.
steps.guidance: Treat any relayed OTP as a live account-takeover-in-progress.
steps.outcome: Account locked before or immediately after attacker use.

steps.title: Remove any attacker-established persistence
steps.desc: Revoke any OAuth app grants, mailbox forwarding rules, or new MFA device enrollments created during the attacker's session.
steps.outcome: Account confirmed free of attacker persistence.

steps.title: Restore access with new credentials and re-enrolled MFA
steps.desc: Have the user set a new password and re-enroll MFA on a verified device before restoring access.
steps.outcome: User has restored, confirmed-clean access with new MFA.

steps.title: Document the relay attempt and reinforce urgent 'never share OTP' guidance
steps.desc: Record the full incident timeline; this pattern indicates deliberate, credential-holding targeting and should be flagged urgently to security awareness.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; urgent awareness reminder issued if part of a wider campaign.

steps.title: Check the account for a completed login using the relayed code
steps.desc: Check identity provider sign-in logs in real time for a successful authentication matching the OTP trigger time.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the attacker successfully authenticated.

steps.title: If a successful login is confirmed, treat as active account takeover
steps.desc: Escalate to the account-takeover/intrusion response process: check for mailbox rules, OAuth grants, downstream system access, and data access performed during the session.
steps.outcome: Full scope of attacker access during the session established.

steps.title: Place the account under short-term heightened monitoring
steps.desc: Flag the account for elevated SIEM monitoring for a defined period following the incident.
steps.outcome: Account under active monitoring.

steps.title: Block the relay-request sender and report
steps.desc: Block and report the number/channel used to request the code relay.
steps.outcome: Sender blocked and reported.

ITID-11334.def: A text message posing as a security alert asking the target to confirm or deny a login attempt by replying (e.g., 'Reply YES to approve' or 'Tap to confirm'), exploiting alert fatigue and the routine nature of such confirmations rather than soliciting an explicit numeric code.
ITID-11334.purpose: Distinguishes smishing that asks the target to reply YES/NO (or tap confirm/deny) to a fake login-confirmation prompt, rather than asking for a code directly.
scopeIncludes: Reply-based confirm/deny prompts framed as routine security alerts
scopeExcludes: Messages explicitly asking the victim to type back a numeric OTP code (ITID-11332, ITID-11333, ITID-11335)
ITID-11334.severity: Medium-High — a mistaken 'approve' reply can directly authorize attacker access.
ITID-11334.priority: P2 default, P1 if a reply of approval is confirmed sent.
ITID-11334.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IAM immediately if an approval reply is confirmed; lock the account pending investigation.
indicators: Text asking for a simple YES/NO or confirm/deny reply framed as a security check
No explicit numeric code present in the message
vectors: Framing account compromise as a routine security confirmation to lower the target's guard
rootCauses: Users conditioned to quickly reply to routine-seeming security confirmations without verifying the request's authenticity
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA not susceptible to reply-based approval
User awareness training on scrutinizing confirm/deny prompts
ITID-11334.detection: Moderate if correlated with an authentication log showing a real pending approval request.
ITID-11334.response: Lock the account and review authentication logs if an approval reply is confirmed; treat any reply as a potential compromise.
metrics: Count of confirm/deny-reply smishing incidents per quarter
sops: MFA Fatigue/OTP Relay Incident Response SOP
ITID-11334.notes: Distinguished from code-relay leaves by the reply-based confirm/deny mechanism rather than a numeric code ask.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Suspicious-Login Confirmation Smishing
playbook.description: For a reported SMS falsely claiming a suspicious login was detected and asking the user to 'confirm' or 'deny' it via a link, which actually harvests credentials or session tokens.

steps.title: Preserve the message and confirm it did not originate from the real identity provider
steps.desc: Screenshot the message and confirm with the actual identity provider/security team whether a genuine suspicious-login alert was sent.
steps.outcome: Message confirmed illegitimate or a genuine alert identified.
steps.abort: If a genuine alert is confirmed, redirect to standard suspicious-login response instead.

steps.title: Reset credentials and revoke sessions on the targeted account
steps.desc: Force password reset and session/token revocation, especially if a correlating real login attempt was found.
steps.outcome: Account secured.

steps.title: Verify no persistent unauthorized access was established
steps.desc: Review the account for unexpected forwarding rules, OAuth grants, or new MFA enrollments.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no residual attacker access.

steps.title: Confirm restored access with fresh MFA
steps.desc: Confirm the user has restored access with re-enrolled MFA.
steps.outcome: User has confirmed-clean access.

steps.title: Log the campaign and clarify legitimate alert formatting
steps.desc: Record findings; consider reminding users what genuine suspicious-login alerts from the identity provider actually look like, to help them distinguish real from fake in future.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; user guidance clarified if warranted.

steps.title: Determine whether the link was clicked and what was entered
steps.desc: Interview the user and check MDM/mobile threat defense logs for interaction with the link.
steps.outcome: Confirmed interaction status.
steps.abort: If no interaction, proceed to blocklisting only.

steps.title: Block the phishing domain and report the sender
steps.desc: Add the domain to the web/DNS blocklist and report the number to the carrier.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked; number reported.

steps.title: Check for a correlating real login attempt
steps.desc: Check identity provider sign-in logs for any real login attempt around the time the message was sent, since this lure is often paired with an actual credential-stuffing attempt.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether a real login attempt exists.

ITID-11335.def: A fake OTP/MFA-related text sent using a spoofed sender ID or short code matching a legitimate service's real OTP sender, causing the fraudulent message to appear in the same conversation thread as the victim's genuine past OTP messages, substantially increasing perceived legitimacy.
ITID-11335.purpose: Distinguishes OTP-fatigue smishing where the attacker spoofs the legitimate sender ID/short code so the fake message appears within the same thread as genuine past OTPs.
scopeIncludes: Cases where sender-ID/short-code spoofing is confirmed or strongly indicated (message appearing in an existing legitimate OTP thread)
scopeExcludes: OTP fatigue tactics using a generic/unspoofed sender number (other sibling leaves)
ITID-11335.severity: High — thread-spoofing substantially increases the odds of victim compliance.
ITID-11335.priority: P1 given the elevated credibility and likely success rate.
ITID-11335.escalation: Escalate to SOC and telecom/carrier fraud team immediately; report the spoofed sender ID for takedown.
indicators: Fraudulent OTP-style message appearing within an existing legitimate sender thread
Sender ID/short code matching a known legitimate service
vectors: SMS sender-ID spoofing to inject a fraudulent message into a trusted, pre-existing conversation thread
rootCauses: Lack of cryptographic sender authentication in SMS/short-code infrastructure
Carrier-level sender verification gaps
controls: Carrier-level sender ID verification/authentication where available
Phishing-resistant MFA not susceptible to SMS spoofing
User awareness training
ITID-11335.detection: Weak at the technical level given SMS's lack of sender authentication; relies on user reporting and carrier fraud teams.
ITID-11335.response: Report the spoofed sender to the carrier/telecom fraud team; lock the account if any code was relayed.
metrics: Count of confirmed sender-ID-spoofed OTP smishing incidents per quarter
sops: MFA Fatigue/OTP Relay Incident Response SOP
ITID-11335.notes: Technique-axis leaf distinguished by confirmed or strongly indicated sender-ID/short-code spoofing.

playbook.name: Response: Spoofed OTP Short Code Impersonation Smishing
playbook.description: For a reported SMS spoofing the actual short code / sender ID normally used by a legitimate service's OTP messages, so it appears in the same message thread as genuine past OTPs.

steps.title: Preserve the message and compare against known legitimate short code history
steps.desc: Screenshot the message and compare the sender ID/short code and message thread against the user's history of genuine OTP messages from that service.
steps.guidance: Sender ID spoofing can make a fake message appear within the same thread as real past OTPs, which is highly deceptive — note this explicitly.
steps.outcome: Spoofing confirmed and thread context documented.

steps.title: If the user acted on the spoofed message, contain the affected account
steps.desc: Force password reset and session revocation on the account associated with the spoofed service.
steps.outcome: Affected account secured.

steps.title: Confirm account restored if affected
steps.desc: Confirm restored access for any affected account.
steps.outcome: User has confirmed-clean access.

steps.title: Log the spoofing technique and brief users on thread-based deception risk
steps.desc: Record findings; brief users that a message appearing in a trusted thread is not proof of legitimacy, since sender IDs can be spoofed.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness content updated.

steps.title: Determine whether the user acted on the spoofed message
steps.desc: Interview the user to confirm whether they clicked a link, replied with a code, or otherwise acted on the spoofed message.
steps.outcome: Confirmed interaction status.
steps.abort: If no interaction, proceed to reporting only.

steps.title: Report the spoofing incident to the carrier
steps.desc: Report the spoofed short code usage to the carrier's fraud team, since sender ID spoofing is a carrier-level abuse issue.
steps.outcome: Carrier notified.

steps.title: Verify with the legitimate service provider whether their short code was spoofed
steps.desc: Report the spoofing to the impersonated service's security/abuse team to confirm and help them address the sender ID abuse.
steps.outcome: Legitimate provider notified and engaged.

ITID-11336.def: A high-frequency barrage of genuine, backend-triggered OTP SMS messages against a single account within a short time window, intended to fatigue or confuse the victim into forwarding or approving one out of frustration.
ITID-11336.purpose: Distinguishes OTP fatigue driven by a high volume of genuinely-triggered authentication attempts against a single account in rapid succession (classic 'MFA bombing' via the SMS channel).
scopeIncludes: Multiple confirmed real authentication attempts against one account within a short window, each generating a genuine OTP SMS
scopeExcludes: A single real trigger followed by a distinct relay ask (ITID-11333)
The equivalent barrage spread across multiple different accounts/services simultaneously (ITID-11339)
Push-notification-based MFA bombing with no SMS/OTP component (ITID-12621, MFA Fatigue)
ITID-11336.severity: High — volume-based fatigue is a well-established precursor to accidental approval and account takeover.
ITID-11336.priority: P1 given active, sustained attack behavior.
ITID-11336.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IAM immediately; lock the account and rate-limit/block further authentication attempts from the source.
indicators: Multiple genuine OTP-triggering authentication attempts against the same account within minutes
Victim reporting a sudden flood of legitimate-looking OTP texts
vectors: Repeated automated or manual login/reset attempts against a single account to generate a barrage of real OTP messages
rootCauses: No rate limiting on authentication attempts or OTP issuance
Lack of automated lockout after repeated failed/abandoned attempts
controls: Rate limiting on authentication attempts and OTP issuance
Automated account lockout after a threshold of rapid attempts
Phishing-resistant MFA
ITID-11336.detection: Strong — authentication logs directly show the volume/frequency pattern, a real technical signal.
ITID-11336.response: Lock the account, apply rate limiting, and investigate the source of the repeated attempts.
metrics: Count of confirmed volume-based OTP fatigue incidents per quarter
Average number of OTPs triggered per incident
sops: MFA Fatigue/OTP Relay Incident Response SOP
ITID-11336.notes: Distinguished from ITID-11333 by volume/frequency (many rapid triggers) rather than a single trigger with a separate relay ask, and from ITID-11339 by being confined to one account/service.

playbook.name: Response: High-Frequency SMS OTP Trigger Barrage
playbook.description: For an incident where an attacker rapidly and repeatedly triggers real OTP requests against a user's account in a short window (MFA-bombing), hoping the user approves one out of frustration or confusion.

steps.title: Confirm the barrage is live and interview the user immediately
steps.desc: Urgently confirm with the user whether any of the rapid-fire OTP prompts were approved, entered, or shared, and get an approximate count/timeframe.
steps.guidance: Treat as an active incident given the speed of MFA-bombing attacks.
steps.outcome: Confirmed approval status and barrage timeframe.

steps.title: Force an immediate password reset and session revocation
steps.desc: Reset credentials and revoke all sessions/tokens without delay — a high-frequency barrage confirms the attacker holds valid credentials and is actively trying to get in.
steps.outcome: Account locked against further attempts on the old password.

steps.title: Verify no approval succeeded during the barrage
steps.desc: Confirm via sign-in logs that no successful authentication occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no unauthorized access.
steps.abort: Escalate to account-takeover response if a successful login is found.

steps.title: Restore account access with new credentials
steps.desc: Confirm the user can authenticate normally with the new password.
steps.outcome: User has restored, confirmed-clean access.

steps.title: Document the barrage and recommend org-wide MFA-bombing mitigations
steps.desc: Record the incident; if number-matching/throttling isn't yet standard org-wide, escalate the recommendation to identity/security engineering.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; mitigation recommendation raised.

steps.title: Pull the full authentication attempt log for the account
steps.desc: Retrieve the complete sign-in log for the barrage window, including source IPs and whether any attempt succeeded.
steps.outcome: Full attempt log retrieved and correlated with the barrage.

steps.title: Block the source IP(s) generating the barrage
steps.desc: Add the identified source IP(s)/ranges to the conditional access/firewall blocklist.
steps.outcome: Attacker source blocked.

steps.title: Enable number-matching or rate-limiting MFA controls if not already active
steps.desc: If the identity provider supports number-matching or MFA request throttling and it isn't already enabled, enable it to blunt future bombing attempts org-wide.
steps.outcome: Bombing-resistant MFA controls enabled.

ITID-11337.def: A text message warning that the target's account will be locked unless they act immediately, driving urgency without necessarily including an OTP code — the call to action is to reply, call back, or click a link 'to prevent lockout.'
ITID-11337.purpose: Distinguishes an OTP/MFA-fatigue-adjacent smishing message that uses an account-lockout warning and urgency, without necessarily containing an actual code, as its primary lever.
scopeIncludes: Lockout-warning/urgency-framed messages with no explicit code content, used to drive a follow-on action (reply, callback, click)
scopeExcludes: Messages that include an explicit OTP code as part of the lockout framing (classify under ITID-11332, ITID-11333, or ITID-11335 instead based on the code-handling tactic)
ITID-11337.severity: Medium — urgency-based social pressure without a direct code-relay mechanism.
ITID-11337.priority: P3 default, P2 if it leads to a follow-on credential or code disclosure.
ITID-11337.escalation: Escalate to SOC if the target acted on the message (called back, clicked, replied); otherwise standard smishing triage.
indicators: Text warning of imminent account lockout with an urgent call to action and no explicit code
vectors: Urgency/fear-based framing designed to provoke an impulsive reply, callback, or click
rootCauses: Users' fear of losing account access overriding normal verification caution
controls: User awareness training on urgency-based social engineering
ITID-11337.response: Assess whether the target acted on the message; if so, treat as a potential precursor to account compromise.
metrics: Count of lockout-warning smishing incidents per quarter
sops: MFA Fatigue/OTP Relay Incident Response SOP
ITID-11337.notes: Distinguished from other siblings by the absence of an explicit code and reliance purely on urgency/lockout framing as the manipulation lever.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Account-Lockout Warning Smishing
playbook.description: For a reported SMS falsely warning the user their account will be locked/suspended unless they act immediately via a link, pressuring them into entering credentials under urgency.

steps.title: Preserve the message and confirm no genuine lockout is in progress
steps.desc: Screenshot the message and check the referenced account/service directly to confirm whether any real lockout or suspension is occurring.
steps.outcome: Message preserved; genuine account status confirmed.
steps.abort: If a genuine lockout is found, redirect the user to the real account-recovery process.

steps.title: If credentials were entered, contain the affected account
steps.desc: Force password reset and session revocation on any corporate account whose credentials were entered.
steps.outcome: Affected account secured.

steps.title: Confirm restored access
steps.desc: Confirm the account is restored and functioning normally.
steps.outcome: User has confirmed-clean access.

steps.title: Log the urgency-pressure lure pattern
steps.desc: Record the lure for awareness content emphasizing skepticism of urgent action-required messages.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine whether the link was clicked and credentials entered
steps.desc: Interview the user and check MDM/mobile threat defense logs.
steps.outcome: Confirmed interaction status.
steps.abort: If no interaction, proceed to blocklisting only.

steps.title: Block the domain and report the sender
steps.desc: Add the domain to the web/DNS blocklist and report the number to the carrier.
steps.outcome: Domain blocked; number reported.

steps.title: Check for a broader campaign
steps.desc: Check for other reports of the same fake lockout lure.
steps.outcome: Campaign scope established.

ITID-11338.def: An OTP/MFA fatigue trigger or barrage deliberately timed to late night, early morning, or other off-hours periods, exploiting reduced alertness and slower verification behavior to increase the odds of an erroneous approval or code relay.
ITID-11338.purpose: Distinguishes OTP/MFA fatigue attacks deliberately timed to off-hours to exploit reduced target alertness.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed or strongly indicated deliberate off-hours timing as a notable feature of the attack
scopeExcludes: Standard-hours OTP fatigue attempts with no notable timing element (classify under the relevant tactic-based sibling leaf instead)
ITID-11338.severity: High — deliberate timing indicates a more sophisticated, premeditated attacker.
ITID-11338.priority: P1 given the premeditation and elevated success likelihood.
ITID-11338.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IAM immediately; lock the account pending investigation.
indicators: OTP fatigue trigger/barrage occurring between roughly 11pm and 5am local time to the victim
Pattern of repeated off-hours attempts against the same or related accounts
vectors: Scheduling or manually timing authentication triggers to off-hours periods when victims are less alert
rootCauses: No time-of-day-based anomaly detection on authentication attempts
controls: Time-of-day anomaly detection on authentication attempts
Phishing-resistant MFA
ITID-11338.detection: Moderate — authentication logs show timing patterns that can be flagged by anomaly detection.
ITID-11338.response: Lock the account, investigate the timing pattern, and correlate with any other suspicious activity against related accounts.
metrics: Count of confirmed off-hours-timed OTP fatigue incidents per quarter
sops: MFA Fatigue/OTP Relay Incident Response SOP
ITID-11338.notes: A timing-axis leaf, applied on top of whatever underlying tactic is used, when off-hours timing is itself the notable classification feature.

playbook.name: Response: Off-Hours Timed OTP Fatigue Smishing
playbook.description: For an incident where OTP/MFA fatigue prompts are deliberately timed to arrive late at night or during off-hours, exploiting reduced alertness or the hope the user will approve just to silence the phone.

steps.title: Interview the user and confirm the off-hours timing pattern
steps.desc: Confirm with the user the exact times prompts were received and whether any were approved, especially any approved while half-asleep or without full attention.
steps.outcome: Timing pattern and approval status confirmed.

steps.title: Force an immediate password reset and session revocation
steps.desc: Reset credentials and revoke all sessions/tokens, since off-hours OTP triggers confirm the attacker holds valid credentials.
steps.outcome: Account secured.

steps.title: Verify no approval succeeded during the off-hours window
steps.desc: Confirm via sign-in logs that no successful authentication occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no unauthorized access.
steps.abort: Escalate to account-takeover response if a successful login is found.

steps.title: Restore account access with new credentials
steps.desc: Confirm the user can authenticate normally with the new password.
steps.outcome: User has restored, confirmed-clean access.

steps.title: Log the off-hours timing pattern for detection tuning
steps.desc: Record the timing pattern; consider whether alerting rules should flag off-hours repeated MFA prompts as higher priority.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; detection tuning recommendation raised if warranted.

steps.title: Pull the authentication attempt log for the off-hours window
steps.desc: Retrieve sign-in logs for the relevant window including source IPs and whether any attempt succeeded.
steps.outcome: Full attempt log retrieved.

steps.title: Block the source IP(s) behind the off-hours attempts
steps.desc: Add the identified source IP(s) to the conditional access/firewall blocklist.
steps.outcome: Attacker source blocked.

ITID-11339.def: An OTP/MFA fatigue attack that triggers authentication attempts across multiple different accounts or services belonging to the same target (e.g., corporate SSO, personal email, and banking simultaneously), overwhelming the victim and increasing the odds that at least one approval or code relay slips through.
ITID-11339.purpose: Distinguishes OTP/MFA fatigue attacks that simultaneously or sequentially target multiple different accounts/services belonging to the same individual.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed correlated OTP fatigue activity across two or more distinct accounts/services for the same individual
scopeExcludes: A volume barrage confined to a single account/service (ITID-11336)
ITID-11339.severity: High — indicates a well-resourced attacker with broad access to the target's account landscape (likely via prior data aggregation/breach data).
ITID-11339.priority: P1 given the scope and sophistication.
ITID-11339.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IAM immediately; lock all affected accounts and coordinate cross-service investigation.
indicators: Correlated OTP triggers across multiple, unrelated services within a short window for the same individual
vectors: Attacker with access to multiple of the victim's usernames/emails (from breach data) triggering simultaneous authentication attempts across services
rootCauses: Credential/PII reuse across services enabling a single attacker to target many accounts at once
No cross-service correlation of authentication anomalies
controls: Cross-service anomaly correlation where feasible
Phishing-resistant MFA
Dark-web/breach-data monitoring for the individual's credentials
ITID-11339.detection: Moderate for the corporate-account leg (via SSO/IAM logs); weak for correlating with the individual's personal-service activity.
ITID-11339.response: Lock the corporate account, advise the individual to secure all other affected personal accounts, and investigate for a common breach-data source.
metrics: Count of confirmed multi-account OTP fatigue incidents per year
sops: MFA Fatigue/OTP Relay Incident Response SOP
ITID-11339.notes: Distinguished from ITID-11336 by scope — multiple accounts/services rather than a single-account volume barrage.

playbook.name: Response: Multi-Account Cross-Service OTP Fatigue Smishing
playbook.description: For an incident where a user receives simultaneous or near-simultaneous OTP/MFA fatigue prompts across multiple, unrelated services, indicating the attacker holds credentials for several of the user's accounts (likely from a credential-stuffing list).

steps.title: Enumerate every service generating OTP prompts
steps.desc: Interview the user and list every distinct service/account that sent an unsolicited OTP or MFA prompt in the incident window.
steps.outcome: Complete list of affected services compiled.

steps.title: Reset credentials and revoke sessions on every affected account
steps.desc: Force password reset and session/token revocation on each of the services identified, prioritizing corporate and financial accounts first.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts secured.

steps.title: Verify no successful authentication occurred on any affected account
steps.desc: Check sign-in logs across all identified services for any successful login during the incident window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no unauthorized access, or further incident opened for any account where access succeeded.
steps.abort: Escalate to account-takeover response for any account with a confirmed successful login.

steps.title: Confirm restored access across all affected accounts
steps.desc: Confirm the user has restored, working access to each affected account with new, unique credentials.
steps.outcome: All accounts restored with unique credentials.

steps.title: Document the cross-service pattern and recommend a password manager/unique-password reminder
steps.desc: Record the full scope; use this as a concrete example in awareness content for why password reuse is dangerous.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness content updated.

steps.title: Confirm none of the prompts were approved or codes shared
steps.desc: Confirm for each listed service whether the user approved, entered, or shared any code.
steps.outcome: Approval status confirmed per service.

steps.title: Advise the user to reset any other accounts sharing the same password
steps.desc: Since multi-service targeting indicates a reused/breached password, advise the user to change that password everywhere it was reused, not just on corporate systems.
steps.outcome: Password reuse risk addressed beyond the immediate corporate scope.

steps.title: Check whether this correlates with a known credential-stuffing list or recent breach
steps.desc: Check breach-monitoring/threat intel feeds for whether the user's email/credentials appear in a recent dump that would explain simultaneous targeting across services.
steps.outcome: Likely source of the credential list identified where possible.

ITID-11411.def: An interaction (email, chat, ticket, in-person, or other non-voice-call channel) in which an attacker poses as a representative of a known or plausible vendor to make a request of staff, logged before the specific request type is confirmed.
ITID-11411.purpose: Catch-all for a pretexting incident involving a fake vendor request that does not yet match a more specific leaf in this Tier-4 group.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific vendor-request type is confirmed
scopeExcludes: A request type clearly matching a more specific sibling leaf
The equivalent pretext delivered via a live phone call (a distinct Vishing-branch ITID, ITID-11214 Vendor/Supplier Representative Impersonation Call)
ITID-11411.severity: Medium; reassess once the request type and channel are confirmed.
ITID-11411.escalation: Escalate to SOC/fraud team; reclassify once the request type is confirmed.
indicators: Staff report of an unusual request from a purported vendor contact
vectors: Impersonation of a vendor via email, chat, ticket, or in-person contact
rootCauses: Insufficient detail available at time of report
controls: Out-of-band vendor-request verification procedures
User awareness training
ITID-11411.response: Document and attempt reclassification under a more specific leaf.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-11411.notes: Intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one. Scoped to non-voice-call channels; the live-call variant is tracked separately under ITID-11214.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Fake Vendor Request
playbook.description: For a report of a phone, email, or chat contact from someone claiming to be a vendor/supplier requesting an action from staff, where the specific ask (password reset, access, payment change, etc.) is not yet known.

steps.title: Capture the report details from the employee who was contacted
steps.desc: Record the contact channel (phone, email, chat), the claimed vendor, the request made, and any contact details used by the caller.
steps.guidance: Get this while details are fresh; ask the employee not to re-contact the number/email in the interim.
steps.outcome: A documented account of the contact and request.

steps.title: Verify the request against the legitimate vendor via a known contact channel
steps.desc: Contact the actual vendor using a phone number or email from the official contract/vendor management record — never the contact info supplied by the requester.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the request did not originate from the real vendor.
steps.abort: If the vendor confirms the request was genuine, close as a false positive and document the confusion for process improvement.

steps.title: Reverse or halt any action taken on the fraudulent request
steps.desc: If any step was completed (e.g. info shared, a change initiated), reverse or halt it immediately.
steps.outcome: No fraudulent action remains in effect.

steps.title: Confirm with the employee that no further contact/compliance is expected
steps.desc: Close the loop with the reporting employee and confirm they know not to act on any follow-up contact from the same source.
steps.outcome: Employee clear on next steps.

steps.title: Log the incident and assess vendor-contact verification process
steps.desc: Record the pretext used and evaluate whether staff have a clear, known process for verifying vendor contacts before acting on requests.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a process recommendation if warranted.

steps.title: Determine whether any action was taken on the request
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee complied with any part of the request (shared info, reset something, approved something) before recognizing it as suspicious.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether any compromise already occurred.

steps.title: Alert relevant teams to be on watch for related contact
steps.desc: Notify finance, IT helpdesk, or other teams likely to be targeted by the same pretext, especially if the caller may attempt other staff.
steps.outcome: Relevant teams briefed and alert.
