ITID-11412.def: An attacker posing as a known vendor's representative, contacting staff to request a password reset, credential handoff, or disclosure of a shared vendor-portal account's login details.
ITID-11412.purpose: Distinguishes a fake vendor pretext specifically requesting a password reset or shared vendor-account credential.
scopeIncludes: Requests to reset, share, or disclose vendor-portal or shared vendor-account credentials
scopeExcludes: The equivalent request delivered via live phone call (ITID-11214)
Internal IT-impersonation password-reset requests (a distinct leaf, ITID-11422, under the Fake IT Support Requests group)
ITID-11412.severity: High — successful credential disclosure can grant direct access to shared vendor systems.
ITID-11412.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if credentials were disclosed.
ITID-11412.escalation: Escalate to SOC and reset the affected credentials immediately if disclosure is confirmed.
indicators: Unsolicited request purportedly from a vendor asking for a password reset or shared login
Request made outside the vendor's normal support channel
vectors: Impersonating a known vendor contact via email or chat to request credential handoff
rootCauses: Use of shared, non-individualized vendor-account credentials
No out-of-band verification process for vendor credential requests
controls: Individualized (non-shared) vendor account credentials
Out-of-band verification for credential requests
User awareness training
ITID-11412.detection: Relies on human reporting; vendor-account login logs can confirm any resulting unauthorized access.
ITID-11412.response: Reset affected credentials, verify with the real vendor through a known channel, and review vendor-account access logs.
metrics: Count of fake vendor password/credential requests per quarter
ITID-11412.notes: Scoped to vendor-impersonation specifically; the internal-IT-impersonation equivalent is tracked under ITID-11422.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Vendor Password/Account Reset Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be a vendor requested that staff reset, share, or provide a password or account credential tied to a vendor-facing system or shared account.

steps.title: Identify which account/system the reset was requested for
steps.desc: Determine which specific account, portal, or shared credential was targeted by the request.
steps.outcome: Target account/system identified.

steps.title: Force a password reset on the targeted account regardless
steps.desc: Reset the credential immediately if there is any chance it was shared or reset by the caller, even if unconfirmed.
steps.outcome: Account secured with a new credential unknown to the caller.

steps.title: Check the account's recent activity for unauthorized use
steps.desc: Review login/activity logs for the account to check for any use of the credential by an unauthorized party before it was reset.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no unauthorized use occurred, or unauthorized use identified and escalated as an account-compromise incident.

steps.title: Communicate the new credential to the vendor through the verified channel
steps.desc: If the account is shared with the legitimate vendor, provide the new credential only through the verified contact channel.
steps.outcome: Legitimate vendor access restored securely.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce credential-request verification policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm staff know that password/credential requests must always be verified through a known channel before action.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a process recommendation.

steps.title: Determine whether the reset/share was completed
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee actually reset the password or disclosed the credential before recognizing the request as suspicious.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether the credential was compromised.

steps.title: Verify the request with the real vendor via a known contact channel
steps.desc: Contact the vendor using contract/vendor-record contact details to confirm whether they made this request.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the request did not originate from the real vendor.
steps.abort: If the vendor confirms the request was genuine, reverse the precautionary reset via the verified channel and close as a false positive.

ITID-11413.def: An attacker posing as a vendor technician, delivery contractor, or maintenance representative, requesting or attempting physical access to a facility under a fabricated service pretext.
ITID-11413.purpose: Distinguishes a fake vendor pretext specifically requesting physical facility access.
scopeIncludes: Requests for physical entry framed as scheduled or emergency vendor service
scopeExcludes: Purely digital vendor requests with no physical-access component (other sibling leaves)
ITID-11413.severity: High — physical access enables direct facility compromise, device tampering, or further reconnaissance.
ITID-11413.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if access was actually granted.
ITID-11413.escalation: Escalate to physical security immediately; verify the vendor's identity and scheduled visit against the real service contract.
indicators: Unscheduled or unverified vendor technician requesting entry
Vendor identity that cannot be confirmed against the organization's contracted vendor list
vectors: Impersonating a known vendor's field technician to gain physical entry under a service pretext
rootCauses: No requirement to verify vendor visits against a pre-scheduled service list
Front-desk/reception staff not trained to challenge unscheduled vendor visits
controls: Pre-scheduled vendor visit verification at reception/security desk
Vendor ID badge/credential verification process
Physical security awareness training
ITID-11413.detection: Relies entirely on physical security controls and staff vigilance; no technical detection surface.
ITID-11413.response: Deny access pending verification; report to physical security and, if access was granted, initiate a facility-compromise review.
metrics: Count of fake vendor physical-access attempts per quarter
ITID-11413.notes: The only leaf in this sibling group with a physical (rather than purely digital) attack surface.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Vendor Physical Access Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be a vendor requested that staff arrange physical site access (badge issuance, a pre-approved visitor pass, gate/dock clearance) for themselves or a third party.

steps.title: Identify what access was requested and for whom
steps.desc: Determine what type of physical access (badge, visitor pass, dock clearance) was requested and who it was requested for.
steps.outcome: Request details recorded.

steps.title: Remove or hold any access already arranged
steps.desc: Revoke any pre-approved visitor pass, remove any name from an access list, or place a hold on badge issuance until verified.
steps.outcome: No unverified access remains active.
steps.tool: Access control system / visitor management system

steps.title: Notify security/reception to watch for the named individual arriving on-site
steps.desc: Brief front-line staff to challenge and verify identity if the named individual attempts to use the arranged access.
steps.outcome: Security/reception briefed and alert.

steps.title: Re-arrange access properly if the request is later confirmed legitimate
steps.desc: If verification later confirms a genuine need, process the access request through the normal verified vendor-visit procedure.
steps.outcome: Legitimate access granted through proper channel if applicable.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce physical-access-request verification policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm reception/security staff verify any vendor-requested physical access before arranging it.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a process recommendation.

steps.title: Determine whether access was already arranged
steps.desc: Check whether reception, security, or facilities already acted on the request (issued a pass, added a name to an access list).
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether access has already been granted.
steps.tool: Access control system / visitor management system

steps.title: Verify the request with the real vendor via a known contact channel
steps.desc: Contact the vendor using contract/vendor-record contact details to confirm whether this access request is genuine.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the request did not originate from the real vendor.
steps.abort: If the vendor confirms the request was genuine, restore the access arrangement through the verified channel and close as a false positive.

ITID-11414.def: An attacker posing as a vendor's representative, asking staff to install a piece of software, a monitoring/support agent, or an 'update' on organization systems — a potential malware-delivery vector achieved through social pretext rather than a malicious link.
ITID-11414.purpose: Distinguishes a fake vendor pretext specifically requesting installation of software, an agent, or an 'update'.
scopeIncludes: Requests to install vendor-branded software, agents, or updates initiated through a social pretext rather than a phishing link
scopeExcludes: Malware delivered via a smishing/phishing link with no live-interaction pretext (Malware Links smishing group, ITID-11321 family)
ITID-11414.severity: High — successful installation can grant the attacker persistent access equivalent to a legitimate vendor tool.
ITID-11414.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if installation was completed.
ITID-11414.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IT immediately; isolate the affected system if installation occurred.
indicators: Unscheduled software/update install request attributed to a vendor with no corresponding change ticket
Installer or package not matching the vendor's known legitimate distribution
vectors: Social-engineering a staff member into manually installing attacker-provided software framed as a vendor update
rootCauses: No change-management verification requirement for vendor-initiated software installs
Lack of software allowlisting/application control
controls: Application allowlisting
Change-management verification for vendor software installs
User awareness training
ITID-11414.detection: EDR/application-control tooling can detect the resulting unauthorized install; the initial pretext itself is only visible via reporting.
ITID-11414.response: Isolate and investigate the affected system if installation occurred; verify with the real vendor through a known channel.
metrics: Count of fake vendor software-install requests per quarter
ITID-11414.notes: Distinguished from link-based malware smishing by the live social-interaction pretext driving a manual install.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Vendor Software/Update Installation Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be a vendor pressured staff to install software, an update, or a patch — potentially delivering malware under the guise of legitimate vendor maintenance.

steps.title: Identify what software/update was requested and whether it was installed
steps.desc: Determine the name/source of the software or update requested, and whether the employee downloaded or installed anything.
steps.outcome: Clear picture of what was requested and the installation status.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint if anything was installed or run
steps.desc: Disconnect the machine from the network (or isolate via EDR) if any file was executed, pending analysis.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated to prevent lateral spread.

steps.title: Scan and remediate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Run a full malware scan and remediate/reimage the endpoint if anything malicious is confirmed.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean or fully remediated.

steps.title: Restore the endpoint to service
steps.desc: Return the cleaned/reimaged endpoint to normal use once confirmed safe.
steps.outcome: Endpoint restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce software-installation verification policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm staff know that software/updates should only be installed through IT-managed channels, never at the direct request of an unverified caller.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a process recommendation.

steps.title: Preserve the installer file/link and any related email for analysis
steps.desc: Retain a copy of the installer, download link, or email without executing it further.
steps.outcome: Artifact preserved for security/malware analysis.

steps.title: Verify the request with the real vendor via a known contact channel
steps.desc: Contact the vendor using contract/vendor-record contact details to confirm whether this update/install request is genuine.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the request did not originate from the real vendor.
steps.abort: If the vendor confirms the request was genuine and nothing malicious was installed, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Check for lateral movement or further compromise
steps.desc: Review logs for any spread from the affected endpoint to other systems.
steps.outcome: Confirmed contained to the single endpoint, or scope expanded and escalated.

ITID-11415.def: An attacker posing as a vendor's representative, requesting sensitive internal data, reports, or exports under a plausible business pretext (e.g., 'we need this for our audit/integration').
ITID-11415.purpose: Distinguishes a fake vendor pretext specifically requesting sensitive data, reports, or exports.
scopeIncludes: Requests for data exports, reports, or sensitive documents framed as routine vendor business need
scopeExcludes: Requests for banking/payment details specifically (a distinct leaf, ITID-11416)
ITID-11415.severity: Medium-High — successful compliance can result in significant data exfiltration.
ITID-11415.escalation: Escalate to SOC and data owner immediately; assess scope of any data actually disclosed.
indicators: Unusual or unscheduled data request attributed to a vendor with no corresponding contractual basis
Request for data broader than the vendor's known legitimate scope
vectors: Impersonating a vendor to request data exports under a business-need pretext
rootCauses: No formal process requiring data-request verification against vendor contract scope
Lack of data classification controls limiting what can be exported to a vendor contact
controls: Data-request verification against contracted vendor scope
Data loss prevention on outbound sensitive data
User awareness training
ITID-11415.detection: DLP tooling can flag unusual outbound data transfers; the initial request is otherwise only visible via reporting.
ITID-11415.response: Verify with the real vendor before any data is sent; if data was already disclosed, assess exposure scope and notify affected data owners.
metrics: Count of fake vendor data-request incidents per quarter
ITID-11415.notes: Scoped to data/report requests specifically, distinct from the banking/payment-detail leaf (ITID-11416).

playbook.name: Response: Fake Vendor Data/Report Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be a vendor requested internal data, reports, or business information they would not normally be entitled to, using the vendor relationship as a pretext.

steps.title: Identify what data/report was requested
steps.desc: Determine exactly what information was asked for and its sensitivity level.
steps.outcome: Request scope and sensitivity documented.

steps.title: Verify the request with the real vendor via a known contact channel
steps.desc: Contact the vendor using contract/vendor-record contact details to confirm whether this data request is genuine and within the scope of the vendor relationship.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the request did not originate from the real vendor, or exceeded their legitimate entitlement.
steps.abort: If the vendor confirms the request was genuine and appropriately scoped, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Assess the scope and sensitivity of any data disclosed
steps.desc: If data was sent, determine exactly what was disclosed and whether it includes PII, financial, or confidential business information.
steps.outcome: Exposure scope documented.

steps.title: Escalate to privacy/legal if sensitive data was disclosed
steps.desc: If PII or confidential data was disclosed, loop in privacy/legal to assess notification obligations and next steps.
steps.outcome: Privacy/legal informed and assessing impact.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce data-request verification policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm staff verify the identity and entitlement of any requester before sharing internal data or reports.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a process recommendation.

steps.title: Determine whether the data was already sent
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee already provided any of the requested information before recognizing the request as suspicious.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether any disclosure already occurred.

ITID-11416.def: An attacker posing as a known vendor's representative, contacting accounts-payable/finance staff to request a change to the vendor's banking or payment details, in order to redirect future payments to an attacker-controlled account.
ITID-11416.purpose: Distinguishes a fake vendor pretext requesting a banking/payment detail change, scoped to non-email interactive channels or to the initial social-engineering contact itself.
scopeIncludes: The social-engineering interaction itself (phone, chat, portal message, in-person) requesting a banking-detail change, when the incident is centered on that interaction rather than a compromised email thread
scopeExcludes: The specifically email-channel version of this scam, tracked as Business Email Compromise under Financial Fraud (ITID-53121 Vendor Invoice Fraud and ITID-53211 Wire Transfer Fraud via Compromised Vendor Banking Details Change Email) — use this leaf only when the incident is not centered on a compromised/spoofed email thread
ITID-11416.severity: High — direct financial fraud risk with potential for significant loss.
ITID-11416.priority: P1 if a payment has already been redirected or is imminent; P2 otherwise.
ITID-11416.escalation: Escalate to finance/fraud team and SOC immediately; freeze any pending payment to the requested new account until verified.
indicators: Unsolicited banking-detail change request attributed to a vendor via a non-email channel
Request bypassing the organization's standard vendor-change verification process
vectors: Direct-contact impersonation of a vendor's finance representative requesting a payment-detail change
rootCauses: No callback verification requirement for vendor banking-detail changes using a number independently sourced from the vendor's known contract
Insufficient segregation of duties in the vendor-master-data change process
controls: Mandatory independent callback verification for all vendor banking-detail changes
Segregation of duties in vendor-master-data updates
ITID-11416.detection: Relies entirely on process controls and staff vigilance; no direct technical detection surface.
ITID-11416.response: Freeze the pending change/payment, verify independently with the real vendor, and report to finance fraud team.
metrics: Count of fake vendor banking-change requests per quarter
Dollar value of payments frozen/prevented
ITID-11416.notes: Deliberately scoped to avoid duplicating ITID-53121 and ITID-53211 under Business Email Compromise, which cover the specifically email-channel version of this same scam; use this leaf for the non-email interactive pretext or the initial social-engineering contact itself.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Vendor Banking/Payment Detail Change Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be a vendor requested that bank account or payment details on file be changed — a common precursor to invoice/payment redirection fraud.

steps.title: Identify what payment/banking change was requested and to which vendor record
steps.desc: Determine the specific vendor account and what banking details were requested to be changed.
steps.outcome: Target vendor record and requested change documented.

steps.title: Freeze the vendor payment record and halt any pending payments
steps.desc: Place a hold on the vendor's payment record in the ERP/finance system and stop any payment run that would use the new details.
steps.outcome: No further payments can go to the unverified account.

steps.title: If a payment was already sent, initiate recall/recovery immediately
steps.desc: Contact the sending bank without delay to attempt a payment recall, and involve finance leadership and, if amounts are significant, law enforcement.
steps.guidance: Speed is critical — fraudulent payment recall success drops sharply after the first 24 hours.
steps.outcome: Recall initiated; bank and law enforcement engaged if warranted.

steps.title: Restore the correct banking details on the vendor record
steps.desc: Ensure the vendor's payment record reflects the verified, legitimate banking details.
steps.outcome: Vendor record accurate and payments can resume safely.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce dual-control verification for payment changes
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm finance requires independent callback verification and/or dual approval for any vendor banking detail change.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a process recommendation.

steps.title: Determine whether the change was already made or any payment sent
steps.desc: Check finance/ERP records to see whether the banking details were updated or any payment was made to the new details.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether funds were exposed.

steps.title: Verify the change with the real vendor via a known, independent contact channel
steps.desc: Contact the vendor's known accounts-payable/finance contact using details from the original contract, not from the request itself, to confirm the change.
steps.guidance: A phone callback to a verified number is strongly preferred over email confirmation for banking changes.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the change did not originate from the real vendor.
steps.abort: If the vendor confirms the change was genuine via the independent channel, lift the hold and process normally.

ITID-11417.def: An attacker posing as a vendor's representative, attempting to manipulate the procurement or contracting process — for example, requesting an approval bypass, an expedited purchase order, or altered contract terms — rather than directly requesting credentials, data, or a payment-detail change.
ITID-11417.purpose: Distinguishes a fake vendor pretext that manipulates the contract or procurement process rather than requesting data, access, or payment directly.
scopeIncludes: Requests to bypass, expedite, or alter procurement/contracting steps under a vendor pretext
scopeExcludes: Direct payment-detail-change requests (ITID-11416)
Requests for data/reports (ITID-11415)
ITID-11417.severity: Medium — primarily a process-integrity risk, though it can enable downstream financial fraud.
ITID-11417.priority: P3 default, P2 if it results in an unauthorized purchase or contract change.
ITID-11417.escalation: Escalate to procurement leadership and SOC; halt any in-progress procurement action pending verification.
indicators: Unusual pressure to bypass standard procurement approval steps attributed to a vendor
Contract terms altered outside the normal review process
vectors: Impersonating a vendor to pressure procurement staff into skipping standard controls
rootCauses: Procurement approval steps that can be bypassed under urgency without secondary verification
controls: Non-bypassable procurement approval workflow
Segregation of duties in contract execution
ITID-11417.detection: Relies entirely on procurement process controls; no technical detection surface.
ITID-11417.response: Halt the in-progress procurement action, verify with the real vendor, and review for policy gaps that allowed the bypass attempt.
metrics: Count of fake vendor procurement-manipulation attempts per quarter
ITID-11417.notes: Scoped to procurement-process manipulation specifically, distinct from direct payment or data requests.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Vendor Contract/Procurement Process Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be a vendor attempted to manipulate the contract or procurement process (rushing a contract signature, bypassing approval steps, requesting an off-cycle purchase order) under false pretenses.

steps.title: Identify the specific procurement action requested
steps.desc: Determine what was requested — a signature, an urgent PO, bypassing approvals, or similar — and which contract/vendor record is involved.
steps.outcome: Request details documented.

steps.title: Halt the procurement action pending verification
steps.desc: Pause any pending signature, PO issuance, or approval step tied to the request.
steps.outcome: No procurement commitment proceeds until verified.

steps.title: Reverse any procurement action taken under false pretenses
steps.desc: If a PO, signature, or approval was already issued, work with procurement/legal to rescind or cancel it.
steps.outcome: No fraudulent commitment remains in effect.

steps.title: Brief procurement staff on the pattern observed
steps.desc: Share the pretext used with the procurement team so they recognize similar attempts.
steps.outcome: Procurement team briefed.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce procurement-approval verification steps
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm procurement approval workflows cannot be bypassed by urgency claims alone.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a process recommendation.

steps.title: Determine whether any procurement action was already taken
steps.desc: Check whether a signature, PO, or approval was already issued based on the request.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether any commitment was made.

steps.title: Verify the request with the real vendor and internal procurement owner
steps.desc: Contact the vendor's known representative and the internal procurement/legal owner of the relationship to confirm the request is genuine.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the request did not originate from the real vendor or authorized process.
steps.abort: If confirmed genuine, resume normal processing.

ITID-11418.def: An attacker posing as a vendor's support representative, requesting elevated access to the organization's internal ticketing system or portal, or asking staff to grant the vendor account elevated permissions, under a support-related pretext.
ITID-11418.purpose: Distinguishes a fake vendor pretext requesting access to the organization's internal support ticketing system or portal — the vendor pretending to need something from the organization's own staff, rather than the vendor's own support brand being impersonated toward the public.
scopeIncludes: Requests for elevated internal ticket-system/portal access attributed to a vendor support contact
scopeExcludes: Impersonation of a vendor's official support team directed outward at customers/the public via a fake support page or channel (a distinct ITID, ITID-22532 Impersonation of SaaS Vendor's Official Support Team, under the Attacks Against the Company Brand domain) — this leaf is the inward-facing request-to-the-organization's-own-staff version
ITID-11418.severity: Medium-High — elevated internal portal access can expose sensitive ticket data or enable further pivoting.
ITID-11418.escalation: Escalate to IT/SOC immediately; review and revoke any access granted pending verification.
indicators: Vendor support contact requesting access beyond their normal contracted scope
Access request made outside the vendor's established support ticket process
vectors: Impersonating a known vendor support contact to request elevated internal portal/ticket-system access
rootCauses: No formal process to verify vendor support access requests against contracted scope
Overly permissive default vendor support-account roles
controls: Least-privilege vendor support-account provisioning
Access-request verification against contracted scope
ITID-11418.detection: Access-management logs can flag unusual permission grants; the initial request is otherwise only visible via reporting.
ITID-11418.response: Revoke any granted access pending verification; review ticket-system access logs for misuse.
metrics: Count of fake vendor support-access requests per quarter
ITID-11418.notes: Deliberately scoped to the inward-facing request-to-organization-staff direction to avoid duplicating ITID-22532, which covers the outward-facing brand-impersonation version of vendor support impersonation.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Vendor Support Ticket/Portal Access Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be a vendor requested access to an internal support ticketing system or vendor portal, potentially to harvest information from past tickets or manipulate ticket status.

steps.title: Identify what system access was requested
steps.desc: Determine which ticketing system or portal access was requested and what level of access.
steps.outcome: Target system and access level documented.

steps.title: Revoke or hold any access granted
steps.desc: Disable any account created or access extended based on the unverified request.
steps.outcome: No unverified access remains active.

steps.title: Review any ticket history or portal data exposed if access was granted
steps.desc: Determine what tickets or data the account could have viewed before it was revoked.
steps.outcome: Exposure scope documented, or confirmed no access occurred.

steps.title: Re-provision access properly if later confirmed legitimate
steps.desc: If verification later confirms a genuine need, provision access through the standard verified vendor-onboarding process.
steps.outcome: Legitimate access granted through proper channel if applicable.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce portal-access-request verification policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm support/IT staff verify vendor identity before granting ticketing or portal access.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a process recommendation.

steps.title: Determine whether access was already granted
steps.desc: Check whether an account was created or access rights were already extended based on the request.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether access was granted.

steps.title: Verify the request with the real vendor via a known contact channel
steps.desc: Contact the vendor using contract/vendor-record contact details to confirm whether this access request is genuine.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the request did not originate from the real vendor.
steps.abort: If the vendor confirms the request was genuine, restore access through the normal verified onboarding process.

ITID-11419.def: A fake vendor request — of any type (access, data, payment, software) — where the attacker's primary lever is manufactured urgency or crisis framing (e.g., 'critical outage, we need this now') intended to short-circuit the target's normal verification process.
ITID-11419.purpose: Flags fake vendor requests where the notable, classification-driving feature is urgency/crisis framing used to override normal verification, cutting across any of the specific request types above.
scopeIncludes: Cases where urgency/crisis framing is the dominant, classification-driving tactic, regardless of the underlying request content
scopeExcludes: Cases where the request content is clear and urgency is incidental — classify under the specific request-type leaf instead (ITID-11412 through ITID-11418)
ITID-11419.severity: Medium-High — urgency framing is a strong indicator of social-engineering intent and correlates with higher compliance rates.
ITID-11419.priority: P2 default given the elevated-risk framing.
ITID-11419.escalation: Escalate to SOC immediately; treat any urgency-driven vendor request as high-risk pending independent verification.
indicators: Explicit crisis/urgency language ('immediately', 'critical', 'right now') combined with pressure to bypass normal process
Request timed to exploit off-hours or reduced staffing
vectors: Manufactured urgency/crisis framing designed to override standard vendor-verification procedures
rootCauses: Verification procedures that can be bypassed under sufficient time pressure
No mandatory 'urgency is not a bypass reason' policy for vendor requests
controls: Policy explicitly prohibiting urgency as grounds for skipping vendor-request verification
User awareness training on urgency-based social engineering
ITID-11419.detection: Relies entirely on staff recognizing and reporting the urgency pattern; no technical detection surface.
ITID-11419.response: Apply standard verification regardless of stated urgency; escalate any bypass attempt to SOC.
metrics: Count of urgency-framed fake vendor requests per quarter
ITID-11419.notes: A tactic-axis leaf, used only when urgency/crisis framing itself is the notable classification driver rather than a specific request type.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Vendor Emergency/Urgent Escalation Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be a vendor invoked a fabricated emergency or urgent escalation (e.g. 'critical outage,' 'security issue on your account') to pressure staff into bypassing normal verification and acting immediately.

steps.title: Capture the claimed emergency and the action demanded
steps.desc: Record exactly what emergency was claimed and what urgent action the caller demanded be taken.
steps.guidance: High-pressure urgency itself is a red flag worth noting explicitly.
steps.outcome: Claim and demand documented.

steps.title: Independently verify the claimed emergency exists
steps.desc: Check internal monitoring/ticketing and contact the vendor via a known channel to determine whether any real issue is actually occurring.
steps.guidance: A real vendor emergency should be independently visible in monitoring or a prior ticket — an emergency that exists only in the caller's claim is a strong fraud indicator.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether a real emergency exists.
steps.abort: If a genuine emergency is independently confirmed, hand off to the appropriate incident process and close this playbook.

steps.title: Alert relevant teams to the urgency-pretext pattern
steps.desc: Warn helpdesk, finance, and other frequently targeted teams about the specific urgency claim used, in case the same actor contacts others.
steps.outcome: Relevant teams briefed and alert.

steps.title: Confirm with the employee that no further compliance is expected
steps.desc: Close the loop with the reporting employee, reassuring them that raising the alarm was correct and they should not act on follow-up pressure.
steps.outcome: Employee clear on next steps and not discouraged from reporting future suspicions.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce a no-bypass-under-pressure policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm staff know that claimed urgency never justifies skipping identity verification steps.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a process/training recommendation.

steps.title: Determine whether any action was taken under the pressure
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee complied with any part of the demand before recognizing it as suspicious.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether any compromise already occurred.

steps.title: Reverse or halt any action taken under the pressure
steps.desc: Undo or stop any step completed in response to the fabricated urgency.
steps.outcome: No fraudulent action remains in effect.

ITID-11421.def: An interaction in which an attacker poses as the organization's own internal IT/help-desk staff to make a request of an employee, logged before the specific request type is confirmed.
ITID-11421.purpose: Catch-all for a pretexting incident involving a fake internal IT support request that does not yet match a more specific leaf in this Tier-4 group.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific IT-support-request type is confirmed
scopeExcludes: A request type clearly matching a more specific sibling leaf
Impersonation of a vendor's (external) support team rather than internal IT (Fake Vendor Requests group, ITID-11411 family)
ITID-11421.severity: Medium; reassess once the request type is confirmed.
ITID-11421.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IT security; reclassify once the request type is confirmed.
indicators: Employee report of an unusual request from a purported internal IT contact
vectors: Impersonation of internal IT/help-desk staff
rootCauses: Insufficient detail available at time of report
controls: Out-of-band verification for IT-support requests
User awareness training
ITID-11421.response: Document and attempt reclassification under a more specific leaf.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
sops: IT Support Impersonation Pretext Response SOP
ITID-11421.notes: Intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Fake IT Support Request
playbook.description: For a report of a phone, email, or chat contact from someone claiming to be internal IT/help desk staff requesting an action from an employee, where the specific ask is not yet known.

steps.title: Capture the report details from the employee who was contacted
steps.desc: Record the contact channel, the claimed IT identity/department, the request made, and any caller ID or sender address used.
steps.outcome: A documented account of the contact and request.

steps.title: Verify against the real IT help desk's ticket/call records
steps.desc: Check the IT service management system for any genuine open ticket or scheduled outreach that would explain the contact, and confirm the caller's identity against the real help desk roster.
steps.guidance: Never use a callback number the caller provided — use the published internal help desk number.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the request did not originate from real IT.
steps.abort: If confirmed genuine, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Reverse or halt any action taken on the fraudulent request
steps.desc: If any step was completed, reverse or halt it immediately.
steps.outcome: No fraudulent action remains in effect.

steps.title: Confirm with the employee that no further compliance is expected
steps.desc: Close the loop with the reporting employee and confirm they should not act on follow-up contact from the same source.
steps.outcome: Employee clear on next steps.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce IT-contact verification awareness
steps.desc: Record the pretext used and evaluate whether staff know how to verify a genuine IT contact.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a training/process recommendation if warranted.

steps.title: Determine whether any action was taken on the request
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee complied with any part of the request before recognizing it as suspicious.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether any compromise already occurred.

steps.title: Alert the security/IT team to the impersonation attempt
steps.desc: Notify IT security so they can watch for related activity and warn other staff who may be targeted by the same pretext.
steps.outcome: IT security aware and alert.

ITID-11422.def: An attacker posing as internal IT/help-desk staff, contacting an employee to request they reveal their current password or perform a password reset in a way that discloses or resets credentials to attacker control.
ITID-11422.purpose: Distinguishes an internal-IT-impersonation pretext specifically requesting a password reset or password disclosure.
scopeIncludes: Requests to reveal a current password, or to reset a password via an attacker-controlled process
scopeExcludes: The equivalent request impersonating a vendor rather than internal IT (ITID-11412)
The equivalent request delivered by live phone call impersonating an executive to the real IT helpdesk (a distinct ITID under a different domain, ITID-22432)
ITID-11422.priority: P1 if the password was disclosed or reset.
ITID-11422.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IAM immediately; force a credential reset regardless of confirmed disclosure.
indicators: Unsolicited password reset/disclosure request purportedly from IT, made outside the normal help-desk ticketing channel
Request pressuring the employee to bypass standard identity-verification steps
vectors: Impersonating internal IT to directly request or reset a password
rootCauses: No mandatory callback-to-known-number verification for password-related IT requests
Weak identity-verification steps in the real help-desk password-reset process itself
controls: Mandatory independent callback verification for IT-initiated password requests
Strong identity verification in the real help-desk reset process
User awareness training
ITID-11422.detection: IAM logs can show the resulting password reset event; the initial impersonation is otherwise only visible via reporting.
ITID-11422.response: Reset the credential through a verified channel, review IAM logs for the reset event's true origin, and lock the account if compromise is suspected.
metrics: Count of fake IT password-reset requests per quarter
sops: IT Support Impersonation Pretext Response SOP
ITID-11422.notes: Scoped to internal-IT impersonation specifically; the vendor-impersonation equivalent is tracked under ITID-11412.

playbook.name: Response: Fake IT Password Reset Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be IT/help desk requested that an employee reset or reveal their account password, or attempted to trigger a reset and extract the resulting temporary credential from the employee.

steps.title: Identify which account was targeted
steps.desc: Determine which system/account the reset request targeted.
steps.outcome: Target account identified.

steps.title: Force a password reset on the account immediately
steps.desc: Reset the credential without delay if there is any chance it was disclosed.
steps.outcome: Account secured with a new credential unknown to the caller.

steps.title: Review account activity for unauthorized access before the reset
steps.desc: Check login and activity logs for the account around the incident time for signs of unauthorized use.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no unauthorized use occurred, or unauthorized use identified and escalated as an account-compromise incident.

steps.title: Help the employee set a new password through the verified self-service channel
steps.desc: Guide the employee to reset their password themselves through the official IT self-service portal.
steps.outcome: Employee has full access restored securely.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce that IT never asks for passwords
steps.desc: Record the incident and reinforce the standing policy that legitimate IT staff never ask an employee to state or share their password.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with an awareness reminder issued.

steps.title: Determine whether the password or a temporary credential was disclosed
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee provided their password or read out a reset code/temporary password to the caller.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether the credential was compromised.

steps.title: Revoke active sessions and check MFA status on the account
steps.desc: Terminate any active sessions and confirm no new MFA device was registered by the attacker.
steps.outcome: Sessions revoked; MFA confirmed intact.

ITID-11423.def: An attacker posing as internal IT staff, instructing an employee to install a remote access/remote support tool (e.g., AnyDesk, TeamViewer, or similar) on their device — granting the attacker direct remote control once installed.
ITID-11423.purpose: Distinguishes an internal-IT-impersonation pretext specifically requesting installation of a remote access tool.
scopeIncludes: Requests to install a remote-access/remote-support tool under an IT-support pretext
scopeExcludes: Legitimate, governance-tracked vendor remote access tooling risk (a distinct architectural/governance ITID, ITID-42141, under the Network Infrastructure domain) — this leaf covers the social-engineering-induced install specifically, not standing legitimate vendor access
ITID-11423.severity: High — successful installation grants the attacker direct, real-time control of the endpoint.
ITID-11423.priority: P1 if installation and remote-control access was achieved.
ITID-11423.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IT immediately; isolate the endpoint and terminate any active remote session.
indicators: Remote-access tool installed outside the organization's approved software/change-management process
Unusual remote-control session activity on the endpoint following the request
vectors: Social-engineering an employee into manually installing a legitimate remote-access tool for illegitimate use
rootCauses: No application allowlisting preventing unauthorized remote-access tool installs
Employees not trained to recognize that IT rarely, if ever, asks them to self-install remote-control software
controls: Application allowlisting blocking unauthorized remote-access tools
EDR alerting on remote-access tool execution
User awareness training
ITID-11423.detection: Strong — EDR can reliably detect and alert on remote-access tool installation and active sessions.
ITID-11423.response: Isolate the endpoint immediately, terminate the remote session, and treat as an active intrusion.
metrics: Count of confirmed unauthorized remote-access tool installs via IT-impersonation per quarter
sops: IT Support Impersonation Pretext Response SOP
ITID-11423.notes: Distinguished from ITID-42141 (a standing vendor-access governance gap) by being a discrete social-engineering-induced install event rather than a persistent architectural risk.

playbook.name: Response: Fake IT Remote Access Tool Installation Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be IT/help desk instructed an employee to install a remote access/remote desktop tool, potentially giving the attacker direct hands-on-keyboard control of the endpoint.

steps.title: Identify what remote access tool was requested or installed
steps.desc: Determine the specific tool name and whether it was actually installed and a session established.
steps.outcome: Tool identified and installation/session status confirmed.

steps.title: Immediately isolate the endpoint from the network
steps.desc: Disconnect the machine from the network or isolate via EDR without delay if any remote session occurred.
steps.guidance: Do not wait to gather more information — sever the connection first.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated and the remote session terminated.

steps.title: Scan and remediate the endpoint for additional malware or persistence
steps.desc: Run a full EDR/malware scan and check for scheduled tasks, added accounts, or other persistence the attacker may have planted during the session.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean or fully remediated.

steps.title: Restore the endpoint to service and reissue any reset credentials
steps.desc: Return the cleaned endpoint to normal use and ensure the employee has working, freshly issued credentials.
steps.outcome: Endpoint and employee access restored.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce remote-tool installation policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and reinforce that remote access tools are only installed by IT-initiated, verified sessions, never at a caller's direction.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a training/process recommendation.

steps.title: Determine how long any remote session lasted and what was visible/done
steps.desc: If a session occurred, establish its duration and what the caller did or could see during it.
steps.outcome: Scope of the remote session established.

steps.title: Uninstall the remote access tool and reset any credentials entered during the session
steps.desc: Remove the installed tool and force a reset of any account credentials the employee typed or that may have been captured while the attacker had visibility.
steps.outcome: Tool removed; potentially exposed credentials reset.

steps.title: Check for lateral movement from the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Review network/authentication logs for any spread to other systems during or after the session.
steps.outcome: Confirmed contained to the single endpoint, or scope expanded and escalated.

ITID-11424.def: An attacker posing as internal IT/help-desk staff via chat, ticket, email, or an in-person/ambiguous-channel interaction, requesting the employee approve an MFA push notification or read out an OTP/security code.
ITID-11424.purpose: Distinguishes an internal-IT-impersonation pretext specifically requesting an MFA push approval or OTP/security code, delivered via a non-voice-call channel.
scopeIncludes: MFA/code requests made via chat, ticket, email, or in-person IT-support-style contact
scopeExcludes: The equivalent request delivered as a live phone call soliciting the code (a distinct Vishing-branch ITID, ITID-11218 Real-Time MFA/OTP Relay Vishing)
ITID-11424.severity: High — successful compliance results in immediate account/MFA bypass.
ITID-11424.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IAM immediately; lock the account regardless of confirmed compliance.
indicators: IT-support-style request for an MFA approval or code outside a verified help-desk ticket
Request timed to coincide with a real pending authentication attempt
vectors: Impersonating IT to request an MFA push approval or code via chat/ticket/email
rootCauses: Employees not trained that legitimate IT never needs their MFA code or push approval
No policy explicitly prohibiting IT from requesting MFA codes
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA
Explicit policy that IT never requests MFA codes/approvals
User awareness training
ITID-11424.detection: Authentication logs can confirm any correlated real login attempt, giving a moderate technical signal.
ITID-11424.response: Lock the account, reset MFA, and review authentication logs for the underlying triggering attempt.
metrics: Count of fake IT MFA/code requests per quarter
sops: IT Support Impersonation Pretext Response SOP
detections: Authentication log correlation for OTP-triggering events
ITID-11424.notes: The non-voice-call counterpart to ITID-11218; use this leaf when the MFA/code ask arrives via chat, ticket, email, or in-person IT-support pretext rather than a live phone call.

playbook.name: Response: Fake IT MFA/Security Code Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be IT/help desk asked an employee to read out an MFA code, approve an unexpected push notification, or otherwise assist in defeating multi-factor authentication on their account.

steps.title: Identify which account's MFA was targeted
steps.desc: Determine which account the MFA code or push approval request related to.
steps.outcome: Target account identified.

steps.title: Immediately reset the account password and MFA registration
steps.desc: Force a password reset and re-register MFA on the account without delay, treating this as a likely active compromise attempt.
steps.guidance: MFA-code/push social engineering is a strong indicator of an imminent account takeover attempt — treat as urgent.
steps.outcome: Account secured with new credentials and MFA the caller cannot access.

steps.title: Review account activity immediately following the disclosed code/approval
steps.desc: Check login, mailbox, and application activity logs for any unauthorized access that occurred using the compromised MFA.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no unauthorized access occurred, or unauthorized access identified and escalated as an account-compromise incident.

steps.title: Help the employee re-enroll MFA through a verified in-person or trusted channel
steps.desc: Have the employee re-register their MFA device through IT directly, not via a link or code from an inbound caller.
steps.outcome: Employee has secure MFA restored.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce that MFA codes are never shared
steps.desc: Record the incident and reinforce the standing rule that MFA codes and push approvals are never given to anyone, including someone claiming to be IT.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with an urgent awareness reminder issued organization-wide if this appears to be a targeted campaign.

steps.title: Determine whether the code was shared or the push was approved
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee actually disclosed the code or approved the push notification.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether MFA was bypassed.

steps.title: Revoke all active sessions on the account
steps.desc: Terminate any existing sessions, tokens, or app passwords that could have been established using the disclosed code/approval.
steps.outcome: All prior sessions terminated.

ITID-11425.def: An attacker posing as internal IT, notifying an employee that their device has been flagged as non-compliant and instructing them to take a remediation action (install an agent, change a setting, provide device access) that in fact compromises the device.
ITID-11425.purpose: Distinguishes an internal-IT-impersonation pretext that uses a fake device-compliance flag to get the target to take a compromising action.
scopeIncludes: Fake compliance-flag notifications driving an employee to install an agent or change a security setting
scopeExcludes: Genuine device-compliance enforcement processes (not applicable — this is inherently a malicious pretext leaf)
ITID-11425.severity: Medium-High — the remediation action requested is typically itself the compromise vector.
ITID-11425.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IT immediately; verify against the real device-compliance/MDM system.
indicators: Compliance-flag notification not corresponding to any real flag in the organization's actual MDM/compliance system
Requested remediation action inconsistent with the organization's real compliance-remediation process
vectors: Fabricated compliance-flag pretext instructing the employee to install an attacker-provided 'remediation' agent
rootCauses: Employees unable to independently verify a compliance flag against the real MDM console
No standardized, employee-recognizable compliance-notification format
controls: Standardized, verifiable compliance-notification format
MDM console cross-check requirement before acting on a compliance flag
User awareness training
ITID-11425.detection: Moderate — the real MDM console can confirm whether a genuine compliance flag exists.
ITID-11425.response: Verify against the real MDM console before any action; if a remediation agent was installed, isolate and investigate the device.
metrics: Count of fake device-compliance pretext incidents per quarter
sops: IT Support Impersonation Pretext Response SOP
ITID-11425.notes: Distinguished from other IT-impersonation leaves by the specific device-compliance/remediation framing.

playbook.name: Response: Fake IT Endpoint/Device Compliance Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be IT told an employee their device was non-compliant, infected, or flagged, and instructed them to take a remediation action (run a tool, change a setting, provide device details) as a pretext to gain access or information.

steps.title: Identify the compliance claim and requested remediation action
steps.desc: Record exactly what the caller claimed was wrong with the device and what action they instructed the employee to take.
steps.outcome: Claim and requested action documented.

steps.title: Determine whether the requested action was taken
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee ran the tool, changed the setting, or provided the requested device details.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of what, if anything, was done to the device.

steps.title: Inspect the endpoint for any malicious tool or configuration change
steps.desc: Check for anything installed or changed as a result of the fraudulent instruction.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean, or issue found and remediated.

steps.title: Restore the endpoint to normal service
steps.desc: Return the device to normal use once confirmed safe.
steps.outcome: Endpoint restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce compliance-notification verification process
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm employees know genuine compliance issues come through the official MDM notification, not an unsolicited call.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a training recommendation.

steps.title: Check the real device management console for any genuine compliance flag
steps.desc: Look up the device in the actual endpoint/device management system to see if a real compliance issue exists.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether a genuine compliance issue exists.
steps.abort: If a genuine compliance issue is found and IT confirms it initiated contact, hand off to normal remediation and close this playbook.

steps.title: Isolate the endpoint if any tool was run or setting changed
steps.desc: Isolate the device via EDR/MDM pending inspection if any action was taken based on the false claim.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated pending inspection.

ITID-11426.def: An attacker posing as internal IT handling a (fabricated) new-hire onboarding or employee-offboarding action, requesting account creation, credential handoff, or an access transfer under that process pretext.
ITID-11426.purpose: Distinguishes an internal-IT-impersonation pretext exploiting the onboarding/offboarding process to manipulate account provisioning or access transfer.
scopeIncludes: Requests to create, transfer, or hand off account access framed as an onboarding or offboarding action
scopeExcludes: Genuine onboarding/offboarding requests initiated through the organization's real HR/IT workflow (not applicable — this is inherently a malicious pretext leaf)
ITID-11426.severity: Medium-High — onboarding/offboarding is a well-known blind spot with less-scrutinized account changes.
ITID-11426.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IAM immediately; verify against the real HR system before any account action.
indicators: Account creation/transfer request not corresponding to any real HR record for the named employee
Request bypassing the standard joiner/leaver workflow
vectors: Impersonating IT during a fabricated onboarding/offboarding scenario to manipulate account provisioning
rootCauses: No mandatory cross-check against the real HR system before account provisioning changes
Onboarding/offboarding workflows treated as lower-scrutiny than other access requests
controls: Mandatory HR-system cross-check before any onboarding/offboarding account action
User awareness training
ITID-11426.detection: IAM provisioning logs can be cross-referenced against HR records to detect discrepancies.
ITID-11426.response: Verify against the real HR system; reverse any unauthorized provisioning change immediately.
metrics: Count of fake onboarding/offboarding pretext incidents per quarter
sops: IT Support Impersonation Pretext Response SOP
ITID-11426.notes: Distinguished from other IT-impersonation leaves by exploiting the joiner/leaver process specifically as the pretext.

playbook.name: Response: Fake IT Onboarding/Offboarding Account Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be IT/HR requested an account be created, modified, or disabled under the pretext of an onboarding or offboarding action, potentially to plant or hijack an account.

steps.title: Identify the specific account action requested
steps.desc: Determine what was requested — new account creation, permission change, or account disablement — and for whom.
steps.outcome: Request details documented.

steps.title: Verify against actual HR onboarding/offboarding records
steps.desc: Confirm with HR directly whether the named individual has a genuine, currently active onboarding or offboarding event.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the account action is legitimate.
steps.abort: If confirmed genuine, allow the action to proceed/stand as normal.

steps.title: Audit what access any fraudulently created/modified account had and used
steps.desc: Check activity logs for any use of the account before it was disabled/reversed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no unauthorized use occurred, or use identified and escalated.

steps.title: Confirm proper onboarding/offboarding proceeds through the normal HR-verified process
steps.desc: If a genuine onboarding/offboarding need exists, process it through the standard verified workflow.
steps.outcome: Correct account state achieved through proper process.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce that account changes require HR-system verification
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm IT staff verify onboarding/offboarding requests against the HR system of record before acting, not on a caller's say-so.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a process recommendation.

steps.title: Determine whether the action was already taken
steps.desc: Check the IAM/HR system for whether the account was actually created, modified, or disabled.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of what, if anything, was done.

steps.title: Reverse any unverified account action immediately
steps.desc: Disable any newly created unverified account, or reverse any permission change made under the false pretext.
steps.outcome: No unauthorized account or access remains active.

ITID-11427.def: An attacker posing as internal IT, contacting an employee to enforce (fabricated) software-license or update-compliance requirements, pushing a malicious 'compliance' download or requesting license-key/account information.
ITID-11427.purpose: Distinguishes an internal-IT-impersonation pretext that uses software-license or update-compliance enforcement as its framing.
scopeIncludes: License/update-compliance-framed requests pushing a download or requesting license/account information
scopeExcludes: The device-compliance-flag pretext, which is scoped to general device-security compliance rather than software licensing specifically (a distinct leaf, ITID-11425)
ITID-11427.severity: Medium-High — the compliance-framed download is typically itself the compromise vector.
ITID-11427.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IT immediately; verify against the real software-asset-management system.
indicators: License-compliance notification not corresponding to any real flag in the organization's software-asset-management system
Requested download inconsistent with the organization's known legitimate software sources
vectors: Fabricated license/update-compliance pretext instructing the employee to download an attacker-provided package
rootCauses: No standardized, verifiable license-compliance-notification process
Employees unable to independently verify licensing status
controls: Standardized, verifiable license-compliance-notification format
Software-asset-management cross-check requirement
User awareness training
ITID-11427.detection: Moderate — the real software-asset-management system can confirm whether a genuine compliance issue exists.
ITID-11427.response: Verify against the real software-asset-management system; if a download occurred, isolate and investigate the device.
metrics: Count of fake license/update-compliance pretext incidents per quarter
sops: IT Support Impersonation Pretext Response SOP
ITID-11427.notes: Distinguished from the general device-compliance leaf (ITID-11425) by its specific software-license/update framing.

playbook.name: Response: Fake IT Software License/Update Compliance Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be IT told an employee their software license was expired/non-compliant and instructed them to click a link, enter credentials, or install something to 'reactivate' or 'update' it.

steps.title: Identify the software/license claim and requested action
steps.desc: Record which software was claimed to be non-compliant and what action (link click, credential entry, install) was requested.
steps.outcome: Claim and requested action documented.

steps.title: Determine whether the employee clicked the link, entered credentials, or installed anything
steps.desc: Establish exactly what the employee did in response to the request.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of the employee's actions.

steps.title: Scan the endpoint and review account activity
steps.desc: Check for malware on the endpoint and review the account's activity logs for unauthorized use.
steps.outcome: Endpoint and account confirmed clean, or issues found and remediated.

steps.title: Restore endpoint/account to normal service
steps.desc: Return the cleaned endpoint and reset account to normal use.
steps.outcome: Endpoint and account restored.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce software-compliance verification process
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm genuine license/compliance issues route through the official IT asset system, not unsolicited links.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a training recommendation.

steps.title: Check the real software asset management system for actual license status
steps.desc: Look up the software license in the real asset management system to confirm whether a genuine compliance issue exists.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether a genuine issue exists.
steps.abort: If genuine and IT confirms it initiated contact, hand off to normal remediation and close this playbook.

steps.title: Reset any credentials entered and isolate the endpoint if anything was installed
steps.desc: Force a password reset for any credentials entered on the fake page, and isolate the endpoint via EDR if software was installed.
steps.outcome: Credentials secured; endpoint isolated if applicable.

ITID-11428.def: An attacker posing as internal IT/help-desk, instructing the employee to call back a given number 'to verify their identity' or resolve an issue — where the number is attacker-controlled, exploiting the general trust placed in callback-based verification.
ITID-11428.purpose: Distinguishes an internal-IT-impersonation pretext that exploits the callback-verification convention itself, instructing the target to call an attacker-controlled number.
scopeIncludes: Direct, non-transactional callback pretexts where no explicit service/benefit is offered in exchange
scopeExcludes: The Quid-Pro-Quo-styled version where a specific service or fix is explicitly offered in exchange for the callback (a distinct ITID under a different Tier-3 branch, ITID-11527 Fake Corporate Help Desk Vendor Callback Scam)
ITID-11428.severity: Medium-High — the callback itself typically leads into a live vishing interaction that can extract credentials or MFA codes.
ITID-11428.priority: P2 default, P1 if the target completed the callback and disclosed information.
ITID-11428.escalation: Escalate to SOC immediately; treat any completed callback as a potential information-disclosure event.
indicators: Instruction to call a number not matching the organization's known, published IT/help-desk contact
Request framed as identity verification with no specific benefit offered in exchange
vectors: Directing the target to an attacker-controlled callback number, exploiting the callback-verification convention itself
rootCauses: Employees not trained to independently verify IT contact numbers against a published directory
No organization-wide single source of truth for the real IT help-desk number
controls: Published, organization-wide single source of truth for the real IT help-desk number
User awareness training on callback-number verification
ITID-11428.detection: Relies entirely on human reporting; no technical detection surface until a resulting compromise generates its own signal.
ITID-11428.response: Confirm whether the callback was completed and what information was disclosed; treat as a potential credential/MFA exposure event.
metrics: Count of fake IT callback pretext incidents per quarter
sops: IT Support Impersonation Pretext Response SOP
ITID-11428.notes: Distinguished from ITID-11527 by the absence of an explicit quid-pro-quo framing — this leaf is a direct identity-verification pretext with no service/benefit offered in exchange.

playbook.name: Response: Fake IT Help Desk Callback Verification Request
playbook.description: For an incident where an attacker instructed a target to call a fraudulent 'IT help desk' number (often left as a callback in a phishing email or voicemail) which was actually staffed by the attacker, who then used the trust of the target-initiated call to extract information or push a malicious action.

steps.title: Identify the phone number called and the pretext that prompted the call
steps.desc: Record the number the employee called, and what email/voicemail/message prompted them to call it.
steps.outcome: Callback number and originating pretext documented.

steps.title: Confirm the number is not a legitimate internal or vendor help desk line
steps.desc: Check the number against the real internal help desk directory and any legitimate vendor support lines.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the number is fraudulent.
steps.abort: If confirmed to be a legitimate number simply mislabeled or misdialed, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Block the fraudulent number/domain where feasible and preserve the originating message
steps.desc: Block the number in relevant systems and retain the original phishing email/voicemail for analysis and reporting.
steps.outcome: Number blocked where possible; artifact preserved.

steps.title: Confirm with the employee that no further compliance is expected
steps.desc: Close the loop with the employee, reassuring them and confirming they should not call back or continue engaging with the number.
steps.outcome: Employee clear on next steps.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce use of the official help desk directory
steps.desc: Record the incident and remind staff to always use the published internal IT help desk number rather than one provided in an email or voicemail.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with an awareness reminder issued.

steps.title: Determine what happened during the call
steps.desc: Establish what information was shared or what action was taken while the employee was on the call.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of what occurred during the call.

steps.title: Reverse or halt any action taken during the call and reset any disclosed credentials
steps.desc: Undo any change made, and force a reset of any credential or code disclosed while on the fraudulent call.
steps.outcome: No fraudulent action remains in effect; disclosed credentials secured.

ITID-11429.def: An attacker posing as internal IT running a (fabricated) data backup or system migration project, requesting the employee provide access, credentials, or a data export under that project pretext.
ITID-11429.purpose: Distinguishes an internal-IT-impersonation pretext that uses a fabricated data backup or system migration project as its framing.
scopeIncludes: Backup/migration-project-framed requests for access, credentials, or data exports
scopeExcludes: Data/report requests framed as a vendor need rather than an internal IT project (Fake Vendor Requests group, ITID-11415)
ITID-11429.severity: Medium-High — successful compliance can grant broad access or result in significant data exposure.
ITID-11429.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IT immediately; verify against the real IT project-management/change-management record.
indicators: Backup/migration project not corresponding to any real, tracked IT change record
Request for access/data broader than any legitimate migration would require
vectors: Fabricated IT project pretext used to justify an unusual access or data-export request
rootCauses: No requirement to verify IT project requests against the real change-management system
Employees unfamiliar with which IT projects are legitimately in progress
controls: Change-management cross-check requirement before granting project-based access
User awareness training
ITID-11429.detection: Moderate — the real change-management system can confirm whether a genuine project exists.
ITID-11429.response: Verify against the real change-management system; reverse any access/data disclosure granted under the false pretext.
metrics: Count of fake backup/migration pretext incidents per quarter
sops: IT Support Impersonation Pretext Response SOP
ITID-11429.notes: Distinguished from the vendor-impersonation data-request leaf (ITID-11415) by the internal-IT-project framing rather than a vendor-business-need framing.

playbook.name: Response: Fake IT Data Backup/Migration Request
playbook.description: For an incident where a caller or emailer claiming to be IT instructed an employee to export, copy, or transfer data to an external location/account under the pretext of a backup, migration, or system upgrade.

steps.title: Identify what data transfer/export was requested and its destination
steps.desc: Determine what data was requested to be exported or transferred, and to where (external drive, cloud link, email address).
steps.outcome: Request scope and destination documented.

steps.title: Verify against real IT's change/migration schedule
steps.desc: Check with IT operations whether a genuine backup or migration project is underway that would explain the request.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the request is legitimate.
steps.abort: If confirmed genuine, allow the process to proceed through proper channels.

steps.title: Assess the scope and sensitivity of any data transferred
steps.desc: Determine exactly what data left the environment and its sensitivity level.
steps.outcome: Exposure scope documented.

steps.title: Escalate to privacy/legal if sensitive data was exposed
steps.desc: If PII or confidential data left the environment, loop in privacy/legal to assess notification obligations.
steps.outcome: Privacy/legal informed and assessing impact.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce data-export verification policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and confirm staff know that data exports/migrations are only performed through verified, IT-initiated change requests.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a process recommendation.

steps.title: Determine whether the transfer was completed
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee actually exported or sent the data before recognizing the request as suspicious.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether data was exposed.

steps.title: Revoke access to the destination and attempt to recall/delete any transferred data
steps.desc: If data was sent to an external destination, act immediately to revoke sharing links, disable the destination account if internal, or request deletion.
steps.outcome: External access to the data curtailed to the extent possible.

ITID-11431.def: A channel-agnostic, interactive impersonation of an organization's executive (phone, text, chat, or in-person) directed at a subordinate or staff member to manipulate them into an action, logged before the specific request type is confirmed.
ITID-11431.purpose: Catch-all for a pretexting incident involving fake executive fraud support requests that does not yet match a more specific leaf in this Tier-4 group.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific executive-fraud request type is confirmed
scopeExcludes: A request type clearly matching a more specific sibling leaf
The templated, scaled email-based version of executive impersonation fraud (a distinct ITID under Financial Fraud/BEC, ITID-53111 Unclassified/General Executive Impersonation Fraud (BEC Context))
The live phone-call script specifically authorizing a wire transfer (a distinct ITID under a different domain, ITID-22431 Executive Impersonation Call Authorizing Urgent Wire Transfer)
ITID-11431.severity: Medium-High; reassess once the request type is confirmed.
ITID-11431.priority: P3 default, escalating quickly given the executive-authority pressure typical of this pretext family.
ITID-11431.escalation: Escalate to SOC/fraud team; reclassify once the request type is confirmed.
indicators: Staff report of an unusual, authority-pressured request purportedly from an executive
vectors: Impersonation of an executive via phone, text, chat, or in-person contact
rootCauses: Insufficient detail available at time of report
controls: Out-of-band executive-request verification procedures
User awareness training
ITID-11431.response: Document and attempt reclassification under a more specific leaf.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-11431.notes: Intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one. Scoped to interactive, non-email, non-pure-voice-call executive impersonation pretexting; the email-templated version rolls up under BEC (ITID-53111) and the wire-transfer-specific live-call script under ITID-22431.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Executive Fraud Support Request
playbook.description: For a report of a message or call impersonating a senior executive requesting an action from an employee, where the specific ask (gift cards, a favor, a document, etc.) is not yet known.

steps.title: Capture the report details from the employee who was contacted
steps.desc: Record the contact channel (email, text, call), the claimed executive, the request made, and any sender address/number used.
steps.guidance: Business email compromise / executive impersonation often uses a lookalike domain or a spoofed display name — check the actual sending address, not just the display name.
steps.outcome: A documented account of the contact and request.

steps.title: Verify with the real executive through a separate, known channel
steps.desc: Contact the executive directly via a known phone number or in person — never by replying to the suspicious message — to confirm whether they sent the request.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the request did not originate from the real executive.
steps.abort: If the executive confirms the request was genuine, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Reverse or halt any action taken on the fraudulent request
steps.desc: If any step was completed, reverse or halt it immediately.
steps.outcome: No fraudulent action remains in effect.

steps.title: Confirm with the employee that no further compliance is expected
steps.desc: Close the loop with the reporting employee, reassuring them that flagging it was correct.
steps.outcome: Employee clear on next steps and not discouraged from reporting.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce executive-request verification policy
steps.desc: Record the pretext used and evaluate whether staff who regularly interact with executives know the verification process for unusual requests.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a training recommendation if warranted.

steps.title: Determine whether any action was taken on the request
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee complied with any part of the request before recognizing it as suspicious.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of whether any compromise already occurred.

steps.title: Alert IT security to check for a compromised executive mailbox
steps.desc: If the message came from what appears to be the executive's real email address (not a lookalike), have IT security check the mailbox for signs of compromise (forwarding rules, unusual login locations).
steps.outcome: Mailbox checked and secured if compromise is found; ruled out if not applicable.
