ITID-11522.detection: Web/proxy logs can identify the scareware domain if the URL is captured; otherwise relies on user reporting.
ITID-11522.response: Have the target force-close the browser without calling the number; scan the device if any interaction occurred.
metrics: Count of scareware pop-up scam reports
Count where the target called the number
ITID-11522.notes: Differentiated from siblings by the pop-up/scareware initiation vector specifically.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Pop-up/Scareware-Initiated Tech Support Scam
playbook.description: For an incident where a browser pop-up or full-screen alert falsely claimed the device was infected/locked and displayed a phone number to call for 'support,' designed to scare the employee into contacting an attacker-controlled number.

steps.title: Capture the pop-up content and the site/context it appeared on
steps.desc: Record the exact warning message, any phone number shown, and what website or action triggered it.
steps.outcome: Pop-up details documented for blocking and analysis.

steps.title: Close the browser without interacting with the pop-up and check for lock-style behavior
steps.desc: If the pop-up is still displayed, close via task manager/force-quit rather than clicking anything in it; verify the browser/OS is not actually locked.
steps.guidance: Scareware pop-ups are typically just a browser tab and can be closed safely without calling any number.
steps.outcome: Pop-up dismissed without further interaction.

steps.title: Block the pop-up's originating site/domain
steps.desc: Add the triggering domain to the web proxy/DNS filter block list.
steps.outcome: Site blocked for other employees.

steps.title: Restore the endpoint to service once confirmed safe
steps.desc: Return the cleaned endpoint to normal use.
steps.outcome: Endpoint restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce that browser pop-ups are never real system alerts
steps.desc: Record the incident and remind staff that a genuine infection alert never appears as a browser pop-up with a phone number — it comes from the managed endpoint security tool.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness note issued.

steps.title: Determine whether the employee called the number or took any action
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee called the displayed number, entered any information, or downloaded anything the pop-up prompted.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of engagement level.

steps.title: If the employee called and granted remote access or installed software, isolate the endpoint
steps.desc: Disconnect or isolate the device via EDR pending inspection.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated if any real engagement occurred.

steps.title: Scan and remediate the endpoint if any software was installed or access granted
steps.desc: Run a full malware scan and remediate/reimage if compromise is confirmed.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean or fully remediated.

ITID-11523.def: An attacker cold-calls the target claiming to be from a well-known technology vendor, alleging a detected problem with the target's device and pressuring them into a paid remediation or remote-access session.
ITID-11523.purpose: Captures a tech support scam initiated by an unsolicited inbound cold call claiming to be from a well-known vendor.
scopeIncludes: Unsolicited inbound calls claiming to be from a major OS/software vendor's support line
Cold calls alleging the target's IP address or device has been 'flagged' for malicious activity
scopeExcludes: Scam initiated by a browser pop-up directing the target to call (see ITID-11522)
Vishing simulations run as authorized testing (see ITID-95121)
ITID-11523.severity: Medium; escalate if the call led to remote access or payment.
ITID-11523.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if remote access was granted.
ITID-11523.escalation: Escalate immediately if the target granted remote access or disclosed payment details during the call.
indicators: Unsolicited call claiming to be from a major vendor's support line
Caller ID spoofing a known vendor's number
vectors: Cold-call campaigns using spoofed caller ID
Purchased/scraped phone number lists targeting a demographic
rootCauses: Lack of awareness that legitimate vendors do not cold-call about device issues
No organizational policy on validating unsolicited support calls
controls: Security awareness training on vendor cold-call scams
Caller-ID spoofing awareness
ITID-11523.detection: Relies entirely on user reporting; no automated technical signal for an inbound phone call.
ITID-11523.response: Advise the target to hang up and never call back the number provided; scan the device if any remote session occurred.
metrics: Count of cold-call tech support scam reports per quarter
ITID-11523.notes: Differentiated from ITID-11522 by the cold-call initiation vector, with no pop-up or prior digital contact.

playbook.name: Response: Unsolicited Cold-Call Tech Support Scam
playbook.description: For an incident where an employee received an unsolicited phone call from someone claiming to be tech support (often claiming to represent a well-known vendor or the company's own IT) offering to fix a supposed problem the employee never reported.

steps.title: Capture the caller's claimed identity and what they offered to fix
steps.desc: Record who the caller claimed to be, the caller ID shown if any, and what issue they claimed to be calling about.
steps.outcome: Call details documented.

steps.title: Isolate the endpoint if remote access was granted or software installed
steps.desc: Disconnect or isolate the device via EDR pending inspection.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated to prevent further compromise.

steps.title: Scan and remediate the endpoint if compromise is suspected
steps.desc: Run a full malware scan and remediate/reimage if anything malicious is confirmed.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean or fully remediated.

steps.title: Restore the endpoint to service once confirmed safe
steps.desc: Return the cleaned endpoint to normal use.
steps.outcome: Endpoint restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce that IT/vendor support never cold-calls unprompted
steps.desc: Record the incident and remind staff that legitimate support is initiated by the employee, not by an unsolicited inbound call about a problem they never reported.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness note issued.

steps.title: Verify against real IT/vendor ticket records
steps.desc: Check whether any genuine support ticket or vendor case exists that would explain this outbound call.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no genuine ticket exists, or a genuine one is found and the caller's legitimacy separately verified.
steps.abort: If a genuine matching ticket is found and the caller can be verified, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Reset any credentials or payment details disclosed
steps.desc: If credentials or payment information were shared, reset/freeze them immediately.
steps.outcome: Disclosed credentials/payment details secured.

steps.title: Determine whether the employee granted access, installed anything, or disclosed information
steps.desc: Establish what, if anything, the employee did during or after the call.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of engagement level.

ITID-11524.def: As part of a tech support scam, the target installs a remote-access tool and grants the attacker a live remote desktop session, during which the attacker may install malware, harvest data, or manipulate the target into authorizing a payment.
ITID-11524.purpose: Captures the specific point in a tech support scam where the target is convinced to grant a remote desktop session, giving the attacker hands-on device access.
scopeIncludes: Installation of a remote-access tool (e.g., screen-sharing/remote-support software) at the scammer's direction
Attacker-driven actions taken during a granted remote session (fake diagnostics, file access, browser manipulation)
scopeExcludes: The initial pop-up or cold-call contact that led to the remote session (see ITID-11522/ITID-11523)
Legitimate corporate IT remote sessions
ITID-11524.severity: High — active remote-hands access materially increases compromise and data-loss risk.
ITID-11524.priority: P1 given live attacker control of the device.
ITID-11524.escalation: Escalate to SOC/endpoint team immediately; treat the device as compromised until proven otherwise.
indicators: Remote-access tool installed shortly after an unsolicited support contact
Unusual outbound network connections during/after the session
Unfamiliar files or scheduled tasks created during the session
vectors: Attacker directing installation of a legitimate remote-support tool for illegitimate purposes
Screen-sharing session used to walk the victim through authorizing a payment
rootCauses: No endpoint control restricting installation of unauthorized remote-access software
Lack of awareness of the risk of granting remote access to an unverified caller
controls: Application allow-listing restricting unauthorized remote-access tools
Endpoint detection and response (EDR) monitoring
ITID-11524.detection: EDR and network logs provide a real technical signal — installation of an unrecognized remote-access tool and its outbound connections are detectable.
ITID-11524.response: Isolate the device, terminate the remote session, run a full compromise assessment, and reset any credentials used during or after the session.
metrics: Count of confirmed remote-session tech support scam compromises
Mean time to isolate an affected device
ITID-11524.notes: This is the leaf in the Tech Support Scams group with the strongest genuine technical detection surface, since a real remote-access tool and session are involved.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Remote Desktop Session Tech Support Scam
playbook.description: For an incident where a fraudulent 'tech support' contact successfully talked an employee into installing a remote-access tool and establishing a live remote session, giving the attacker direct hands-on-keyboard control of the endpoint.

steps.title: Confirm whether the remote session is still active
steps.desc: Immediately determine if the attacker currently has an active remote connection to the endpoint.
steps.outcome: Current session status established.

steps.title: Immediately disconnect the endpoint from the network
steps.desc: Physically unplug/disable Wi-Fi or isolate via EDR without delay to terminate the remote session.
steps.guidance: Do this before anything else — every minute the session remains active increases exposure.
steps.outcome: Remote session terminated and endpoint isolated.

steps.title: Scan and remediate the endpoint for malware and persistence
steps.desc: Run a full EDR scan and check for scheduled tasks, added accounts, or other persistence the attacker may have planted; reimage if in doubt.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean or fully remediated.

steps.title: Restore the endpoint to service and reissue reset credentials
steps.desc: Return the cleaned/reimaged endpoint to normal use and ensure the employee has working, freshly issued credentials.
steps.outcome: Endpoint and employee access restored.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce that remote sessions are only ever IT-initiated and verified
steps.desc: Record the incident and reinforce organization-wide that remote access tools are never installed at an unsolicited caller's direction.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; organization-wide awareness reminder issued given the severity.

steps.title: Establish what the attacker did or could see during the session
steps.desc: Determine session duration and what applications, files, or credentials were visible or accessed.
steps.outcome: Scope of the session established.

steps.title: Uninstall the remote access tool and reset all credentials used or visible during the session
steps.desc: Remove the installed tool and force a reset of any account credentials the employee typed or that may have been captured, including email, VPN, and any application accessed during the session.
steps.outcome: Tool removed; all potentially exposed credentials reset.

steps.title: Check for lateral movement and review financial/banking exposure
steps.desc: Review network/authentication logs for spread to other systems, and check whether the employee had online banking or corporate finance tools open/accessible during the session.
steps.guidance: Tech support scams frequently pivot to convincing the victim to log into banking sites 'to verify a refund' — check for this specifically.
steps.outcome: Confirmed contained to the endpoint and no financial exposure, or issues identified and escalated.

ITID-11525.def: An attacker claims to owe the target a refund for prior tech support services, deliberately 'overpays' (often via a fabricated bank transfer receipt or manipulated on-screen balance), and pressures the target to return the difference via gift cards or wire transfer.
ITID-11525.purpose: Captures the follow-on 'refund' scam where an attacker who previously scammed the target (or poses as their support provider) claims to have overpaid a refund and demands the difference back.
scopeIncludes: Fake refund calls claiming an accidental overpayment requiring the target to send money back
Manipulated on-screen bank balance display used to fabricate the appearance of an overpayment during a remote session
scopeExcludes: The initial remote-session compromise itself (see ITID-11524)
Fake tech support requests unrelated to a refund claim (see ITID-11521)
ITID-11525.severity: High — this stage typically results in direct financial loss via gift cards or wire transfer.
ITID-11525.priority: P1 once a refund/overpayment demand is identified, given imminent financial-loss risk.
ITID-11525.escalation: Escalate to fraud/finance immediately; advise the target not to send any funds back regardless of an apparent bank balance change.
indicators: Claim of an accidental refund overpayment
Pressure to repay via gift card codes or wire transfer
On-screen balance change during a remote session that does not match the target's actual bank statement
vectors: Manipulated browser display during a remote session faking a bank transfer
Fabricated refund confirmation email or fake bank portal page
rootCauses: Target unable to distinguish a manipulated on-screen display from a real bank balance
Gift cards accepted as a legitimate repayment method by the target
controls: Security awareness training on refund/overpayment scams
Financial institution alerts on large gift-card purchases
ITID-11525.detection: Relies mainly on user/bank reporting; some signal from retailers flagging large gift-card purchases matching known scam patterns.
ITID-11525.response: Advise the target to contact their bank directly and never repay via gift card or wire transfer.
metrics: Count of refund/overpayment scam reports
Total confirmed financial loss
ITID-11525.notes: Scoped to the refund/overpayment stage specifically, which typically follows an ITID-11524 remote session but is tracked separately as the point of actual financial loss.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Tech Support Refund/Overpayment Scam
playbook.description: For an incident where a fraudulent 'tech support' contact claimed to owe the employee a refund or claimed to have accidentally overpaid them, then directed the employee to log into banking/payment tools to 'return' the difference — a scam designed to manipulate the employee into transferring real funds to the attacker.

steps.title: Capture the refund/overpayment claim and what financial action was requested
steps.desc: Record the claimed refund amount, the pretext given, and exactly what the employee was asked to do (log into banking, wire money, buy gift cards).
steps.outcome: Claim and requested action documented.

steps.title: Contact the bank/payment provider immediately if any transfer occurred
steps.desc: Call the bank's fraud line right away to attempt to halt or recall any transfer initiated during the scam.
steps.guidance: Speed is critical — act within minutes, not hours.
steps.outcome: Bank notified and recall/halt requested if still possible.

steps.title: Review the affected account for further unauthorized transactions
steps.desc: Check the bank/payment account statement for any additional unauthorized activity.
steps.outcome: No further unauthorized activity found, or activity identified and disputed.

steps.title: File a report with the bank's fraud department and, for significant loss, law enforcement
steps.desc: Formalize the fraud report and, if the loss is significant or funds cannot be recovered, file with local law enforcement/relevant fraud reporting body.
steps.outcome: Loss documented and reported through appropriate channels.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce that no legitimate support requests a bank login or transfer
steps.desc: Record the incident and issue an awareness reminder that this specific refund/overpayment pretext is a well-known scam pattern.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness note issued.

steps.title: Determine whether the employee logged into any financial account or transferred funds
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee accessed banking/payment tools during the call and whether any transfer occurred.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of financial exposure.

steps.title: Isolate the endpoint if remote access was granted during the call
steps.desc: Disconnect or isolate the device via EDR if the scam also involved a remote session (this scam type is frequently paired with ITID-11524).
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated if applicable.

ITID-11526.def: During a tech support scam, the target is directed to download and run a fake diagnostic or 'PC health check' tool that displays fabricated errors, malware detections, or performance warnings to justify a paid remediation service.
ITID-11526.purpose: Captures a tech support scam where the target is convinced to install a fake diagnostic tool that reports fabricated errors to justify a paid 'fix'.
scopeIncludes: Fake diagnostic/registry-scan tools that fabricate error counts or malware detections
Command Prompt output (e.g., Event Viewer errors) misrepresented by the attacker as proof of infection
scopeExcludes: Installation of an actual remote-access tool for hands-on control (see ITID-11524)
Legitimate diagnostic software used for its intended purpose
ITID-11526.severity: Medium-High; the installed tool may itself be malicious beyond the fabricated diagnostics.
ITID-11526.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the diagnostic tool is confirmed to carry a malicious payload.
ITID-11526.escalation: Escalate to endpoint/SOC team to assess whether the installed diagnostic tool carries additional malicious functionality.
indicators: Download and execution of an unrecognized 'PC health check' or registry-scan tool
Fabricated error/malware counts inconsistent with actual system state
vectors: Attacker-guided download of a fake diagnostic utility during a call or remote session
Fake diagnostic tool bundled with genuine-looking branding
rootCauses: No application allow-listing preventing installation of unrecognized diagnostic tools
Target unable to independently verify system health claims
controls: Application allow-listing
Endpoint detection and response (EDR) monitoring
ITID-11526.detection: EDR can detect installation and execution of an unrecognized/unsigned diagnostic binary.
ITID-11526.response: Remove the installed tool, scan the device for additional malicious payloads, and verify with the target what data or access the tool had.
metrics: Count of fake diagnostic tool installations reported
ITID-11526.notes: Distinguished from ITID-11524 by the tool being a fabricated diagnostic utility rather than a genuine remote-access application.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Diagnostic Tool Installation Scam
playbook.description: For an incident where a fraudulent 'tech support' contact convinced an employee to download and run a 'diagnostic' or 'cleaner' tool that was actually malware, spyware, or a vector for further compromise.

steps.title: Identify the diagnostic tool and confirm whether it was run
steps.desc: Determine the name/source of the tool and whether it was downloaded and executed.
steps.outcome: Tool identified and execution status confirmed.

steps.title: Immediately isolate the endpoint from the network
steps.desc: Disconnect or isolate the device via EDR without delay.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated to prevent further spread.

steps.title: Scan and remediate the endpoint
steps.desc: Run a full malware scan and remediate/reimage the endpoint, since 'diagnostic tools' in this scam pattern frequently install additional payloads or persistence.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean or fully remediated.

steps.title: Restore the endpoint to service once confirmed safe
steps.desc: Return the cleaned/reimaged endpoint to normal use.
steps.outcome: Endpoint restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce software-installation policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and reinforce that diagnostic/cleanup tools are only run at IT's direction through approved software.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness note issued.

steps.title: Preserve the installer/download link for analysis
steps.desc: Retain a copy of the file or link without running it further.
steps.outcome: Artifact preserved for security analysis.

steps.title: Reset any credentials entered or visible while the tool ran
steps.desc: Force a reset of any account credentials the employee typed or that may have been captured during the tool's execution.
steps.outcome: Potentially exposed credentials reset.

steps.title: Check for lateral movement from the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Review network/authentication logs for any spread to other systems.
steps.outcome: Confirmed contained to the single endpoint, or scope expanded and escalated.

ITID-11527.def: An attacker impersonates a legitimate third-party vendor's technical support representative, calling an organization's IT/help desk staff to offer unsolicited 'assistance' with a supposed vendor-side issue, aiming to gain remote access to corporate systems.
ITID-11527.purpose: Captures a tech support scam where an attacker impersonates a known third-party vendor's support line calling back a corporate help desk or IT staff member.
scopeIncludes: Unsolicited vendor-support callback claiming to address a ticket the organization never opened
Vendor impersonation targeting IT/help desk staff specifically, distinct from end-user targeting
scopeExcludes: An attacker impersonating the organization's own internal IT help desk to harvest an employee's credentials (see ITID-11428)
Consumer-facing tech support scams targeting a general end user's personal device (see ITID-11521 through ITID-11526)
ITID-11527.severity: High given the corporate/IT-staff target and potential for broad system access.
ITID-11527.priority: P1 if remote access to any corporate system was granted.
ITID-11527.escalation: Escalate to SOC immediately; treat any system accessed during the call as potentially compromised.
indicators: Unsolicited vendor callback referencing a ticket number IT staff cannot verify
Request for remote access to corporate infrastructure from an unverified vendor contact
vectors: Spoofed caller ID matching a known vendor's support line
Social-engineering of the IT service desk using vendor terminology and account details gathered via reconnaissance
rootCauses: No formal callback-verification procedure for inbound vendor support contacts
IT staff not trained to independently verify vendor support tickets before granting access
controls: Vendor callback verification procedure via a known-good number
Privileged access management restricting vendor remote-access grants
ITID-11527.detection: Privileged access management and remote-access logs provide signal if the attacker attempts to establish a session; the initial call itself has no technical signal.
ITID-11527.response: Verify any vendor support contact through an independently sourced number before granting access; treat unverified requests as a security incident.
metrics: Count of unverified vendor callback attempts reported by IT/help desk staff
ITID-11527.notes: Scope decision: distinguished from ITID-11428 (internal IT help-desk impersonation targeting an employee) by targeting IT/help desk staff with a fabricated third-party vendor identity, rather than an employee being contacted by someone posing as internal IT.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Corporate Help Desk Vendor Callback Scam
playbook.description: For an incident where an attacker impersonated the company's own outsourced/managed help desk vendor, exploiting employees' familiarity with routing IT issues to a third-party support line to gain trust and extract access or information.

steps.title: Capture the contact details and what the caller claimed/requested
steps.desc: Record the number/email used, which vendor they claimed to represent, and what was requested.
steps.outcome: Contact details and request documented.

steps.title: Isolate the endpoint if remote access was granted or software installed
steps.desc: Disconnect or isolate the device via EDR pending inspection.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated to prevent further compromise.

steps.title: Scan and remediate the endpoint if compromise is suspected
steps.desc: Run a full malware scan and remediate/reimage if anything malicious is confirmed.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean or fully remediated.

steps.title: Restore the endpoint to service once confirmed safe
steps.desc: Return the cleaned endpoint to normal use.
steps.outcome: Endpoint restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce genuine help desk vendor verification steps
steps.desc: Record the incident and issue a reminder of exactly how to verify a genuine contact from the outsourced help desk vendor (e.g. ticket number lookup, callback via internal portal).
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness note issued.

steps.title: Verify against the actual managed help desk vendor
steps.desc: Contact the real outsourced help desk vendor directly, using the officially published contact channel, to confirm whether this contact originated from them.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the contact did not originate from the real vendor.
steps.abort: If confirmed genuine, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Reset any credentials disclosed
steps.desc: If any credential was shared, reset it immediately.
steps.outcome: Disclosed credentials secured.

steps.title: Determine whether the employee granted access or disclosed information
steps.desc: Establish what, if anything, the employee did during the interaction.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of engagement level.

ITID-11528.def: An attacker poses as printer or peripheral-device support (often via a fake support number found through a poisoned search result), convincing the target to grant remote access or pay for a service to resolve a fabricated printer/peripheral issue.
ITID-11528.purpose: Captures a tech support scam narrowly focused on a printer or other peripheral device as the pretext for gaining remote access or payment.
scopeIncludes: Fake printer manufacturer support numbers surfaced via search-engine poisoning
Peripheral-driver 'fix' pretexts (scanners, webcams, external drives) used to justify remote access
scopeExcludes: General OS/software tech support scams not centered on a peripheral device (see ITID-11521 through ITID-11527)
Fake software update/installer downloads unrelated to a peripheral (see ITID-11627)
ITID-11528.severity: Medium; escalate if remote access was granted to resolve the fabricated peripheral issue.
ITID-11528.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if remote access was granted.
ITID-11528.escalation: Escalate to SOC/endpoint team if any remote session occurred.
indicators: Search for printer/peripheral support surfacing a non-official phone number
Unsolicited remote-access request to fix a peripheral issue
vectors: Search-engine poisoning placing a fake support number above the legitimate manufacturer's listing
Fake peripheral driver download bundled with a remote-access tool
rootCauses: Users searching for support numbers rather than using the manufacturer's official site
No organizational guidance directing staff to procurement-approved support channels for peripherals
controls: Security awareness training on verifying support numbers via official manufacturer sites
Web filtering for known scam support-number domains
ITID-11528.detection: Limited; relies on user reporting and web-filtering categorization of the fake support page.
ITID-11528.response: Advise the target to locate support numbers only via the manufacturer's official website; scan the device if remote access occurred.
metrics: Count of peripheral/printer support scam reports
detections: Web filtering for known scam support domains
ITID-11528.notes: Differentiated from other Tech Support Scams siblings by the peripheral-device-specific pretext (printer, scanner, webcam) rather than a general OS/security issue.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Printer/Peripheral Support Scam
playbook.description: For an incident where a fraudulent 'support' contact offered to fix a printer or peripheral device issue, using a low-stakes-seeming device as a pretext to gain remote access or install software on the connected endpoint.

steps.title: Capture the claimed issue and support contact details
steps.desc: Record the device involved, the claimed problem, and how the 'support' contact reached the employee or was reached.
steps.outcome: Contact and claim details documented.

steps.title: Isolate the connected endpoint if any access was granted
steps.desc: Disconnect or isolate the device via EDR pending inspection.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated to prevent further compromise.

steps.title: Scan and remediate the endpoint if compromise is suspected
steps.desc: Run a full malware scan and remediate/reimage if anything malicious is confirmed.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean or fully remediated.

steps.title: Restore the endpoint to service once confirmed safe
steps.desc: Return the cleaned endpoint to normal use.
steps.outcome: Endpoint restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce that peripheral issues route through the normal IT help desk
steps.desc: Record the incident and remind staff that even seemingly low-stakes device issues (printers, monitors) should be reported to the internal help desk, not resolved via an unsolicited contact.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness note issued.

steps.title: Determine whether remote access was granted or software installed on the connected endpoint
steps.desc: Establish whether, in the course of 'fixing' the peripheral, the employee gave the caller access to the actual computer.
steps.guidance: Peripheral scams frequently use the device as a pretext to gain access to the far more valuable connected computer — treat this the same as any other remote-access scam.
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of what access, if any, was granted.

steps.title: Reset any credentials disclosed
steps.desc: If any credential was shared during the interaction, reset it immediately.
steps.outcome: Disclosed credentials secured.

ITID-11529.def: A fake renewal or upgrade notice for security/antivirus software (often referencing a real vendor the target already uses) prompts a call to a fraudulent support number, leading into a paid remediation or remote-access scam.
ITID-11529.purpose: Captures a tech support scam that uses a fake security software renewal or upgrade notice as the initial pretext.
scopeIncludes: Fake antivirus/security-suite renewal invoices referencing a real vendor
Fake 'your subscription has expired, call now' notices for security software
scopeExcludes: Scareware pop-ups claiming active infection without a renewal/billing framing (see ITID-11522)
Legitimate security software renewal emails later exploited by a separate scam step (tracked under the resulting scam leaf, e.g., ITID-11524 or ITID-11525, once escalated)
ITID-11529.severity: Medium; escalate if the target called the fraudulent number and granted access or paid.
ITID-11529.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if payment or remote access resulted.
ITID-11529.escalation: Escalate to SOC/finance depending on whether remote access or payment occurred.
indicators: Renewal invoice referencing an unusually high charge with an urgent callback number
Invoice email from a domain not matching the actual vendor
vectors: Spoofed renewal invoice email impersonating a well-known security vendor
Fake billing statement PDF with an embedded fraudulent support number
rootCauses: Recipients unable to verify legitimate vendor billing domains
No corporate process for validating unexpected software renewal invoices before acting
controls: Email authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) enforcement
Security awareness training on verifying renewal invoices directly with the vendor
ITID-11529.detection: Email gateway can flag spoofed sender domains impersonating the security vendor.
ITID-11529.response: Advise the target to verify any renewal directly through the vendor's official account portal, not the number in the email.
metrics: Count of fake security-renewal scam reports per quarter
ITID-11529.notes: Differentiated from ITID-11522 by the billing/renewal framing as the initiation pretext rather than an active-infection scareware claim.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Security Software Renewal/Upgrade Scam
playbook.description: For an incident where an employee received a notification (pop-up, email, or call) claiming their antivirus/security software subscription had expired or needed an urgent upgrade, directing them to a fraudulent payment page or a malicious 'upgrade' download.

steps.title: Capture the notification details and claimed security vendor
steps.desc: Record the channel, claimed vendor/product, and what action (payment, download, link click) was requested.
steps.outcome: Notification details documented.

steps.title: Determine whether payment was made or a download occurred
steps.desc: Establish whether the employee paid for the fake renewal or downloaded/installed the fraudulent 'upgrade.'
steps.outcome: Clear understanding of financial and endpoint exposure.

steps.title: Scan and remediate the endpoint
steps.desc: Run a full malware scan and remediate/reimage if anything malicious is confirmed — fake 'security upgrades' frequently install the very malware they claim to protect against.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean or fully remediated.

steps.title: Restore the endpoint to service once confirmed safe
steps.desc: Return the cleaned endpoint to normal use.
steps.outcome: Endpoint restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Log the incident and reinforce that security software is centrally managed, never user-renewed
steps.desc: Record the incident and remind staff that corporate endpoint security is managed and renewed centrally by IT — they should never see or need to act on a renewal prompt themselves.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness note issued.

steps.title: Check the actual endpoint security console for the real subscription/agent status
steps.desc: Look up the endpoint in the real security management console to confirm whether the managed security agent is actually expired or in need of action.
steps.guidance: Corporate endpoints are typically centrally managed — a genuine renewal need would show here, not as a pop-up to the end user.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether a genuine issue exists.
steps.abort: If a genuine issue is found and it is IT-initiated, hand off to normal remediation and close this playbook.

steps.title: Isolate the endpoint if a download/install occurred; notify card issuer if payment was made
steps.desc: Disconnect or isolate the device via EDR if anything was installed, and if a payment card was used, have finance/the employee dispute the charge.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated and/or payment dispute initiated as applicable.

steps.title: Confirm the real security agent is present and functioning correctly
steps.desc: Verify the legitimate managed security agent on the endpoint has not been disabled, uninstalled, or tampered with.
steps.outcome: Legitimate security agent confirmed active and healthy.

ITID-11611.def: An adversary leaves a removable USB device somewhere a target is likely to find and plug it in out of curiosity or good intent, without enough detail captured to classify the specific drop location or lure mechanism.
ITID-11611.purpose: Catch-all for a USB drop baiting attempt that does not fit a more specific leaf under USB Drop.
scopeIncludes: USB drop reports logged before the location/lure mechanism is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID once the drop location/lure is known
Authorized USB drop security-awareness testing exercises (see ITID-95131, ITID-95132, ITID-95133)
ITID-11611.severity: Medium by default; reassess once the drop context and whether the device was plugged in are known.
ITID-11611.priority: P2 by default given the risk of a plugged-in device leading to compromise.
ITID-11611.escalation: Escalate to SOC/endpoint team immediately if the device was plugged into any corporate system.
indicators: Report of an unattended/unexplained USB device found on premises or personal property
vectors: Unattended USB device left in an unclear location
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of report
Lack of awareness that an unknown USB device should never be plugged in
controls: Security awareness training
USB port control/allow-listing
ITID-11611.detection: Relies primarily on human reporting; endpoint USB-device-control logs provide signal if the device was plugged in.
ITID-11611.response: Document, recover the device without plugging it into a live system, and attempt to reclassify.
metrics: Count of USB drop reports pending reclassification
ITID-11611.notes: Intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one. This entire USB Drop Type covers only the social-engineering lure/delivery vector — getting a human to find and insert the device; the resulting technical payload/execution mechanism (e.g., keystroke injection, worm propagation, data exfiltration) is covered separately by ITID-33411, the ITID-3132x USB worm family, and the ITID-3431x USB exfiltration family. Authorized red-team/awareness USB drop exercises are excluded and tracked under ITID-95131 through ITID-95133.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General USB Drop
playbook.description: For a report of an unidentified/unlabeled USB storage device found or plugged in, where the specific drop scenario (location/vector) is not yet determined.

steps.title: Establish device location and status
steps.desc: Determine where the device was found, whether it has been plugged into any machine, and by whom.
steps.guidance: Interview the finder/user directly; do not rely on secondhand reports. Note exact location and time found.
steps.outcome: Documented chain of custody: who found it, where, when, and current physical location of the device.

steps.title: Isolate any host the device was inserted into
steps.desc: Immediately network-isolate any endpoint the USB device was plugged into, pending forensic review.
steps.guidance: Use EDR network containment rather than powering off, to preserve volatile memory for analysis.
steps.outcome: Affected host(s) isolated from the network but still running.

steps.title: Forensically image and analyze the device
steps.desc: Using an isolated, non-production analysis workstation (write-blocked), image the USB device and scan/analyze its contents for malware.
steps.guidance: Never analyze on a production or user endpoint. Use a dedicated malware-analysis sandbox or air-gapped forensic workstation.
steps.outcome: Full inventory of device contents and malware verdict (clean, malicious, or inconclusive).

steps.title: Restore host to network
steps.desc: Release network containment once the host is confirmed clean and re-verify endpoint protection is active.
steps.outcome: Host returned to normal operation with no residual indicators.

steps.title: Document findings and reinforce USB policy awareness
steps.desc: Record device origin theory, malware verdict, and affected systems; remind staff of the found-media reporting procedure.
steps.outcome: Case closed with findings logged and an awareness reminder issued if warranted.

steps.title: Determine if the device has been inserted into any host
steps.desc: Check the reporting user's machine and ask whether the device was plugged in before reporting.
steps.guidance: Check USB device history in the endpoint's registry/EDR telemetry (e.g. USBSTOR entries, EDR device-insertion events) rather than relying solely on user recall.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of any host(s) the device was connected to, with timestamps.

steps.title: Secure the physical device
steps.desc: Take physical custody of the USB device in an anti-static evidence bag; do not insert it into any further machines.
steps.guidance: Label with finder, location, and time. Store in a locked evidence location.
steps.outcome: Device secured with documented chain of custody, no further uncontrolled insertions.

steps.title: Remediate any affected host
steps.desc: If malware executed on the inserted host, run full EDR remediation (removal, or reimage if persistence/rootkit indicators are found).
steps.outcome: Affected host confirmed clean by EDR scan or reimaged.

ITID-11612.def: A USB device is deliberately left in a parking lot, sidewalk, smoking area, or other external grounds area near a facility, relying on a passerby's curiosity to pick it up and plug it into a device.
ITID-11612.purpose: Captures a USB drop staged in a parking lot or external grounds area, relying on chance discovery by anyone entering the facility.
scopeIncludes: USB devices found in parking lots, exterior walkways, smoking areas, or building entrances
scopeExcludes: USB devices found inside the facility (see ITID-11616)
Authorized parking-lot USB drop testing (see ITID-95131)
ITID-11612.severity: Medium; untargeted external drops have lower confirmed-intent likelihood than internal or branded drops but still carry compromise risk.
ITID-11612.escalation: Escalate to physical security and SOC if the device is recovered or was plugged in.
indicators: USB device found in an exterior area with no owner identifiable
Multiple devices found in the same external area suggesting a deliberate drop
vectors: Device left near a building entrance or in visitor/employee parking
rootCauses: No policy/signage reminding staff not to plug in found USB devices
Lack of physical security monitoring of exterior grounds
controls: Security awareness training
USB port control/allow-listing
Physical security patrol of exterior grounds
ITID-11612.detection: Endpoint USB-device-control logs provide signal only if the device was plugged into a monitored system.
ITID-11612.response: Recover the device without plugging it in; submit to security for forensic handling.
metrics: Count of exterior-grounds USB drops found per quarter
ITID-11612.notes: Differentiated from siblings by the external/untargeted drop location.

playbook.name: Response: Parking Lot/External Grounds USB Drop
playbook.description: For a USB storage device deliberately left in a parking lot, walkway, or other external grounds area to bait an employee into picking it up and plugging it in.

steps.title: Confirm find location and canvass for additional devices
steps.desc: Document the exact external location the device was found and have security/facilities sweep the surrounding grounds for additional dropped devices.
steps.guidance: Baiting drops are often seeded in multiples across a lot or entrance to increase odds of pickup.
steps.outcome: Confirmed count and locations of all dropped devices found.

steps.title: Isolate any host with a confirmed insertion
steps.desc: Network-isolate any endpoint the device was plugged into.
steps.outcome: Affected host isolated pending analysis.

steps.title: Forensically analyze recovered devices
steps.desc: Image and analyze each device on an isolated forensic workstation for malware payloads or autorun scripts.
steps.outcome: Malware verdict recorded for each device.

steps.title: Restore normal operations and increase physical monitoring
steps.desc: Release containment on cleaned hosts; request increased security patrols/camera coverage of drop-prone external areas for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Host restored; heightened physical monitoring active for the observation window.

steps.title: Document and brief staff on found-media risk
steps.desc: Record the incident and send an awareness reminder about never plugging in unknown found media, referencing this specific incident (without identifying the finder).
steps.outcome: Case documented; awareness communication sent.

steps.title: Review physical security camera footage
steps.desc: Pull CCTV covering the drop location for the relevant time window to identify who placed the device(s).
steps.guidance: Coordinate with facilities/physical security team for footage retrieval.
steps.outcome: Footage reviewed; suspect vehicle/person identified or ruled unavailable.

steps.title: Recover and secure all dropped devices
steps.desc: Have security collect every device found in the sweep into evidence custody.
steps.outcome: All known dropped devices in secured custody.

steps.title: Remediate any affected host
steps.desc: Remove confirmed malware or reimage the host if rootkit/persistence indicators are present.
steps.outcome: Affected host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Determine if any device was inserted into a host
steps.desc: Interview anyone who picked up a device and check EDR telemetry for USB insertion events.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any device reached a corporate endpoint.

ITID-11613.def: A USB device bearing a curiosity-provoking label or branding (e.g., 'Confidential', 'Salaries', 'Executive Bonuses') is left where a target will find it, exploiting curiosity to drive a higher plug-in rate than an unlabeled device.
ITID-11613.purpose: Captures a USB drop that uses a deliberately provocative label (e.g., 'Payroll 2024', 'Confidential') to maximize the target's curiosity and likelihood of plugging it in.
scopeIncludes: USB devices with handwritten or printed labels designed to provoke curiosity
Devices labeled to suggest sensitive or high-value content
scopeExcludes: Vendor/partner-branded USB devices relying on trust rather than curiosity (see ITID-11618)
Unlabeled/generic USB drops (see ITID-11612 or ITID-11616 depending on location)
ITID-11613.severity: Medium-High — a targeted curiosity label indicates deliberate psychological engineering and a higher expected plug-in rate.
ITID-11613.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if plugged in.
ITID-11613.escalation: Escalate to SOC/endpoint team immediately if the labeled device was plugged in.
indicators: USB device with a label designed to provoke curiosity or urgency
Multiple similarly labeled devices found in the same period, suggesting a coordinated campaign
vectors: Labeled device left in a common area or desk
Labeling exploiting curiosity about compensation, layoffs, or confidential data
rootCauses: Lack of awareness that a provocative label increases rather than decreases risk
No USB port control preventing execution from an inserted device
controls: Security awareness training specifically addressing curiosity-labeled devices
USB port control/allow-listing
ITID-11613.detection: Endpoint USB-device-control logs provide signal if the device was plugged in.
ITID-11613.response: Recover without plugging in; submit to security for forensic handling; consider a targeted awareness reminder if multiple labeled drops are found.
metrics: Count of curiosity-labeled USB drops found per quarter
ITID-11613.notes: Differentiated from siblings by the deliberate curiosity-provoking label as the psychological lure mechanism, independent of drop location.

playbook.name: Response: Labeled/Branded USB Drop (Curiosity Bait)
playbook.description: For a USB device deliberately labeled with enticing text (e.g. 'Salaries 2026', 'Confidential', 'Executive Bonuses') to exploit curiosity and drive pickup and use.

steps.title: Document the label/branding used as bait
steps.desc: Record the exact text/branding on the device, which is a strong indicator of the attacker's targeting intent and social-engineering theme.
steps.guidance: A payroll/salary or 'confidential' label suggests broad curiosity targeting; a department- or project-specific label suggests targeted reconnaissance of that team.
steps.outcome: Label content documented and assessed for targeting intent.

steps.title: Isolate the host
steps.desc: Network-isolate any host the device was inserted into, regardless of whether execution is confirmed.
steps.outcome: Host isolated pending forensic clearance.

steps.title: Analyze device contents and any executed payload
steps.desc: Image the device on an isolated forensic workstation; analyze the decoy document and any payload for malware behavior.
steps.outcome: Malware verdict and behavior profile documented.

steps.title: Restore host and monitor
steps.desc: Release containment and place the host under elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Host restored; monitoring active.

steps.title: Document targeting theme and update awareness training
steps.desc: Record the bait theme used and add a specific example to security awareness materials warning against curiosity-driven found-media use.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness material updated.

steps.title: Determine if the device was inserted and files opened
steps.desc: Check EDR telemetry for USB insertion and any subsequent file execution from the device.
steps.guidance: Curiosity bait often includes a decoy document alongside a malicious payload — check whether the user only viewed the decoy or also triggered the payload.
steps.outcome: Confirmed insertion status and whether any file was opened/executed.

steps.title: Secure the device and interview the user
steps.desc: Take custody of the device and interview the user about what they saw/opened, without judgment, to get an accurate account.
steps.outcome: Device in evidence custody; accurate account of user actions obtained.

steps.title: Remediate the host
steps.desc: Remove confirmed malware or reimage if persistence is found; check for data staged for exfiltration if the theme suggests targeted intent.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

ITID-11614.def: A USB device is mailed or couriered to a target — often accompanied by a letter impersonating a known brand, government agency, or internal department — to lend it legitimacy and increase the likelihood it is plugged in.
ITID-11614.purpose: Captures a USB device delivered to a target through the postal/courier system rather than physically dropped on-site.
scopeIncludes: USB devices received via postal mail or courier delivery
Mailed devices accompanied by a fabricated cover letter or branding
scopeExcludes: Devices physically found/dropped on premises (see ITID-11612, ITID-11616, ITID-11619)
Conference/event swag USB devices (see ITID-11615)
ITID-11614.severity: Medium-High — the mail delivery channel lends an appearance of legitimacy that can increase plug-in likelihood.
ITID-11614.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if plugged in.
ITID-11614.escalation: Escalate to SOC/mailroom security immediately upon receipt of an unsolicited mailed USB device.
indicators: Unsolicited USB device received by mail/courier
Accompanying letter impersonating a known brand or agency
vectors: Mailed device with a cover letter claiming a prize, survey incentive, or official notice
Courier delivery impersonating a known vendor or government sender
rootCauses: No mailroom screening process for unsolicited physical media
Lack of awareness that a mailed USB device should be treated as untrusted regardless of apparent sender
controls: Mailroom screening procedure for unsolicited physical media
USB port control/allow-listing
ITID-11614.detection: Endpoint USB-device-control logs provide signal if the device was plugged in; mailroom intake logging can flag the delivery itself.
ITID-11614.response: Route any unsolicited mailed USB device to security before it reaches an end recipient's desk.
metrics: Count of mailed USB drops intercepted or reported per quarter
ITID-11614.notes: Differentiated from siblings by the postal/courier delivery channel rather than an on-site physical drop.

playbook.name: Response: Mailed/Delivered USB Drop
playbook.description: For a USB device sent through postal mail or courier to an employee or the organization, often impersonating a vendor, gift, or official notice.

steps.title: Preserve the mailing/packaging and any accompanying letter
steps.desc: Collect the envelope/box, postage/tracking information, and any included letter or covering material without discarding anything.
steps.guidance: Return address, postmark, and courier tracking number can help identify the sender or shipment origin.
steps.outcome: Full mailing package preserved intact for evidence.

steps.title: Isolate any affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate any host the device was connected to.
steps.outcome: Host isolated pending analysis.

steps.title: Forensically analyze the device
steps.desc: Image and analyze the device on an isolated forensic workstation for malware.
steps.outcome: Malware verdict documented.

steps.title: Restore host and monitor
steps.desc: Release containment and place the host under elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: Host restored; monitoring active for the observation window.

steps.title: Document and coordinate with mailroom/facilities on future screening
steps.desc: Record sender/tracking details, note whether other similarly addressed packages arrived, and recommend a mailroom screening step for unsolicited electronic media.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; mailroom procedure recommendation made if warranted.

steps.title: Determine intended recipient and targeting rationale
steps.desc: Establish whether the mailing was addressed to a specific named individual/role (suggesting targeted spear-baiting) or generic (suggesting mass mailing).
steps.guidance: Check whether the addressee is a high-value role (finance, executive, IT admin) which would indicate deliberate targeting.
steps.outcome: Targeting assessment documented.

steps.title: Secure the device and mailing materials
steps.desc: Place the device and all mailing materials into evidence custody.
steps.guidance: Consider notifying mailroom/facilities to flag similar incoming packages for other staff.
steps.outcome: Materials secured; mailroom alerted to watch for similar packages.

steps.title: Remediate any affected host
steps.desc: Remove confirmed malware or reimage if persistence indicators are present.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Determine insertion status
steps.desc: Check whether the recipient plugged the device in before reporting, and pull EDR USB telemetry to confirm.
steps.outcome: Confirmed insertion status and any host affected.

ITID-11615.def: A USB device is distributed as apparent promotional swag at a conference, trade show, or networking event — either from a fraudulent booth/vendor or by tampering with a legitimate sponsor's giveaway stock — exploiting the trust attendees place in event-branded items.
ITID-11615.purpose: Captures a USB device distributed as free promotional swag at a conference, trade show, or industry event.
scopeIncludes: USB swag distributed from an unregistered or fraudulent event booth
Legitimate sponsor swag tampered with prior to or during distribution
scopeExcludes: Vendor/partner-branded USB drops outside an event context (see ITID-11618)
Mailed/delivered USB devices (see ITID-11614)
ITID-11615.severity: Medium-High — event context lends significant apparent legitimacy, increasing expected plug-in rate.
ITID-11615.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if plugged in.
ITID-11615.escalation: Escalate to SOC and notify staff who attended the event if a compromised swag device is identified.
indicators: USB device received as event swag later found to contain unexpected content or behavior
Multiple employees returning from the same event report similar devices
vectors: Fraudulent booth distributing branded USB devices
Tampering with a legitimate vendor's swag supply chain before the event
rootCauses: No corporate policy restricting use of event-received USB swag on corporate devices
Lack of vetting of event exhibitor legitimacy
controls: Policy prohibiting use of event-received removable media on corporate devices
USB port control/allow-listing
ITID-11615.detection: Endpoint USB-device-control logs provide signal if the device was plugged in.
ITID-11615.response: Advise staff to submit event swag USB devices to IT for inspection before use; recall/notify if a bad batch is identified.
metrics: Count of event-swag USB drop reports per quarter
ITID-11615.notes: Differentiated from siblings by the conference/trade-show swag distribution channel specifically.

playbook.name: Response: Conference/Event Swag USB Drop
playbook.description: For a USB device received as apparent promotional swag at a conference, trade show, or industry event, later found to contain malicious content.

steps.title: Establish event, vendor booth, and distribution context
steps.desc: Identify which event, booth, or vendor the device was received from, and whether it matches known legitimate swag distributed by that vendor.
steps.guidance: Contact the vendor directly (via a known-good channel, not contact info printed on the device) to confirm whether they distributed this item.
steps.outcome: Confirmed or refuted legitimate origin of the device.

steps.title: Isolate any affected hosts
steps.desc: Network-isolate every endpoint the device was inserted into.
steps.outcome: All affected hosts isolated.

steps.title: Forensically analyze a sample device
steps.desc: Image and analyze at least one representative device on an isolated forensic workstation for malware.
steps.outcome: Malware verdict documented and applicable to all matching units.

steps.title: Restore hosts and monitor
steps.desc: Release containment on cleaned hosts and place them under elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: Hosts restored; monitoring active.

steps.title: Document and update conference/travel security guidance
steps.desc: Record the event, vendor, and findings; update travel/conference security guidance to discourage using unvetted promotional USB media.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; guidance updated and communicated ahead of future events.

steps.title: Canvass other attendees who may have received the same item
steps.desc: Check with other employees who attended the same event/booth for the same swag item.
steps.outcome: Full list of employees who may possess the same device.

steps.title: Recall and secure all instances of the device
steps.desc: Instruct all identified holders to stop using and surrender the device for analysis.
steps.outcome: All known devices recovered into evidence custody.

steps.title: Remediate all affected hosts
steps.desc: Remove confirmed malware or reimage each affected host.
steps.outcome: All affected hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Determine insertion status across affected employees
steps.desc: For each identified device holder, check whether it was plugged into a corporate or personal device used for work.
steps.guidance: Check EDR USB telemetry; also ask about personal devices used to access corporate email/VPN.
steps.outcome: Confirmed insertion status for each device holder.

ITID-11616.def: A USB device is deliberately left inside a secured internal facility area (desk, break room, printer station) rather than an external or public location, indicating the attacker gained some level of physical facility access to place it.
ITID-11616.purpose: Captures a USB device deliberately placed inside a secured facility, indicating the attacker already had some level of physical access.
scopeIncludes: USB devices found on desks, in break rooms, near printers, or other internal-only areas
Devices found in areas requiring badge access to reach
scopeExcludes: USB devices found in external/public areas (see ITID-11612)
Lost-and-found staged devices intentionally left near a lost-and-found desk (see ITID-11619)
ITID-11616.severity: High — placement inside a secured area implies the attacker already achieved unauthorized physical access, a materially higher-severity precondition than an external drop.
ITID-11616.priority: P1 given the implied physical-access breach.
ITID-11616.escalation: Escalate to physical security and SOC immediately; investigate how the attacker gained access to place the device.
indicators: USB device found in a badge-access-controlled internal area with no known owner
Access-control/CCTV review showing an unrecognized individual in the area
vectors: Insider or tailgating attacker placing the device on an employee's desk
Device left in a shared space during an authorized but unescorted visit (e.g., vendor visit)
rootCauses: Insufficient visitor escort/access controls enabling unauthorized presence in internal areas
No routine sweep for unattended devices in sensitive areas
controls: Visitor escort policy
Access-control/CCTV review process
USB port control/allow-listing
ITID-11616.detection: CCTV and access-control logs provide a real technical signal for reconstructing how the device was placed; endpoint logs cover any resulting plug-in.
ITID-11616.response: Treat as a physical security breach investigation in addition to a baiting incident; review access logs for the affected area.
metrics: Count of internal-facility USB drops found per quarter
ITID-11616.notes: Differentiated from ITID-11612 by requiring the device to be placed inside a secured, badge-controlled internal area, implying a prior physical-access breach.

playbook.name: Response: Internal Facility USB Drop
playbook.description: For a USB device found dropped inside a controlled internal facility area (break room, lobby, meeting room, desk), suggesting the dropper had internal access or exploited a physical access gap.

steps.title: Document find location and assess how the dropper gained access
steps.desc: Record the exact internal location found, and assess badge/access logs for the area to identify who had access during the likely drop window.
steps.guidance: An internal drop location is significant — it implies either an insider, a visitor with unescorted access, or a badge/tailgating failure. Treat this differently from an external parking-lot drop.
steps.outcome: Drop location documented and access-control gap (or insider possibility) assessed.

steps.title: Isolate any affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate any endpoint the device was inserted into.
steps.outcome: Host isolated pending analysis.

steps.title: Forensically analyze the device
steps.desc: Image and analyze the device on an isolated forensic workstation for malware.
steps.outcome: Malware verdict documented.

steps.title: Restore host and close physical access gap
steps.desc: Release network containment and confirm the identified physical access control gap has a remediation plan or ticket.
steps.outcome: Host restored; physical security ticket opened if a gap was confirmed.

steps.title: Document and brief facilities/security on the access gap
steps.desc: Record how internal access was likely obtained and recommend a specific physical security control improvement.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendation delivered to facilities/physical security.

steps.title: Review interior CCTV for the area and window
steps.desc: Pull camera footage covering the find location for the relevant time period.
steps.outcome: Footage reviewed; person who placed the device identified or footage gap noted.

steps.title: Tighten physical access controls for the affected area
steps.desc: Coordinate with physical security to review visitor logs, escort compliance, and badge access for the area where the device was found.
steps.outcome: Access gap identified and interim mitigation (e.g. escort enforcement, badge reader check) applied.

steps.title: Remediate any affected host
steps.desc: Remove confirmed malware or reimage if persistence is found.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Determine insertion status
steps.desc: Check whether the device was plugged into any host, via user interview and EDR USB telemetry.
steps.outcome: Confirmed insertion status and any affected host.

ITID-11617.def: An adversary leaves or gifts a USB charging cable, adapter, or other small accessory that has been modified to act as a keystroke-injection or data-exfiltration device, exploiting the fact that a cable is far less likely to be treated with suspicion than a flash drive.
ITID-11617.purpose: Captures a baiting attack using a malicious charging cable or accessory rather than a traditional USB flash drive form factor.
scopeIncludes: Modified/malicious charging cables left in common areas or given as apparent gifts
USB adapters, hubs, or fans found unattended that could conceal a malicious implant
scopeExcludes: Traditional USB flash-drive-form-factor drops (see ITID-11611 through ITID-11616, ITID-11618, ITID-11619)
The technical keystroke-injection payload/execution itself once connected (see ITID-33411, BadUSB/HID Emulation Attack)
ITID-11617.severity: High — a cable/accessory form factor is far less likely to be recognized as suspicious, increasing both plug-in likelihood and stealth.
ITID-11617.priority: P1 given the low detectability and high compromise potential of a modified cable.
ITID-11617.escalation: Escalate to SOC/endpoint team immediately upon discovery of any charging cable or accessory of unknown origin in use.
indicators: Unfamiliar charging cable or accessory found or given as a gift
Unusual keyboard/HID input events on a device shortly after a cable was connected
vectors: Modified cable left near a shared charging station
Cable given as a promotional gift or 'found' item
rootCauses: No policy restricting use of non-issued charging cables/accessories with corporate devices
Lack of awareness that a cable can conceal an active electronic implant
controls: Policy restricting use of non-issued charging accessories on corporate devices
USB port control/HID device restriction
ITID-11617.detection: Endpoint HID-device monitoring can detect an unexpected keyboard-emulation device appearing on connection, though the cable form factor itself is not detectable until connected.
ITID-11617.response: Confiscate and forensically examine any suspect cable/accessory; treat the connected device as potentially compromised.
metrics: Count of malicious cable/accessory baiting reports per quarter
ITID-11617.notes: Scope decision: this ITID covers the delivery/lure of a cable-form-factor bait item; the resulting keystroke-injection compromise once connected is classified under ITID-33411 (BadUSB/HID Emulation Attack) to avoid double-counting the same incident across the lure and execution stages.

playbook.name: Response: USB Charging Cable/Accessory Bait
playbook.description: For a malicious USB charging cable or accessory (e.g. a 'O.MG'-style cable with an embedded implant) left as bait, which can inject keystrokes or exfiltrate data even without a traditional storage payload.

steps.title: Identify the accessory and where/how it was obtained
steps.desc: Document exactly what the accessory is (cable, charger, adapter) and where it was found, received, or picked up.
steps.guidance: Malicious cables are visually near-identical to legitimate ones — do not assume safety based on appearance; treat any unverified cable/accessory as suspect.
steps.outcome: Accessory type and origin documented.

steps.title: Isolate any connected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate any host the accessory was plugged into, even briefly.
steps.outcome: Host isolated pending analysis.

steps.title: Inspect host for HID-injected commands or credential theft
steps.desc: Review the host's command history, EDR process telemetry, and any new scheduled tasks/scripts for signs of injected keystrokes or automated exploitation.
steps.guidance: Malicious HID cables typically execute a scripted payload within seconds of connection — check process creation events immediately following the connection timestamp.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of injected commands/payload execution.
steps.abort: If no HID enumeration or process activity is found around the connection time, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Restore host and monitor
steps.desc: Release containment and place the host under elevated monitoring for a defined period.
steps.outcome: Host restored; monitoring active.

steps.title: Document and remind staff to use only issued/verified accessories
steps.desc: Record the incident and reinforce policy that staff should use only IT-issued charging accessories, not found or unverified ones.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness reminder issued.

steps.title: Determine what it was connected to and for how long
steps.desc: Establish which device(s) (phone, laptop) the accessory was plugged into and the duration of connection.
steps.guidance: Check EDR HID/keyboard-injection alerts and unusual USB device enumeration events (malicious cables often enumerate as a keyboard/HID device, not storage).
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of connected devices and connection duration.

steps.title: Physically confiscate the accessory
steps.desc: Take the cable/accessory into evidence custody and instruct the user not to reuse it or any similar unverified accessory.
steps.outcome: Accessory secured; user briefed not to use unverified peripherals going forward.

steps.title: Remediate the host and rotate any exposed credentials
steps.desc: Remove any malicious artifacts found and force a credential reset for any account that was logged in during the connection window.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean; potentially exposed credentials rotated.

ITID-11618.def: A USB device bearing the branding of a trusted vendor or business partner is left or delivered to the target, exploiting the existing trust relationship rather than curiosity, to increase the likelihood it is plugged in without suspicion.
ITID-11618.purpose: Captures a USB drop that impersonates a known vendor or business partner's branding to exploit the trust relationship rather than curiosity.
scopeIncludes: USB devices branded to appear as an official item from a known vendor/partner
Devices delivered alongside apparently legitimate vendor materials
scopeExcludes: Curiosity-labeled devices with no vendor branding (see ITID-11613)
Conference/event swag USB devices (see ITID-11615)
ITID-11618.severity: High — exploiting an established trust relationship increases expected plug-in likelihood beyond a generic or curiosity-based lure.
ITID-11618.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if plugged in.
ITID-11618.escalation: Escalate to SOC and notify the vendor relationship owner to confirm whether the branded item is legitimate.
indicators: USB device bearing vendor/partner branding not verified as an authorized distribution
Device delivered alongside other apparently legitimate vendor correspondence
vectors: Device left at a shared reception/mailroom area addressed to a specific team
Impersonation of a known vendor's account manager delivering 'promotional' hardware
rootCauses: No process for verifying unsolicited vendor-branded hardware before use
Trust in vendor branding not extended to verification of the specific delivery
controls: Vendor-item verification procedure before use of unsolicited hardware
USB port control/allow-listing
ITID-11618.detection: Endpoint USB-device-control logs provide signal if the device was plugged in.
ITID-11618.response: Verify with the vendor relationship owner before use; submit to security for inspection.
metrics: Count of vendor/partner-branded USB drop reports per quarter
ITID-11618.notes: Differentiated from ITID-11613 by exploiting an existing vendor/partner trust relationship rather than generic curiosity.

playbook.name: Response: Vendor/Partner-Branded USB Drop
playbook.description: For a USB device bearing the branding/logo of a known vendor or business partner, exploiting trust in that relationship to encourage use.

steps.title: Verify legitimacy with the impersonated vendor/partner
steps.desc: Contact the named vendor/partner through a known-good channel (not any contact info on the device) to confirm whether they distributed this item.
steps.outcome: Confirmed or refuted legitimate origin.

steps.title: Isolate any affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate any endpoint the device was inserted into.
steps.outcome: Host isolated pending analysis.

steps.title: Forensically analyze the device
steps.desc: Image and analyze the device on an isolated forensic workstation for malware.
steps.outcome: Malware verdict documented.

steps.title: Restore host and monitor
steps.desc: Release containment and place the host under elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: Host restored; monitoring active.

steps.title: Document and brief the affected team on vendor-impersonation risk
steps.desc: Record findings and brief the team that regularly interacts with the impersonated vendor on verifying unsolicited physical media.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; targeted awareness briefing delivered.

steps.title: Assess targeting and distribution scope
steps.desc: Determine how the device reached the organization (mailed, hand-delivered, left at a meeting) and whether other employees who interact with this vendor also received one.
steps.guidance: Vendor-branded bait is often targeted at specific teams (procurement, IT, finance) that regularly deal with that vendor.
steps.outcome: Distribution scope and targeting rationale documented.

steps.title: Recall devices and alert the legitimate vendor
steps.desc: Recover all known instances of the device from staff, and if the vendor confirms they did not distribute it, notify the vendor their brand is being impersonated.
steps.outcome: Devices recovered; vendor notified of brand impersonation if applicable.

steps.title: Remediate any affected host
steps.desc: Remove confirmed malware or reimage if persistence indicators are present.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Determine insertion status
steps.desc: Check EDR USB telemetry and interview recipients to confirm whether any device was plugged in.
steps.outcome: Confirmed insertion status and any affected host.

ITID-11619.def: A USB device is deliberately placed to appear as though someone innocently lost it (e.g., near a lost-and-found desk, in a common area with an apparent personal item attached), exploiting the target's good-faith intent to identify the owner by plugging it in.
ITID-11619.purpose: Captures a USB drop staged to appear as a genuinely lost item, exploiting the target's good-faith intent to find the owner.
scopeIncludes: Devices staged with an attached personal item (keychain, lanyard) to appear genuinely lost
Devices deliberately placed near or turned in to a lost-and-found desk
scopeExcludes: Devices dropped without any attempt to simulate a genuine loss (see ITID-11612 or ITID-11616 depending on location)
ITID-11619.severity: Medium-High — exploiting good-faith intent to find an owner is a distinct and effective psychological lure.
ITID-11619.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if plugged in.
ITID-11619.escalation: Escalate to SOC/physical security if a staged lost-and-found device is identified or was plugged in.
indicators: USB device with an attached personal item found and turned in as 'lost'
Device deliberately placed near a lost-and-found desk with no legitimate owner ever coming forward
vectors: Device staged with a keychain or lanyard to simulate personal ownership
Device turned in directly to a lost-and-found or reception desk by the attacker
rootCauses: No policy directing lost-and-found staff to avoid plugging in found electronic devices
Good-faith intent to identify an owner not weighed against plug-in risk
controls: Policy directing lost-and-found staff never to plug in found electronic devices
USB port control/allow-listing
ITID-11619.detection: Endpoint USB-device-control logs provide signal if the device was plugged in.
ITID-11619.response: Hold the device in lost-and-found without plugging it in; submit to security if no owner is identified within a reasonable period.
metrics: Count of staged lost-and-found USB drop reports per quarter
ITID-11619.notes: Differentiated from siblings by the staged 'genuine loss' presentation intended to exploit good-faith return behavior specifically.

playbook.name: Response: Lost-and-Found Staged USB Drop
playbook.description: For a USB device deliberately placed in or near a legitimate lost-and-found area/box to exploit the expectation that items there are safe and awaiting a rightful owner.

steps.title: Confirm how the device entered the lost-and-found process
steps.desc: Determine who placed the device in the lost-and-found and whether it was logged through the normal intake process (if one exists).
steps.guidance: A device with no legitimate intake record, or placed outside normal hours, is a strong indicator of deliberate staging rather than a genuine lost item.
steps.outcome: Intake circumstances documented and staging likelihood assessed.

steps.title: Isolate any affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate any endpoint the device was inserted into.
steps.outcome: Host isolated pending analysis.

steps.title: Forensically analyze the device
steps.desc: Image and analyze the device on an isolated forensic workstation for malware.
steps.outcome: Malware verdict documented.

steps.title: Restore host and reinstate a hardened lost-and-found process
steps.desc: Release containment on the host and reinstate the lost-and-found process with a rule that found electronic media is handed to security/IT, never returned or used directly.
steps.outcome: Host restored; updated lost-and-found handling procedure in place.

steps.title: Document and update facilities lost-and-found policy
steps.desc: Record the incident and formalize a policy that electronic media found or turned in is routed to IT/security for screening rather than returned to a claimant.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; policy update proposed to facilities.

steps.title: Review lost-and-found area camera coverage
steps.desc: Pull CCTV covering the lost-and-found location/box for the relevant window to identify who placed the device.
steps.outcome: Footage reviewed; placer identified or footage gap noted.

steps.title: Secure the device and review lost-and-found handling procedure
steps.desc: Take the device into evidence custody and pause the lost-and-found box/area pending a review of its handling procedure.
steps.outcome: Device secured; lost-and-found process temporarily paused for review.

steps.title: Remediate any affected host
steps.desc: Remove confirmed malware or reimage if persistence indicators are present.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean.

steps.title: Determine insertion status
steps.desc: Check whether anyone who handled the device (staff processing lost-and-found, or a claimant) plugged it in, via interview and EDR USB telemetry.
steps.outcome: Confirmed insertion status and any affected host.
