steps.desc: Determine, where possible, the scope of accounts the user had saved in their browser password store on the affected device.
steps.guidance: Users often have far more saved passwords than they remember — treat every saved credential store entry as compromised, not just recently-used ones.
steps.outcome: Best-available list of exposed accounts.
steps.tool: Browser password manager export (if accessible) / user interview

steps.title: Reset every exposed saved credential
steps.desc: Force password resets and session revocation for every account identified as saved in the browser store, prioritizing corporate and financial accounts.
steps.outcome: All exposed credentials invalidated.

ITID-12133.def: Malware or tooling that dumps and parses credential material directly from process memory (e.g. LSASS memory on Windows holding cached logon credentials/hashes).
ITID-12133.purpose: Captures malware performing in-memory extraction of credentials or password hashes from a running process, most notably LSASS memory dumping on Windows.
scopeIncludes: LSASS memory dumping via tools such as Mimikatz or comparable credential-dumping utilities
In-memory extraction of plaintext credentials or hashes from any running process
scopeExcludes: Reuse of an already-extracted hash for authentication without cracking it (Pass-the-Hash, ITID-12721 series, a different Tier-4 type)
Extraction of credentials from an on-disk file rather than memory (ITID-12132, ITID-12136)
ITID-12133.severity: Critical - in-memory dumping typically yields multiple cached credentials including privileged accounts.
ITID-12133.escalation: Escalate immediately to SOC/IR; treat as active credential-access-stage compromise requiring domain-wide credential rotation assessment.
indicators: EDR alert on LSASS process access from an unrelated process
Detection of known credential-dumping tool signatures or command-line patterns
vectors: Post-exploitation credential-dumping tool executed after initial endpoint compromise
rootCauses: LSASS not running in Protected Process Light (PPL) mode
Endpoint protection gap allowing credential-dumping tool execution
mitreTechniques: T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
controls: LSASS Protected Process Light (PPL) enforcement
Credential Guard
EDR behavioral detection of LSASS access
ITID-12133.detection: EDR provides strong, well-established detection for LSASS access patterns and known credential-dumping tool signatures/command-line telemetry.
ITID-12133.response: Isolate the endpoint immediately, assume every credential cached on that host is compromised, and initiate domain-wide credential rotation for affected accounts.
metrics: Count of in-memory credential dumping incidents per year
Number of accounts rotated per incident
ITID-12133.notes: Scoped strictly to the extraction of the credential/hash itself; subsequent reuse of the extracted hash without cracking it is a distinct technique tracked under ITID-12721 series and excluded here to avoid duplication.

playbook.name: Response: In-Memory Credential Dumping Malware
playbook.description: For malware that dumps credentials directly from process memory (e.g. LSASS memory scraping), typically yielding cached domain credentials and enabling severe lateral movement.

steps.title: Confirm the credential-dumping technique and target process
steps.desc: Identify the specific dumping technique (e.g. LSASS access) via EDR and confirm which process/credential store was targeted.
steps.guidance: Treat as high-severity from the outset — this technique commonly yields domain admin or service account credentials with severe lateral-movement potential.
steps.outcome: Confirmed technique and targeted process.

steps.title: Isolate the endpoint immediately
steps.desc: Isolate the device from the network via EDR without delay.
steps.outcome: Device isolated.

steps.title: Hunt for lateral movement from the affected device
steps.desc: Search the environment for authentication events using the dumped credentials from other systems since the dump occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of lateral movement.

steps.title: Restore with enhanced monitoring across the affected identity scope
steps.desc: Restore the device and place all affected accounts, especially privileged ones, under elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: Device restored; monitoring active across the affected identity scope.

steps.title: Conduct a full post-incident review
steps.desc: Document the full incident given the severity of credential-dumping techniques and recommend credential-hardening measures (e.g. Credential Guard, LSA protection).
steps.outcome: Post-incident review completed.

steps.title: Determine which credentials were cached and likely dumped
steps.desc: Establish which accounts had active sessions/cached credentials on the device at the time of the dump, including any privileged or service accounts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of likely-exposed accounts, prioritized by privilege level.

steps.title: Reset all cached/dumped credentials, prioritizing privileged accounts
steps.desc: Force password resets and session/ticket revocation (including Kerberos ticket invalidation where applicable) for every account confirmed cached on the device, starting with privileged and service accounts.
steps.guidance: A password reset alone does not invalidate an already-issued Kerberos ticket — coordinate with the domain team on ticket invalidation (e.g. krbtgt considerations) if domain admin credentials were exposed.
steps.outcome: All exposed credentials, including any issued tickets, invalidated.

steps.title: Remove the malware and reimage
steps.desc: Reimage the device given the severity of this technique, rather than attempting in-place removal.
steps.outcome: Device rebuilt from a trusted baseline.

ITID-12134.def: Malware that locates and attempts to decrypt or exfiltrate a dedicated password manager application's local vault (e.g. a local encrypted vault file, unlocked in-memory vault contents, or clipboard capture during vault access).
ITID-12134.purpose: Captures malware specifically targeting a dedicated third-party password manager's local vault file for extraction.
scopeIncludes: Extraction/exfiltration of an encrypted password manager vault file
In-memory capture of decrypted vault contents while the vault is unlocked
scopeExcludes: Browser's own built-in password store (ITID-12132)
ITID-12134.severity: Critical - a compromised password manager vault can expose the totality of a user's credentials across every system.
ITID-12134.escalation: Escalate immediately to SOC/IR; treat as a full credential inventory compromise requiring reset of every credential stored in the vault.
indicators: EDR alert on process accessing password manager vault file or process memory
Unusual clipboard-monitoring process active while the password manager is in use
vectors: Infostealer malware with a dedicated password-manager-vault-parsing module
rootCauses: Password manager master password not protected by additional hardware-key factor
Endpoint protection gap allowing infostealer execution
mitreTechniques: T1555.005 Credentials from Password Stores: Password Managers
controls: Hardware-key second factor for password manager unlock
EDR behavioral detection of vault-file access
ITID-12134.detection: EDR can detect anomalous access to known password manager vault file paths and clipboard-monitoring behavior, giving concrete host-level telemetry.
ITID-12134.response: Isolate the endpoint, force reset of every credential stored in the compromised vault, and rotate the vault master password with a fresh, uncompromised device.
metrics: Count of password manager vault extraction incidents per year
Number of credentials reset per incident
ITID-12134.notes: Differentiated from ITID-12132 by target: a dedicated third-party vault holding potentially hundreds of credentials, versus a browser's own smaller built-in store.

playbook.name: Response: Password Manager Vault Extraction Malware
playbook.description: For malware specifically designed to locate and extract an encrypted password manager vault file (or its unlocked in-memory contents), potentially exposing a user's entire credential set.

steps.title: Confirm the malware and vault-targeting capability
steps.desc: Identify the malware family via EDR and confirm it targets password manager vault files or the unlocked in-memory vault.
steps.guidance: This is a maximum-blast-radius scenario for the individual user — every credential in the vault should be considered exposed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malware identity and capability.

steps.title: Isolate the endpoint
steps.desc: Isolate the device from the network via EDR.
steps.outcome: Device isolated; further exfiltration stopped.

steps.title: Remove the malware and rotate the vault master password
steps.desc: Remove the malware via EDR remediation (or reimage if needed), and have the user rotate their password manager master password/key from a known-clean device.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean; vault re-secured with a new master credential.

steps.title: Monitor exposed accounts
steps.desc: Place the highest-priority exposed accounts under elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: Monitoring active on priority accounts.

steps.title: Document scope and recommend enterprise password-manager hardening
steps.desc: Record the full scope and recommend hardening measures for the password manager deployment (e.g. requiring MFA on the vault itself, enterprise-managed deployment with device-trust requirements).
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine whether the vault was locked or unlocked, and enumerate contents
steps.desc: Establish whether the vault was unlocked (full plaintext exposure) or only the encrypted vault file was taken (exposure contingent on master password/key strength), and obtain an inventory of vault contents if accessible.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exposure state and best-available inventory of vault contents.
steps.tool: Password manager admin console (if enterprise-managed) / user interview

steps.title: Reset every credential stored in the vault
steps.desc: Treat every account in the vault as compromised and force a reset for each, prioritizing corporate, financial, and email accounts.
steps.guidance: This can be a large number of accounts — coordinate with the user to work through the list systematically rather than missing entries.
steps.outcome: All vault-stored credentials invalidated.

ITID-12135.def: Malware running on an infected endpoint that locates and exfiltrates cached browser session cookies, OAuth/SSO tokens, or other locally-stored authentication artifacts, typically to enable session replay without needing the original password.
ITID-12135.purpose: Captures malware that extracts cached authentication tokens or session cookies from an infected endpoint for offline reuse, distinguishing local malware-based extraction from network- or web-application-based session theft.
scopeIncludes: Infostealer malware harvesting browser session cookie stores from an infected endpoint
Local extraction of cached SSO/OAuth tokens from disk or browser storage by malware
scopeExcludes: Session/cookie theft achieved via a web application vulnerability such as XSS, which is tracked under ITID-32434 (XSS Used for Session Token/Cookie Theft), a different attack surface entirely
Trusted-device cookie/token theft in the MFA-bypass context of ITID-12637, which concerns bypassing an MFA-trust decision specifically rather than general malware-based token exfiltration
General session hijacking via malware-resident token theft as classified under ITID-12925 in the separate Session Hijacking Tier-4 type
ITID-12135.severity: High - stolen session tokens can grant account access without triggering a password-based or even MFA-based authentication event.
ITID-12135.priority: P1 if the token grants access to SSO or privileged systems; P2 otherwise.
ITID-12135.escalation: Escalate immediately to IAM to revoke the specific sessions/tokens (not just reset the password, since token replay bypasses password reset alone).
indicators: EDR alert on process reading browser cookie/token storage files
Session activity from an unrecognized device/IP using a token issued to a known-infected endpoint
vectors: Commodity infostealer malware with a cookie/token-harvesting module
rootCauses: Long-lived session tokens without frequent re-authentication requirements
Endpoint protection gap allowing infostealer execution
controls: Short session/token lifetimes with re-authentication requirements
Session-binding to device fingerprint or IP range
ITID-12135.detection: EDR detects local file access to cookie/token stores; IAM/SSO logs detect anomalous reuse of the stolen token from a new device or location, giving two independent, concrete technical signals.
ITID-12135.response: Revoke the specific compromised sessions/tokens at the identity provider (password reset alone is insufficient), isolate the endpoint, and remove the malware.
metrics: Count of token/cookie extraction incidents per quarter
Number of sessions revoked per incident
ITID-12135.notes: Scope decision: this leaf is limited to malware-based local extraction of cached tokens/cookies from an infected endpoint. Web-application-vulnerability-based theft (XSS) is ITID-32434; MFA-trust-decision cookie theft is ITID-12637; and the downstream act of hijacking a session with a stolen token is tracked separately under the Session Hijacking type (ITID-12921 series) to avoid duplicating that Tier-4 group.

playbook.name: Response: Cached Authentication Token/Cookie Extraction Malware
playbook.description: For malware that extracts cached session cookies or authentication tokens from the browser/OS, enabling session hijacking that can bypass MFA since the victim already completed authentication.

steps.title: Confirm the malware and token/cookie-targeting capability
steps.desc: Identify the malware family via EDR and confirm it targets session cookies/authentication tokens rather than (or in addition to) plaintext passwords.
steps.guidance: This technique is particularly dangerous because it bypasses MFA entirely — the attacker inherits an already-authenticated session.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malware identity and capability.

steps.title: Isolate the endpoint
steps.desc: Isolate the device from the network via EDR.
steps.outcome: Device isolated; further exfiltration stopped.

steps.title: Remove the malware
steps.desc: Remove the malware via EDR remediation, or reimage if clean removal cannot be confirmed.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore access and verify no attacker activity occurred on the stolen sessions
steps.desc: Restore the user's access with freshly authenticated sessions, and review each exposed application for any activity by the attacker before revocation.
steps.outcome: Access restored; any attacker activity on the stolen sessions identified.

steps.title: Document and recommend session-security hardening
steps.desc: Record the finding and recommend hardening measures (e.g. shorter session lifetimes, device-bound tokens, continuous access evaluation) given the MFA-bypass risk.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Identify which sessions were active/cached at time of theft
steps.desc: Determine which application sessions (email, SSO, SaaS, banking) were logged in on the device at the time of compromise.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of exposed sessions.

steps.title: Revoke every exposed session/token, not just reset passwords
steps.desc: Explicitly revoke each affected session/token at the identity provider and application level for every exposed account.
steps.guidance: A password reset does NOT invalidate a stolen session cookie/token in most platforms — explicit session revocation is the required control here, and MFA re-authentication alone will not stop a valid stolen session.
steps.outcome: All stolen sessions/tokens invalidated, forcing re-authentication everywhere.

ITID-12136.def: Malware that reads stored email account credentials from a desktop email client's configuration files, registry entries, or credential cache.
ITID-12136.purpose: Captures malware that extracts stored credentials from a desktop email client (e.g. Outlook, Thunderbird) configuration or credential cache.
scopeIncludes: Extraction of stored IMAP/POP3/Exchange credentials from a desktop email client's configuration
Malware reading Outlook profile credential cache
scopeExcludes: Webmail credential theft via phishing (ITID-12116)
OAuth token abuse against mailbox access (ITID-33142)
ITID-12136.severity: High - email credentials enable both mailbox access and further password-reset-chain attacks.
ITID-12136.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the account has delegate or administrative mailbox access.
ITID-12136.escalation: Escalate to IAM/messaging team for credential reset and mailbox rule/delegate audit.
indicators: EDR alert on process accessing email client configuration/credential store
Unusual mailbox access pattern shortly after malware execution
vectors: Commodity infostealer malware with an email-client-credential-parsing module
rootCauses: Email client storing credentials in a recoverable/reversible format
Endpoint protection gap allowing infostealer execution
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Modern authentication (OAuth) replacing stored basic-auth credentials in email clients
EDR behavioral detection of credential-store access
ITID-12136.detection: EDR can detect process access to known email-client credential-storage locations; mailbox audit logs detect subsequent anomalous access.
ITID-12136.response: Isolate the endpoint, force reset of the email credential, and review mailbox activity/rules for the exposure window.
metrics: Count of email client credential extraction incidents per quarter
ITID-12136.notes: Differentiated from ITID-12116 (Phished Email/Webmail Credential) by mechanism: this leaf is malware-based local extraction from a configured desktop client, not phishing.

playbook.name: Response: Email Client Stored Credential Extraction Malware
playbook.description: For malware that extracts stored credentials from a local email client's configuration (e.g. saved IMAP/POP/SMTP/Exchange credentials cached by Outlook or another mail client).

steps.title: Confirm the malware and mail-client-targeting capability
steps.desc: Identify the malware family via EDR and confirm it targets locally stored mail-client credentials.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malware identity and capability.

steps.title: Isolate the endpoint
steps.desc: Isolate the device from the network via EDR.
steps.outcome: Device isolated; further exfiltration stopped.

steps.title: Check for mailbox persistence and outbound abuse
steps.desc: Review each exposed mailbox for attacker-added forwarding/inbox rules and any spear-phishing sent from the account.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of persistence and outbound abuse.

steps.title: Restore mailbox access with re-enrolled MFA
steps.desc: Restore access with new credentials and re-enrolled MFA for corporate mail accounts.
steps.outcome: Access restored securely.

steps.title: Document finding
steps.desc: Record the scope and remediation taken.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine which mail accounts were configured on the client
steps.desc: Enumerate every email account configured in the mail client on the affected device (the user may have multiple accounts configured, including personal ones).
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of exposed mail accounts.

steps.title: Reset credentials and revoke sessions for every exposed mail account
steps.desc: Force password resets and session/token revocation for every mail account identified as configured on the client.
steps.outcome: All exposed mail credentials invalidated.

steps.title: Remove the malware
steps.desc: Remove the malware via EDR remediation, or reimage if clean removal cannot be confirmed.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.

ITID-12137.def: Malware that reads stored Wi-Fi network profile credentials or other cached network authentication material (e.g. saved VPN pre-shared keys) from an endpoint's operating system configuration.
ITID-12137.purpose: Captures malware that extracts stored Wi-Fi network credentials (SSID/pre-shared keys) or other locally cached network authentication material from an endpoint.
scopeIncludes: Extraction of saved Wi-Fi SSID/password profiles from an operating system's network configuration
Extraction of cached network-share or VPN pre-shared-key credentials
scopeExcludes: Wi-Fi PIN/WPS brute forcing, a different technique tracked as ITID-42122 (WPS PIN Brute Force Exploitation) elsewhere in the taxonomy
ITID-12137.severity: Medium - primarily enables physical-proximity network access rather than direct account compromise.
ITID-12137.priority: P2, escalating if the network is a sensitive segment (e.g. OT/ICS Wi-Fi).
ITID-12137.escalation: Escalate to network security to rotate the affected Wi-Fi/network credential and review for unauthorized network joins.
indicators: EDR alert on process accessing OS network-profile credential store
Unrecognized device joining the network using the affected credential
vectors: Commodity infostealer malware with a network-credential-parsing module
rootCauses: Static, long-lived Wi-Fi pre-shared keys not rotated regularly
Endpoint protection gap allowing infostealer execution
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Rotation schedule for shared Wi-Fi/network pre-shared keys
802.1X per-device authentication replacing shared PSK
ITID-12137.detection: EDR can detect process access to OS network-credential storage; wireless access point logs detect unrecognized device joins using the affected credential.
ITID-12137.response: Rotate the affected network credential, isolate the endpoint, and review network access logs for unauthorized joins.
metrics: Count of network credential extraction incidents per quarter
ITID-12137.notes: Scoped to malware-based extraction of stored network credentials; active WPS PIN brute forcing is a distinct technique tracked under ITID-42122.

playbook.name: Response: Wi-Fi/Network Credential Extraction Malware
playbook.description: For malware that extracts saved Wi-Fi network credentials (SSIDs and pre-shared keys) or other stored network authentication material from the device, enabling physical/network-proximity access.

steps.title: Confirm the malware and network-credential-targeting capability
steps.desc: Identify the malware family via EDR and confirm it targets saved Wi-Fi/network credentials.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malware identity and capability.

steps.title: Isolate the endpoint
steps.desc: Isolate the device from the network via EDR.
steps.outcome: Device isolated; further exfiltration stopped.

steps.title: Remove the malware
steps.desc: Remove the malware via EDR remediation, or reimage if clean removal cannot be confirmed.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.

steps.title: Monitor for unauthorized wireless association attempts
steps.desc: Monitor wireless infrastructure logs for association attempts using the old credential or from unrecognized devices.
steps.outcome: No unauthorized wireless access observed post-rotation.

steps.title: Document and recommend moving to certificate-based Wi-Fi authentication
steps.desc: Record the finding and, if the network still relies on a shared PSK, recommend migrating to per-user/per-device 802.1X certificate authentication to avoid the operational cost of future org-wide rotations.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Enumerate exposed networks
steps.desc: Determine which Wi-Fi networks (corporate office, guest, home) were saved on the device and therefore potentially exposed.
steps.guidance: Corporate Wi-Fi exposure is the priority concern given it can enable physical-proximity network access.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of exposed networks.

steps.title: Rotate exposed corporate Wi-Fi pre-shared keys
steps.desc: If a corporate Wi-Fi network using a shared PSK was exposed, rotate the key and redistribute securely; if using per-user certificate/802.1X authentication instead, revoke and reissue the affected device/user's credential.
steps.guidance: A shared corporate Wi-Fi PSK exposure requires an org-wide rotation, which has broad operational impact — escalate the decision and timing to network operations.
steps.outcome: Exposed network credential rotated.

ITID-12138.def: Infection by a widely available, commercially or freely distributed commodity infostealer malware family with built-in multi-target credential harvesting capability (browsers, wallets, FTP clients, etc.), delivered via a human-targeted vector (phishing, malicious ad, cracked software).
ITID-12138.purpose: Captures infection by a commodity, off-the-shelf infostealer family (e.g. RedLine, Raccoon, Vidar-class malware) obtained readily by low-sophistication actors, distinguishing mass-market tooling from bespoke credential-harvesting malware.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed infection by a known commodity infostealer family delivered via phishing or a human-interaction vector
Any commodity infostealer regardless of the specific credential store it targeted, when the classification interest is the malware family/campaign itself
scopeExcludes: Bespoke/custom-built credential harvesting malware not matching a known commodity family (ITID-12131 unclassified, or a more specific mechanism leaf if known)

Infostealer classified from a malware-family/technical-infrastructure perspective under the Malware domain's own infostealer leaves (ITID-31231 through ITID-31234), which track delivery model, anti-analysis capability, and campaign infrastructure rather than the human-targeted credential-theft outcome tracked here
ITID-12138.severity: High - commodity infostealers typically exfiltrate all available credential stores in a single run.
ITID-12138.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if corporate SSO or privileged credentials are confirmed among the exfiltrated data.
ITID-12138.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR for full-scope credential reset across every application/browser profile on the affected endpoint.
indicators: EDR/AV signature match to a known commodity infostealer family
C2 beaconing to a known infostealer log-panel domain
vectors: Phishing email with malicious attachment
Malicious advertisement (malvertising) leading to a fake software download
Cracked/pirated software bundled with the infostealer
rootCauses: Endpoint protection gap allowing initial execution
Users downloading unvetted or pirated software
controls: EDR signature/behavioral detection of known infostealer families
Web filtering blocking malvertising and known malware-distribution domains
ITID-12138.detection: EDR/AV signature and behavioral detection for well-known commodity infostealer families is mature and reliable; network telemetry on C2 log-panel domains adds a second concrete signal.
ITID-12138.response: Isolate the endpoint, treat every stored credential on it as compromised, force a full reset, and remove the malware via reimage.
metrics: Count of commodity infostealer incidents per quarter
Average number of credentials reset per incident
ITID-12138.notes: Scope decision: this leaf tracks the human-targeted, credential-theft-outcome view of a commodity infostealer infection under Attacks Against the Human. The Malware domain's own infostealer leaves (ITID-31231 through ITID-31234) track the same malware family from a technical/infrastructure perspective (delivery model, MaaS subscription, anti-analysis); an incident should be logged under this leaf for credential-impact reporting and may additionally reference the malware-domain leaf for infrastructure tracking, avoiding double-counting the same technical facts twice under this leaf.

playbook.name: Response: Commodity Infostealer (Off-the-Shelf) Malware
playbook.description: For a widely available, off-the-shelf commodity infostealer (e.g. broadly distributed credential/cookie/wallet-stealing malware sold or shared among many low-sophistication actors) as opposed to a bespoke or targeted tool.

steps.title: Confirm the commodity infostealer family and its known capability set
steps.desc: Identify the specific infostealer family via EDR signature/threat-intel match, and reference known public reporting on its typical capabilities (browser passwords, cookies, crypto wallets, system info, screenshots).
steps.guidance: Commodity infostealers are well-documented — use public threat-intel reporting on the specific family to quickly determine the full scope of what it typically exfiltrates, rather than assuming only what was directly observed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malware family and its documented full capability set applied to scope this incident.

steps.title: Isolate the endpoint
steps.desc: Isolate the device from the network via EDR.
steps.outcome: Device isolated.

steps.title: Remove the malware
steps.desc: Remove the malware via EDR remediation, or reimage if clean removal cannot be confirmed.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore and monitor
steps.desc: Return the clean device to service and place affected accounts under elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: Device restored; monitoring active.

steps.title: Document infection vector and recommend control improvement
steps.desc: Record how the commodity malware was delivered and recommend the control improvement that should have prevented or caught it earlier (e.g. email filtering, endpoint protection tuning).
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine exfiltration destination and whether data has left the network
steps.desc: Review network/EDR telemetry for the exfiltration destination (often a Telegram bot, Discord webhook, or dedicated panel) and confirm whether data transfer completed before containment.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exfiltration status and destination.

steps.title: Reset all credentials and sessions per the family's known full capability
steps.desc: Based on the documented capability set, reset passwords and revoke sessions/tokens for all browser-saved credentials, active sessions, and any other credential stores the family is known to target.
steps.outcome: All plausibly exposed credentials and sessions invalidated.

steps.title: Block known distribution/exfiltration infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the delivery vector and exfiltration destination (domains, webhook endpoints) identified during analysis.
steps.outcome: Infrastructure blocked org-wide.

ITID-12139.def: Credential harvesting malware bundled within a trojanized copy of otherwise legitimate or expected software (a cracked application, a fake update, or a supply-chain-compromised installer) that the victim knowingly installs believing it to be genuine.
ITID-12139.purpose: Captures credential harvesting malware delivered by trojanizing a legitimate or seemingly legitimate software package, distinguishing supply-chain-adjacent delivery from mass-phishing delivery.
scopeIncludes: Malware bundled in a cracked/pirated software installer
Fake software update package containing a credential-harvesting payload
Trojanized legitimate installer distributed via a compromised download source
scopeExcludes: True upstream supply-chain compromise of a vendor's build pipeline affecting many downstream customers, which is tracked under the organization's supply-chain/third-party risk domain leaves rather than this individually-scoped leaf
Phishing-email-delivered infostealer with no trojanized-software component (ITID-12138)
ITID-12139.severity: High - trojanized software often achieves broader and more trusted execution context than a phishing attachment.
ITID-12139.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for confirmed privileged-account or widespread-deployment scenarios.
ITID-12139.escalation: Escalate to SOC/IR for full-scope credential reset and to assess whether the trojanized package was deployed to multiple endpoints.
indicators: EDR alert on unsigned or anomalously-signed installer executing credential-harvesting behavior
Software downloaded from an unofficial or non-vendor-verified source
vectors: Cracked/pirated software download
Fake browser or application update prompt
Compromised third-party download mirror
rootCauses: Users downloading software from unofficial sources
No application allowlisting/software restriction policy
controls: Application allowlisting/software restriction policy
Code-signing verification enforcement
ITID-12139.detection: EDR detects unsigned/anomalous installer execution and subsequent credential-store access behavior, giving concrete host-level detection.
ITID-12139.response: Isolate the endpoint, remove the trojanized software, force credential reset, and check for the same package deployed elsewhere in the environment.
metrics: Count of trojanized-software credential harvesting incidents per year
Number of additional endpoints found with the same package
ITID-12139.notes: Scoped to endpoint-level trojanized software the victim knowingly installed; a genuine upstream vendor build-pipeline compromise affecting many organizations is tracked as a supply-chain incident elsewhere, not duplicated here.

playbook.name: Response: Credential Harvesting Malware via Trojanized Software
playbook.description: For credential-harvesting malware bundled within a trojanized legitimate-looking application (e.g. a cracked software download, fake installer, or supply-chain-compromised update) rather than delivered via phishing/email.

steps.title: Identify the trojanized software and its source
steps.desc: Identify the specific application/installer that carried the malware and trace how/where the user obtained it (download site, torrent, supply-chain-compromised legitimate vendor update).
steps.guidance: Determine whether this is an isolated user-initiated download (e.g. pirated software) or a supply-chain compromise of a legitimately-used vendor update, which would affect many more users.
steps.outcome: Confirmed source and scope classification (isolated vs. supply-chain).

steps.title: Isolate affected endpoint(s)
steps.desc: Isolate the affected device(s) from the network via EDR.
steps.outcome: Device(s) isolated.

steps.title: Remove the trojanized software and malware
steps.desc: Remove the trojanized application and any dropped malware via EDR remediation, or reimage if clean removal cannot be confirmed.
steps.outcome: Device(s) confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore and monitor
steps.desc: Return clean device(s) to service and place affected accounts under elevated monitoring.
steps.outcome: Device(s) restored; monitoring active.

steps.title: Document and reinforce software-installation policy
steps.desc: Record the finding and recommend reinforcement of policy around unauthorized software installation, or if supply-chain related, recommend vendor-risk follow-up.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: If supply-chain related, determine full organizational exposure
steps.desc: If the trojanized software is a legitimately-used vendor application/update, determine how many other endpoints in the organization have it installed.
steps.outcome: Full scope of exposure across the organization determined, if supply-chain related.

steps.title: Reset credentials exposed on affected device(s)
steps.desc: Force password resets and session revocation for accounts accessed on the affected device(s) during the exposure window.
steps.outcome: Potentially captured credentials invalidated.

steps.title: Block the malicious download source or hold the compromised update
steps.desc: Block the malicious download source at the web proxy, or if supply-chain related, pause deployment of the compromised vendor update and notify the vendor.
steps.outcome: Further distribution of the trojanized software prevented.

ITID-12211.def: Automated login attempts using previously breached username/password pairs against an organization's authentication endpoint, where the specific source (combolist, botnet, low-and-slow, API/mobile, SSO, SaaS, CAPTCHA-bypass) has not yet been identified.
ITID-12211.purpose: Catch-all for credential stuffing incidents where the specific source list or delivery method has not yet been determined.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific credential-stuffing method is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Any case where the method is known and matches ITID-12212 through ITID-12219
Password spraying, which uses a small set of passwords against many usernames rather than known valid pairs (ITID-12221 series)
ITID-12211.priority: P3 by default, escalating once account-takeover is confirmed.
ITID-12211.escalation: Reclassify once the specific method/source is confirmed via log analysis.
indicators: Spike in failed logins using distinct, valid-format username/password pairs of unclear origin
vectors: Unclear/unconfirmed at time of initial detection
rootCauses: Insufficient triage detail captured at time of detection
controls: Login rate limiting and anomaly detection
ITID-12211.detection: Authentication logs and WAF/bot-management telemetry give the same core signal as the specific sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-12211.response: Investigate and reclassify to a specific sibling leaf once the source/method is confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-12211.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification within Credential Stuffing, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Credential Stuffing Attempt
playbook.description: General triage playbook for a suspected credential-stuffing attack (automated login attempts using previously breached username/password pairs) where the specific technique has not yet been identified.

steps.title: Confirm the stuffing pattern in logs
steps.desc: Review authentication logs for a high volume of login attempts using distinct username/password pairs (one attempt per pair), consistent with a breach-list replay rather than a brute-force of one account.
steps.guidance: Key signature: unique usernames, each tried once or twice, at volume — not many passwords against one account.
steps.outcome: Confirmed credential-stuffing pattern, or ruled out.
steps.abort: If volume/pattern doesn't match, close as false positive.

steps.title: Block the source and enable bot mitigation
steps.desc: Block/rate-limit the source IP(s) and enable CAPTCHA or bot-management challenge on the login endpoint.
steps.outcome: Stuffing traffic blocked or significantly throttled.

steps.title: Enforce MFA on affected/at-risk accounts
steps.desc: Confirm MFA is enforced for all compromised accounts and recommend org-wide MFA enforcement if gaps are found.
steps.outcome: MFA enforced where gaps existed.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts and advise unique password use going forward.
steps.outcome: Users notified per policy.

steps.title: Document and recommend breach-list monitoring
steps.desc: Record scope and recommend subscribing to a breach-credential monitoring feed if not already in place.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify any successful authentications within the attack traffic to determine which accounts were actually compromised.
steps.guidance: Even a low success rate (e.g. 0.1-2%) against a large list can yield real account takeovers — always check, don't assume the whole batch failed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts, if any.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Immediately reset passwords and revoke sessions for any account with a successful login match.
steps.outcome: Compromised accounts secured.

ITID-12212.def: Credential stuffing where the username/password pairs used are traceable to a specific, identified prior data breach combolist circulating on breach forums or dark-web marketplaces.
ITID-12212.purpose: Captures credential stuffing driven by a specific known breach combolist (a leaked username/password dump traceable to an identified prior breach).
scopeIncludes: Stuffing attack correlated to a named, identified breach dataset via threat intelligence
scopeExcludes: Stuffing where the source list cannot be attributed to a specific known breach (ITID-12211)
ITID-12212.severity: Medium-High depending on how recently the combolist was published and how many organizational accounts appear in it.
ITID-12212.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if a large percentage of attempted accounts are valid organizational users.
ITID-12212.escalation: Escalate to IAM to proactively force-reset any organizational accounts confirmed present in the combolist.
indicators: Threat intelligence match between attempted username/password pairs and a known published breach dataset
vectors: Automated stuffing tooling loaded with a specific breach combolist
rootCauses: Widespread password reuse between the breached third-party service and the organization's own accounts
mitreTechniques: T1589.001 Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
controls: Proactive breach-monitoring feed cross-referenced against employee identities
Login rate limiting and bot management
ITID-12212.detection: Threat intelligence feeds combined with authentication log correlation give a strong, specific technical signal tying the attack to a known dataset.
ITID-12212.response: Force reset for any organizational account confirmed in the combolist, and monitor for continued attempts using the same dataset.
metrics: Count of combolist-driven stuffing incidents per quarter
Number of proactively reset accounts per incident
ITID-12212.notes: Distinct from ITID-12521 series (Dark Web Credential Listing), which tracks the exposure/listing event itself; this leaf tracks the active login-attempt attack that uses such a list against this organization.

playbook.name: Response: Breach Combolist-Sourced Credential Stuffing
playbook.description: For credential stuffing traced to a specific known third-party breach combolist (a published username/password dump from an unrelated compromised service).

steps.title: Identify the source combolist
steps.desc: Correlate the attempted username/password pairs against known public breach combolists to identify the originating breach.
steps.guidance: Threat-intel feeds or breach-monitoring services can help match pair patterns to a specific known dump.
steps.outcome: Source combolist identified where possible.

steps.title: Block source and enable bot mitigation
steps.desc: Block/rate-limit source IPs and enable CAPTCHA/bot management on affected login endpoints.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic blocked or throttled.

steps.title: Cross-check the full combolist against the user directory
steps.desc: If the source breach list is obtainable via threat intel, proactively check all corporate identities against it, not just the ones targeted in this attack.
steps.guidance: Attackers often only test a subset first; the full list may re-target the remainder later.
steps.outcome: Full exposure list identified and proactively reset if matches found.

steps.title: Notify affected users with context
steps.desc: Notify users, referencing the specific breached third-party service so they understand the password-reuse risk.
steps.outcome: Users notified with actionable context.

steps.title: Document and reinforce password-reuse awareness
steps.desc: Record the source breach and recommend awareness messaging on password reuse and password manager adoption.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify successful logins from the attack to determine which employees reused a breached password on a corporate account.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12213.def: Credential stuffing where login attempts originate from a large number of distinct IP addresses consistent with a distributed botnet, used to evade IP-based rate limiting and blocklisting.
ITID-12213.purpose: Captures credential stuffing conducted through a distributed botnet infrastructure, distinguishing large-scale, multi-source attacks from single-origin attempts.
scopeIncludes: Stuffing attack with login attempts distributed across hundreds/thousands of source IPs in a short window
scopeExcludes: Single-source or small-IP-range stuffing attempts (ITID-12211/12212)

Botnet infrastructure classified from an infrastructure/campaign perspective across multiple victim organizations (ITID-31722 series in the Malware/Botnet domain), which tracks the botnet itself rather than this organization's specific incident of being targeted by it
ITID-12213.severity: High - distributed sourcing indicates a well-resourced, evasion-aware attacker.
ITID-12213.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if any accounts are confirmed compromised.
ITID-12213.escalation: Escalate to network security/WAF team to enable bot-management/device-fingerprinting controls beyond simple IP blocking.
indicators: Large number of distinct source IPs each attempting a small number of logins
Device/browser fingerprint anomalies consistent with automated tooling
vectors: Commercial or criminal botnet-for-hire credential stuffing service
rootCauses: Authentication endpoint relying solely on IP-based rate limiting
controls: Bot management/device-fingerprinting solution
Behavioral/velocity-based login anomaly detection
ITID-12213.detection: WAF and bot-management platforms provide strong technical detection via device fingerprinting, velocity analysis, and known botnet IP reputation feeds.
ITID-12213.response: Enable/tune bot-management rules, block the identified botnet signature, and audit for any successful logins during the attack window.
metrics: Count of distributed stuffing incidents per quarter
Number of distinct source IPs observed per incident
ITID-12213.notes: Scoped to this organization's victim-side incident of being targeted by a distributed stuffing attack; the botnet infrastructure itself, if tracked for multi-organization campaign purposes, is logged under ITID-31722 in the Malware domain to avoid duplicating that infrastructure-centric classification.

playbook.name: Response: Distributed/Botnet-Driven Credential Stuffing
playbook.description: For credential stuffing conducted via a distributed botnet spreading requests across many source IPs to evade per-IP rate limiting.

steps.title: Confirm distributed sourcing
steps.desc: Review logs for the attack's IP diversity, geographic spread, and ASN distribution consistent with botnet infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Look for shared TLS/JA3 fingerprints or user-agent strings across the diverse IPs as corroborating evidence of a single coordinated tool.
steps.outcome: Confirmed botnet-driven pattern.

steps.title: Enable bot-management/fingerprint-based blocking
steps.desc: Since per-IP blocking is ineffective against a botnet, enable device/behavioral fingerprinting and bot-management challenge rather than relying on IP blocklists alone.
steps.outcome: Botnet traffic identified and blocked/challenged despite IP diversity.

steps.title: Share botnet indicators with threat intel
steps.desc: Submit observed botnet infrastructure indicators to threat-intel sharing channels/vendor for broader blocklisting.
steps.outcome: Indicators shared.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Users notified.

steps.title: Document and evaluate bot-management coverage
steps.desc: Record the finding and assess whether current bot-management coverage is adequate across all public login surfaces.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; coverage gaps identified if any.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify successful logins across the distributed attack traffic.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12214.def: Credential stuffing conducted at a deliberately slow rate (e.g. one or a few attempts per account per hour/day, spread across a long campaign window) specifically to stay under automated detection thresholds.
ITID-12214.purpose: Captures credential stuffing deliberately paced below standard rate-limiting/lockout thresholds to evade detection.
scopeIncludes: Stuffing campaign with attempt rate and pattern consistent with deliberate lockout/detection-threshold evasion
scopeExcludes: High-volume, rapid stuffing attempts (ITID-12211/12213)
ITID-12214.severity: High - the deliberate evasion behavior indicates a more sophisticated, patient attacker and often evades standard alerting entirely.
ITID-12214.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if any accounts are confirmed compromised, given the extended undetected dwell time typical of this pattern.
ITID-12214.escalation: Escalate to detection engineering to tune long-window behavioral baselines, since standard short-window alerting will have missed this activity.
indicators: Long-window statistical analysis reveals a slow, steady trickle of failed logins per account below standard alert thresholds
Login attempts spread evenly across an extended time period rather than in a burst
vectors: Deliberately throttled automated stuffing tooling
rootCauses: Detection thresholds tuned only for short-window/high-volume attack patterns
controls: Long-window behavioral baselining (days/weeks) in addition to short-window rate limiting
ITID-12214.detection: Requires SIEM long-window aggregation and UEBA-style baselining rather than simple rate-limit thresholds; a real but less immediate technical signal than the high-volume variants.
ITID-12214.response: Once identified, block the source pattern, force reset for any confirmed-attempted accounts, and extend detection baselines to catch similar future campaigns.
metrics: Count of low-and-slow stuffing campaigns detected per year
Average detection latency
ITID-12214.notes: Detection latency is expected to be materially higher for this leaf than for high-volume stuffing; do not treat delayed detection as an indicator of control failure.

playbook.name: Response: Low-and-Slow Credential Stuffing
playbook.description: For credential stuffing conducted at a deliberately low rate over an extended period to evade volume-based detection thresholds.

steps.title: Confirm low-and-slow pattern over an extended window
steps.desc: Query logs over a wider time window (days to weeks) rather than the default short lookback, since the attack is designed to stay under short-window thresholds.
steps.guidance: Look for a slow, steady trickle of unique-username login attempts from consistent or slowly-rotating infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Confirmed low-and-slow stuffing pattern.

steps.title: Tune detection to a longer aggregation window
steps.desc: Adjust the relevant SIEM/WAF detection rule to aggregate failed-login counts over a longer sliding window so future low-and-slow attempts are caught earlier.
steps.outcome: Detection threshold adjusted.

steps.title: Enable behavioral/bot detection for slow patterns
steps.desc: Enable or tune bot-management behavioral detection, which is more effective than volume thresholds against low-rate attacks.
steps.outcome: Behavioral detection active.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Users notified.

steps.title: Document detection gap and fix
steps.desc: Record how long the campaign ran undetected and the detection-tuning change made.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine cumulative success and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Aggregate successful logins across the full attack window to identify compromised accounts, since success may be spread thin over time.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts across the full campaign.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12215.def: Credential stuffing conducted directly against a backend API or mobile application authentication endpoint, often bypassing web-layer bot-management controls that only cover the browser-based login form.
ITID-12215.purpose: Captures credential stuffing directed at an API or mobile-app authentication endpoint rather than a standard web login form.
scopeIncludes: Stuffing traffic hitting a mobile app's authentication API directly
Stuffing traffic against an API endpoint lacking the same bot-management coverage as the web login page
scopeExcludes: Stuffing against the standard web login form (ITID-12211 through ITID-12214)
ITID-12215.severity: High - API endpoints frequently have weaker bot-detection coverage than the primary web login.
ITID-12215.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if account takeovers are confirmed.
ITID-12215.escalation: Escalate to API security/engineering team to extend bot-management and rate-limiting coverage to the affected API endpoint.
indicators: Spike in failed authentication API calls with mobile/API user-agent strings and no corresponding web-session activity
API traffic lacking expected mobile app telemetry/attestation headers
vectors: Automated tooling calling the mobile app's authentication API directly, bypassing the app's own client logic
rootCauses: API authentication endpoint not covered by the same bot-management/WAF rules as the web login page
No mobile app attestation (e.g. Play Integrity/App Attest) enforced
controls: API gateway rate limiting and bot management
Mobile app attestation enforcement (Play Integrity/App Attest)
ITID-12215.detection: API gateway logs provide concrete technical telemetry once instrumented; a common control gap is that this endpoint is not monitored to the same standard as the web login, which detection engineering should close.
ITID-12215.response: Extend bot-management coverage to the API endpoint, block the identified attack pattern, and audit for successful authentications during the attack window.
metrics: Count of API/mobile stuffing incidents per quarter
Time to extend bot-management coverage post-incident
ITID-12215.notes: This leaf frequently surfaces a genuine control gap (API endpoint outside standard web bot-management scope); the root-cause field should be reviewed for control-coverage remediation, not just incident closure.

playbook.name: Response: API/Mobile Endpoint Credential Stuffing
playbook.description: For credential stuffing directed at a mobile app or backend API authentication endpoint rather than the standard web login form, often bypassing web-focused bot defenses.

steps.title: Confirm the API/mobile endpoint targeted
steps.desc: Review API gateway logs for the specific mobile/API authentication endpoint receiving the stuffing traffic, and confirm it lacks the same bot-mitigation controls as the web login.
steps.guidance: Attackers often target the mobile API directly because it's less protected than the browser-facing login page.
steps.outcome: Confirmed targeted endpoint and its current protection level.

steps.title: Apply rate limiting and bot mitigation to the API endpoint
steps.desc: Extend rate limiting, CAPTCHA/challenge, or mobile app attestation (e.g. device integrity checks) to the API endpoint to bring it to parity with web login protections.
steps.outcome: API endpoint protected against automated stuffing.

steps.title: Audit all API endpoints for equivalent gaps
steps.desc: Request an inventory review of other mobile/API endpoints to confirm they carry equivalent anti-automation protection as public web forms.
steps.outcome: Audit initiated; gaps tracked for remediation.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Users notified.

steps.title: Document parity gap and fix
steps.desc: Record the protection gap between web and API surfaces and the remediation taken.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify successful authentications against the API/mobile endpoint.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions/tokens for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12216.def: Credential stuffing attempts made directly against the corporate SSO/identity provider login page.
ITID-12216.purpose: Captures credential stuffing directed specifically at the organization's SSO/identity provider login, the highest-consequence stuffing target given downstream federated access.
scopeIncludes: Stuffing attack against the corporate IdP login endpoint specifically
scopeExcludes: Stuffing against a standalone SaaS application not federated through SSO (ITID-12217)
ITID-12216.severity: Critical - any successful hit grants federated access across every downstream application.
ITID-12216.priority: P1 always for the attack itself; escalate further if any hit is confirmed.
ITID-12216.escalation: Escalate immediately to IAM; enable conditional access risk policies to block or challenge the observed attack pattern.
indicators: Spike in failed SSO logins with valid-format username/password pairs from varied sources
IdP risk-scoring engine flags high volume of credential-stuffing-pattern sign-in attempts
vectors: Automated stuffing tooling targeting the IdP login endpoint directly
rootCauses: IdP conditional access policy not configured to challenge/block high-risk sign-in patterns
controls: IdP risk-based conditional access (block/challenge on stuffing-pattern risk)
Phishing-resistant MFA reducing blast radius of any successful hit
ITID-12216.detection: IdP sign-in logs and native risk-detection engines (e.g. Entra ID Identity Protection, Okta ThreatInsight) provide strong, purpose-built technical detection for this exact pattern.
ITID-12216.response: Enable/verify conditional access blocking, force reset for any accounts with a successful hit, and review downstream application access granted to any compromised identity.
metrics: Count of SSO stuffing incidents per quarter
Percentage blocked by conditional access
ITID-12216.notes: Differentiated from ITID-12217 by target: this leaf is the federated identity provider itself, not an individual downstream SaaS application.

playbook.name: Response: Credential Stuffing Against SSO/Identity Provider
playbook.description: For credential stuffing directed at the corporate SSO/identity provider login, where a single successful match grants access across all federated applications.

steps.title: Confirm the attack against the IdP login
steps.desc: Review identity provider logs for the stuffing pattern and volume against the primary SSO login.
steps.guidance: This is high-severity given the blast radius — a single successful match yields access to every federated app.
steps.outcome: Confirmed pattern and scope.

steps.title: Block source and enable bot mitigation at the IdP
steps.desc: Enable CAPTCHA/bot-management and block source infrastructure at the identity provider login.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic blocked or throttled.

steps.title: Enforce MFA org-wide on the IdP
steps.desc: Confirm/enforce MFA for all accounts at the SSO layer if any gap allowed this attack to succeed.
steps.outcome: MFA enforced across the identity provider.

steps.title: Review each compromised identity for downstream impact
steps.desc: Check each federated application accessed by compromised identities for signs of data access or further compromise.
steps.outcome: Downstream impact assessed per application.

steps.title: Document and escalate as high-severity finding
steps.desc: Record the incident with emphasis on the blast-radius risk of SSO-targeted attacks and confirm MFA/bot-mitigation coverage going forward.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and reviewed at appropriate severity.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify successful logins and, for each, enumerate every downstream application the compromised identity had access to via SSO.
steps.outcome: Confirmed compromised accounts and their full downstream application access.

steps.title: Force reset and revoke all federated sessions
steps.desc: Reset the password and revoke every SSO session and downstream application token for each compromised identity.
steps.guidance: Revoking only the IdP session is not sufficient — federated app sessions can outlive it; revoke explicitly at each connected app if the IdP doesn't cascade automatically.
steps.outcome: All access, including downstream federated sessions, terminated.

ITID-12217.def: Credential stuffing attempts made against a specific, individually-authenticated SaaS or third-party application login page.
ITID-12217.purpose: Captures credential stuffing directed at a specific standalone SaaS application portal not federated through corporate SSO.
scopeIncludes: Stuffing attack against a specific named SaaS portal's own login page
scopeExcludes: Stuffing against the corporate SSO/IdP login (ITID-12216)
ITID-12217.severity: Medium-High depending on the sensitivity of data held in the targeted SaaS application.
ITID-12217.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for high-sensitivity applications (financial, HR, customer data).
ITID-12217.escalation: Escalate to the application owner and IAM to enable the application's own bot-management/lockout controls and evaluate SSO onboarding.
indicators: Spike in failed logins against the specific SaaS portal with valid-format credential pairs
vectors: Automated stuffing tooling targeting the specific SaaS application's login endpoint
rootCauses: SaaS application not integrated with corporate SSO/conditional access
Weak or absent native lockout/bot-management controls on the SaaS platform
controls: SaaS application onboarding to SSO
CASB-enforced login anomaly detection for non-SSO SaaS apps
ITID-12217.detection: Detection depends on the SaaS provider's own login telemetry plus CASB visibility; a real but sometimes less centralized technical signal than SSO-integrated stuffing detection.
ITID-12217.response: Work with the SaaS vendor/application owner to block the attack pattern, force reset for any successful hits, and evaluate bringing the application under SSO.
metrics: Count of SaaS-portal stuffing incidents per quarter
Percentage of targeted SaaS apps subsequently brought under SSO
ITID-12217.notes: Differentiated from ITID-12216 by target scope: a single standalone SaaS application, not the federated identity provider.

playbook.name: Response: Credential Stuffing Against a Specific SaaS Portal
playbook.description: For credential stuffing directed at a single third-party SaaS application's own login (not the corporate SSO), where the application maintains its own separate credential store.

steps.title: Confirm the targeted SaaS portal and pull its logs
steps.desc: Identify the specific SaaS application targeted and obtain authentication logs from the vendor (via admin console or support request if not natively available).
steps.guidance: Access to detailed logs may be limited depending on the vendor's tier — engage vendor support early if needed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed attack pattern and scope from available logs.

steps.title: Enable available anti-automation controls in the SaaS platform
steps.desc: Enable any vendor-provided rate limiting, CAPTCHA, or IP allowlisting features for the SaaS login.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic blocked or throttled to the extent the platform allows.

steps.title: Migrate the application to corporate SSO if not already federated
steps.desc: If the SaaS app maintains standalone credentials rather than federating through corporate SSO, open a project to migrate it, since standalone credential stores are a recurring stuffing target.
steps.outcome: Migration recommendation logged/ticketed.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Users notified.

steps.title: Document and update SaaS security inventory
steps.desc: Record the finding and update the organization's SaaS security posture tracking for this vendor.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify any successful logins within the SaaS portal.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions for compromised accounts within the SaaS platform.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12218.def: Credential stuffing where the automated tooling successfully solves or bypasses CAPTCHA/bot-verification challenges, typically via a CAPTCHA-solving service, browser automation mimicking human behavior, or a CAPTCHA-farm.
ITID-12218.purpose: Captures credential stuffing that specifically employs CAPTCHA-solving or bypass techniques, indicating a more sophisticated and resourced attacker than basic automated stuffing.
scopeIncludes: Stuffing traffic confirmed to have successfully passed CAPTCHA challenges at high volume
Automated tooling using headless-browser fingerprint evasion to defeat bot-detection challenges
scopeExcludes: Stuffing blocked by CAPTCHA (not a successful bypass, and thus lower-severity, tracked under ITID-12211/12213)
ITID-12218.severity: High - CAPTCHA-bypass capability indicates a well-resourced, evasion-focused attacker with a materially higher success rate.
ITID-12218.priority: P1, given the demonstrated ability to defeat a key layered control.
ITID-12218.escalation: Escalate to detection engineering/bot-management vendor immediately to identify and close the specific CAPTCHA-bypass technique used.
indicators: High CAPTCHA-pass rate correlated with known automated-traffic fingerprints
Bot-management platform flags CAPTCHA solutions consistent with a solving-service signature
vectors: Commercial CAPTCHA-solving service (human-farm or AI-based) integrated into stuffing tooling
rootCauses: CAPTCHA used as the sole bot-detection layer, with no supplementary device-fingerprinting or behavioral analysis
controls: Layered bot management (device fingerprinting + behavioral analysis, not CAPTCHA alone)
Invisible/risk-based challenge escalation
ITID-12218.detection: Requires an advanced bot-management platform capable of detecting CAPTCHA-solving-service signatures and behavioral automation patterns beyond the CAPTCHA outcome itself.
ITID-12218.response: Deploy supplementary bot-detection layers beyond CAPTCHA, block the identified pattern, and audit for successful account takeovers.
metrics: Count of CAPTCHA-bypass stuffing incidents per year
CAPTCHA pass-rate anomaly trend
ITID-12218.notes: This leaf signals a control-effectiveness gap in relying on CAPTCHA alone; remediation should focus on adding layered, behavior-based bot detection.

playbook.name: Response: CAPTCHA-Bypass/Automated Credential Stuffing
playbook.description: For credential stuffing where the attacker's tooling has demonstrated the ability to solve or bypass CAPTCHA/bot-challenge defenses, indicating a more sophisticated automation capability (e.g. CAPTCHA-solving service, headless browser automation).

steps.title: Confirm the CAPTCHA bypass
steps.desc: Review bot-management/CAPTCHA logs to confirm the challenge was actually being solved (not simply not triggered) and characterize the automation signature.
steps.guidance: Distinguish between a CAPTCHA that wasn't triggered due to misconfiguration versus one genuinely being solved by the attacker's tooling — the remediation differs.
steps.outcome: Confirmed genuine bypass and characterized automation method.

steps.title: Escalate to bot-management vendor and layer additional controls
steps.desc: Report the bypass to the CAPTCHA/bot-management vendor, and layer additional signals (device fingerprinting, behavioral analysis, velocity checks) since CAPTCHA alone is no longer sufficient.
steps.outcome: Additional defensive layer(s) enabled.

steps.title: Enforce MFA as the durable mitigation
steps.desc: Since CAPTCHA has been defeated, treat MFA enforcement as the primary durable control against this attacker's continued attempts.
steps.outcome: MFA enforced on all at-risk accounts.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Users notified.

steps.title: Document the bypass capability for threat-intel tracking
steps.desc: Record the CAPTCHA-bypass technique/tooling observed as a threat-intel note, since this indicates a more capable and likely recurring adversary.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; threat profile updated.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify successful logins within the bypass traffic.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12219.def: A credential stuffing incident in which at least one login attempt succeeded and account takeover is confirmed via subsequent unauthorized activity, session establishment, or account-setting changes.
ITID-12219.purpose: Captures confirmed successful credential stuffing resulting in account takeover, distinguishing outcome-confirmed compromise from mere stuffing attempts for severity/priority purposes.
scopeIncludes: Any credential stuffing variant (ITID-12212 through ITID-12218) where a successful login and subsequent unauthorized account activity is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Stuffing attempts blocked or unsuccessful (the specific method-based sibling leaves)
ITID-12219.severity: Critical - confirmed account takeover, markedly higher than any attempt-only sibling leaf.
ITID-12219.escalation: Escalate immediately to IAM/SOC for session revocation, credential reset, and full account-activity audit.
indicators: Successful login from a stuffing-pattern source followed by account-setting changes, data access, or lateral use of the account
User report of unrecognized account activity coinciding with a known stuffing campaign
vectors: Any credential stuffing vector where the credential pair happened to be valid and unprotected by MFA
rootCauses: No MFA on the affected account
Password reuse by the account holder against a previously breached third-party service
controls: MFA enforcement on all accounts
Forced password reset and session revocation workflow
ITID-12219.detection: Authentication success logs correlated with a known stuffing-pattern source IP/fingerprint, combined with post-login activity monitoring, provide a strong technical confirmation trail.
ITID-12219.response: Revoke sessions, force password reset, and conduct a full audit of actions taken by the account during the compromise window.
metrics: Count of confirmed account takeovers via stuffing per quarter
Mean time to detection and containment
ITID-12219.notes: This is the confirmed-outcome escalation applicable across any credential stuffing method sibling leaf; it does not restate the delivery-method scoping of ITID-12212 through ITID-12218.

playbook.name: Response: Successful Credential Stuffing with Confirmed Account Takeover
playbook.description: For a confirmed incident where credential stuffing resulted in one or more successful account takeovers, regardless of the specific stuffing technique used.

steps.title: Confirm scope of all compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reconstruct the full attack and identify every account with a confirmed successful login match, not just the first one discovered.
steps.outcome: Complete list of compromised accounts.

steps.title: Force reset and revoke sessions on all compromised accounts
steps.desc: Immediately reset passwords and revoke all active sessions/tokens for every confirmed compromised account.
steps.outcome: Attacker access terminated across all affected accounts.

steps.title: Check for persistence on each compromised account
steps.desc: Review each compromised account for attacker-added persistence (forwarding rules, new MFA devices, OAuth grants, API keys).
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of persistence per account.

steps.title: Restore accounts with monitoring
steps.desc: Restore legitimate access and place affected accounts under elevated monitoring for a defined window.
steps.outcome: Accounts restored securely with monitoring active.

steps.title: Conduct post-incident review
steps.desc: Document the full incident, notify stakeholders per policy, and confirm anti-stuffing and MFA controls are adequate going forward.
steps.outcome: Post-incident review completed.

steps.title: Determine what each compromised account was used for
steps.desc: Review post-compromise activity for each affected account to identify data accessed, actions taken, or lateral movement.
steps.outcome: Full scope of attacker activity documented per account.

steps.title: Block the attacking infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the source IP(s)/infrastructure used in the attack.
steps.outcome: Attack infrastructure blocked.

steps.title: Remove confirmed persistence and enforce MFA
steps.desc: Remove any attacker-established persistence and enforce MFA on all affected accounts going forward.
steps.outcome: No attacker foothold remains; MFA active.

ITID-12221.def: Login attempts using a small number of common passwords against many usernames, staying under per-account lockout thresholds, where the specific pattern (seasonal, botnet, low-and-slow, SSO, legacy protocol, org wordlist, VPN) has not yet been identified.
ITID-12221.purpose: Catch-all for password spraying incidents where the specific pattern or target has not yet been determined.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific spraying pattern is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Any case where the pattern is known and matches ITID-12222 through ITID-12228
Credential stuffing, which uses known valid username/password pairs rather than guessed common passwords (ITID-12211 series)
ITID-12221.priority: P3 by default, escalating once account-takeover is confirmed.
ITID-12221.escalation: Reclassify once the specific pattern/target is confirmed via log analysis.
indicators: Single or small set of passwords attempted across many distinct usernames within a short window
vectors: Unclear/unconfirmed at time of initial detection
rootCauses: Insufficient triage detail captured at time of detection
controls: Account lockout/throttling policy tuned for spray-resistant thresholds
ITID-12221.detection: Authentication logs showing a many-usernames/few-passwords ratio give the same core signal as the specific sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-12221.response: Investigate and reclassify to a specific sibling leaf once the pattern is confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-12221.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification within Password Spraying, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Password Spraying Attempt
playbook.description: General triage playbook for a suspected password-spraying attack (a small set of common passwords tried against many accounts) where the specific technique has not yet been identified.

steps.title: Confirm the spraying pattern in logs
steps.desc: Review authentication logs for one or a few passwords being tried against many distinct usernames, spread out to avoid per-account lockout.
steps.guidance: Signature is the inverse of stuffing: few passwords, many usernames, each account tried only once or twice.
steps.outcome: Confirmed spraying pattern, or ruled out.
steps.abort: If pattern doesn't match, close as false positive.

steps.title: Block the source and enable bot mitigation
steps.desc: Block/rate-limit the source IP(s) and enable CAPTCHA/bot-management challenge on the login endpoint.
steps.outcome: Spraying traffic blocked or throttled.

steps.title: Enforce MFA and password-policy review
steps.desc: Confirm MFA is enforced on affected accounts and review whether the sprayed passwords indicate a weak org-wide password policy.
steps.outcome: MFA enforced; policy reviewed.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Users notified.

steps.title: Document findings
steps.desc: Record scope and remediation taken.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify any successful authentications within the spray traffic.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts, if any.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12222.def: Password spraying using a set of passwords derived from predictable seasonal/date-based patterns commonly adopted by users under mandatory password rotation policies.
ITID-12222.purpose: Captures password spraying using seasonally predictable password patterns (e.g. 'Summer2026!', 'CompanyName2026'), a common low-effort attack correlated with the calendar.
scopeIncludes: Spraying attack using passwords matching a season/year/quarter naming pattern
scopeExcludes: Spraying using an organization-specific wordlist not based on seasonal patterns (ITID-12227)
ITID-12222.severity: Medium-High - seasonal patterns have an unusually high hit rate against organizations with mandatory rotation policies.
ITID-12222.escalation: Escalate to IAM to review password policy for seasonal-pattern susceptibility (e.g. banning season+year combinations).
indicators: Attempted passwords matching a season/year/quarter naming convention across many usernames
vectors: Automated spraying tooling using a curated seasonal-password wordlist
rootCauses: Mandatory password rotation policy without a banned-password-pattern list, driving predictable seasonal password creation
controls: Banned-password-list enforcement including seasonal/date patterns
Move away from mandatory periodic rotation toward risk-based reset
ITID-12222.detection: Authentication logs showing the specific seasonal-pattern password attempted across many accounts provide a clear, attributable technical signal.
ITID-12222.response: Block the identified source, review and strengthen password policy to ban seasonal patterns, and force reset for any accounts using a matching password.
metrics: Count of seasonal-pattern spraying incidents per quarter
Percentage of accounts found using a matching pattern
ITID-12222.notes: This leaf frequently surfaces a password-policy design weakness; remediation should include banned-password-list updates, not just incident closure.

playbook.name: Response: Seasonal/Predictable Password Pattern Spraying
playbook.description: For password spraying using predictable, seasonally/contextually themed passwords (e.g. 'Summer2026!', 'CompanyName2026') that exploit weak organizational password conventions.

steps.title: Confirm the seasonal/predictable pattern used
steps.desc: Review the sprayed password values to confirm they follow a seasonal or organization-name-based pattern.
steps.guidance: This strongly suggests the attacker has reconnaissance on the org's password policy/naming convention — investigate how they learned it.
steps.outcome: Confirmed pattern and, where possible, the likely reconnaissance source.

steps.title: Block source and enable bot mitigation
