steps.desc: Block/rate-limit source IPs and enable CAPTCHA/bot-management challenge.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic blocked or throttled.

steps.title: Ban the predictable pattern from the password policy
steps.desc: Add the observed pattern (and common variants) to the organization's banned-password list/dictionary check.
steps.outcome: Pattern blocked from future use org-wide.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts and reinforce guidance against predictable seasonal passwords.
steps.outcome: Users notified.

steps.title: Document and recommend awareness reinforcement
steps.desc: Record the finding and recommend security-awareness messaging timed ahead of the next likely seasonal password rotation.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify successful authentications within the spray traffic.
steps.guidance: A predictable-pattern spray often has a higher success rate than random spraying — treat as elevated risk.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12223.def: Password spraying where login attempts originate from a large number of distinct IP addresses consistent with a distributed botnet.
ITID-12223.purpose: Captures password spraying conducted through a distributed botnet infrastructure to evade IP-based detection.
scopeIncludes: Spraying attack with login attempts distributed across many source IPs
scopeExcludes: Single-source spraying attempts (ITID-12221/12222)
Botnet infrastructure classified from an infrastructure/campaign perspective (ITID-31722 series in the Malware domain), which tracks the botnet itself rather than this organization's incident
ITID-12223.severity: High - distributed sourcing indicates a well-resourced attacker evading standard IP-based defenses.
ITID-12223.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if any accounts are confirmed compromised.
ITID-12223.escalation: Escalate to network security/IdP team to enable device-fingerprinting and risk-based conditional access beyond IP blocking.
indicators: Large number of distinct source IPs each attempting the same small password set against different usernames
vectors: Commercial or criminal botnet-for-hire spraying service
rootCauses: Authentication endpoint relying solely on IP-based rate limiting
controls: IdP risk-based conditional access
Device-fingerprinting bot management
ITID-12223.detection: IdP native risk-detection engines and bot-management platforms provide strong technical detection via distributed-source correlation and device fingerprinting.
ITID-12223.response: Enable/tune conditional access blocking, force reset for any accounts with a successful attempt, and review for downstream account activity.
metrics: Count of distributed spraying incidents per quarter
Number of distinct source IPs observed per incident
ITID-12223.notes: Scoped to this organization's victim-side incident; the botnet infrastructure itself, if tracked for multi-organization campaign purposes, is logged under ITID-31722 to avoid duplication.

playbook.name: Response: Distributed/Botnet-Driven Password Spraying
playbook.description: For password spraying conducted via a distributed botnet spreading requests across many source IPs to evade per-IP rate limiting.

steps.title: Confirm distributed sourcing
steps.desc: Review logs for IP diversity, geographic spread, and ASN distribution consistent with botnet infrastructure behind the spray.
steps.guidance: Look for shared fingerprints (JA3, user-agent) across the diverse sources as corroborating evidence.
steps.outcome: Confirmed botnet-driven pattern.

steps.title: Enable bot-management/fingerprint-based blocking
steps.desc: Enable device/behavioral fingerprinting since per-IP blocking alone is ineffective against botnet-distributed spraying.
steps.outcome: Botnet traffic blocked/challenged despite IP diversity.

steps.title: Share botnet indicators with threat intel
steps.desc: Submit observed infrastructure indicators to threat-intel sharing channels/vendor.
steps.outcome: Indicators shared.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Users notified.

steps.title: Document and evaluate bot-management coverage
steps.desc: Record the finding and assess bot-management coverage across all login surfaces.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify successful logins across the distributed spray traffic.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12224.def: Password spraying conducted at a deliberately slow rate (e.g. one attempt per account per lockout-observation-window) specifically to remain under automated lockout and alerting thresholds.
ITID-12224.purpose: Captures password spraying deliberately paced below standard lockout/detection thresholds to evade detection over an extended period.
scopeIncludes: Spraying campaign with attempt rate and pattern consistent with deliberate lockout-threshold evasion, often spanning days or weeks
scopeExcludes: High-volume, rapid spraying attempts (ITID-12221/12223)
ITID-12224.severity: High - the deliberate evasion behavior indicates a patient, sophisticated attacker and typically evades standard short-window alerting.
ITID-12224.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if any accounts are confirmed compromised.
ITID-12224.escalation: Escalate to detection engineering to tune long-window behavioral baselines for this exact evasion pattern.
indicators: Long-window statistical analysis reveals the same one or two passwords attempted against many usernames at a very low per-account rate over an extended period
vectors: Deliberately throttled automated spraying tooling
rootCauses: Lockout policy resets its attempt counter faster than the attacker's per-account attempt rate, and detection thresholds are tuned only for short-window bursts
controls: Long-window behavioral baselining (days/weeks) in addition to per-account lockout policy
ITID-12224.detection: Requires SIEM long-window aggregation across the many-usernames/single-password ratio; a real but delayed technical signal compared to high-volume spraying.
ITID-12224.response: Once identified, block the source pattern, force reset for confirmed-attempted accounts, and extend detection baselines.
metrics: Count of low-and-slow spraying campaigns detected per year
Average detection latency
ITID-12224.notes: Detection latency is expected to be materially higher for this leaf; do not treat delayed detection as an indicator of control failure.

playbook.name: Response: Low-and-Slow Password Spraying
playbook.description: For password spraying conducted at a deliberately low rate over an extended period (often one attempt per account per day) to evade both lockout thresholds and volume-based detection.

steps.title: Confirm low-and-slow pattern over an extended window
steps.desc: Query logs over an extended time window (days to weeks) since the attack is designed to evade short-window detection thresholds.
steps.guidance: Look for a steady trickle of the same password(s) tried against a rotating/expanding set of accounts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed low-and-slow spraying pattern.

steps.title: Tune detection to a longer aggregation window
steps.desc: Adjust the relevant SIEM/IAM detection rule to aggregate failed logins across a longer sliding window.
steps.outcome: Detection threshold adjusted for earlier catch of future low-and-slow attempts.

steps.title: Enforce MFA as durable mitigation
steps.desc: Enforce MFA on all accounts, which neutralizes the value of a correctly-guessed password even if detection remains imperfect.
steps.outcome: MFA enforced org-wide.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Users notified.

steps.title: Document detection gap and fix
steps.desc: Record how long the campaign ran undetected and the detection-tuning change made.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine cumulative success and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Aggregate successful logins across the full campaign window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts across the campaign.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12225.def: Password spraying attempts made directly against the corporate SSO/identity provider login page.
ITID-12225.purpose: Captures password spraying directed specifically at the organization's SSO/identity provider login, the highest-consequence spraying target given downstream federated access.
scopeIncludes: Spraying attack against the corporate IdP login endpoint specifically
scopeExcludes: Spraying against a standalone SaaS application not federated through SSO
Spraying against a legacy protocol endpoint that bypasses the SSO/MFA layer entirely (ITID-12226)
ITID-12225.severity: Critical - any successful hit grants federated access across every downstream application.
ITID-12225.priority: P1 always for the attack itself.
ITID-12225.escalation: Escalate immediately to IAM; enable conditional access risk policies to block or challenge the observed attack pattern.
indicators: Same one or two passwords attempted against many usernames at the IdP login endpoint
IdP risk-scoring engine flags high volume of spraying-pattern sign-in attempts
vectors: Automated spraying tooling targeting the IdP login endpoint directly
rootCauses: IdP conditional access policy not configured to challenge/block spraying-pattern sign-in risk
controls: IdP risk-based conditional access
Phishing-resistant MFA reducing blast radius of any successful hit
ITID-12225.detection: IdP sign-in logs and native risk-detection engines provide strong, purpose-built technical detection for this exact pattern.
ITID-12225.response: Enable/verify conditional access blocking, force reset for any accounts with a successful hit, and review downstream application access.
metrics: Count of SSO spraying incidents per quarter
Percentage blocked by conditional access
ITID-12225.notes: Differentiated from ITID-12226 by target: this leaf targets the modern, MFA-protected SSO endpoint; ITID-12226 specifically covers legacy protocol endpoints that bypass MFA entirely.

playbook.name: Response: Password Spraying Against SSO/Identity Provider
playbook.description: For password spraying directed at the corporate SSO/identity provider login, where a single successful match grants access across all federated applications.

steps.title: Confirm the attack against the IdP login
steps.desc: Review identity provider logs for the spraying pattern and volume against the primary SSO login.
steps.guidance: High-severity given the blast radius — a single successful guess yields access to every federated app.
steps.outcome: Confirmed pattern and scope.

steps.title: Block source and enable bot mitigation at the IdP
steps.desc: Enable CAPTCHA/bot management and block source infrastructure at the identity provider login.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic blocked or throttled.

steps.title: Enforce MFA org-wide on the IdP
steps.desc: Confirm/enforce MFA for all accounts at the SSO layer.
steps.outcome: MFA enforced across the identity provider.

steps.title: Review each compromised identity for downstream impact
steps.desc: Check each federated application accessed by compromised identities for signs of further compromise.
steps.outcome: Downstream impact assessed per application.

steps.title: Document and escalate as high-severity finding
steps.desc: Record the incident with emphasis on SSO blast-radius risk and confirm MFA/bot-mitigation coverage.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and reviewed at appropriate severity.

steps.title: Determine success rate and downstream exposure
steps.desc: Identify successful logins and, for each, enumerate every downstream application the compromised identity had access to via SSO.
steps.outcome: Confirmed compromised accounts and their full downstream application access.

steps.title: Force reset and revoke all federated sessions
steps.desc: Reset the password and revoke every SSO session and downstream application token for each compromised identity.
steps.outcome: All access, including downstream federated sessions, terminated.

ITID-12226.def: Password spraying attempts made against a legacy protocol endpoint that lacks modern authentication/MFA support, such that any successful password guess grants immediate account access with no secondary factor to stop it.
ITID-12226.purpose: Captures password spraying directed at a legacy authentication protocol endpoint (e.g. IMAP, POP3, SMTP AUTH, ActiveSync, legacy basic auth) that does not support or enforce MFA, making a successful spray immediately consequential.
scopeIncludes: Spraying against IMAP/POP3/SMTP AUTH, legacy ActiveSync, or other basic-auth endpoints not protected by MFA
Spraying against a legacy on-premises authentication endpoint lacking conditional access enforcement
scopeExcludes: Spraying against the modern, MFA-enforced SSO/IdP endpoint (ITID-12225)
ITID-12226.severity: Critical - because there is no MFA at all on this protocol, a single successful guess equals immediate compromise with no secondary control to stop it.
ITID-12226.priority: P1 always, given the complete absence of a compensating MFA control on this path.
ITID-12226.escalation: Escalate immediately to IAM/messaging team to disable or block the legacy protocol entirely if not business-required, or restrict it to a managed VPN/allowlist.
indicators: Spraying pattern observed specifically against a legacy authentication protocol endpoint
Successful legacy-protocol login with no corresponding MFA challenge event in the logs
vectors: Automated spraying tooling targeting legacy basic-auth/IMAP/POP3/ActiveSync endpoints specifically because they lack MFA
rootCauses: Legacy protocol left enabled for a small number of business-required use cases without compensating controls
Conditional access policy not configured to block legacy authentication entirely
controls: Conditional access policy blocking legacy authentication protocols organization-wide
Disabling unused legacy protocols (IMAP/POP3/basic auth) at the tenant level
ITID-12226.detection: Authentication logs specifically flagging legacy-protocol sign-ins (which by definition carry no MFA claim) provide a clear, high-confidence technical signal once legacy-auth logging is enabled.
ITID-12226.response: Block or disable the legacy protocol immediately where not strictly business-required, force reset for any accounts confirmed attempted, and audit for successful legacy-protocol logins.
metrics: Count of legacy-protocol spraying incidents per quarter
Percentage of tenant with legacy authentication blocked
ITID-12226.notes: This leaf frequently surfaces a genuine control gap (legacy protocol left enabled); remediation should prioritize disabling the protocol entirely over per-incident credential reset alone. Distinct from MFA-bypass-technique leaves in the separate Advanced Credential Attacks/MFA Bypass branch, since MFA is entirely absent on this path rather than being circumvented.

playbook.name: Response: Password Spraying Against Legacy/Non-MFA Protocol Endpoint
playbook.description: For password spraying directed at a legacy authentication protocol (e.g. IMAP, POP3, SMTP AUTH, legacy Exchange ActiveSync) that does not support or enforce MFA, bypassing modern-auth protections.

steps.title: Confirm the legacy protocol targeted
steps.desc: Identify the specific legacy protocol/endpoint receiving the spray traffic and confirm it is not subject to Conditional Access/MFA enforcement.
steps.guidance: This is a very common real-world bypass technique — legacy protocols are frequently overlooked in MFA rollouts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed targeted legacy endpoint and its current protection gap.

steps.title: Block or disable the legacy protocol
steps.desc: Disable legacy authentication for the affected protocol org-wide, or restrict it via Conditional Access/network ACL if a business need remains.
steps.guidance: This is the direct, durable fix — most organizations should be disabling legacy auth entirely.
steps.outcome: Legacy protocol access blocked or brought under MFA enforcement.

steps.title: Audit for remaining legacy-auth exposure
steps.desc: Request an inventory of any remaining legacy-auth-dependent applications/devices to plan their migration off legacy protocols.
steps.outcome: Audit initiated; migration plan tracked.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Users notified.

steps.title: Document as a high-priority MFA-coverage gap
steps.desc: Record the finding and escalate legacy-auth disablement as a priority control gap if not already fully closed.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; gap tracked to closure.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify successful authentications against the legacy endpoint.
steps.guidance: Because legacy protocols bypass MFA, any successful match here is a full account compromise, not just a password exposure.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions/tokens for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12227.def: Password spraying using a custom wordlist built from organization-specific or industry-specific terminology, indicating attacker reconnaissance beyond generic common-password lists.
ITID-12227.purpose: Captures password spraying using a wordlist specifically curated from organization- or industry-specific terms (company name, product names, local sports teams, industry jargon) rather than a generic common-password list.
scopeIncludes: Spraying attack using passwords incorporating the company name, branded products, or industry-specific terms
scopeExcludes: Spraying using a generic, non-targeted common-password list (ITID-12221)
Seasonal/date-pattern spraying (ITID-12222)
ITID-12227.severity: High - the targeted wordlist indicates prior reconnaissance and a materially higher hit rate.
ITID-12227.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if any accounts are confirmed compromised.
ITID-12227.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence to assess what reconnaissance/OSINT the attacker likely used to build the wordlist.
indicators: Attempted passwords incorporating company name, product names, or industry jargon across many usernames
vectors: Manually curated or OSINT-derived organization-specific wordlist used in automated spraying tooling
rootCauses: Banned-password-list policy not extended to cover company/product/industry-specific terms
mitreTechniques: T1589.001 Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
controls: Organization-specific banned-password-list enforcement
Employee password policy training addressing brand-name password risk
ITID-12227.detection: Authentication logs showing organization-specific term patterns attempted across many accounts provide a clear, attributable technical signal.
ITID-12227.response: Block the identified source, extend the banned-password list to cover the identified terms, and force reset for any matching accounts.
metrics: Count of org-specific wordlist spraying incidents per quarter
Percentage of accounts found using a matching pattern
ITID-12227.notes: Distinguished from ITID-12222 (seasonal pattern) by the source of the wordlist: this leaf is organization/industry-derived terminology, not calendar-based patterns.

playbook.name: Response: Password Spraying Using Organization-Specific Wordlist
playbook.description: For password spraying using a custom wordlist tailored to the organization (e.g. company name variants, product names, local sports teams, known former passwords), indicating targeted reconnaissance rather than a generic attack.

steps.title: Confirm the org-specific wordlist pattern
steps.desc: Review the sprayed password values to confirm they are tailored to the organization rather than a generic common-password list.
steps.guidance: This indicates deliberate targeting and reconnaissance — treat with elevated concern versus opportunistic spraying.
steps.outcome: Confirmed tailored wordlist and, where possible, likely reconnaissance source (e.g. scraped from public website, social media, prior breach).

steps.title: Block source and enable bot mitigation
steps.desc: Block/rate-limit source IPs and enable CAPTCHA/bot-management challenge.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic blocked or throttled.

steps.title: Ban observed patterns and assess targeted-attack likelihood
steps.desc: Add the observed org-specific terms to the banned-password dictionary, and assess whether this campaign is likely a precursor to a more targeted attack given the deliberate reconnaissance.
steps.outcome: Patterns blocked; targeting assessment documented.

steps.title: Notify affected users
steps.desc: Notify users of compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Users notified.

steps.title: Document as evidence of targeted reconnaissance
steps.desc: Record the finding, flag as potential targeted-actor activity, and share with threat-intel/hunting for correlation with other alerts.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and shared for broader correlation.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify successful authentications within the spray traffic.
steps.guidance: A tailored wordlist typically yields a higher success rate — treat as elevated risk.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts.

steps.title: Force reset on compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke sessions for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Accounts secured.

ITID-12228.def: Password spraying attempts made against a VPN client or remote-access gateway login.
ITID-12228.purpose: Captures password spraying directed at the organization's VPN or remote-access authentication endpoint.
scopeIncludes: Spraying attack against a VPN concentrator or remote-access portal login
scopeExcludes: Spraying against the SSO/IdP login (ITID-12225)
Spraying against a legacy non-VPN protocol endpoint (ITID-12226)
ITID-12228.severity: High - VPN access often bypasses perimeter network controls entirely.
ITID-12228.priority: P1 if VPN lacks MFA; P2 if MFA is enforced on the VPN.
ITID-12228.escalation: Escalate to network security team to review VPN lockout policy and confirm MFA enforcement.
indicators: Same one or two passwords attempted against many VPN usernames within a short window
vectors: Automated spraying tooling targeting the VPN login endpoint directly
rootCauses: VPN portal not enforcing MFA
VPN account lockout policy not tuned against low-volume-per-account spraying
controls: MFA enforcement on VPN/remote access
VPN concentrator login-anomaly alerting
ITID-12228.detection: VPN concentrator authentication logs provide concrete technical signal for the many-usernames/single-password pattern characteristic of spraying.
ITID-12228.response: Block the identified source, force reset for confirmed-attempted accounts, and confirm/enforce MFA on the VPN.
metrics: Count of VPN spraying incidents per quarter
Percentage of VPN accounts with MFA enforced
sops: VPN Account Lockout Policy Review SOP
ITID-12228.notes: Scoped to the spraying technique against VPN specifically; phishing-sourced VPN credential theft is tracked separately under ITID-12114.

playbook.name: Response: Password Spraying Against VPN/Remote Access
playbook.description: For password spraying directed at the organization's VPN or remote-access gateway, where a successful match can grant network-level access rather than just application access.

steps.title: Confirm the attack against the VPN/remote-access gateway
steps.desc: Review VPN gateway/remote-access logs for the spraying pattern and volume.
steps.guidance: Successful VPN compromise is high-severity — it can grant internal network access, not just an application session.
steps.outcome: Confirmed pattern and scope.

steps.title: Block source and enable bot mitigation at the gateway
steps.desc: Block/rate-limit source IPs at the VPN gateway/firewall and enable available anti-automation controls.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic blocked or throttled.

steps.title: Enforce MFA on the VPN gateway
steps.desc: Confirm/enforce MFA for VPN authentication if any gap allowed this attack to succeed.
steps.outcome: MFA enforced on VPN access.

steps.title: Investigate for internal lateral movement
steps.desc: If any successful VPN session occurred, review internal network logs/EDR for lateral movement from that access point.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of internal compromise.

steps.title: Document and escalate as high-severity finding
steps.desc: Record the incident given the network-access blast radius and confirm VPN MFA coverage going forward.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and reviewed at appropriate severity.

steps.title: Determine success rate and compromised accounts
steps.desc: Identify successful VPN authentications within the spray traffic and check for any subsequent internal network activity from that session.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of compromised accounts and any internal activity observed.

steps.title: Force reset and terminate active VPN sessions
steps.desc: Reset passwords and forcibly terminate any active VPN session for compromised accounts.
steps.outcome: Attacker network access terminated.

ITID-12229.def: A password spraying incident in which at least one login attempt succeeded and account takeover is confirmed via subsequent unauthorized activity, session establishment, or account-setting changes.
ITID-12229.purpose: Captures confirmed successful password spraying resulting in account takeover, distinguishing outcome-confirmed compromise from mere spraying attempts for severity/priority purposes.
scopeIncludes: Any password spraying variant (ITID-12222 through ITID-12228) where a successful login and subsequent unauthorized account activity is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Spraying attempts blocked or unsuccessful (the specific pattern-based sibling leaves)
ITID-12229.severity: Critical - confirmed account takeover, markedly higher than any attempt-only sibling leaf.
ITID-12229.escalation: Escalate immediately to IAM/SOC for session revocation, credential reset, and full account-activity audit.
indicators: Successful login from a spraying-pattern source followed by account-setting changes, data access, or lateral use of the account
vectors: Any password spraying vector where the guessed password happened to be valid and unprotected by MFA
rootCauses: No MFA on the affected account
Weak or predictable password chosen by the account holder
controls: MFA enforcement on all accounts
Forced password reset and session revocation workflow
ITID-12229.detection: Authentication success logs correlated with a known spraying-pattern source, combined with post-login activity monitoring, provide a strong technical confirmation trail.
ITID-12229.response: Revoke sessions, force password reset, and conduct a full audit of actions taken by the account during the compromise window.
metrics: Count of confirmed account takeovers via spraying per quarter
Mean time to detection and containment
ITID-12229.notes: This is the confirmed-outcome escalation applicable across any password spraying pattern sibling leaf; it does not restate the pattern-specific scoping of ITID-12222 through ITID-12228.

playbook.name: Response: Successful Password Spraying with Confirmed Account Takeover
playbook.description: For a confirmed incident where password spraying resulted in one or more successful account takeovers, regardless of the specific spraying technique used.

steps.title: Confirm scope of all compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reconstruct the full attack and identify every account with a confirmed successful login match.
steps.outcome: Complete list of compromised accounts.

steps.title: Force reset and revoke sessions on all compromised accounts
steps.desc: Immediately reset passwords and revoke all active sessions/tokens for every confirmed compromised account.
steps.outcome: Attacker access terminated across all affected accounts.

steps.title: Check for persistence on each compromised account
steps.desc: Review each compromised account for attacker-added persistence (forwarding rules, new MFA devices, OAuth grants, API keys).
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of persistence per account.

steps.title: Restore accounts with monitoring
steps.desc: Restore legitimate access and place affected accounts under elevated monitoring for a defined window.
steps.outcome: Accounts restored securely with monitoring active.

steps.title: Conduct post-incident review
steps.desc: Document the full incident, notify stakeholders per policy, and confirm anti-spraying and MFA controls are adequate going forward.
steps.outcome: Post-incident review completed.

steps.title: Determine what each compromised account was used for
steps.desc: Review post-compromise activity for each affected account to identify data accessed, actions taken, or lateral movement.
steps.outcome: Full scope of attacker activity documented per account.

steps.title: Block the attacking infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the source IP(s)/infrastructure used in the attack.
steps.outcome: Attack infrastructure blocked.

steps.title: Remove confirmed persistence and enforce MFA
steps.desc: Remove any attacker-established persistence and enforce MFA on all affected accounts going forward.
steps.outcome: No attacker foothold remains; MFA active.

ITID-12231.def: Unauthorized or inappropriate use of a legitimately-shared or reused credential where the specific context (shared team account, vendor account, departed employee, cross-system reuse, service account, family device, documented password, or M&A legacy account) has not yet been identified.
ITID-12231.purpose: Catch-all for shared credential exploitation incidents where the specific sharing context has not yet been determined.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific sharing context is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Any case where the context is known and matches ITID-12232 through ITID-12239
ITID-12231.escalation: Reclassify once the specific sharing context is confirmed.
indicators: Account activity inconsistent with a single named user, of unclear cause
vectors: Unclear/unconfirmed at time of initial detection
rootCauses: Insufficient triage detail captured at time of detection
controls: Access review and account-ownership auditing
ITID-12231.detection: IAM access-review and account-activity-attribution telemetry give the same core signal as the specific sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-12231.response: Investigate and reclassify to a specific sibling leaf once the sharing context is confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-12231.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification within Shared Credential Exploitation, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Shared Credential Exploitation
playbook.description: General triage playbook for a suspected incident involving misuse of a shared (multi-person) credential, where the specific context has not yet been identified.

steps.title: Identify the shared credential and its legitimate user population
steps.desc: Determine which account is shared, who is authorized to use it, and from what locations/devices it is normally accessed.
steps.guidance: Shared-credential incidents hinge entirely on establishing a baseline of 'normal' since there is no single owner to interview first.
steps.outcome: Documented list of authorized users and normal access baseline.

steps.title: Reset the shared credential
steps.desc: Rotate the password for the shared account immediately.
steps.outcome: Prior credential invalidated.

steps.title: Distribute new credential only to verified authorized users
steps.desc: Redistribute the new credential only to the confirmed authorized-user list via a secure channel (e.g. password manager vault, not plaintext chat/email).
steps.outcome: New credential securely distributed only to legitimate users.

steps.title: Evaluate eliminating the shared account
steps.desc: Assess whether the shared account can be replaced with individual accounts plus role-based access, which is the durable fix for this class of risk.
steps.outcome: Recommendation made and tracked.

steps.title: Document findings and shared-account policy gap
steps.desc: Record the incident and recommend a policy against creating new shared accounts going forward.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Identify anomalous use of the shared account
steps.desc: Compare recent access logs against the baseline to identify use inconsistent with any authorized user (unusual location, time, device, or activity).
steps.outcome: Confirmed anomalous activity, or ruled out as normal variation among authorized users.
steps.abort: If all activity is explainable by an authorized user, close as false positive.

steps.title: Revoke active sessions
steps.desc: Terminate all active sessions/tokens for the account.
steps.outcome: Any unauthorized session terminated.

ITID-12232.def: Exploitation of a credential legitimately shared among multiple members of a team or department (e.g. a shared support mailbox login, a shared operations dashboard account) beyond its authorized use, by an authorized team member acting improperly or by an external party who obtained the shared credential.
ITID-12232.purpose: Captures inappropriate or unauthorized use of a credential intentionally shared among a team or department for legitimate operational convenience.
scopeIncludes: Misuse of a known team/department shared account by an authorized member outside their scope
External compromise of a team/department shared account
scopeExcludes: Shared vendor/contractor accounts (ITID-12233)
Shared application/automation service accounts (ITID-12236)
ITID-12232.severity: Medium-High - shared accounts complicate attribution and often carry broader access than an individual account.
ITID-12232.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if externally compromised.
ITID-12232.escalation: Escalate to the account owner's manager and IAM to review whether the shared account should be eliminated in favor of individual named accounts.
indicators: Activity on a known shared account inconsistent with any legitimate team member's known behavior/location
Login to the shared account from an unrecognized device/location
vectors: Legitimate team member credential shared beyond the intended distribution list
External phishing/credential theft targeting the shared account specifically
rootCauses: Lack of individual named accounts with role-based access as an alternative to a shared account
No periodic review of who has access to shared account credentials
controls: Migration from shared accounts to individual named accounts with role-based access
Periodic access review of shared account credential distribution
ITID-12232.detection: IAM/SIEM correlation of login source, timing, and behavioral pattern against the known population of legitimate shared-account users provides a workable, if imperfect, attribution signal.
ITID-12232.response: Rotate the shared credential, investigate all recent activity for attribution, and evaluate migrating to individual accounts.
metrics: Count of shared team account misuse incidents per year
Number of shared accounts migrated to individual accounts post-incident
ITID-12232.notes: This leaf frequently surfaces a governance weakness (reliance on shared accounts); remediation should prioritize migration to individual named accounts.

playbook.name: Response: Shared Team/Department Account Exploitation
playbook.description: For misuse of a shared team or department account (e.g. a support inbox, shared social-media login, or team distribution account) by someone outside the authorized team.

steps.title: Confirm the team's authorized member list
steps.desc: Obtain the current authoritative list of team members authorized to use the account from the team lead/manager.
steps.guidance: Team rosters change frequently — always get a fresh list rather than relying on a stale document.
steps.outcome: Current authorized-user list confirmed.

steps.title: Reset the shared credential and revoke sessions
steps.desc: Rotate the password and terminate all active sessions for the team account.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access terminated.

steps.title: Determine how the credential leaked outside the team
steps.desc: Investigate how the departed/unauthorized individual obtained the credential (e.g. former member never removed, credential shared in an unsecured document).
steps.outcome: Leak vector identified.

steps.title: Redistribute securely to the current roster only
steps.desc: Distribute the new credential to the current authorized roster via a secure channel.
steps.outcome: Credential securely redistributed.

steps.title: Document and recommend individual accounts or a managed vault
steps.desc: Recommend migrating the team account to individual logins with role-based access, or at minimum a managed shared-credential vault with rotation-on-departure.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendation tracked.

steps.title: Identify the out-of-team access
steps.desc: Compare access logs against the confirmed team roster to identify access from someone not on the list.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized access, or ruled out.

ITID-12233.def: Exploitation of a credential provided to a vendor or contractor organization and shared among multiple individuals at that vendor beyond the organization's authorization, or compromised at the vendor and reused against the organization.
ITID-12233.purpose: Captures inappropriate or unauthorized use of a credential shared with or among an external vendor/contractor's staff.
scopeIncludes: Vendor staff turnover where a departed vendor employee retains and uses shared vendor account access
Vendor account credential compromised at the vendor's own environment and reused against this organization
scopeExcludes: Shared internal team/department accounts (ITID-12232)

A genuine third-party/supply-chain breach tracked under the organization's vendor risk domain, when the incident's primary character is the vendor's own breach rather than this organization's credential-sharing exposure
ITID-12233.severity: High - vendor credential sharing often lacks the visibility/offboarding rigor of internal accounts.
ITID-12233.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the vendor account has privileged or broad access.
ITID-12233.escalation: Escalate to vendor management and IAM to immediately rotate the vendor credential and review the vendor's own access-control practices.
indicators: Vendor account activity from an individual known to have left the vendor organization
Vendor account login pattern inconsistent with the vendor's documented access schedule
vectors: Vendor's own poor internal credential-sharing hygiene
Lack of individual-attribution requirement in the vendor access agreement
rootCauses: No contractual requirement for individually attributable vendor access
No offboarding notification process between the vendor and the organization
controls: Contractual requirement for individually attributable, named vendor access
Vendor offboarding notification and immediate access revocation process
ITID-12233.detection: IAM access logs combined with vendor-provided personnel-change notifications (where contractually required) give the primary detection signal; often reactive rather than proactive absent strong vendor coordination.
ITID-12233.response: Rotate the vendor credential immediately, review the vendor contract for individual-attribution requirements, and audit vendor account activity for unauthorized use.
metrics: Count of vendor shared-credential incidents per year
Percentage of vendor contracts requiring individual attribution
ITID-12233.notes: Scope decision: when the incident's primary character is a genuine breach of the vendor's own environment, log it under the organization's third-party/supply-chain risk domain instead of duplicating it here; this leaf is for the credential-sharing exposure specifically.

playbook.name: Response: Shared Vendor/Contractor Account Exploitation
playbook.description: For misuse of a credential shared among multiple vendor/contractor personnel, where an individual outside the current engagement uses the account after their access should have ended.

steps.title: Confirm current vendor engagement and authorized personnel
steps.desc: Contact the vendor management/procurement owner to confirm the current engagement status and the list of vendor personnel currently authorized.
steps.outcome: Current authorized personnel list and engagement status confirmed.

steps.title: Reset the shared credential and revoke sessions
steps.desc: Rotate the password and terminate all active sessions for the vendor account.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access terminated.

steps.title: Verify offboarding process for vendor accounts
steps.desc: Confirm whether the standard vendor-offboarding process failed to disable this account at contract end, and file a process-gap ticket if so.
steps.outcome: Process gap identified and ticketed, or confirmed the process was followed correctly.

steps.title: Restore access only if engagement is active
steps.desc: If the vendor engagement is still active and legitimate, redistribute the new credential securely to currently authorized personnel only.
steps.outcome: Access restored appropriately, or fully terminated if engagement has ended.

steps.title: Document and recommend individual vendor accounts
steps.desc: Recommend individual, time-bound vendor accounts tied to the contract lifecycle rather than a persistent shared credential.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; recommendation tracked.

steps.title: Identify unauthorized or post-engagement access
steps.desc: Compare access logs against the confirmed list and engagement dates to identify access after contract end or by unlisted personnel.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized access, or ruled out.

steps.title: Notify the vendor's account manager
steps.desc: Formally notify the vendor of the unauthorized access finding and request their internal investigation if the access originated from their side.
steps.outcome: Vendor notified and engaged.

ITID-12234.def: Authentication or access using a credential belonging to an individual whose employment or engagement has ended, indicating an offboarding process failure.
ITID-12234.purpose: Captures use of a credential belonging to a former employee that was not properly deactivated as part of offboarding, a classic identity-lifecycle control failure.
scopeIncludes: Login activity on an account belonging to a confirmed departed employee/contractor after their termination date
Departed employee retaining and using access after offboarding
scopeExcludes: Current employee credential shared with another current employee (ITID-12232)
ITID-12234.severity: High - represents a direct identity-lifecycle control failure with unbounded access duration.
ITID-12234.priority: P1, given the offboarding process failure and unknown duration of unauthorized access.
ITID-12234.escalation: Escalate immediately to HR and IAM to confirm termination date, disable the account, and audit all activity since the termination date.
indicators: Login activity on an account after the individual's confirmed last day of employment
HR system termination record with no corresponding IAM deprovisioning event
vectors: Manual, non-automated offboarding process with a gap between HR termination and IAM deprovisioning
rootCauses: No automated HR-to-IAM deprovisioning integration
Offboarding checklist not consistently followed
controls: Automated HR-to-IAM deprovisioning integration (joiner-mover-leaver process)
Periodic access review reconciling active accounts against HR employment status
ITID-12234.detection: IAM/HR reconciliation reporting provides a concrete, auditable technical signal comparing active account status against HR termination records.
ITID-12234.response: Disable the account immediately, audit all activity since termination, and review the offboarding process for the gap that allowed continued access.
metrics: Count of departed-employee access incidents per year
Average days between termination and deprovisioning
ITID-12234.notes: This leaf is a direct process-failure indicator; every occurrence should trigger a review of the joiner-mover-leaver deprovisioning pipeline, not just the individual account.

playbook.name: Response: Departed Employee Credential Reuse
playbook.description: For a former employee's account or credential being used to access systems after their termination/departure date, whether their individual account was not disabled or their credential was shared/retained by others.

steps.title: Confirm departure date and account status
steps.desc: Confirm the employee's official last day with HR and check whether the standard offboarding process disabled their account(s).
steps.outcome: Confirmed departure date and current account status (should have been disabled).

steps.title: Immediately disable the account
steps.desc: Disable the account and revoke all active sessions/tokens/API keys if not already done.
steps.guidance: This should have happened automatically at offboarding — treat any live account past departure date as an urgent gap.
steps.outcome: Account fully disabled; no residual access.

steps.title: Review and remediate the offboarding process failure
steps.desc: Identify why the automated/manual offboarding step failed to disable this account and fix the process gap (e.g. missing system in the offboarding checklist, HR-to-IT sync failure).
steps.outcome: Root cause of the offboarding failure identified and fixed.

steps.title: Audit for other recently departed employees with live accounts
steps.desc: Proactively check other recent departures for the same offboarding gap to catch any other live accounts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no other affected departures, or additional accounts found and disabled.

steps.title: Document and address any policy violation
steps.desc: Record the incident, address any policy violation with the individual/manager involved if a current employee retained and shared the credential, and confirm the offboarding process fix.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; HR/management follow-up completed if warranted.

steps.title: Identify post-departure access
steps.desc: Review access logs for any activity on the account after the departure date, including source and what was accessed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of post-departure access, if any.

steps.title: Determine who used the credential post-departure
steps.desc: Where possible, determine whether the departed employee themselves accessed the account, or whether someone else (e.g. a colleague who retained the password) used it.
steps.guidance: This determines whether the issue is an offboarding process failure, a policy violation by a current employee, or genuine unauthorized access by the former employee.
steps.outcome: Determination made on who accessed the account and why.

ITID-12235.def: Unauthorized access to a system achieved by reusing a password/credential obtained from a different system where the same individual had set an identical or closely similar password.
ITID-12235.purpose: Captures exploitation enabled by an individual reusing the same password across multiple internal or external systems, where compromise of one system's credential grants access to another.
scopeIncludes: Password obtained from a compromise on System A confirmed reused to access System B by the same user
Internal cross-system password reuse discovered via password-hash comparison during a security assessment
scopeExcludes: Credential stuffing using breach-list pairs against many unrelated accounts (ITID-12211 series), which is an external mass-attack technique rather than a single individual's password-reuse pattern discovered internally
ITID-12235.severity: High - demonstrates a systemic weakness whenever a single point of compromise cascades across systems.
ITID-12235.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the second system is a privileged or sensitive one.
ITID-12235.escalation: Escalate to IAM to force reset across every system where reuse is confirmed, not just the originally compromised one.
indicators: Password hash comparison across systems reveals identical or closely similar passwords for the same user
Confirmed unauthorized access to System B shortly after a known compromise of the same user's credential on System A
vectors: Attacker manually testing a stolen credential against other systems the same user is known to access
rootCauses: No enforcement of unique passwords across internal systems
Lack of a centralized password manager to encourage unique password generation
controls: Enterprise password manager deployment encouraging unique passwords per system
Periodic internal password-hash-reuse auditing
ITID-12235.detection: Internal password-hash comparison tooling and cross-system login correlation provide a concrete, if periodic rather than real-time, technical detection method.
ITID-12235.response: Force reset across every system where reuse is confirmed, and review for any unauthorized access already taken using the reused credential.
metrics: Count of cross-system reuse incidents per year
Percentage of accounts found reusing passwords in periodic audits
ITID-12235.notes: Differentiated from credential stuffing (ITID-12211 series) by origin: this leaf covers reuse discovered/exploited within the organization's own systems by a single-user password pattern, not a mass external breach-list attack.

playbook.name: Response: Cross-System Password Reuse Exploitation
playbook.description: For an attacker who compromised a user's password on one (often lower-security) system and successfully reused it to access a separate, unrelated corporate system.

steps.title: Identify the originating and target systems
steps.desc: Determine which system the password was originally compromised on (e.g. a personal account breach, a lower-tier internal system) and which corporate system it was successfully reused against.
steps.outcome: Both systems identified and the reuse confirmed.

steps.title: Reset the password on the target (and originating, if internal) system
steps.desc: Force a password reset on the affected corporate system, and on the originating system too if it is also an internal/managed system.
steps.outcome: Reused credential invalidated everywhere it applies.

steps.title: Check for the same password reused elsewhere
steps.desc: Where feasible, check whether the same user has the same or a similar password on other internal systems and force resets there too.
steps.guidance: Password-reuse habits are rarely limited to one pair of systems.
steps.outcome: Other exposed systems identified and remediated.

steps.title: Enforce MFA and provide password-manager guidance
steps.desc: Confirm MFA is enforced on the target system and provide the user guidance on using a password manager to avoid reuse.
steps.outcome: MFA confirmed; user guidance delivered.

steps.title: Document and reinforce reuse awareness
steps.desc: Record the finding and recommend broader password-reuse awareness messaging.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Determine scope of access gained on the target system
steps.desc: Review what the attacker accessed or did on the target system using the reused credential.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of access/impact.

steps.title: Revoke sessions on the target system
steps.desc: Terminate all active sessions/tokens on the compromised target system.
steps.outcome: Attacker access terminated.

ITID-12236.def: Unauthorized use of a non-human service/automation account credential that is shared across multiple applications, scripts, or integration points, typically discovered hardcoded or broadly distributed.
ITID-12236.purpose: Captures exploitation of a shared application, automation, or service account credential embedded in scripts, integrations, or scheduled jobs.
scopeIncludes: Service account credential embedded in multiple scripts/applications and exploited from one of those exposure points
Automation account credential shared across teams beyond its intended integration scope
scopeExcludes: Service account credential exploited due to never being rotated, which is tracked under ITID-12423 (a different Tier-4 type focused on the rotation-failure root cause specifically) rather than the sharing/distribution aspect tracked here
ITID-12236.severity: High - service accounts frequently hold broad, standing privileges and lack MFA by design.
ITID-12236.priority: P1 if the service account has privileged/cross-system access; P2 otherwise.
ITID-12236.escalation: Escalate to engineering/DevOps and IAM to rotate the credential and migrate to a managed secrets solution with scoped, individually-tracked access.
indicators: Service account authentication from an unexpected source/script not on the documented list of authorized integrations
Credential found hardcoded in multiple repositories or configuration files
vectors: Credential copy-pasted across multiple scripts/integrations without a central secrets management system
Departing engineer retaining a copy of a shared automation credential
rootCauses: No centralized secrets management (vault) for service account credentials
Service accounts not scoped to least-privilege, single-purpose access
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Centralized secrets management (vault) with automated rotation
Least-privilege, single-purpose service account scoping
ITID-12236.detection: Service account authentication source monitoring (comparing observed source IPs/hosts against a documented allowlist of authorized integrations) provides a concrete technical signal.
ITID-12236.response: Rotate the credential immediately, migrate it to a managed secrets vault, and audit all systems/scripts referencing the old credential.
metrics: Count of shared service account exploitation incidents per year
Percentage of service accounts under centralized secrets management
ITID-12236.notes: Scope decision: this leaf covers the sharing/distribution of the service account credential across multiple scripts or teams; exploitation specifically enabled by the credential never having been rotated is the distinct root cause tracked under ITID-12423.

playbook.name: Response: Shared Application/Automation Account Exploitation
playbook.description: For misuse of a shared service/automation account (e.g. a CI/CD credential, scheduled-task account, or integration API key) used by multiple systems or scripts, where the credential is compromised or misused outside its intended automation.

steps.title: Inventory legitimate consumers of the account
steps.desc: Identify every system, script, or pipeline authorized to use the service account/API key, and its expected access pattern (source IPs, times, actions).
steps.guidance: Service accounts often have poorly documented ownership — check CI/CD configs, scheduled tasks, and integration settings directly if no central inventory exists.
steps.outcome: Documented list of legitimate consumers and expected behavior baseline.

steps.title: Rotate the credential/API key
steps.desc: Rotate the service account's password or API key/secret immediately.
steps.outcome: Prior credential invalidated.

steps.title: Update legitimate automation with the new credential
steps.desc: Coordinate with each legitimate consumer to update their configuration with the rotated credential to avoid breaking production automation.
steps.outcome: All legitimate automation restored with the new credential.

steps.title: Move to per-integration credentials where feasible
steps.desc: Assess whether the account can be split into distinct credentials per consuming system, so a future compromise doesn't require rotating one credential shared by everything.
steps.outcome: Recommendation made and tracked.

steps.title: Document and recommend secrets-management improvement
steps.desc: Record the finding and recommend a managed secrets-rotation process if the credential was static/long-lived.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Identify anomalous use of the account
steps.desc: Compare recent activity against the baseline to identify use from an unexpected source, at an unexpected time, or performing actions outside the automation's normal scope.
steps.outcome: Confirmed anomalous use, or ruled out.

steps.title: Revoke active tokens/sessions
steps.desc: Invalidate any active tokens or sessions issued under the old credential.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access terminated.

steps.title: Restrict the account's scope and source
steps.desc: Where possible, scope the service account to least privilege and restrict allowed source IPs/networks to reduce future exploitability.
steps.outcome: Account scope hardened.

ITID-12237.def: A corporate credential shared with a family member (e.g. for convenience, or by a minor using a parent's device) or otherwise exposed via use on a shared, multi-user personal/family device without adequate profile separation.
ITID-12237.purpose: Captures exposure or misuse of a corporate credential shared with a family member or used on a shared family/personal device.
scopeIncludes: Corporate credential known/used by a family member of the employee
Corporate session/credential exposed via browser autofill on a shared family device
scopeExcludes: Credential exposure via a personal account phished with corporate password reuse (ITID-12118, a different mechanism)
ITID-12237.severity: Medium - typically low sophistication but represents a genuine unauthorized-access pathway.
ITID-12237.priority: P3, escalating to P2 if any actual unauthorized access or data exposure is confirmed.
ITID-12237.escalation: Escalate to the employee's manager and IAM for credential reset and a reminder of acceptable-use policy regarding shared devices.
indicators: Corporate account activity confirmed performed by someone other than the authorized employee, attributed to a family member
Corporate session found active in a browser profile on a shared family device
vectors: Employee sharing corporate login for convenience (e.g. shared streaming-style password-sharing habit extended to work accounts)
Corporate credential saved in a browser autofill on a device also used by other household members
rootCauses: No corporate policy or awareness training addressing credential sharing on personal devices
Corporate BYOD policy not enforcing device/profile separation
controls: Acceptable use policy explicitly prohibiting credential sharing with family/household members
BYOD/MDM policy requiring separated work profiles on personal devices
ITID-12237.detection: Limited direct technical telemetry; typically identified via activity-attribution investigation (behavioral inconsistency, self-report, or a specific incident) rather than automated detection.
ITID-12237.response: Reset the credential, counsel the employee on acceptable use policy, and review for any unauthorized data access during the exposure window.
metrics: Count of family/personal device sharing incidents per year
ITID-12237.notes: This leaf typically relies on human reporting or investigation rather than automated telemetry, consistent with its low-sophistication, human-behavior-driven origin.

playbook.name: Response: Family/Personal Device Shared Credential Exploitation
playbook.description: For unauthorized access to a corporate account resulting from a family member or other household user of a personal/BYOD device using a saved or shared corporate credential.

steps.title: Interview the account owner
steps.desc: Contact the account owner to determine whether they shared their device or credential with a family member, and gather details on the device and circumstances.
steps.guidance: Approach non-punitively to get an honest account — this is a common and often unintentional policy violation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed circumstances of the credential sharing.

steps.title: Reset the credential and revoke sessions
steps.desc: Force a password reset and revoke all active sessions for the account.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access terminated.

steps.title: Remove saved credentials from the personal device
steps.desc: Guide the user to remove any saved corporate credentials/sessions from the shared personal device, or trigger a remote wipe of corporate data if MDM-managed.
steps.outcome: Corporate credential no longer accessible on the shared device.

steps.title: Reinforce BYOD/credential-sharing policy with the user
steps.desc: Remind the user of the acceptable-use policy regarding credential sharing and personal device use for corporate access.
steps.outcome: User acknowledgment of policy.

steps.title: Document and assess broader BYOD policy exposure
steps.desc: Record the incident and note whether it points to a broader BYOD policy or MFA-on-personal-device gap.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Confirm the scope of unauthorized access
steps.desc: Review access logs for what the unauthorized family member accessed or did while using the account.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of access/impact.

ITID-12238.def: Unauthorized access achieved by discovering a credential that was written down or stored in plaintext in an easily accessible location, such as a sticky note, notebook, or unencrypted document.
ITID-12238.purpose: Captures exploitation of a corporate credential that was physically written down or stored in an easily discoverable unencrypted format (sticky note, unencrypted spreadsheet on a shared drive).
scopeIncludes: Credential found written on a physical note near a workstation and used for unauthorized access
Credential found in an unencrypted document/spreadsheet on a shared drive and used for unauthorized access
scopeExcludes: Credential accidentally sent via unencrypted email (ITID-12532, a different exposure mechanism)
Credential left in a shared document primarily as an accidental-disclosure event without confirmed subsequent misuse (ITID-12534), when no exploitation has occurred; log there instead if unexploited
ITID-12238.severity: Medium-High depending on the privilege level of the discovered credential.
ITID-12238.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for privileged credentials.
ITID-12238.escalation: Escalate to the credential owner's manager and IAM for immediate reset and a review of physical/document security practices.
indicators: Physical security sweep discovers a written credential near a workstation
Unauthorized access traced to a credential found in an unencrypted shared document
vectors: Physical discovery of a written-down password by an insider or on-site visitor
Discovery of a plaintext credential in an easily browsable shared drive location
rootCauses: No password manager provided/mandated, driving users to write down complex passwords
Insufficient clean-desk policy enforcement
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Enterprise password manager deployment removing the need to write down passwords
Clean-desk policy enforcement and periodic physical security sweeps
ITID-12238.detection: Limited direct technical telemetry; detection relies on physical security sweeps, document discovery, and correlating the exploitation event's timing/access pattern with the exposure.
ITID-12238.response: Reset the credential immediately, remove the physical/document exposure, and review for any unauthorized access already taken.
metrics: Count of written-credential exploitation incidents per year
ITID-12238.notes: Distinguished from ITID-12534 by requiring confirmed subsequent exploitation, not merely the discovery/disclosure of the written-down credential.

playbook.name: Response: Documented/Written-Down Shared Credential Exploitation
playbook.description: For unauthorized access resulting from a credential that was written down or stored insecurely (e.g. a sticky note, shared spreadsheet, unencrypted document) and discovered/used by an unauthorized party.

steps.title: Locate and secure the insecure credential record
steps.desc: Identify exactly where and how the credential was written down/stored (physical note, shared drive file, chat message) and secure or remove it to prevent further exposure.
steps.outcome: Insecure credential record located and removed/secured.

steps.title: Reset the credential and revoke sessions
steps.desc: Force a password reset and revoke all active sessions for the affected account.
steps.outcome: Exposed credential invalidated.

steps.title: Purge the credential from all discovered insecure locations
steps.desc: Confirm the credential has been removed or redacted from every location it was found (document, chat history, shared drive) including version history where applicable.
steps.outcome: No remaining copies of the credential in insecure storage.

steps.title: Provide the user a secure alternative
steps.desc: Provide the user with a password manager and guidance on secure credential storage.
steps.outcome: User equipped with a secure storage method.

steps.title: Document and reinforce secure credential storage awareness
steps.desc: Record the incident and recommend broader awareness messaging on secure credential storage, plus a scan for similar exposed credentials elsewhere in the organization if feasible.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; broader scan considered.

steps.title: Determine who had access to the insecure record
steps.desc: Assess who could plausibly have seen the written-down credential (e.g. who has access to the shared drive/document) to scope potential unauthorized users.
steps.outcome: Scope of potential exposure documented.

ITID-12239.def: Unauthorized use of a credential belonging to a legacy system or account structure inherited from a merged or acquired entity, where post-merger identity consolidation and access review was incomplete or delayed.
ITID-12239.purpose: Captures exploitation of a legacy shared credential left over from a merger or acquisition, where account consolidation or access review was incomplete.
scopeIncludes: Legacy acquired-entity account still active and shared/known beyond its intended user base after the merger
Credential from a pre-merger legacy identity system exploited due to incomplete consolidation
scopeExcludes: Standard departed-employee credential reuse unrelated to M&A activity (ITID-12234)
ITID-12239.severity: High - M&A transition periods frequently carry incomplete visibility into legacy access, and legacy systems may lack current security controls.
ITID-12239.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for privileged legacy accounts.
ITID-12239.escalation: Escalate to the integration/IAM team to accelerate consolidation of the legacy identity system and disable orphaned legacy accounts.
indicators: Activity on a legacy acquired-entity account not yet migrated to the parent organization's IAM system
Credential known to multiple former employees of the acquired entity still functioning post-acquisition
vectors: Legacy account credential known to multiple former employees of the acquired company
Legacy system's own weaker security controls exploited during the transition window
rootCauses: Incomplete or delayed post-merger identity consolidation project
Legacy system retained without a defined decommissioning timeline
controls: Prioritized post-merger identity consolidation timeline with executive sponsorship
Interim compensating monitoring on legacy acquired-entity systems pending consolidation
ITID-12239.detection: Detection depends on whatever logging the legacy system provides, which is often weaker than the parent organization's standard telemetry; this is an explicit, tracked control gap during the M&A transition window.
ITID-12239.response: Disable the legacy account, accelerate consolidation planning, and audit legacy system access logs to the extent available.
metrics: Count of legacy M&A credential exploitation incidents per year
Percentage of acquired-entity accounts consolidated into parent IAM
ITID-12239.notes: This leaf explicitly flags an M&A-transition-period control gap; expect reduced detection coverage on the legacy system side until consolidation is complete.

playbook.name: Response: Post-Merger/Acquisition Legacy Shared Credential Exploitation
playbook.description: For unauthorized access via a legacy shared credential inherited from a merger/acquisition that was never rotated, individualized, or brought under current identity governance.

steps.title: Confirm the credential's origin and current governance status
steps.desc: Identify the legacy system/account, confirm it originated from the M&A-acquired entity, and determine whether it is currently under the acquiring organization's identity governance (MFA, rotation policy, ownership).
steps.guidance: Post-M&A environments frequently retain untracked legacy accounts outside normal IAM processes — treat discovery of the account itself as a finding.
steps.outcome: Account origin and governance gap confirmed.

steps.title: Reset the credential and revoke sessions
steps.desc: Force a password reset and revoke all active sessions for the account.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access terminated.

steps.title: Bring the account under current identity governance
steps.desc: Migrate the account into the acquiring organization's IAM (individual ownership, MFA enforcement, standard rotation) or decommission it if no longer needed.
steps.outcome: Account brought into governance or decommissioned.

steps.title: Audit for other ungoverned M&A-legacy accounts
steps.desc: Request a broader audit of the acquired entity's remaining systems for other legacy accounts not yet integrated into current identity governance.
steps.outcome: Audit initiated; additional legacy accounts tracked for remediation.

steps.title: Document and escalate M&A integration gap
steps.desc: Record the incident and escalate to the M&A integration/IT leadership team as an example of an identity-integration gap requiring prioritization.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and escalated.

steps.title: Identify the unauthorized use
steps.desc: Review access logs for the anomalous/unauthorized use of the account.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of unauthorized access.

ITID-12311.def: Systematic, exhaustive automated attempts to guess a password (as opposed to dictionary/wordlist or rainbow-table-based methods) where the specific method (offline hash, online interactive, GPU cluster, mask-based, SSH/admin protocol, API, PIN) has not yet been identified.
ITID-12311.purpose: Catch-all for brute force attack incidents where the specific method or target has not yet been determined.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific brute force method is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Any case where the method is known and matches ITID-12312 through ITID-12318
Dictionary attacks using a curated wordlist rather than exhaustive character-space guessing (ITID-12321 series)
Rainbow table attacks using precomputed hash lookups rather than live guessing (ITID-12331 series)
ITID-12311.escalation: Reclassify once the specific method/target is confirmed via log or forensic analysis.
indicators: High-volume sequential or exhaustive password-guessing pattern of unclear origin
vectors: Unclear/unconfirmed at time of initial detection
rootCauses: Insufficient triage detail captured at time of detection
controls: Account lockout policy
Rate limiting on authentication endpoints
ITID-12311.detection: Authentication logs showing exhaustive/sequential guessing patterns give the same core signal as the specific sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-12311.response: Investigate and reclassify to a specific sibling leaf once the method/target is confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-12311.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification within Brute Force Attack, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Brute Force Attack
playbook.description: Baseline response for a detection or report of repeated, systematic password-guessing attempts against an account or system, where the specific technique (online, offline, distributed, etc.) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm the brute force pattern from authentication logs
steps.desc: Pull the authentication log for the targeted account/system and confirm a pattern of repeated failed login attempts.
steps.guidance: Note volume, rate, source IP(s), and whether attempts are against one account or many.
steps.outcome: Confirmed brute force pattern with supporting log evidence.

steps.title: Block the source of the attempts
steps.desc: Block the identified source IP(s)/ASN at the firewall or authentication gateway.
steps.outcome: Source blocked from further attempts.

steps.title: Audit for persistence on any compromised account
steps.desc: If any account was accessed, check for new MFA enrollments, forwarding rules, or OAuth grants added.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of persistence.

steps.title: Confirm lockout/rate-limiting thresholds are in place
steps.desc: Verify the affected system enforces account lockout or rate-limiting after repeated failed attempts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed rate-limiting/lockout controls are effective.

steps.title: Document the attack and recommend control improvements
steps.desc: Record the technique and volume observed and recommend rate-limiting, lockout policy, or MFA enforcement improvements if gaps were found.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a concrete control recommendation.

steps.title: Determine the attack surface and technique
steps.desc: Classify whether the attack is online/interactive against a live login, offline against stolen hashes, GPU/distributed cracking, mask-based, or targeting SSH/API/PIN specifically.
steps.guidance: Reclassify to the more specific ITID playbook once known and continue from there if one exists.
steps.outcome: Attack correctly classified by technique.

steps.title: Force password reset on any account with a successful login
steps.desc: Reset the password and revoke sessions for any account where a brute-force attempt succeeded.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated and sessions terminated for compromised accounts.
steps.abort: If no account was successfully accessed, this step is not required.

steps.title: Determine whether any attempt succeeded
steps.desc: Check whether any of the brute-force attempts resulted in a successful authentication.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the attack resulted in unauthorized access.

ITID-12312.def: Exhaustive password guessing performed offline against a stolen password hash using local computing resources, with no interaction with the target system and therefore no lockout or rate-limiting exposure during the cracking process itself.
ITID-12312.purpose: Captures brute forcing performed offline against an already-exfiltrated password hash, where the attacker has unlimited attempts with no lockout exposure.
scopeIncludes: Offline exhaustive brute forcing of an exfiltrated hash file using standard CPU/single-machine cracking tools
scopeExcludes: GPU/distributed cracking cluster use for the same offline cracking activity, tracked separately given its distinct scale/severity implications (ITID-12314)
Rainbow table (precomputed lookup) attacks against the same stolen hash, a distinct method (ITID-12331 series)
ITID-12312.severity: Critical - the hash exfiltration itself represents a significant prior compromise, and offline cracking has no rate-limiting defense.
ITID-12312.priority: P1 always, given that hash exfiltration already occurred as a prerequisite.
ITID-12312.escalation: Escalate immediately to SOC/IR - focus first on how the hash was exfiltrated (the prerequisite breach), not solely on the cracking activity, which is likely undetectable once offline.
indicators: Confirmed prior exfiltration of a password hash database/file
Threat intelligence or dark-web monitoring shows the hash or cracked plaintext being traded
vectors: Prior database breach or credential dumping malware yielding the hash file
rootCauses: Weak hashing algorithm or insufficient salting allowing feasible offline cracking
The underlying breach that exposed the hash in the first place
controls: Strong adaptive hashing algorithm (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2) with proper salting
Rapid password reset upon confirmed hash exfiltration
ITID-12312.detection: The cracking process itself occurs offline and is not directly observable; detection instead focuses on the upstream hash-exfiltration event and downstream monitoring for the cracked plaintext being used or traded.
ITID-12312.response: Force reset for every account in the exfiltrated hash set immediately, regardless of whether cracking has been confirmed, since offline cracking cannot be reliably detected in progress.
metrics: Time from hash exfiltration confirmation to full password reset
Percentage of exfiltrated accounts reset within 24 hours
ITID-12312.notes: The response imperative here is to treat every exfiltrated hash as eventually crackable and reset proactively, since the offline cracking step itself typically cannot be detected.

playbook.name: Response: Offline Hash Brute Force
playbook.description: For an attack where an adversary obtained a stolen password hash dump and is attempting to brute force the plaintext values offline, without generating authentication attempts against the live system.

steps.title: Confirm the hash exposure and scope the exfiltrated data
steps.desc: Determine how the hash dump was obtained (database breach, memory dump, credential store access) and identify exactly which accounts' hashes were exposed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hash exposure with full account scope.

steps.title: Force password reset for every account whose hash was exposed
steps.desc: Reset the password for every affected account regardless of hash strength, since offline cracking time cannot be reliably bounded.
steps.guidance: Treat weak/unsalted hashes as effectively already cracked.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts have rotated credentials.

steps.title: Audit for use of any already-cracked password against the live system
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for any login attempt using a plaintext password that matches a hash from the dump, indicating successful offline cracking already in use.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any cracked password has been used.

steps.title: Restore access with new credentials and enforce MFA
steps.desc: Confirm affected users have completed password resets and enforce MFA on affected accounts if not already required.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts restored with new credentials and MFA enforced.

steps.title: Document the exposure and remediate the root-cause access path
steps.desc: Record how the hash dump was obtained and ensure the underlying vulnerability (e.g., SQL injection, over-permissioned database access) is fully remediated.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with root cause remediated or tracked to closure.

steps.title: Assess the hashing algorithm strength
