steps.guidance: Salting alone defeats rainbow tables — this is the definitive fix, not just a mitigation.
steps.outcome: Password storage upgraded to a salted, rainbow-table-resistant algorithm.

steps.title: Determine whether any password has already been recovered and used
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for any login using a plaintext password matching an exposed hash.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any recovered password has been used for unauthorized access.

ITID-12332.def: Recovery of plaintext passwords from a stolen unsalted hash database using a precomputed rainbow table, exploiting the absence of a per-password salt.
ITID-12332.purpose: Captures rainbow table attacks feasible specifically because the stolen password hashes were unsalted, allowing a single precomputed table to work against every account in the dataset.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed or threat-intelligence-indicated rainbow table recovery against an unsalted hash dataset
scopeExcludes: Salted-hash datasets, which are not practically vulnerable to standard precomputed rainbow tables (not applicable to this leaf)
ITID-12332.severity: Critical - unsalted hashing represents a severe, fundamental cryptographic control failure enabling mass, efficient password recovery.
ITID-12332.escalation: Escalate immediately to engineering leadership; this indicates a fundamental application security defect requiring urgent remediation, not just incident response.
indicators: Confirmed exfiltration of a hash database using an unsalted hashing scheme
Threat intelligence/dark-web indicates cracked plaintexts being circulated at unusually high volume/speed for the dataset size
vectors: Exfiltration of a database using a legacy or poorly implemented unsalted hashing scheme
rootCauses: Application/database never implemented per-password salting
Legacy system predating modern password-hashing standards
controls: Mandatory migration to a salted, adaptive hashing algorithm (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2) for every credential store
ITID-12332.detection: Shares the limited-observability profile of offline cracking; detection focuses on the upstream exfiltration event and confirming the hashing scheme lacked salting.
ITID-12332.response: Force reset for the entire affected account population immediately, and treat the unsalted hashing scheme itself as a critical vulnerability requiring urgent remediation.
metrics: Time from exfiltration confirmation to hashing scheme remediation
Percentage of credential stores confirmed salted
detections: Application security review of hashing implementation
ITID-12332.notes: This leaf should always trigger an application-security defect ticket for the unsalted hashing implementation itself, not just an incident-response credential reset.

playbook.name: Response: Unsalted Hash Rainbow Table Attack
playbook.description: For an attack exploiting password hashes stored without a per-user salt, making them directly vulnerable to precomputed rainbow table lookup regardless of algorithm.

steps.title: Confirm the hash exposure and verify the absence of salting
steps.desc: Determine which accounts' hashes were exposed and confirm from the database schema/code that no per-user salt is applied.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unsalted hash exposure with full account scope.

steps.title: Force password reset for every account whose hash was exposed, immediately
steps.desc: Reset the password for every affected account without delay.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts have rotated credentials.

steps.title: Audit for use of any recovered password against the live system
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for use of any password recovered from the dump.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any unauthorized access.

steps.title: Restore access with new credentials and enforce MFA
steps.desc: Confirm affected users have completed password resets and enforce MFA on affected accounts.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts restored with new credentials and MFA enforced.

steps.title: Audit other systems for the same unsalted-storage defect
steps.desc: Check whether other applications in the estate share this unsalted-hashing implementation and open remediation tickets for each.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; estate-wide remediation tracked.

steps.title: Determine whether any password has already been recovered and used
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for any login using a plaintext password matching an exposed hash.
steps.guidance: Unsalted hashes are the fastest possible rainbow-table target — treat the entire exposed set as compromised immediately.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any recovered password has been used.

steps.title: Revoke sessions and close the exfiltration path
steps.desc: Terminate active sessions for affected accounts and remediate the access path that allowed the hash dump to be exfiltrated.
steps.outcome: Sessions terminated; exfiltration path closed.

steps.title: Add per-user salting and migrate to a strong algorithm
steps.desc: Update the password-storage implementation to apply a unique, random salt per user with a strong algorithm (bcrypt/argon2).
steps.guidance: This is the root-cause fix — unsalted storage is the defect being exploited, not just a hardening opportunity.
steps.outcome: All stored passwords now use per-user salting with a strong algorithm.

ITID-12333.def: Recovery of plaintext passwords from a stolen hash database using a precomputed rainbow table, exploiting the use of a legacy or cryptographically weak hashing algorithm for which comprehensive public rainbow tables already exist.
ITID-12333.purpose: Captures rainbow table attacks feasible because the stolen hashes used a legacy or cryptographically weak algorithm (e.g. MD5, SHA1, unsalted DES) for which large precomputed tables are widely available.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed rainbow table recovery against a hash database using MD5, SHA1, or a comparable legacy algorithm
scopeExcludes: Modern adaptive hashing algorithm (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2) datasets, which are not practically vulnerable regardless of salting (not applicable to this leaf)
ITID-12333.severity: Critical - legacy weak hashing algorithms have comprehensive, freely available precomputed tables, making recovery near-instantaneous.
ITID-12333.escalation: Escalate immediately to engineering leadership for urgent hashing algorithm migration.
indicators: Confirmed exfiltration of a hash database using a legacy weak algorithm (MD5/SHA1/etc.)
Extremely rapid appearance of cracked plaintexts in threat intelligence, consistent with precomputed-table lookup rather than live cracking
vectors: Exfiltration of a database still using a legacy hashing algorithm despite modern alternatives being available
rootCauses: Application/database never migrated from a legacy hashing algorithm to a modern adaptive standard
controls: Mandatory migration to a modern adaptive hashing algorithm (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2)
ITID-12333.detection: Shares the limited-observability profile of offline cracking; detection focuses on the upstream exfiltration event and confirming the legacy algorithm was in use.
ITID-12333.response: Force reset for the entire affected account population immediately and prioritize urgent hashing algorithm migration.
metrics: Time from exfiltration confirmation to hashing algorithm migration
Percentage of credential stores on a modern adaptive algorithm
detections: Application security review of hashing implementation
ITID-12333.notes: Differentiated from ITID-12332 by the specific failure: this leaf is algorithm weakness (legacy MD5/SHA1) rather than absence of salting on an otherwise-acceptable algorithm.

playbook.name: Response: Legacy/Weak Hash Algorithm Rainbow Table Attack
playbook.description: For an attack exploiting passwords hashed with a deprecated, fast algorithm (e.g., MD5, SHA1, unsalted SHA256) for which large precomputed rainbow tables are widely available, even if a salt is present but the algorithm itself is weak.

steps.title: Confirm the hash exposure and identify the specific algorithm in use
steps.desc: Determine which accounts' hashes were exposed and confirm the specific weak/legacy algorithm used.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hash exposure with algorithm identified.

steps.title: Force password reset for every account whose hash was exposed
steps.desc: Reset the password for every affected account.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts have rotated credentials.

steps.title: Audit for use of any recovered password against the live system
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for use of any password recovered from the dump.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any unauthorized access.

steps.title: Restore access with new credentials and enforce MFA
steps.desc: Confirm affected users have completed password resets and enforce MFA on affected accounts.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts restored with new credentials and MFA enforced.

steps.title: Inventory other systems still using legacy hash algorithms
steps.desc: Conduct or request an inventory of applications across the estate still using MD5/SHA1/unsalted SHA256 for password storage and open remediation tickets.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; estate-wide remediation tracked.

steps.title: Determine whether any password has already been recovered and used
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for any login using a plaintext password matching an exposed hash.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any recovered password has been used.

steps.title: Revoke sessions and close the exfiltration path
steps.desc: Terminate active sessions for affected accounts and remediate the access path that allowed the hash dump to be exfiltrated.
steps.outcome: Sessions terminated; exfiltration path closed.

steps.title: Migrate to a modern, memory-hard algorithm
steps.desc: Replace the legacy algorithm with argon2/bcrypt/scrypt, re-hashing passwords at next successful login or forcing a reset for all affected accounts.
steps.outcome: Password storage upgraded to a modern algorithm.

ITID-12334.def: Recovery of plaintext passwords from a stolen hash database using a precomputed table custom-built by the attacker for a specific character-set, length, or policy-constrained keyspace not covered by publicly available generic rainbow tables.
ITID-12334.purpose: Captures rainbow table attacks using a custom-generated table built specifically to target this organization's known password policy or a particular character-set/length combination, indicating attacker investment beyond off-the-shelf tables.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed rainbow table recovery using a table attributed to custom generation for this specific target's keyspace/policy
scopeExcludes: Use of a generic, publicly available rainbow table (ITID-12332, ITID-12333)
ITID-12334.severity: High - custom table generation indicates a resourced, deliberate attacker investing specifically in this target.
ITID-12334.priority: P1, given the demonstrated attacker investment and targeting.
ITID-12334.escalation: Escalate immediately to threat intelligence to assess the broader campaign this custom investment may be part of.
indicators: Cracked password recovery pattern consistent with a keyspace/policy-constrained table not matching any known public rainbow table
Attribution indicating dedicated attacker infrastructure investment
vectors: Attacker generating a custom precomputed table specifically constrained to the organization's known password policy
rootCauses: Weak or moderately weak hashing algorithm making custom table generation a worthwhile attacker investment
Password policy characteristics (length/character set) publicly known or inferable
controls: Mandatory migration to a modern adaptive, memory-hard hashing algorithm resistant to any precomputed-table approach
ITID-12334.detection: Shares the limited-observability profile of offline cracking; detection relies on the upstream exfiltration event and threat-intelligence attribution of custom attacker tooling investment.
ITID-12334.response: Force reset for the entire affected account population immediately and prioritize migration to a memory-hard hashing algorithm.
metrics: Count of custom rainbow table attack incidents per year
ITID-12334.notes: This leaf's severity is driven primarily by the demonstrated attacker investment/targeting rather than a distinct detectable technical signature versus the generic table leaves.

playbook.name: Response: Custom/Targeted Rainbow Table Generation
playbook.description: For an attack where the adversary generated a custom precomputed rainbow table specifically tailored to the target organization's known password policy or conventions (e.g., a specific length/charset rule), rather than using a generic public table.

steps.title: Confirm the hash exposure and assess evidence of a custom table
steps.desc: Determine which accounts' hashes were exposed, and look for evidence (e.g., unusually fast recovery of passwords fitting the org's specific policy) suggesting a custom-generated table.
steps.guidance: A custom table implies the attacker knows the organization's password policy specifics (length, charset, required characters) — investigate how that was learned.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hash exposure with custom-table indicators noted.

steps.title: Force password reset for every account whose hash was exposed
steps.desc: Reset the password for every affected account.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts have rotated credentials.

steps.title: Audit for use of any recovered password against the live system
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for use of any password recovered from the dump.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any unauthorized access.

steps.title: Restore access with new credentials that don't follow the previously-known policy pattern
steps.desc: Restore affected accounts with new passwords, and consider revising the password policy so it no longer follows a publicly-inferable, narrow pattern.
steps.outcome: Accounts restored under a less-predictable password policy.

steps.title: Investigate how the password policy details became known to the attacker
steps.desc: Record the incident and investigate whether the policy specifics were publicly documented, leaked, or learned through reconnaissance.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with the disclosure vector investigated.

steps.title: Determine whether any password has already been recovered and used
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for any login using a plaintext password matching an exposed hash.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any recovered password has been used.

steps.title: Revoke sessions and close the exfiltration path
steps.desc: Terminate active sessions for affected accounts and remediate the access path that allowed the hash dump to be exfiltrated.
steps.outcome: Sessions terminated; exfiltration path closed.

steps.title: Migrate to a salted, memory-hard algorithm
steps.desc: Migrate password storage to a salted, memory-hard algorithm, which neutralizes any precomputed table, custom or otherwise.
steps.outcome: Password storage upgraded to defeat any precomputed table approach.

ITID-12335.def: Recovery of plaintext passwords from a stolen hash by submitting the hash to a commercial or criminal cloud-based rainbow table lookup service rather than performing the lookup with locally-held infrastructure.
ITID-12335.purpose: Captures rainbow table attacks performed using a commercial or criminal cloud-based hash lookup service, lowering the barrier to entry for attackers who lack their own cracking infrastructure.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed or attributed use of a cloud-based hash lookup service (e.g. an online rainbow table lookup site) against exfiltrated hashes
scopeExcludes: Locally-held custom or standard rainbow table use (ITID-12332 through ITID-12334)
ITID-12335.severity: High - cloud lookup services dramatically lower the sophistication bar, meaning even low-resourced attackers can crack legacy-algorithm hashes quickly.
ITID-12335.priority: P1 if the hash algorithm is confirmed vulnerable to public lookup services (legacy/unsalted); P2 otherwise.
ITID-12335.escalation: Escalate immediately if the hashing scheme is known to be covered by public lookup services, since recovery is likely near-instantaneous.
indicators: Extremely rapid appearance of cracked plaintexts following exfiltration, consistent with a lookup-service query rather than local computation
Network/DNS telemetry (if available pre-exfiltration containment) showing queries to a known hash-lookup service domain
vectors: Low-sophistication attacker submitting a stolen hash to a free or paid public/criminal rainbow table lookup website
rootCauses: Legacy or unsalted hashing algorithm covered by widely available public lookup-service databases
controls: Mandatory migration to a salted, adaptive hashing algorithm not covered by public lookup-service databases
ITID-12335.detection: Shares the limited-observability profile of offline cracking on the attacker side; the notable signal here is the unusually fast turnaround from exfiltration to cracked plaintext appearing in the wild.
ITID-12335.response: Force reset for the entire affected account population immediately given the near-certainty of rapid recovery via lookup service.
metrics: Time from exfiltration to observed cracked-plaintext circulation
ITID-12335.notes: This leaf underscores that even low-sophistication attackers can achieve rapid password recovery once a hash using a lookup-service-covered algorithm is exfiltrated; treat detection latency assumptions accordingly.

playbook.name: Response: Cloud-Based Rainbow Table Lookup Service Attack
playbook.description: For an attack where an adversary submitted a stolen hash to a commercial/cloud-based rainbow table lookup service (a hash-cracking-as-a-service platform) rather than running their own precomputed table.

steps.title: Confirm the hash exposure and identify the affected accounts
steps.desc: Determine which accounts' hashes were exposed and confirm any available indicators of submission to an external lookup service.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hash exposure with full account scope.

steps.title: Force password reset for every account whose hash was exposed, immediately
steps.desc: Reset the password for every affected account without delay, given how quickly a cloud lookup service can return results.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts have rotated credentials.

steps.title: Audit for use of any recovered password against the live system
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for use of any password recovered from the dump.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any unauthorized access.

steps.title: Restore access with new credentials and enforce MFA
steps.desc: Confirm affected users have completed password resets and enforce MFA on affected accounts.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts restored with new credentials and MFA enforced.

steps.title: Document the exposure and the speed of cloud-based cracking observed
steps.desc: Record the incident, noting how quickly the attacker was able to recover a plaintext password, to emphasize urgency in future similar incidents.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a timeline emphasizing response urgency.

steps.title: Determine whether any password has already been recovered and used
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for any login using a plaintext password matching an exposed hash — cloud lookup services can return results within minutes for weak hashes.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any recovered password has been used.

steps.title: Revoke sessions and close the exfiltration path
steps.desc: Terminate active sessions for affected accounts and remediate the access path that allowed the hash dump to be exfiltrated.
steps.outcome: Sessions terminated; exfiltration path closed.

steps.title: Migrate to a salted, memory-hard algorithm
steps.desc: Migrate password storage to a salted, memory-hard algorithm, which cloud lookup services (built on precomputed unsalted tables) cannot defeat.
steps.outcome: Password storage upgraded to defeat cloud rainbow-table lookup services.

ITID-12336.def: Recovery of plaintext passwords from a Windows environment by exploiting the presence of the legacy LAN Manager (LM) hash format, either because it remains stored alongside NTLM or because an attacker forced a downgrade to generate it, and then using a precomputed table against its structurally weak design.
ITID-12336.purpose: Captures rainbow table attacks enabled by an attacker forcing or exploiting the legacy Windows LM hash format, which is trivially reversible via widely available precomputed tables due to its weak design (case-insensitive, split into two 7-character halves).
scopeIncludes: Confirmed extraction and rainbow table cracking of an LM hash present in a Windows SAM/AD database
Attacker-forced authentication downgrade specifically to generate/capture an LM hash
scopeExcludes: NTLM hash extraction/reuse without an LM-specific downgrade or exploitation, tracked under the Pass-the-Hash Tier-4 type (ITID-12721 series) rather than here
ITID-12336.severity: Critical - LM hash structure makes cracking almost trivially fast regardless of the underlying password's actual complexity.
ITID-12336.escalation: Escalate immediately to Active Directory/infrastructure engineering to confirm LM hash storage is disabled domain-wide.
indicators: Extracted SAM/AD database confirmed to contain LM hash values
Authentication protocol downgrade to LM/NTLMv1 observed in domain controller logs
vectors: Legacy AD/domain configuration still generating and storing LM hashes for backward compatibility
Attacker-forced protocol downgrade during an authentication exchange
rootCauses: Domain policy not disabling LM hash storage (a known, decades-old Windows hardening baseline item)
Legacy applications requiring LM/NTLMv1 compatibility
mitreTechniques: T1003.002 OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
controls: Group Policy setting disabling LM hash storage domain-wide (NoLMHash)
Disabling NTLMv1/LM authentication protocol support entirely
ITID-12336.detection: Domain controller security logs can detect LM/NTLMv1 protocol usage directly, and a security configuration baseline scan can confirm whether LM hash storage is disabled - both concrete, well-established technical signals.
ITID-12336.response: Disable LM hash storage and legacy protocol support immediately, force reset for every account with an LM hash present, and audit for legacy application dependencies blocking remediation.
metrics: Percentage of domain controllers with LM hash storage disabled
Count of LM hash-related incidents per year
detections: Domain controller LM/NTLMv1 protocol usage alerting
ITID-12336.notes: This leaf is scoped to the LM-hash-specific cracking weakness; NTLM hash reuse without cracking (Pass-the-Hash) is a distinct technique in a different Tier-4 type and is excluded here.

playbook.name: Response: Windows LM Hash Downgrade Rainbow Table Attack
playbook.description: For an attack exploiting the legacy Windows LM (LAN Manager) hash format — either still stored alongside NTLM or obtained via a forced downgrade — which is trivially broken by widely available rainbow tables due to its weak design (case-insensitive, split into two 7-character halves).

steps.title: Confirm LM hashes were present/obtained and identify affected accounts
steps.desc: Determine whether LM hashes were stored (vs. NTLM-only) or whether a protocol downgrade forced their use, and identify every account affected.
steps.outcome: Confirmed LM hash exposure/use with full account scope.

steps.title: Force password reset for every affected account, immediately
steps.desc: Reset the password for every affected account without delay.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts have rotated credentials.

steps.title: Audit for use of any recovered password against the domain
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for use of any password recovered via the LM hash weakness.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any unauthorized access.

steps.title: Restore access with new credentials and enforce MFA
steps.desc: Confirm affected users have completed password resets and enforce MFA on affected accounts where supported.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts restored with new credentials and MFA enforced where possible.

steps.title: Document the finding and audit the domain for other legacy protocol weaknesses
steps.desc: Record the incident and conduct a broader audit for other legacy authentication protocol weaknesses (e.g., NTLMv1 still enabled) across the domain.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; broader legacy-protocol audit initiated.

steps.title: Determine whether any password has already been recovered and used
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for any login using a plaintext password recovered from an LM hash — recovery is typically extremely fast given the format's weakness.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any recovered password has been used.

steps.title: Disable LM hash storage and block protocol downgrade
steps.desc: Apply the domain policy setting to prevent LM hash storage and disable authentication protocols that allow downgrade to LM/NTLMv1.
steps.guidance: This is a well-documented Windows hardening setting (NoLMHash policy, enforcing NTLMv2-only) — verify it is applied domain-wide, not just to the affected account.
steps.outcome: LM hash storage disabled; downgrade path blocked domain-wide.

steps.title: Remove legacy LM hash values from the domain database
steps.desc: Confirm that after the policy change and password resets, no LM hash values remain stored for any account.
steps.outcome: No LM hashes remain in the domain database.

ITID-12337.def: Recovery of plaintext passwords via precomputed table lookup against a hash dataset confirmed to have been exfiltrated from a specific, identified compromised database or application breach.
ITID-12337.purpose: Captures rainbow table attacks performed against a hash database that was exfiltrated from a specific compromised database/application, tying the cracking activity directly to a known prior breach event.
scopeIncludes: Rainbow table cracking activity directly attributed to a specific, known database exfiltration event affecting this organization
scopeExcludes: Cracking activity against a hash set of unknown/unconfirmed origin (ITID-12331 unclassified)
ITID-12337.severity: Critical - ties directly to a confirmed database breach, implying both the breach impact and the downstream cracking risk.
ITID-12337.escalation: Escalate jointly with the database breach incident response effort; this leaf should be tracked alongside, not instead of, the underlying breach incident record.
indicators: Confirmed database breach with subsequent threat intelligence showing cracked plaintexts from that specific dataset circulating
vectors: The underlying database breach/exfiltration event, followed by rainbow table cracking of the stolen hash column
rootCauses: The root cause of the underlying database breach (e.g. SQL injection, misconfigured access control) combined with weak hashing of the password column
controls: Salted, adaptive hashing algorithm limiting the impact of any future database exfiltration
Database access controls and injection-prevention controls addressing the root-cause breach vector
ITID-12337.detection: Detection ties directly to the confirmed database breach's own forensic timeline, supplemented by threat-intelligence monitoring for the cracked plaintexts' appearance.
ITID-12337.response: Force reset for the entire affected account population as part of the broader database-breach response, and confirm the hashing scheme is remediated to a modern standard.
metrics: Time from breach confirmation to full password reset
ITID-12337.notes: This leaf tracks the cracking-activity dimension specifically; the underlying database compromise itself should also be logged under the appropriate data-breach/network-intrusion domain ITID to avoid this leaf standing in as the sole record of the breach.

playbook.name: Response: Exfiltrated Database Hash Rainbow Table Attack
playbook.description: For an attack following a confirmed database breach/exfiltration where the stolen password hash table is now being cracked via rainbow table lookup — the incident encompasses both the original breach and the ongoing cracking activity.

steps.title: Confirm the database breach and scope the exfiltrated hash table
steps.desc: Confirm the database breach occurred, identify exactly which table/records were exfiltrated, and determine total account count affected.
steps.guidance: This incident starts with a data breach investigation, not just a cracking-activity detection.
steps.outcome: Confirmed breach with full scope of exfiltrated hash data.

steps.title: Close the exfiltration vector immediately
steps.desc: Patch or remediate the vulnerability/misconfiguration that allowed the database exfiltration.
steps.outcome: Exfiltration path closed.

steps.title: Audit for use of any recovered password against the live system
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for use of any password recovered from the exfiltrated table.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any unauthorized access.

steps.title: Restore access with new credentials and enforce MFA
steps.desc: Confirm affected users have completed password resets and enforce MFA on affected accounts.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts restored with new credentials and MFA enforced.

steps.title: Conduct a formal breach post-incident review, including notification obligations
steps.desc: Document the breach's root cause, scope, and response, and assess whether regulatory or customer breach-notification obligations apply.
steps.outcome: Formal after-action report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned.

steps.title: Determine the exfiltration vector and whether it is still open
steps.desc: Identify how the database was accessed (e.g., SQL injection, stolen credentials, misconfigured access) and confirm whether that path is still exploitable.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exfiltration vector, open or closed.

steps.title: Force password reset for every account in the exfiltrated table
steps.desc: Reset the password for every account in the breached table, regardless of algorithm strength, given the confirmed breach.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts have rotated credentials.

steps.title: Migrate to a salted, memory-hard algorithm
steps.desc: Migrate password storage to a salted, memory-hard algorithm so future exfiltration events cannot be rainbow-tabled.
steps.outcome: Password storage upgraded.

steps.title: Determine whether any password has already been recovered and used
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for any login using a plaintext password recovered from the exfiltrated hash table.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any recovered password has been used.

ITID-12338.def: Recovery of plaintext passwords via precomputed table lookup against a hash exfiltrated from an unpatched, end-of-life, or otherwise unsupported legacy system that inherently uses a weak/legacy hashing scheme and cannot be readily upgraded.
ITID-12338.purpose: Captures rainbow table attacks succeeding specifically because the target system is an unpatched or end-of-life legacy system that could not be upgraded to a modern hashing standard.
scopeIncludes: Rainbow table cracking against a hash from a confirmed unpatched/end-of-life legacy system
scopeExcludes: Modern, actively maintained systems that happen to use a weak algorithm by misconfiguration rather than platform/support limitation (ITID-12332, ITID-12333)
ITID-12338.severity: High - the inability to readily remediate the legacy system's hashing scheme means the exposure may persist even after the initial incident is resolved.
ITID-12338.priority: P1 for the immediate credential exposure; treat the legacy system itself as a standing risk-acceptance item requiring executive visibility.
ITID-12338.escalation: Escalate to IT leadership for a decommissioning or compensating-control decision on the legacy system, since the hashing weakness itself often cannot be patched.
indicators: Confirmed hash exfiltration from a system identified as unpatched/end-of-life in the asset inventory
vectors: Exfiltration of a hash database from a legacy system that cannot be upgraded to a modern hashing library
rootCauses: Legacy system retained past end-of-support without a decommissioning timeline or compensating controls
controls: Compensating controls for legacy systems that cannot be upgraded (network isolation, enhanced monitoring, accelerated decommissioning timeline)
ITID-12338.detection: Shares the limited-observability profile of offline cracking; the asset inventory's legacy/end-of-life flag is the key contextual signal tying the incident to this specific root cause.
ITID-12338.response: Force reset for the affected account population, and escalate the underlying legacy-system risk for a formal risk-acceptance or decommissioning decision.
metrics: Count of legacy-system rainbow table incidents per year
Number of legacy systems with a documented decommissioning timeline
ITID-12338.notes: This leaf should trigger a governance-level risk-acceptance review for the legacy system, since the underlying hashing weakness is often not immediately fixable through the incident response process alone.

playbook.name: Response: Rainbow Table Attack Against Unpatched Legacy System
playbook.description: For an attack exploiting an unpatched or end-of-life legacy system that stores passwords using an outdated, unsalted or otherwise weak hashing method the vendor never updated.

steps.title: Confirm the hash exposure and identify the legacy system involved
steps.desc: Determine which accounts' hashes were exposed and confirm the specific legacy system, its patch level, and its hashing implementation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hash exposure with the legacy system and its weakness identified.

steps.title: Force password reset for every account whose hash was exposed
steps.desc: Reset the password for every affected account.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts have rotated credentials.

steps.title: Audit for use of any recovered password against the system
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for use of any password recovered from the exposed hashes.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any unauthorized access.

steps.title: Restore access with new credentials and enforce MFA where possible
steps.desc: Confirm affected users have completed password resets and enforce MFA on the legacy system or a fronting proxy if the system itself doesn't support it.
steps.outcome: Affected accounts restored with new credentials and MFA enforced where feasible.

steps.title: Document the finding and prioritize legacy system decommissioning/replacement
steps.desc: Record the incident and use it to justify prioritizing the legacy system's replacement or decommissioning given it cannot support modern password security.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a decommissioning/replacement recommendation escalated to system owners.

steps.title: Determine whether any password has already been recovered and used
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for any login using a plaintext password matching an exposed hash.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any recovered password has been used.

steps.title: Isolate or restrict access to the legacy system pending remediation
steps.desc: Restrict network access to the legacy system to only what is strictly necessary while a longer-term fix is planned.
steps.outcome: Legacy system's exposure reduced.

steps.title: Apply available patches or compensating controls to the legacy system
steps.desc: Apply any available vendor patch, or if the system is end-of-life with no patch available, implement compensating controls (e.g., proxy authentication through a modern identity provider) since the underlying weak hashing cannot be fixed directly.
steps.outcome: Legacy system patched or compensating controls in place.

ITID-12339.def: A rainbow table attack incident (any of ITID-12332 through ITID-12338) in which plaintext password recovery is confirmed and subsequent unauthorized use of that recovered credential is observed.
ITID-12339.purpose: Captures confirmed successful rainbow table attack resulting in plaintext password recovery and subsequent account/system access, distinguishing outcome-confirmed compromise from mere cracking-attempt indicators for severity/priority purposes.
scopeIncludes: Any rainbow table method variant where recovered plaintext credentials are confirmed subsequently used for unauthorized access
scopeExcludes: Hash exfiltration/rainbow-table-feasibility cases where subsequent recovery and use has not been confirmed (the specific method-based sibling leaves)
ITID-12339.severity: Critical - confirmed recovery and use, markedly higher than any feasibility-only sibling leaf.
ITID-12339.escalation: Escalate immediately to IAM/SOC for session revocation, credential reset, and full access audit across every account in the exfiltrated dataset.
indicators: Successful authentication using a credential known to have been in an exfiltrated hash dataset, followed by observed account/system activity
Threat intelligence confirms cracked plaintext credentials being actively traded or used
vectors: Any rainbow table method where the recovered plaintext was subsequently used for unauthorized access, particularly against accounts lacking MFA
rootCauses: No MFA on the affected account
Delayed or incomplete credential reset following the initial hash exfiltration
controls: MFA enforcement on all accounts
Rapid, complete credential reset workflow following any confirmed hash exfiltration
ITID-12339.detection: Authentication success logs correlated with the known exfiltrated-account population, combined with post-login activity monitoring, provide a strong technical confirmation trail.
ITID-12339.response: Revoke sessions, force reset for the full affected population if not already completed, and conduct a full audit of actions taken during the compromise window.
metrics: Count of confirmed rainbow table compromises per quarter
Mean time from exfiltration to full reset completion
ITID-12339.notes: This is the confirmed-outcome escalation applicable across any rainbow table method sibling leaf; it does not restate the method-specific scoping of ITID-12332 through ITID-12338.

playbook.name: Response: Successful Rainbow Table Attack with Confirmed Recovery
playbook.description: For a confirmed case where a rainbow table attack (of any variant) successfully recovered one or more plaintext passwords and those passwords were used for unauthorized access — the high-severity, post-compromise variant requiring full account/system-takeover response.

steps.title: Confirm and scope the successful recovery and its use
steps.desc: Establish, from logs, that one or more passwords were recovered and used for unauthorized access, and determine the accounts/systems affected and access timestamps.
steps.outcome: Confirmed successful recovery and use with full timeline documented.

steps.title: Force credential reset and revoke sessions/tokens for all affected accounts
steps.desc: Reset the compromised credentials and invalidate all active sessions and tokens for every affected account.
steps.outcome: Credentials rotated; sessions and tokens terminated.

steps.title: Remove all attacker persistence across affected accounts/systems
steps.desc: Remove rogue MFA enrollments, keys, accounts, or backdoors found across the full scope.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access mechanism remains anywhere in scope.

steps.title: Restore access and validate with the user/owner
steps.desc: Restore access for all affected accounts/systems and confirm with the owner that access and data look correct.
steps.outcome: Verified-clean access restored.

steps.title: Conduct a formal post-incident review
steps.desc: Document root cause, full timeline, blast radius, and required control changes; report to relevant stakeholders per incident severity policy.
steps.outcome: Formal after-action report completed with assigned remediation owners.

steps.title: Determine full extent of attacker activity post-access
steps.desc: Review all activity performed by the attacker during their access window: data accessed, files touched, systems reached, configuration changes.
steps.outcome: Complete activity timeline for the compromised access.

steps.title: Contain any downstream systems or accounts affected
steps.desc: Apply containment (credential reset, session revocation, isolation) to any secondary account or system identified in the blast-radius assessment.
steps.outcome: Blast radius fully contained.

steps.title: Migrate the underlying system to a salted, memory-hard algorithm
steps.desc: Complete the root-cause fix by migrating password storage to a salted, memory-hard algorithm to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Password storage upgraded to defeat future rainbow-table attempts.

steps.title: Extended monitoring of all affected accounts/systems
steps.desc: Place all affected accounts/systems under elevated monitoring for at least 30 days.
steps.outcome: No further anomalous activity observed during the window.

steps.title: Assess blast radius to other accounts and systems
steps.desc: Determine whether the attacker used this access to pivot to other accounts, shared resources, or connected systems.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of impact beyond the initial account/system.

ITID-12411.def: An incident involving use of an administrative credential in a manner inconsistent with its authorized purpose, not yet matched to a more specific misuse pattern.
ITID-12411.purpose: Catch-all for misuse of an administrative credential that does not fit a more specific leaf under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific misuse pattern is confirmed
General admin credential misuse pending reclassification
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Misused Admin Credentials
ITID-12411.severity: Medium pending triage; reassess once the specific pattern is known.
ITID-12411.priority: P2 by default given privileged scope.
ITID-12411.escalation: Escalate to IAM/security engineering once the specific misuse pattern is identified; reclassify accordingly.
indicators: Privileged-account activity flagged by SIEM correlation rule without a clear specific pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector involving an administrative account
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Privileged access management (PAM) session logging
ITID-12411.detection: Same PAM/SIEM telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-12411.response: Investigate and reclassify to a specific leaf once the misuse pattern is confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-12411.notes: Intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Misused Admin Credential
playbook.description: Baseline response for a report or detection of an administrative credential being used inappropriately, where the specific nature of the misuse has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm the anomalous use of the admin credential
steps.desc: Review the alert or report and confirm the specific action, time, and source that appears to constitute misuse.
steps.outcome: Confirmed anomalous use with supporting evidence.
steps.abort: If the action is explained by a documented, approved activity, close as a false positive.

steps.title: Suspend or restrict the admin credential pending investigation
steps.desc: Temporarily disable or restrict the admin account's access while the investigation is underway.
steps.outcome: Admin credential access halted or restricted.

steps.title: Review all actions taken with the credential during the period in question
steps.desc: Conduct a full review of privileged actions taken using the credential to determine the extent of any unauthorized change.
steps.outcome: Complete inventory of actions taken with the credential.

steps.title: Restore appropriate access under normal governance
steps.desc: Restore the account to normal, governed access if the legitimate holder is confirmed clean, or reassign/decommission if compromise is confirmed.
steps.outcome: Account access restored appropriately based on investigation findings.

steps.title: Document the finding and recommend privileged access control improvements
steps.desc: Record the incident and, if a systemic gap in privileged access monitoring or governance is identified, recommend a concrete improvement.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a concrete control recommendation.

steps.title: Determine the nature of the misuse
steps.desc: Classify whether this is external attacker use of a compromised credential, out-of-window use, unauthorized data access, disabling of security controls, shared-account misuse, privilege creep, break-glass misuse, or lateral movement.
steps.guidance: Reclassify to the more specific ITID playbook once known and continue from there if one exists.
steps.outcome: Misuse correctly classified by nature.

steps.title: Revoke active sessions tied to the credential
steps.desc: Terminate any active sessions or tokens associated with the admin credential.
steps.outcome: Sessions terminated.

steps.title: Reverse any unauthorized change and rotate the credential
steps.desc: Reverse any confirmed unauthorized change and rotate the admin credential.
steps.outcome: Environment restored; credential rotated.

steps.title: Determine the identity behind the credential use
steps.desc: Determine whether the action was performed by the legitimate credential holder, an external attacker, or another insider with access to the credential.
steps.outcome: Confirmed or reasonably assessed actor behind the action.

ITID-12412.def: Use of a valid administrative credential by an external threat actor who obtained it through compromise (phishing, credential stuffing, malware, purchase), distinguishing attacker-driven misuse from insider misuse of the same credential class.
ITID-12412.purpose: Captures the case where an external adversary, not an insider, is operating with a compromised administrative credential.
scopeIncludes: Admin logon from external/unrecognized geography or ASN following credential compromise
Admin session activity inconsistent with the legitimate account holder's known behavior pattern
scopeExcludes: Misuse of an admin credential by its legitimate holder (see other siblings in this Type)
Initial credential theft itself (tracked under Credential Leakage ITIDs) when no admin use has yet occurred
ITID-12412.severity: High to Critical — external control of a privileged account.
ITID-12412.escalation: Immediate escalation to incident response for containment (credential revocation, session termination, forced re-auth) and threat hunting for lateral movement.
indicators: Admin logon from anomalous geolocation/ASN with impossible-travel from the legitimate user's last known location
New privileged session immediately followed by reconnaissance-style commands
MFA fatigue/push-bombing accepted just before privileged action
vectors: Phishing-obtained admin credential reuse
Credential-stuffing success against an admin account lacking MFA
Purchase of previously leaked admin credential from an access broker
rootCauses: Admin account not enrolled in phishing-resistant MFA
No conditional access / impossible-travel policy on privileged accounts
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA on all administrative accounts
Conditional access / impossible-travel detection for privileged logons
ITID-12412.detection: Strong: identity provider and SIEM impossible-travel/anomalous-geo alerting on privileged accounts is a real technical signal.
ITID-12412.response: Immediately revoke/rotate the credential, terminate active sessions, and hunt for downstream lateral movement.
metrics: Mean time to revoke compromised admin credentials
Count of external-origin privileged logons detected
ITID-12412.notes: Scoped to attacker-driven misuse specifically; misuse by the legitimate insider holder is tracked under sibling leaves (e.g. ITID-12413 through ITID-12417) to avoid duplication.

playbook.name: Response: External Attacker Using Compromised Admin Credential
playbook.description: For a confirmed case where an external attacker obtained and is actively using a legitimate administrative credential, representing a high-severity account-takeover of a privileged account.

steps.title: Confirm external attacker use and escalate severity immediately
steps.desc: Confirm from source IP/geolocation/device fingerprint that the credential is being used by someone other than the legitimate holder, and escalate incident severity given the privileged nature of the account.
steps.outcome: Confirmed external compromise with severity escalated per policy.

steps.title: Suspend the admin account immediately
steps.desc: Disable the compromised admin account without delay.
steps.outcome: Account access halted immediately.

steps.title: Remove all attacker persistence
steps.desc: Remove any rogue account, disabled logging setting, permission grant, or other persistence mechanism created by the attacker.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access mechanism remains anywhere in scope.

steps.title: Restore privileged access on hardened, monitored terms
steps.desc: Reissue the admin credential with a new password, phishing-resistant MFA, and place the account under enhanced monitoring.
steps.outcome: Admin access restored on hardened, monitored terms.

steps.title: Conduct a formal post-incident review
steps.desc: Document root cause (how the credential was compromised), full timeline, blast radius, and required control changes (phishing-resistant MFA, PAM adoption); report to relevant stakeholders per incident severity policy.
steps.outcome: Formal after-action report completed with assigned remediation owners.

steps.title: Determine the full extent of attacker activity
steps.desc: Review every privileged action taken by the attacker during their access window: config changes, new accounts, permission grants, log deletions, data access.
steps.guidance: An attacker with admin access will often try to create persistence or disable logging quickly — check both explicitly.
steps.outcome: Complete inventory of attacker actions.

steps.title: Revoke all sessions, tokens, and standing elevated-access grants
steps.desc: Terminate all sessions and review/revoke any just-in-time or standing privileged access grants tied to the account.
steps.outcome: All sessions and elevated grants terminated.

steps.title: Reverse all unauthorized configuration changes
steps.desc: Undo any unauthorized change made by the attacker to restore the environment to its pre-incident state.
steps.outcome: Environment restored to pre-incident state.

steps.title: Extended monitoring of the account and affected systems
steps.desc: Place the account and all affected systems under elevated monitoring for at least 30 days.
steps.outcome: No further anomalous activity observed during the window.

steps.title: Assess blast radius across the environment
steps.desc: Determine what other systems, accounts, or data the compromised admin credential could reach, and check for evidence of lateral movement.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of potential and actual impact.

steps.title: Contain any downstream systems or accounts affected by lateral movement
steps.desc: Apply containment to any secondary system/account identified in the blast-radius assessment.
steps.outcome: Blast radius fully contained.

ITID-12413.def: Use of an administrative credential to make changes to a system or environment outside the time boundaries of an approved change ticket, whether by an insider or by an attacker exploiting the change process's blind spot.
ITID-12413.purpose: Captures administrative credential use that falls outside an approved change-management window.
scopeIncludes: Privileged change activity with no corresponding open/approved change ticket
Change activity that extends materially beyond the approved window
scopeExcludes: Change activity within an approved window (not an incident)
Unauthorized data access or control-disabling using an admin credential (see ITID-12414, ITID-12415)
ITID-12413.severity: Medium, escalating to High if the change affects production security controls or sensitive systems.
ITID-12413.escalation: Escalate to change management and the system owner for verification; escalate to security if the change cannot be attributed to an approved activity.
indicators: Privileged configuration change logged with no matching CAB/change ticket
Change timestamp outside the ticket's approved maintenance window
vectors: Insider making unauthorized changes under cover of routine admin access
Attacker with a compromised admin credential making changes timed to avoid staffed hours
rootCauses: Change management process not technically enforced (no automated ticket-to-action correlation)
Weak out-of-hours monitoring of privileged change activity
controls: Change-ticket-to-privileged-action correlation in SIEM
Out-of-hours privileged activity alerting
ITID-12413.detection: Change management system and privileged-session logs correlated in SIEM provide a concrete technical signal.
ITID-12413.response: Verify business justification with the account holder and change owner; treat as a security incident if unattributable.
metrics: Count of out-of-window privileged changes detected per quarter
ITID-12413.notes: Scoped to the timing/process-control dimension of admin misuse; the nature of the change itself (data access, control disabling) is scoped to ITID-12414/ITID-12415 to avoid overlap.

playbook.name: Response: Admin Credential Used Outside Approved Change Window
playbook.description: For an incident where an administrative credential performed changes outside an organization's approved change management window, without a corresponding emergency change approval.

steps.title: Confirm the change and its timing against the change schedule
steps.desc: Confirm the specific change made and its timestamp, and cross-reference against the approved change calendar to confirm it fell outside an approved window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed out-of-window change with supporting evidence.
steps.abort: If an emergency change record exists covering this action, close as compliant.
steps.tool: Change management system / privileged access audit log

steps.title: Assess whether the change should be rolled back
steps.desc: Determine, with the system owner, whether the out-of-window change is safe to leave in place or should be reverted pending proper review.
steps.outcome: Rollback decision made and documented.

steps.title: Confirm no other unauthorized changes were made in the same session
steps.desc: Review the full session for any other change made at the same time that may also require review.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of the session limited to the identified change(s).

steps.title: Restore normal operations and confirm system stability
steps.desc: Confirm the affected system is stable and operating normally following any rollback or retroactive approval.
steps.outcome: System confirmed stable.

steps.title: Document the process gap and reinforce change management policy
steps.desc: Record the incident, address it through the appropriate disciplinary/coaching process if warranted, and reinforce the change management policy including the emergency-change process to the wider admin team.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; process reinforcement communicated.

steps.title: Determine what the change actually did
steps.desc: Assess the technical content and impact of the change made outside the window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed nature and impact of the unauthorized-timing change.

steps.title: Roll back the change if determined unsafe or unauthorized
steps.desc: Revert the change to its pre-change state if the review determines it should not stand.
steps.outcome: System restored to its prior, approved state if warranted.
steps.abort: If the change is deemed safe and beneficial, formally retroactively approve it instead of rolling back.

steps.title: Interview the credential holder for justification
steps.desc: Ask the account holder why the change was made outside the approved window and whether it was an emergency, an oversight, or unauthorized.
steps.outcome: Documented explanation from the credential holder.

ITID-12414.def: Use of an administrative credential's elevated data-access rights to view, export, or exfiltrate data not required for the holder's legitimate duties.
ITID-12414.purpose: Captures use of an administrative credential specifically to access data outside the account holder's job need.
scopeIncludes: Admin account used to browse or query databases/file shares unrelated to assigned duties
Bulk export of sensitive data using administrative access rights
scopeExcludes: Administrative changes to system configuration (see ITID-12413)
Disabling of security controls using admin access (see ITID-12415)
ITID-12414.severity: High — privileged data-access abuse often implicates regulated or sensitive data.
ITID-12414.priority: P1 if sensitive/regulated data is involved, otherwise P2.
ITID-12414.escalation: Escalate to data protection/privacy and legal if regulated data (PII, PHI, financial) is confirmed accessed.
indicators: Admin account querying/exporting data unrelated to its functional role
Large or bulk data export via privileged access with no business ticket
vectors: Insider abusing standing admin rights to browse sensitive records
Compromised admin credential used for data staging prior to exfiltration
rootCauses: Admin roles scoped too broadly (no data-domain segmentation)
No DLP/UEBA monitoring on privileged data access
controls: UEBA baselining of privileged-account data access
DLP monitoring on privileged export activity
ITID-12414.detection: UEBA/DLP telemetry on privileged accounts gives a concrete, real signal distinct from generic activity logging.
ITID-12414.response: Investigate data accessed, determine business justification, and notify data protection/legal if unauthorized access to regulated data is confirmed.
metrics: Count of unauthorized privileged data-access events confirmed per quarter
ITID-12414.notes: Scoped to the data-access dimension of admin misuse only; disabling controls or off-window changes are tracked in sibling leaves to avoid duplication.

playbook.name: Response: Admin Credential Used for Unauthorized Data Access
playbook.description: For an incident where an administrative credential was used to access data outside the legitimate scope of the holder's job duties or an approved investigation — an insider-risk-flavored privilege abuse case.

steps.title: Confirm the data accessed and compare against the holder's legitimate need
steps.desc: Identify exactly what data was accessed, and confirm it falls outside the credential holder's job function or any approved investigation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized data access with scope documented.
steps.abort: If the access is explained by a documented job duty or approved investigation, close as a false positive.
steps.tool: Data access audit log / privileged access audit log

steps.title: Restrict the credential's data access scope pending investigation
steps.desc: Narrow or suspend the admin credential's access to the data category in question while the investigation proceeds.
steps.outcome: Further unauthorized access to the data category prevented.

steps.title: Determine whether the accessed data was copied, exported, or shared
steps.desc: Check for evidence the data was downloaded, emailed, or otherwise moved outside its authorized location.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the data left its authorized boundary.

steps.title: Adjust the credential's access based on the investigation outcome
steps.desc: Restore, permanently restrict, or revoke the credential's data access based on the investigation's outcome.
steps.outcome: Access rights finalized consistent with the investigation outcome.

steps.title: Document the incident and review access scoping for similar roles
steps.desc: Record the incident and assess whether other admin roles have overly broad data access that should be scoped down to least privilege.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with an access-scoping recommendation.

steps.title: Assess sensitivity of the accessed data
steps.desc: Determine whether the accessed data includes PII, financial records, HR data, or other sensitive categories that carry regulatory or contractual notification obligations.
steps.outcome: Confirmed data sensitivity classification.

steps.title: Preserve evidence of the access for HR/legal review
steps.desc: Export and securely preserve the relevant access logs, since this incident may lead to an HR or legal process.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved in a manner suitable for HR/legal use.

steps.title: Engage HR/legal and determine formal next steps
steps.desc: Hand off the findings to HR and/or legal for a determination on disciplinary or legal action, per the organization's insider-risk process.
steps.outcome: HR/legal engaged with a documented handoff.

ITID-12415.def: Use of administrative access rights to disable, tamper with, or degrade a security control (EDR, logging, firewall rule, MFA enforcement) rather than to access data or make routine changes.
ITID-12415.purpose: Captures use of an administrative credential to weaken or disable a security control.
scopeIncludes: Disabling or uninstalling endpoint security agents via admin rights
Disabling audit logging, alerting rules, or MFA enforcement using admin access
scopeExcludes: Legitimate, ticketed maintenance disabling of a control within an approved window (not an incident)
Unauthorized data access using admin rights without control tampering (see ITID-12414)
ITID-12415.severity: Critical — control tampering frequently precedes or accompanies a broader compromise.
ITID-12415.escalation: Immediate escalation to incident response; treat as probable precursor to further compromise and initiate threat hunting.
indicators: EDR/AV agent stopped, uninstalled, or tampered with via admin command
Audit/logging service disabled or log retention policy altered
MFA enforcement policy disabled for one or more accounts
vectors: Attacker with compromised admin credential disabling EDR ahead of payload deployment
Insider disabling logging to cover fraudulent activity
rootCauses: Admin accounts able to modify security tooling without secondary approval
No tamper-protection/alerting on security-control configuration changes
mitreTechniques: T1562.001 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging
controls: EDR tamper protection
Security-control configuration-change alerting
ITID-12415.detection: EDR tamper-protection alerts and SIEM configuration-change monitoring provide a strong, concrete technical signal.
ITID-12415.response: Immediately restore the disabled control, isolate affected hosts, and hunt for concurrent or follow-on malicious activity.
metrics: Mean time to detect security-control tampering
Count of control-tampering events per quarter
ITID-12415.notes: Scoped narrowly to control-tampering; data access and change-window violations are tracked in ITID-12414 and ITID-12413 respectively.

playbook.name: Response: Admin Credential Used to Disable Security Controls
playbook.description: For a high-severity incident where an administrative credential was used to disable, weaken, or delete a security control (e.g., EDR, logging, firewall rule, MFA requirement) — a classic pre-cursor to or indicator of a broader compromise.

steps.title: Confirm the specific control disabled and escalate severity immediately
steps.desc: Confirm exactly which security control was disabled/weakened/deleted and by which credential, and escalate severity given this is a common attacker technique to enable further compromise.
steps.guidance: Treat this as a probable active-attacker indicator until proven otherwise, even if the credential appears to be a legitimate admin's.
steps.outcome: Confirmed control disablement with severity escalated per policy.

steps.title: Re-enable the disabled security control immediately
steps.desc: Restore the disabled control to its proper operating state without delay.
steps.outcome: Security control restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Hunt for compromise indicators across the environment
steps.desc: Given the control disablement, conduct a proactive threat hunt across the environment for indicators of compromise that the disabled control may have been intended to hide.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of broader compromise.

steps.title: Restore access under enhanced monitoring and control-change alerting
steps.desc: Restore appropriate access and ensure the environment now alerts specifically on future security-control-disabling actions.
steps.outcome: Access restored; control-disablement alerting confirmed active.

steps.title: Conduct a formal post-incident review
steps.desc: Document root cause, full timeline, and required control changes (e.g., requiring dual-approval for disabling security controls); report to relevant stakeholders per incident severity policy.
steps.outcome: Formal after-action report completed with assigned remediation owners.

steps.title: Determine whether the credential holder authorized this or is compromised
steps.desc: Interview the credential holder and review source IP/device to assess whether they legitimately made the change or whether the credential is being used by an attacker.
steps.outcome: Confirmed or reasonably assessed actor behind the change.

steps.title: Suspend the credential and revoke sessions pending investigation
steps.desc: Disable the admin account and terminate its active sessions while the investigation proceeds.
steps.outcome: Credential access halted.

steps.title: Remediate any compromise found and rotate the credential
steps.desc: Remediate any confirmed compromise from the threat hunt, and rotate the admin credential with new MFA enrollment.
steps.outcome: Environment confirmed clean; credential rotated.

steps.title: Assess what activity occurred while the control was disabled
steps.desc: Review whatever alternate telemetry remains (network logs, other systems' logs) for any suspicious activity that occurred during the window the control was down.
steps.guidance: This is critical — if EDR/logging was disabled specifically to hide activity, that activity needs to be found via other means.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of activity during the control-down window, to the extent determinable.

ITID-12416.def: Misuse of an administrative account that is shared among multiple individuals or systems, where the lack of individual attribution is itself a contributing factor to the incident.
ITID-12416.purpose: Captures misuse tied specifically to a shared or generic (non-individually-attributable) administrative account.
scopeIncludes: Misuse traced to a generic admin login (e.g. "admin", "root", shared team account) with multiple known users
Inability to attribute a confirmed misuse event to a specific individual due to account sharing
scopeExcludes: Misuse of an individually-assigned admin account (see other siblings in this Type)
Service account misuse (tracked under Service Account Exploitation)
ITID-12416.severity: Medium-High; the attribution gap itself elevates investigative and control-failure severity.
ITID-12416.escalation: Escalate to IAM to force immediate credential rotation and individual-account migration for the shared account.
indicators: Privileged activity logged under a generic/shared account identifier with no session-level user mapping
Multiple concurrent sessions from a single shared admin credential
vectors: Legacy shared admin account never migrated to individual privileged accounts
Shared credential distributed via insecure channel to multiple staff
rootCauses: No policy enforcing individually attributable privileged accounts
PAM solution not deployed or not enforced for legacy shared accounts
controls: PAM enforcement of individually attributable privileged access
Prohibition of shared/generic administrative credentials
ITID-12416.detection: Limited by design — shared-account use is itself the detection gap; PAM session recording is the primary mitigating control once deployed.
ITID-12416.response: Investigate using available session recordings/logs; remediate by decommissioning the shared account in favor of individual PAM-vaulted accounts.
metrics: Count of remaining shared/generic admin accounts in inventory
ITID-12416.notes: This leaf's differentiator is the account-sharing/attribution-gap dimension itself, distinguishing it from siblings scoped by the nature of the misuse.

playbook.name: Response: Shared/Generic Admin Account Misuse
playbook.description: For an incident involving misuse of a shared or generic administrative account (e.g., a common 'admin' login used by multiple people), where individual accountability for the action is unclear by design.

steps.title: Confirm the misuse and identify everyone with access to the shared credential
steps.desc: Confirm the specific misuse and pull the list of everyone who has legitimate access to the shared account's credential.
steps.outcome: Confirmed misuse with the full access list identified.

steps.title: Suspend the shared account and rotate its credential
steps.desc: Disable the shared account and rotate its password via the formal vault/rotation process.
steps.outcome: Shared account access halted; credential rotated.

steps.title: Review all actions taken with the shared credential in the relevant period
steps.desc: Conduct a full review of actions taken with the shared credential to determine the extent of the misuse.
steps.outcome: Complete inventory of actions taken with the credential.

steps.title: Reissue the credential only to currently-authorized individuals
steps.desc: Restore the account's availability but reissue access only to a verified, currently-authorized list of individuals.
steps.outcome: Account restored with a validated access list.

steps.title: Recommend eliminating the shared account in favor of individual accountability
steps.desc: Document the accountability gap this incident exposed and recommend replacing the shared account with individual named accounts plus role-based access, or at minimum enabling PAM session recording for all shared-account use.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a concrete governance recommendation.

steps.title: Attempt attribution using secondary evidence
steps.desc: Use secondary evidence (source IP, device fingerprint, badge/VPN logs, PAM session recording if available) to narrow down which individual likely performed the action.
steps.outcome: Best-effort attribution to a specific individual, or confirmed inability to attribute.

steps.title: Reverse any unauthorized action found
steps.desc: Reverse or remediate any confirmed unauthorized change made with the shared credential.
steps.outcome: Environment restored to pre-incident state.

ITID-12417.def: Misuse of administrative access that an individual retains due to accumulated, un-reviewed privilege grants (role changes, project assignments) rather than a fresh or deliberate grant, where the excess privilege itself is the root cause of the exposure.
ITID-12417.purpose: Captures misuse enabled by privilege creep — accumulated administrative rights beyond current job need.
scopeIncludes: Misuse by a current employee using admin rights left over from a prior role
Access-review finding confirming misuse potential from unreviewed accumulated privileges
scopeExcludes: Misuse by an account holder whose admin rights are current and appropriately scoped (see other siblings)
Misuse of a departed employee's account (tracked under Abandoned Accounts)
ITID-12417.severity: Medium, escalating if the excess privilege was actively exploited.
ITID-12417.escalation: Escalate to IAM governance for immediate rights right-sizing; escalate to security if active exploitation is confirmed.
indicators: Access review flags admin rights inconsistent with current role
Privileged activity in a system unrelated to the individual's current job function
vectors: Insider exploiting retained rights from a previous role for unauthorized access
Attacker exploiting an over-privileged compromised account for broader lateral movement than a right-sized account would allow
rootCauses: No periodic access recertification process
Role changes not triggering automatic deprovisioning of prior entitlements
controls: Periodic access recertification / entitlement review
Role-based access control with automatic deprovisioning on role change
ITID-12417.detection: Access-review and IAM governance tooling (entitlement analytics) provide the primary technical signal; supplemented by UEBA on privileged activity outside role norms.
ITID-12417.response: Right-size the account's entitlements immediately; investigate any activity that occurred under the excess privilege.
metrics: Count of excess-privilege findings remediated per review cycle
ITID-12417.notes: Differentiator is root cause (accumulated, un-reviewed privilege) rather than the misuse action itself.

playbook.name: Response: Admin Credential Privilege Creep Misuse
playbook.description: For an incident where an admin account's accumulated, never-reviewed excess permissions (privilege creep from past roles/projects) were used to take an action outside the individual's current legitimate scope.

steps.title: Confirm the action and the permission that enabled it
steps.desc: Identify the specific action taken and the specific permission grant that made it possible.
steps.outcome: Confirmed action and enabling permission.

steps.title: Remove the stale permission immediately
steps.desc: Revoke the excess permission from the account.
steps.outcome: Stale permission removed; account scoped to current legitimate role.

steps.title: Reverse any unauthorized change made using the permission
steps.desc: If the action taken with the stale permission caused an unauthorized change, reverse it.
steps.outcome: Environment restored to appropriate state.
steps.abort: If the action was benign or authorized despite the technicality, no reversal is needed.

steps.title: Confirm the account's access now matches current role requirements
steps.desc: Verify the account's permissions are fully aligned with the individual's current job function.
steps.outcome: Confirmed least-privilege alignment.

steps.title: Recommend periodic access recertification
steps.desc: Document the finding and recommend implementing or tightening a periodic (e.g., quarterly) access recertification process to catch privilege creep proactively.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a governance process recommendation.

steps.title: Trace the permission's origin and determine if it is stale
steps.desc: Determine when and why the permission was originally granted, and confirm it is no longer relevant to the individual's current role.
steps.guidance: This is the defining characteristic of privilege creep — a legitimately-granted permission from a past role that was never revoked.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the permission is stale and unrelated to current duties.
steps.abort: If the permission is still relevant to the current role, this may not be privilege creep — reassess classification.

steps.title: Run a broader access review for similar stale permissions
steps.desc: Search for other accounts with similarly stale, unreviewed permissions from past roles or projects.
steps.outcome: Other accounts with stale permissions identified for remediation.

steps.title: Assess whether the action itself was malicious, negligent, or a reasonable mistake
steps.desc: Interview the credential holder and assess intent behind using the stale permission.
steps.outcome: Documented intent assessment.

ITID-12418.def: Unauthorized or unjustified use of a break-glass/emergency administrative account outside a declared emergency, or failure to follow required post-use review of a legitimate break-glass activation.
ITID-12418.purpose: Captures misuse of a break-glass or emergency-access administrative account.
scopeIncludes: Break-glass account activated with no corresponding declared incident/emergency
Break-glass credential used and not rotated/reviewed per policy after use
scopeExcludes: Legitimately declared emergency use, reviewed and closed per policy (not an incident)
Misuse of a standing (non-break-glass) admin account (see other siblings)
ITID-12418.severity: High — break-glass accounts typically carry the highest privilege tier in the environment.
ITID-12418.escalation: Escalate immediately to IAM and security leadership; break-glass activation without justification is treated as a potential active compromise until proven otherwise.
indicators: Break-glass account credential checked out/used with no matching emergency ticket
Break-glass credential not rotated within required post-use window
vectors: Attacker who has compromised the break-glass credential vault
Insider abusing break-glass access to bypass normal approval workflows
rootCauses: Break-glass account not subject to automated post-use rotation
No real-time alerting on break-glass account checkout
controls: PAM real-time alerting on break-glass checkout
Mandatory post-use credential rotation for break-glass accounts
ITID-12418.detection: PAM vault checkout logging and real-time alerting provide a strong, concrete technical signal.
ITID-12418.response: Verify emergency justification immediately; if unjustified, treat as a confirmed privileged compromise and initiate full incident response.
metrics: Count of break-glass activations reviewed and closed vs. unjustified
sops: Break-Glass Account Usage and Review SOP
ITID-12418.notes: Scoped specifically to the break-glass account class, distinct from standing admin account misuse covered by sibling leaves.

playbook.name: Response: Break-Glass/Emergency Admin Account Misuse
playbook.description: For an incident where a break-glass/emergency admin account (intended only for use when normal privileged access is unavailable) was used outside a genuine emergency, or without following the required post-use review process.

steps.title: Confirm the break-glass account was used and identify who used it
steps.desc: Confirm the usage event from the vault/PAM checkout log and identify who checked out the credential.
steps.outcome: Confirmed usage with individual identified.

steps.title: Rotate the break-glass credential per standard post-use procedure
steps.desc: Rotate the break-glass account's credential immediately after use, per the organization's break-glass policy, regardless of whether the use was justified.
steps.guidance: Break-glass credentials should always be rotated after every use as standard procedure.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated.

steps.title: Review all actions taken during the break-glass session
steps.desc: Conduct a full review of actions taken during the session to confirm they were limited to the claimed emergency purpose.
steps.outcome: Complete inventory of actions taken, assessed for scope creep beyond the claimed emergency.
steps.tool: PAM session recording / privileged access audit log

steps.title: Confirm the break-glass account is returned to its dormant, monitored state
steps.desc: Confirm the account is disabled/locked in its normal at-rest state pending the next legitimate emergency, with monitoring/alerting active on any future checkout.
