steps.outcome: Accounts restored and under monitoring.

steps.title: Document combolist source and stuffing exposure
steps.desc: Record the combolist source and any control gaps in anti-stuffing protections identified during response.
steps.outcome: Finding logged.

steps.title: Validate matched accounts against the directory
steps.desc: Confirm which matched entries correspond to current, active organizational accounts.
steps.guidance: Combolists often contain stale entries from old breaches; check account status and credential age.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of current active accounts in the combolist.
steps.abort: If no current accounts match, log as informational only.

steps.title: Enable credential-stuffing protections
steps.desc: Confirm rate limiting, bot detection, and MFA are enforced on all externally-facing login portals given elevated stuffing risk.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the WAF/application security team.
steps.outcome: Anti-stuffing controls confirmed active on external portals.

ITID-12527.def: Threat-intelligence-confirmed interest, reconnaissance, or general marketplace reputation activity by a known Initial Access Broker (IAB) actor concerning the organization, without yet a discrete access-for-sale listing.
ITID-12527.purpose: Captures ongoing tracking of an Initial Access Broker's known interest in or general activity concerning the organization, distinct from a specific active listing.
scopeIncludes: Threat-intel report naming a known IAB actor as having expressed interest in or scanned the organization
IAB forum activity referencing the organization without a discrete priced listing
scopeExcludes: A specific, active, priced access-for-sale listing (see ITID-12522)
ITID-12527.severity: Medium-High — a precursor signal warranting proactive hardening rather than a confirmed active sale.
ITID-12527.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if a listing subsequently appears.
ITID-12527.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence and security engineering for proactive hardening of likely-targeted external services.
indicators: Threat-intelligence feed correlating known IAB actor TTPs/infrastructure with reconnaissance against organizational assets
vectors: IAB actor conducting reconnaissance/scanning against externally facing services as a precursor to obtaining and listing access
rootCauses: Externally facing attack surface not proactively monitored for reconnaissance activity
controls: Threat intelligence monitoring for known IAB actor activity
Proactive external attack-surface hardening
ITID-12527.detection: Threat-intelligence feeds tracking known IAB actors and their targeting patterns provide the primary, real technical signal.
ITID-12527.response: Proactively review and harden externally facing services likely to be targeted; monitor for escalation to a confirmed listing.
metrics: Count of IAB-interest signals tracked per quarter
ITID-12527.notes: Differentiator vs. ITID-12522 is the absence of a discrete, priced, active listing — this leaf is precursor/reconnaissance-stage tracking.

playbook.name: Response: Initial Access Broker (IAB) Listing
playbook.description: For a listing by an initial access broker offering to sell established network access (VPN, RDP, citrix, admin panel, etc.) into the organization, representing a high-severity precursor to ransomware or other major intrusion.

steps.title: Capture the IAB listing and escalate immediately
steps.desc: Preserve the listing including described access type, price, and any proof-of-access screenshots, and immediately escalate to the incident commander given the high severity of an active-access sale.
steps.guidance: Treat as a potential precursor to imminent ransomware deployment; do not wait for full triage before escalating.
steps.outcome: Listing preserved and incident escalated.

steps.title: Immediately disable or rotate the specific access vector
steps.desc: Disable the identified account/VPN credential/remote access method or rotate its credentials without delay.
steps.outcome: Identified access vector disabled or rotated.

steps.title: Hunt for signs of buyer activity or persistence
steps.desc: Conduct a focused threat hunt on the affected system and account for lateral movement, new persistence mechanisms, or reconnaissance activity consistent with a purchased-access intrusion.
steps.guidance: Escalate to full incident response if any persistence or lateral movement is found.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of buyer activity.

steps.title: Restore access only after confirmed clean
steps.desc: Restore the access vector only once the hunt confirms no persistence, using new credentials and hardened configuration.
steps.outcome: Access restored on a confirmed-clean, hardened basis.

steps.title: Document access vector, broker, and remediation timeline
steps.desc: Record how the access was likely obtained, the broker's listing details, and the full remediation timeline for leadership review.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and shared with leadership given the severity of this incident class.

steps.title: Identify the specific access vector and affected systems
steps.desc: Determine from the listing description and any proof screenshots exactly which system, credential, or access method is being sold (VPN account, RDP host, admin panel, etc.).
steps.outcome: Specific access vector and affected system identified.

steps.title: Isolate or restrict the affected system pending investigation
steps.desc: Apply network isolation or restrict remote access to the affected host/service until confirmed clean.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the network team for isolation without disrupting unrelated business operations.
steps.outcome: Affected system isolated or access-restricted.

steps.title: Check for evidence the access has already been sold or used
steps.desc: Review listing status, buyer comments, and escrow indicators, and cross-reference against recent authentication and network logs for the identified access vector.
steps.guidance: This is the single most important step for an IAB listing — a completed sale means an active intrusion may already be underway.
steps.outcome: Determined whether the access has already been sold and/or used.

ITID-12528.def: A dark web credential listing where the seller, a threat-intelligence provider, or internal verification has confirmed the credential is currently valid and functional against the target system, as opposed to a stale or already-rotated credential.
ITID-12528.purpose: Captures a dark web credential listing that has been independently confirmed as still valid/working, elevating urgency over an unverified listing.
scopeIncludes: Listing explicitly marketed by the seller as "verified" or "checked" working
Internal verification (via safe, authorized means) confirming the listed credential currently authenticates successfully
scopeExcludes: Unverified listings where validity is unknown or unconfirmed (tracked under the relevant channel-specific sibling, e.g. ITID-12523, ITID-12526)
ITID-12528.severity: Critical — confirmed-valid credentials represent an immediate, proven path to compromise.
ITID-12528.escalation: Immediate escalation to incident response for emergency credential rotation and session termination; treat as an active intrusion risk.
indicators: Dark-web monitoring feed classification tag indicating verified/checked status
Internal authorized verification test confirming credential validity
vectors: Seller pre-validates credentials before listing to command a higher price
Threat-intelligence provider's automated checking service confirms validity as part of its monitoring feed
rootCauses: Underlying exposure/theft event that produced the credential (root-caused under the originating leakage ITID, not duplicated here)
mitreTechniques: T1589.001 Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
controls: Dark-web monitoring with credential-validity verification/tagging
Emergency credential rotation playbook triggered on verified-valid listings
ITID-12528.detection: Dark-web monitoring providers offering validity verification/checking give a real, concrete, high-confidence technical signal.
ITID-12528.response: Rotate the credential and terminate all active sessions immediately upon confirmation, without waiting for further investigation.
metrics: Mean time to rotate a verified-valid listed credential
ITID-12528.notes: Differentiator is confirmed current validity, a status/urgency dimension layered on top of any channel-specific sibling leaf.

playbook.name: Response: Credential Listed with Verified/Confirmed Working Status
playbook.description: For a dark web credential listing explicitly marked by the seller as verified or confirmed working, indicating the seller has tested the credential and it currently grants access — the most urgent class of dark web credential listing.

steps.title: Capture the listing and escalate as high-urgency
steps.desc: Preserve the listing and immediately escalate given the seller's explicit claim that the credential is currently valid and working.
steps.guidance: Do not wait for full triage; a 'verified working' claim means the credential is very likely still active right now.
steps.outcome: Listing preserved and escalated for urgent response.

steps.title: Immediately disable the account pending reset
steps.desc: Disable sign-in for the affected account immediately, ahead of a full password reset, to stop the window of exposure without delay.
steps.outcome: Account sign-in disabled immediately.

steps.title: Hunt for persistence and lateral movement from the account
steps.desc: Given the confirmed-working status, conduct a focused hunt for persistence mechanisms, mailbox rule changes, OAuth grants, or lateral movement originating from the account.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of persistence or lateral movement.

steps.title: Re-enable access only after confirmed clean
steps.desc: Re-enable the account only once the hunt confirms no persistence remains, and maintain extended monitoring.
steps.outcome: Account re-enabled under active monitoring.

steps.title: Document confirmed-active exposure and response timeline
steps.desc: Record the full timeline from detection to containment, given the elevated severity of a confirmed-working credential listing.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and shared with leadership.

steps.title: Identify the exact account(s) and access level claimed
steps.desc: Determine precisely which account, system, or access level the seller claims to have verified.
steps.outcome: Specific account and access level identified.

steps.title: Force credential rotation and MFA re-enrollment
steps.desc: Reset the account's password and require MFA re-enrollment from a verified clean device before re-enabling.
steps.outcome: New credentials and MFA in place.

steps.title: Review recent authentication activity for the account
steps.desc: Check sign-in logs for the identified account for any recent anomalous logins that might correspond to the seller's verification test.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether recent anomalous access has occurred.

ITID-12529.def: A dark web listing specifically curated and packaged around the organization's own employees/domain — a targeted credential bundle assembled and marketed as being about this specific organization, rather than the organization's credentials appearing incidentally within a larger, unrelated dataset.
ITID-12529.purpose: Captures a curated, targeted bundle of employee credentials specific to the organization, as opposed to an incidental appearance within an unrelated bulk dataset.
scopeIncludes: Listing explicitly titled/marketed by organization or company name, containing a curated set of employee credentials
Infostealer-log collection specifically packaged and sold by targeted victim organization
scopeExcludes: Organizational credentials appearing as an incidental subset of a much larger, unrelated bulk dump (see ITID-12523)
General combolist aggregation (see ITID-12526)
ITID-12529.severity: Critical — deliberate targeting indicates focused attacker interest in the organization specifically.
ITID-12529.escalation: Immediate escalation to incident response and threat intelligence; treat as evidence of active, specific targeting warranting broader threat-hunting.
indicators: Listing title or description explicitly naming the organization
Curated credential set exclusively containing the organization's employee email domain
vectors: Targeted infostealer campaign against organizational employees, packaged and sold as an organization-specific bundle
Attacker who breached the organization curating and reselling the resulting employee credential set
rootCauses: Underlying targeted compromise event producing the bundle (root-caused under the originating incident, not duplicated here)
mitreTechniques: T1589.001 Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
controls: Dark-web monitoring specifically for organization-named/branded listings
Emergency organization-wide credential rotation playbook for confirmed targeted bundles
ITID-12529.detection: Dark-web monitoring configured with organization-specific keyword/brand alerting provides a real, concrete, high-priority technical signal.
ITID-12529.response: Initiate organization-wide threat hunting and consider a broad, forced password reset for all employees represented in the bundle.
metrics: Count of organization-specific targeted bundle listings detected per year
ITID-12529.notes: Differentiator is deliberate, organization-specific curation and marketing, distinct from incidental appearance within an unrelated bulk dataset (ITID-12523).

playbook.name: Response: Employee Credential Bundle (Targeted Organization Listing)
playbook.description: For a listing packaging multiple credentials specifically curated and marketed as belonging to a named employee or the targeted organization as a whole, indicating deliberate targeting rather than incidental inclusion in a generic dump.

steps.title: Capture the listing and escalate as high-urgency, broad-scope
steps.desc: Preserve the listing and escalate immediately given that deliberate, organization-targeted bundling suggests broader compromise than a single account.
steps.guidance: Treat as a potential indicator of a targeted campaign against the organization, not an opportunistic leak.
steps.outcome: Listing preserved and escalated.

steps.title: Force broad credential rotation across the entire bundle
steps.desc: Reset credentials for every account included in the bundle, treating the deliberate targeting as elevated risk.
steps.outcome: Credentials rotated for all accounts in the bundle.

steps.title: Hunt for a common compromised asset feeding the bundle
steps.desc: If a common source is suspected (e.g., shared endpoint malware or a targeted phishing kit), investigate and remediate that asset directly.
steps.outcome: Common source identified and remediated, or ruled out.

steps.title: Restore access and notify all affected employees
steps.desc: Confirm all affected accounts operate normally under new credentials and brief affected employees given the targeted nature of the incident.
steps.outcome: Access restored and employees notified.

steps.title: Document targeting pattern and recommend organizational controls
steps.desc: Record the bundle composition, suspected source, and recommend any organization-wide control improvements given evidence of deliberate targeting.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and shared with leadership.

steps.title: Enumerate every account and credential in the bundle
steps.desc: Identify all employees, accounts, and credential types included in the bundle, not just the named individual.
steps.outcome: Complete inventory of all accounts in the bundle.

steps.title: Enforce MFA and review for a common compromise source
steps.desc: Enforce MFA across all affected accounts and investigate whether a shared device, application, or phishing campaign is the common source needing separate containment.
steps.outcome: MFA enforced; common source investigation opened if applicable.

steps.title: Assess likely source and whether targeting indicates insider or external compromise
steps.desc: Evaluate whether the bundled credentials suggest a common source (e.g., a compromised endpoint, a targeted phishing campaign, or an insider) rather than coincidental overlap from separate breaches.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the insider threat and CTI teams as appropriate.
steps.outcome: Likely source and targeting pattern assessed.

ITID-12531.def: An incident involving unintentional, non-malicious disclosure of a credential by an internal party, not yet matched to a more specific disclosure channel.
ITID-12531.purpose: Catch-all for an accidental credential disclosure that does not fit a more specific leaf under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before the specific accidental disclosure channel is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID under Accidental Disclosure
Deliberate/malicious credential disclosure (tracked under insider-threat ITIDs)
ITID-12531.escalation: Escalate to security engineering once the specific disclosure channel is confirmed; reclassify accordingly.
indicators: Report of unclear specific accidental disclosure channel
vectors: Disclosure of unclear specific channel
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Data loss prevention scanning for credential patterns
Secrets scanning in code repositories and shared drives
Employee security awareness training on credential handling
ITID-12531.detection: Same reporting/DLP telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-12531.response: Investigate and reclassify to a specific leaf once confirmed; rotate the credential immediately.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-12531.notes: Intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Accidental Credential Disclosure
playbook.description: For a general case where an employee has inadvertently disclosed credentials through an unspecified channel, without malicious intent, that has not yet been categorized into a more specific disclosure type.

steps.title: Interview the reporting employee to establish what was disclosed
steps.desc: Speak with the employee who disclosed or reported the disclosure to determine exactly what credential(s) were shared and by what means.
steps.guidance: Approach the conversation as fact-finding, not as discipline — accurate detail depends on the employee feeling safe to explain fully.
steps.outcome: Clear account of what was disclosed and how.

steps.title: Rotate the disclosed credential
steps.desc: Reset the password or key that was disclosed.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated and old value invalidated.

steps.title: Confirm no misuse of the disclosed credential occurred
steps.desc: Review authentication logs for the affected account for any activity between disclosure and rotation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of misuse.

steps.title: Confirm restored access and close out the report
steps.desc: Verify the employee can authenticate normally with the new credential.
steps.outcome: Access confirmed restored.

steps.title: Document the disclosure and offer corrective guidance
steps.desc: Record how the disclosure occurred and provide the employee with brief, non-punitive guidance on secure credential handling.
steps.guidance: Frame as a coaching opportunity consistent with the organization's approach to other negligent-insider incidents.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and guidance delivered.

steps.title: Determine who received the disclosure and whether it has been viewed
steps.desc: Identify the recipient(s) of the disclosure and, where possible, confirm whether the material has actually been opened or accessed.
steps.guidance: Check read receipts, access logs, or ask the recipient directly if they are a known/trusted party.
steps.outcome: Recipient identified and viewing status determined.

steps.title: Attempt removal or recall of the disclosed material where feasible
steps.desc: Where the disclosure landed somewhere retrievable, ask the recipient to delete it, revoke sharing permissions, or recall the message.
steps.guidance: Not always possible once sent externally; document the attempt regardless of outcome.
steps.outcome: Material removed/recalled where feasible, or attempt documented.
steps.abort: If recall is not possible, proceed to eradication with rotation as the primary control.

ITID-12532.def: A credential (password, API key, temporary access token) transmitted via email without encryption or adequate protection, exposing it to interception or later inbox compromise.
ITID-12532.purpose: Captures a credential sent via unencrypted or otherwise insecure email.
scopeIncludes: Plaintext password sent via standard corporate or personal email
Credential sent via email to the wrong recipient due to autocomplete or manual error (a specific subtype tracked separately if misdirection is the primary factor — see ITID-12536)
scopeExcludes: Credential disclosed via a support/help-desk ticket system rather than direct email (see ITID-12535)
Misdirected communication where the wrong-recipient error, not the lack of encryption, is the primary factor (see ITID-12536)
ITID-12532.severity: Medium, escalating if the credential is for a privileged or externally facing account.
ITID-12532.escalation: Escalate to security to rotate the credential and to the sender's manager for awareness/training.
indicators: DLP rule match on password-pattern content in outbound email
Employee self-report of having sent a credential via email
vectors: New-account or password-reset credentials sent in plaintext rather than via a secure, one-time-view channel
IT support sending a temporary password via standard email as a matter of habit
rootCauses: No secure credential-delivery mechanism (e.g. one-time-view secret link) provisioned for IT/HR workflows
No DLP policy scanning outbound email for credential patterns
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: DLP scanning of outbound email for credential patterns
Secure, one-time-view credential delivery mechanism for IT/HR workflows
ITID-12532.detection: DLP email-content scanning provides a concrete, real technical signal for this pattern.
ITID-12532.response: Rotate the affected credential and reinforce use of the approved secure delivery mechanism.
metrics: Count of DLP credential-pattern matches in outbound email per quarter
ITID-12532.notes: Scoped to the insecure-channel dimension of email disclosure; wrong-recipient misdirection is tracked separately under ITID-12536 to avoid double-counting the same event under two leaves.

playbook.name: Response: Credential Sent via Unencrypted/Insecure Email
playbook.description: For a case where an employee sent a password or other credential in plaintext over unencrypted email, either internally or to an external party.

steps.title: Locate and review the email content
steps.desc: Retrieve the sent email to confirm exactly which credential(s) were included and whether the message was encrypted in transit.
steps.guidance: Check mail flow/transport logs for TLS status if encryption-in-transit is in question.
steps.outcome: Email content and encryption status confirmed.

steps.title: Rotate the disclosed credential
steps.desc: Reset the password or key that was sent by email.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated.

steps.title: Confirm no misuse of the credential occurred
steps.desc: Review authentication logs for the affected account between the time of the email and rotation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of misuse.

steps.title: Confirm restored access
steps.desc: Verify the account operates normally under the new credential.
steps.outcome: Access confirmed restored.

steps.title: Coach on secure credential-sharing methods
steps.desc: Document the incident and remind the employee of approved secure methods for sharing credentials (e.g., a password manager's sharing feature).
steps.guidance: Corrective, not punitive, in tone.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and guidance delivered.

steps.title: Confirm recipient(s) and whether the message has been opened or forwarded
steps.desc: Identify all recipients including any CC/BCC and forwards, and check for read receipts or mail tracking data.
steps.outcome: Full recipient list and viewing status confirmed.

steps.title: Request deletion of the email from recipient and any mail stores
steps.desc: Ask the recipient to delete the message, and use mail admin tooling to purge copies from internal mailboxes and archives where policy allows.
steps.guidance: External recipient deletion cannot be enforced, only requested — document the request.
steps.outcome: Message removed from internal stores; external deletion requested.

ITID-12533.def: A credential visible in a screen-sharing session (video call, remote presentation) or captured in a screenshot that was subsequently shared, recorded, or published.
ITID-12533.purpose: Captures a credential inadvertently exposed via a shared screen or screenshot.
scopeIncludes: Password/API key visible on-screen during a recorded or live-shared video conference
Screenshot including visible credentials shared in chat, a ticket, or documentation
scopeExcludes: Credential exposed via a third-party remote support session specifically (see ITID-12539)
Credential left directly within a shared document/spreadsheet's text content rather than visible on-screen incidentally (see ITID-12534)
ITID-12533.severity: Medium, escalating if the recording/screenshot has wide or external distribution.
ITID-12533.escalation: Escalate to security to rotate the credential and, if externally shared/recorded, assess further distribution.
indicators: Employee or meeting participant reports credentials visible during a screen share
Screenshot containing visible credential content found in a chat tool or shared drive
vectors: Password manager or terminal window left open and visible during a screen-shared demo/meeting
Screenshot taken for troubleshooting purposes without redacting visible credential fields
rootCauses: No staff training/habit of closing sensitive windows before screen-sharing
No screenshot-redaction practice for support/troubleshooting workflows
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Staff training on screen-share hygiene before meetings
Screenshot-redaction requirement for troubleshooting/support content
ITID-12533.detection: Primarily relies on self-report/participant observation, supplemented by DLP scanning of shared screenshots/recordings where content-scanning tooling is deployed.
ITID-12533.response: Rotate the exposed credential and check the extent of recording/screenshot distribution.
metrics: Count of screen-share/screenshot credential exposures reported per quarter
detections: DLP image/recording content-scanning alerting where deployed
ITID-12533.notes: Scoped to visible on-screen exposure specifically, distinct from third-party remote support sessions (ITID-12539) and shared document text content (ITID-12534).

playbook.name: Response: Credential Included in Shared Screen/Screenshot
playbook.description: For a case where a credential was inadvertently exposed during a screen-share (e.g., video call, remote presentation) or captured in a screenshot that was then shared or posted.

steps.title: Identify exactly what was visible and to whom
steps.desc: Determine what credential was shown on screen, for how long, and who was present in the call or received the screenshot.
steps.guidance: Check meeting attendee/recording lists where available.
steps.outcome: Exposure scope and audience confirmed.

steps.title: Rotate the exposed credential
steps.desc: Reset the password or key that was visible on screen.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated.

steps.title: Confirm no misuse of the credential occurred
steps.desc: Review authentication logs for the affected account between exposure and rotation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of misuse.

steps.title: Confirm restored access
steps.desc: Verify the account operates normally under the new credential.
steps.outcome: Access confirmed restored.

steps.title: Coach on screen-share hygiene
steps.desc: Document the incident and remind the employee to close credential managers/sensitive windows before screen-sharing or presenting.
steps.guidance: Corrective, not punitive, in tone.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and guidance delivered.

steps.title: Check whether the session or screenshot was recorded or further distributed
steps.desc: Determine if the call was recorded, whether a recording is retained, and whether the screenshot was posted or forwarded anywhere beyond the original recipient.
steps.guidance: Check meeting platform recording settings and any chat/collaboration tool where a screenshot may have been posted.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether a persistent record exists and where it has spread.

steps.title: Remove or restrict any recording or posted screenshot
steps.desc: Delete or restrict access to any meeting recording, and request removal of the screenshot from wherever it was posted (chat channel, ticket, shared drive).
steps.outcome: Recording/screenshot removed or access restricted.
steps.abort: If content cannot be removed (e.g., already downloaded by a third party), document and rely on rotation as the primary control.

ITID-12534.def: A credential typed or pasted into the text content of a document or spreadsheet (e.g. a password tracking sheet, a runbook) that is then shared more broadly than intended, via a collaboration platform.
ITID-12534.purpose: Captures a credential left as text content within a shared document or spreadsheet.
scopeIncludes: Password/API key stored as plain text in a spreadsheet shared with a broad group or externally
Runbook or wiki page containing embedded credentials, shared beyond its intended audience
scopeExcludes: Credential visible incidentally on-screen during a screen share/screenshot (see ITID-12533)
Credential exposed in published, finished public documentation (tracked under Public Exposure, ITID-12518)
ITID-12534.severity: Medium-High, especially where the sheet functions as an informal team-wide password store.
ITID-12534.escalation: Escalate to security to rotate all credentials in the document and migrate the team to an approved password/secrets manager.
indicators: DLP or CASB scan of shared drives flags credential-pattern content in a spreadsheet/document
Discovery during an access review that a broadly shared document contains live credentials
vectors: Team maintaining an informal shared spreadsheet of shared account passwords instead of using a password manager
Document with embedded setup credentials shared with a broader distribution list than intended
rootCauses: No enforced use of an approved enterprise password manager for shared/team credentials
Overly permissive default sharing settings on collaboration platform documents
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: CASB/DLP scanning of shared drive content for credential patterns
Mandatory enterprise password manager for shared/team credentials
ITID-12534.detection: CASB/DLP scanning of cloud collaboration platforms for credential-pattern content provides a real, concrete technical signal.
ITID-12534.response: Rotate all credentials found in the document and migrate the team to an approved secrets/password management tool.
metrics: Count of shared documents found containing credential patterns per quarter
ITID-12534.notes: Scoped to persistent document/spreadsheet text content specifically, distinct from incidental on-screen exposure (ITID-12533).

playbook.name: Response: Credential Left in Shared Document/Spreadsheet
playbook.description: For a case where a credential was left in a document or spreadsheet stored on a shared drive or collaboration platform, accessible to a broader audience than intended.

steps.title: Locate the document and confirm its credential content
steps.desc: Identify the specific document/spreadsheet and confirm exactly which credentials it contains.
steps.outcome: Document located and credential content confirmed.

steps.title: Rotate every credential contained in the document
steps.desc: Reset all passwords/keys found in the document, not just the one initially reported.
steps.guidance: Documents of this kind often contain more than one credential — review the full contents.
steps.outcome: All credentials in the document rotated.

steps.title: Confirm no misuse of the exposed credentials occurred
steps.desc: Review authentication logs for each affected account between exposure and rotation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of misuse.

steps.title: Confirm restored access and proper document permissions
steps.desc: Verify affected accounts operate normally and the document now has appropriate, minimal sharing permissions.
steps.outcome: Access restored and document permissions corrected.

steps.title: Coach on secrets management and recommend a vault solution
steps.desc: Document the incident and recommend the team use a proper secrets/password manager instead of storing credentials in shared documents.
steps.guidance: Corrective, not punitive, in tone.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and guidance delivered.

steps.title: Determine the document's sharing scope and access history
steps.desc: Review sharing permissions and access/view logs to determine who could and did access the document.
steps.guidance: Check for organization-wide links, external sharing, or link-based access with no authentication.
steps.outcome: Sharing scope and actual access history confirmed.

steps.title: Restrict sharing permissions and remove the credentials from the document
steps.desc: Revoke overly broad sharing permissions immediately and edit the document to remove the credentials (or replace with a reference to a secure vault).
steps.outcome: Sharing scope restricted and credentials removed from the document.

ITID-12535.def: A credential included, typically by an end user seeking assistance, in the free-text description or attachment of an IT support/help-desk ticket, exposing it to the ticket's broader audience (support staff, ticket history, integrated tools).
ITID-12535.purpose: Captures a credential disclosed within the text of a support or help-desk ticket.
scopeIncludes: End user pasting a password into a ticket description to illustrate a login problem
Screenshot or log attachment on a ticket that includes visible credential content
scopeExcludes: Credential exposed via a live third-party remote support session (see ITID-12539)
General email disclosure not routed through a ticketing system (see ITID-12532)
ITID-12535.severity: Medium — ticket systems often retain content indefinitely and are broadly visible to support staff.
ITID-12535.escalation: Escalate to security to rotate the credential and redact/purge it from the ticket record.
indicators: DLP scanning of ticketing system content flags credential patterns
Support staff identify and report a credential included in an incoming ticket
vectors: User pastes a password directly into a ticket to demonstrate a login failure
Support staff request and receive a password via ticket reply rather than an approved secure channel
rootCauses: No user guidance/prompt in the ticketing form warning against including credentials
Ticketing system content not included in DLP scanning scope
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: DLP scanning extended to ticketing system content
Ticket form guidance/warning against submitting credentials
ITID-12535.detection: DLP scanning extended to the ticketing platform provides a real, concrete technical signal.
ITID-12535.response: Rotate the credential, redact it from the ticket record, and reinforce guidance to end users and support staff.
metrics: Count of credential-pattern matches in ticketing content per quarter
ITID-12535.notes: Scoped to the ticketing-system channel specifically, distinct from general email (ITID-12532) and live remote support sessions (ITID-12539).

playbook.name: Response: Credential Disclosed in Support/Help Desk Ticket
playbook.description: For a case where an employee or customer included a password or other credential in the free-text body of a support/help desk ticket, exposing it to support staff and ticketing system logs beyond the intended scope.

steps.title: Locate the ticket and confirm the credential content
steps.desc: Retrieve the ticket and confirm exactly which credential(s) were included in the ticket body, attachments, or comments.
steps.outcome: Ticket located and credential content confirmed.

steps.title: Rotate the disclosed credential
steps.desc: Reset the password or key included in the ticket.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated.

steps.title: Confirm no misuse of the credential occurred
steps.desc: Review authentication logs for the affected account between ticket submission and rotation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of misuse.

steps.title: Confirm restored access
steps.desc: Verify the account operates normally under the new credential.
steps.outcome: Access confirmed restored.

steps.title: Coach the reporter and remind support staff of ticket handling policy
steps.desc: Document the incident, remind the reporter never to include credentials in ticket text, and confirm support staff know to redact/report such content when seen.
steps.guidance: Corrective, not punitive, in tone.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and guidance delivered.

steps.title: Determine who has visibility into the ticket
steps.desc: Identify all support staff, integrations, or third parties with access to the ticket, including any downstream systems that mirror ticket content.
steps.guidance: Check for automatic forwarding to third-party support vendors if applicable.
steps.outcome: Full visibility scope of the ticket confirmed.

steps.title: Redact the credential from the ticket record
steps.desc: Edit or redact the ticket to remove the plaintext credential from the visible record and any indexed/searchable copies.
steps.outcome: Credential redacted from the ticket record.
steps.abort: If redaction is not possible in the platform, document the residual exposure and rely on rotation.

ITID-12536.def: A credential disclosed because the communication carrying it (email, chat message, file share) was sent to the wrong recipient — due to autocomplete error, similarly named contact, or manual mistake — as distinct from a credential sent correctly but over an insecure channel.
ITID-12536.purpose: Captures a credential sent to an unintended recipient due to a misdirection error.
scopeIncludes: Password reset email sent to the wrong address due to email client autocomplete
Credential-containing file shared with an incorrect external contact due to a similarly named entry
scopeExcludes: Correctly addressed but unencrypted/insecure credential transmission (see ITID-12532)
Third-party support session disclosure (see ITID-12539)
ITID-12536.severity: Medium, escalating if the unintended recipient is external to the organization.
ITID-12536.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the recipient is external and unresponsive to a recall/deletion request.
ITID-12536.escalation: Escalate to security immediately to rotate the credential; escalate to legal/privacy if the recipient is external and does not confirm deletion.
indicators: Email/chat system recall or bounce indicating a send-error correction attempt
Sender self-report of a misdirected message containing credential content
vectors: Autocomplete selecting a similarly named but incorrect contact in an email client
Distribution list misconfiguration including unintended external recipients
rootCauses: No confirmation/warning step for external or first-time recipients when sending sensitive content
Autocomplete not restricted to a verified/trusted contact list for sensitive communications
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Outbound-email warning/confirmation for external or first-time recipients
DLP with recipient-anomaly detection for sensitive content
ITID-12536.detection: DLP with recipient-anomaly/external-recipient warning integration provides a concrete technical signal; supplemented by self-report.
ITID-12536.response: Rotate the credential immediately and attempt message recall/deletion confirmation from the unintended recipient.
metrics: Count of misdirected-communication credential disclosures per quarter
ITID-12536.notes: Differentiator is the wrong-recipient error mechanism specifically, distinct from insecure-channel transmission to the correct recipient (ITID-12532).

playbook.name: Response: Credential Disclosed via Misdirected Communication
playbook.description: For a case where a credential was sent to the wrong recipient entirely — a misaddressed email, a message sent to the wrong chat/channel, or a similar send-to-wrong-party error.

steps.title: Confirm the intended versus actual recipient and content sent
steps.desc: Determine who the communication was intended for, who actually received it, and exactly what credential(s) it contained.
steps.outcome: Intended and actual recipients confirmed along with credential content.

steps.title: Rotate the disclosed credential
steps.desc: Reset the password or key that was sent to the wrong party.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated.

steps.title: Confirm no misuse of the credential occurred
steps.desc: Review authentication logs for the affected account between the misdirected send and rotation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of misuse.

steps.title: Confirm restored access
steps.desc: Verify the account operates normally under the new credential.
steps.outcome: Access confirmed restored.

steps.title: Coach on address/recipient verification habits
steps.desc: Document the incident and remind the employee to double-check recipients before sending sensitive content, particularly with autocomplete enabled.
steps.guidance: Corrective, not punitive, in tone.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and guidance delivered.

steps.title: Assess the actual recipient's trust level and likelihood of misuse
steps.desc: Determine whether the unintended recipient is an internal colleague, a known external party, or a stranger, to gauge risk of misuse.
steps.guidance: An internal misdirect (wrong colleague) carries materially lower risk than an external stranger.
steps.outcome: Recipient trust level assessed and documented.

steps.title: Request the unintended recipient delete the communication
steps.desc: Contact the unintended recipient and ask them to delete the message and confirm they have not acted on its content.
steps.guidance: For a known/trusted internal recipient this is usually straightforward; for an external stranger it may not be possible — document either way.
steps.outcome: Deletion requested and, where possible, confirmed.

ITID-12537.def: A real, valid production credential accidentally included in a training, demo, or sandbox environment that has broader or less-controlled access than production (e.g. shared with trainees, contractors, or a wider internal audience).
ITID-12537.purpose: Captures a live production credential mistakenly exposed within a training or demo environment.
scopeIncludes: Live credential accidentally left in demo environment configuration used for training sessions
Production data/credential set copied into a sandbox without proper sanitization
scopeExcludes: Test/dev account left active in production itself (the inverse direction — see ITID-12434 under Abandoned Accounts)
ITID-12537.severity: Medium-High, given the training/demo audience is typically broader and less trusted than production access norms.
ITID-12537.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the credential is privileged.
ITID-12537.escalation: Escalate to the environment owner and security engineering to rotate the credential and sanitize the environment.
indicators: Post-training audit or self-report identifying a live credential in demo/training material
Data sanitization review of a sandbox environment identifies an unmasked production secret
vectors: Production database or configuration cloned into a training environment without a data-sanitization/masking step
Trainer inadvertently uses live production credentials in a demo walkthrough
rootCauses: No mandatory data-masking/sanitization process for cloning production data into non-production environments
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Mandatory data masking/sanitization when cloning production data to non-production environments
Environment segregation with distinct, non-production-valid credentials for demo/training use
ITID-12537.detection: Sandbox/demo environment audits and secret-scanning extended to non-production environments provide a concrete technical signal.
ITID-12537.response: Rotate the exposed production credential immediately and enforce data-sanitization controls before future environment refreshes.
metrics: Count of live credentials found in non-production environments per audit cycle
ITID-12537.notes: This is the mirror case of ITID-12434 (a test artifact left in production); here a production artifact is left in a lower-trust test/demo environment.

playbook.name: Response: Credential Exposed in Training/Demo Environment
playbook.description: For a case where a real production credential was inadvertently used or left visible within a training session, demo environment, or sample dataset intended for a non-production audience.

steps.title: Confirm the credential is a real production credential, not a sample
steps.desc: Verify whether the exposed value is a genuine live credential or a placeholder/dummy value mistaken for one.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the credential is real and live, or ruled out as a dummy value.
steps.abort: If confirmed to be a placeholder/dummy value only, close as a non-incident.

steps.title: Rotate the exposed production credential
steps.desc: Reset the real credential that was inadvertently exposed.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated.

steps.title: Confirm no misuse of the credential occurred
steps.desc: Review authentication logs for the affected account between the training session and rotation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of misuse.

steps.title: Confirm restored access and verify demo environment uses synthetic credentials
steps.desc: Verify the production account operates normally, and confirm the training/demo environment is reconfigured to use synthetic, non-production credentials going forward.
steps.outcome: Access restored and demo environment corrected.

steps.title: Recommend a standing synthetic-credential policy for training/demo environments
steps.desc: Document the incident and recommend a control ensuring training/demo environments are seeded with synthetic data by default.
steps.guidance: Corrective, not punitive, in tone.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and recommendation delivered.

steps.title: Determine the training/demo audience and whether it was recorded
steps.desc: Identify who attended the session or has access to the demo environment, and whether the session was recorded or the environment is persistently accessible.
steps.outcome: Audience scope and recording/persistence status confirmed.

steps.title: Remove the credential from the training/demo environment and any recording
steps.desc: Scrub the credential from the demo environment configuration and delete or edit any recording that captured it.
steps.outcome: Credential removed from the environment and any recording.

ITID-12538.def: A credential disclosed as an unintended side effect of the offboarding handoff process itself — e.g. shared passwords communicated to a successor insecurely, or account contents (including saved credentials) transferred without proper review.
ITID-12538.purpose: Captures a credential exposed during the process of handing off accounts/access at employee offboarding.
scopeIncludes: Departing employee's account credentials/password vault shared insecurely with a successor during handoff
Shared account password communicated to a team during offboarding via an insecure channel
scopeExcludes: The departed employee's own account remaining active due to a deprovisioning failure (tracked under Abandoned Accounts, ITID-12432)
ITID-12538.escalation: Escalate to IAM and HR to rotate affected credentials and formalize the handoff process.
indicators: Offboarding checklist review identifies an insecure credential handoff step
Successor or manager self-reports receiving credentials via an insecure channel during offboarding
vectors: Manager verbally or via chat shares a departing employee's account password with a successor rather than following a formal transfer process
Password vault export shared broadly during team transition
rootCauses: No formal, secure process for transferring shared-account ownership during offboarding
Offboarding checklist lacking a credential-handoff-specific step
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Formal secure credential-transfer process integrated into offboarding SOP
Enterprise password manager with role-based, auditable access transfer
ITID-12538.detection: Relies primarily on offboarding process audit and self-report; supplemented by DLP where the handoff channel is monitored.
ITID-12538.response: Rotate all credentials involved in the handoff and formalize a secure transfer process for future offboarding events.
metrics: Count of insecure credential handoffs identified per audit cycle
ITID-12538.notes: Scoped to the handoff/transfer process itself, distinct from the departed employee's own account being left active (ITID-12432).

playbook.name: Response: Credential Exposed via Improper Offboarding Handoff
playbook.description: For a case where a departing employee's credentials, or credentials they managed, were inadvertently exposed or improperly transferred during the offboarding handoff process — e.g., shared in a handoff document, left in an inherited mailbox, or not revoked before the handoff.

steps.title: Review the offboarding handoff materials for exposed credentials
steps.desc: Examine handoff documents, transition notes, or inherited accounts/mailboxes for any plaintext credentials.
steps.outcome: Confirmed which credentials were exposed in the handoff materials.

steps.title: Confirm or complete revocation of the departing employee's access
steps.desc: Ensure the departing employee's own accounts and credentials are fully disabled if not already done.
steps.guidance: This should already be standard offboarding practice — verify it was actually completed.
steps.outcome: Departing employee's access confirmed fully revoked.

steps.title: Remove plaintext credentials from handoff documentation
steps.desc: Edit handoff documents to remove plaintext credentials, replacing with references to a secrets vault, and confirm no other copies remain.
steps.outcome: Handoff documentation scrubbed of plaintext credentials.

steps.title: Confirm the receiving employee has correct, minimal access via proper channels
steps.desc: Verify the receiving employee's access to needed systems was granted through standard access-provisioning rather than via the inherited credentials.
steps.outcome: Receiving employee has proper, independently-provisioned access.

steps.title: Recommend offboarding process improvement
steps.desc: Document the gap in the offboarding checklist that allowed credential exposure and recommend a process fix (e.g., mandatory secrets rotation as a checklist item).
steps.guidance: Corrective, not punitive, in tone.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and recommendation delivered to the offboarding process owner.

steps.title: Determine who received the handoff materials and current access status
steps.desc: Identify the receiving employee(s) and confirm whether the departing employee's own access has already been revoked per standard offboarding process.
steps.guidance: Check offboarding checklist completion status.
steps.outcome: Recipient and revocation status confirmed.

steps.title: Rotate any shared/system credentials exposed in the handoff
steps.desc: Reset any shared service accounts, system credentials, or other passwords that appeared in the handoff materials.
steps.outcome: Exposed shared/system credentials rotated.

ITID-12539.def: A credential disclosed to, or visible to, a third-party support technician during a live remote-assistance session (screen sharing, remote desktop control) — whether shared verbally/typed for the technician to use, or incidentally visible on-screen.
ITID-12539.purpose: Captures a credential exposed during a live remote support session with a third party.
scopeIncludes: Credential provided directly to a third-party vendor's support technician to allow them to log in on the customer's behalf
Credential incidentally visible on-screen during a vendor-initiated remote support/screen-control session
scopeExcludes: Internal screen-share/screenshot exposure with no third party involved (see ITID-12533)
Compromise of a third-party integration's own service account credential (tracked under Service Account Exploitation, ITID-12428)
ITID-12539.severity: Medium-High, given the credential is exposed directly to an external party.
ITID-12539.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the credential is privileged or the vendor's own security posture is unverified.
ITID-12539.escalation: Escalate to security to rotate the credential following every such session as standard practice, and to vendor risk management if the vendor's handling practices are in question.
indicators: Support ticket/session log confirming a credential was provided or visible during a remote support session
Post-session credential rotation not performed per policy
vectors: Vendor support technician requests and receives a live credential to remediate an issue directly
Screen-control session exposing a credential-entry field or password manager visible to the remote technician
rootCauses: No standard policy of mandatory credential rotation after any third-party remote support session
No use of temporary, scoped access grants for vendor support instead of sharing standing credentials
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Mandatory credential rotation after any third-party remote support session
Temporary, scoped access grants issued for vendor support instead of standing credential sharing
ITID-12539.detection: Relies on support-session logging/ticketing review and policy compliance auditing rather than automated technical detection.
ITID-12539.response: Rotate the credential immediately following the session as standard practice, regardless of whether misuse is suspected.
metrics: Percentage of third-party remote support sessions followed by policy-compliant credential rotation
ITID-12539.notes: Scoped to live, human-to-human support session exposure specifically, distinct from a compromised standing third-party service-account credential (ITID-12428).

playbook.name: Response: Credential Exposed via Third-Party Support Session
playbook.description: For a case where a credential was inadvertently disclosed to a third-party vendor or support technician during a remote support/troubleshooting session — e.g., spoken aloud on a call, typed into a shared remote-control session, or pasted into a shared chat with the vendor.

steps.title: Confirm what was disclosed to the third party and through which channel
steps.desc: Determine exactly which credential(s) were shared with the vendor/support technician and whether via voice, remote-control screen visibility, or chat/text.
steps.outcome: Disclosed credential and channel confirmed.

steps.title: Rotate the disclosed credential
steps.desc: Reset the password or key shared during the support session.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated.

steps.title: Confirm no misuse of the credential or system occurred
steps.desc: Review authentication and endpoint logs for the affected account/system between the support session and rotation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of misuse.

steps.title: Confirm restored access
steps.desc: Verify the account/system operates normally under the new credential.
steps.outcome: Access confirmed restored.

steps.title: Coach on secure practices for vendor support sessions
steps.desc: Document the incident and remind staff never to speak or type live credentials during support sessions, using temporary access or screen-sharing exclusions instead.
steps.guidance: Corrective, not punitive, in tone.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and guidance delivered.

steps.title: Identify the third party and verify legitimacy of the support session
steps.desc: Confirm the support session was with a legitimate, authorized vendor and not an impersonation or social-engineering attempt.
steps.guidance: If the session appears to be a scam/impersonation rather than a genuine vendor, treat as a separate social-engineering incident with its own response.
steps.outcome: Legitimacy of the vendor and session confirmed.
steps.abort: If the session was fraudulent, escalate as a social-engineering incident instead.

steps.title: End the remote session and confirm no persistent third-party access remains
steps.desc: Terminate the remote-support session and confirm any temporary remote-access tool or account granted to the vendor has been disabled.
steps.outcome: Remote session ended and any temporary access revoked.

ITID-12611.def: An incident of MFA token phishing not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type, logged before enough detail is available to reclassify.
ITID-12611.purpose: Catch-all for cases where an adversary phishes a user for an MFA token/code but the specific factor or delivery method targeted is not yet known or does not match a more specific leaf.
scopeIncludes: Reports of an MFA phishing attempt where the targeted factor (TOTP, push, hardware key, backup code, biometric, QR) has not yet been determined
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID once the targeted factor is known
Vishing-based real-time OTP relay over a phone call (ITID-11218)
ITID-12611.severity: Medium by default; reassess once the specific factor targeted is confirmed.
ITID-12611.priority: P3 pending reclassification, P2 if a privileged account was targeted.
ITID-12611.escalation: Reclassify to the specific phishing sub-technique once confirmed; escalate immediately if any MFA approval was granted.
indicators: User-reported suspicious MFA prompt or login page
Alert of unclear specific MFA phishing vector
vectors: Phishing email or SMS directing the user to a credential/MFA harvesting page
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
User not yet trained to recognize MFA-relay phishing pages
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn) rollout for high-value accounts
Number-matching / context-rich push approval prompts
AiTM-aware conditional access (token binding, IP/device continuity checks)
User security awareness training on real-time credential relay phishing
ITID-12611.detection: Strong technical signal: IdP logs surface impossible-travel and new-device sign-ins immediately following a phishing click, reverse-proxy/AiTM kits leave detectable TLS and referrer fingerprints, and session tokens issued through a phishing relay show anomalous issuance velocity compared to genuine logins.
ITID-12611.response: Force sign-out and reset credentials plus MFA re-enrollment for the targeted user immediately on confirmation; hunt for reuse of any session token or code captured during the phishing window; block the phishing infrastructure at the email/web gateway.
metrics: Count of MFA phishing attempts detected per month
Median time from click to credential reset
Percentage of targeted users on phishing-resistant MFA
ITID-12611.notes: Intake/catch-all classification for this Type, not a terminal one; reclassify once the targeted factor is confirmed.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General MFA Token Phishing
playbook.description: Baseline response for a report or detection of phishing directed at capturing a user's multi-factor authentication token or approval, where the specific MFA method targeted has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Collect the phishing artifact and initial report
steps.desc: Gather the phishing message, link, or user report describing what MFA prompt or code they were asked to provide.
steps.guidance: Capture screenshots, URLs, and timestamps; ask the reporting user exactly what they were shown and what they entered or approved.
steps.outcome: Case file contains the phishing artifact and a clear timeline of user interaction.

steps.title: Force password reset and revoke active sessions
steps.desc: Reset the account password and invalidate all active sessions and refresh tokens.
steps.guidance: Do this even if the token itself wasn't the password, since most phishing kits also harvest the password in the same flow.
steps.outcome: Account credential rotated; prior sessions terminated.

steps.title: Audit the account for attacker-added persistence
steps.desc: Review the account for new MFA method enrollments, mail forwarding rules, OAuth grants, or role changes made after the phishing timestamp.
steps.guidance: This is the step most likely to be skipped and is where attackers retain access even after a password reset.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of attacker persistence.

steps.title: Restore user access with re-enrolled MFA
steps.desc: Guide the user through re-enrolling MFA from a known-clean device with a fresh password.
steps.outcome: User regains full, verified-clean access.

steps.title: Document the campaign and recommend a control improvement
steps.desc: Record the delivery vector, targeted MFA factor, and one concrete improvement (filter rule, phishing-resistant MFA rollout, or awareness point).
steps.outcome: Finding logged and, where applicable, a ticket opened against email security or identity teams.

steps.title: Determine which MFA factor was targeted
steps.desc: Classify whether the attack targeted a TOTP code, push approval, hardware token response, backup code, biometric prompt, or QR enrollment.
steps.guidance: The correct containment path differs sharply by factor type — reclassify to the specific ITID playbook once known and continue from there if a more specific playbook exists.
steps.outcome: Attack correctly classified by targeted factor.

steps.title: Block the phishing infrastructure
steps.desc: Add the phishing domain/URL to the web and mail blocklists and purge the message from any unread mailboxes.
steps.outcome: Phishing domain blocked org-wide; message purged where not yet opened.

steps.title: Remove any confirmed persistence
steps.desc: Delete any rogue MFA enrollment, forwarding rule, or OAuth grant identified in the prior step.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access mechanism remains.

steps.title: Check authentication logs for a successful sign-in near the phishing timestamp
steps.desc: Review identity provider sign-in logs for the affected account around the time of the phishing interaction.
steps.guidance: Look for logins from unfamiliar IPs, ASNs, or device fingerprints immediately following the reported interaction.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the phishing attempt resulted in a successful attacker authentication.

ITID-12612.def: An adversary lures a victim to a fake login page that captures the victim's password and time-based one-time passcode (TOTP) in real time and relays both to the legitimate service before the code expires.
ITID-12612.purpose: Captures phishing attacks that trick a user into typing a TOTP/authenticator-app code into an attacker-controlled page for real-time relay.
scopeIncludes: Fake login pages that prompt for a TOTP code alongside credentials
Manual or AiTM-proxy relay of a captured TOTP code within its validity window
scopeExcludes: Phishing targeting push-notification approval instead of a typed code (ITID-12613)
Phishing for hardware-token responses (ITID-12614)
ITID-12612.severity: High — a relayed TOTP code grants an authenticated session if used before expiry.
ITID-12612.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the account is privileged.
ITID-12612.escalation: Escalate immediately on any indication the code was successfully relayed and used.
indicators: Phishing page requesting both password and a 6-digit code
IdP sign-in immediately following a phishing-page submission from a different IP/ASN
vectors: Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) reverse-proxy phishing kit
Manual real-time relay by a human operator
rootCauses: TOTP as sole second factor with no phishing-resistant alternative
No conditional-access check for session/device continuity
mitreTechniques: T1556.006 Modify Authentication Process: Multi-Factor Authentication
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn) rollout for high-value accounts
Number-matching / context-rich push approval prompts
AiTM-aware conditional access (token binding, IP/device continuity checks)
User security awareness training on real-time credential relay phishing
ITID-12612.detection: Strong technical signal: IdP logs surface impossible-travel and new-device sign-ins immediately following a phishing click, reverse-proxy/AiTM kits leave detectable TLS and referrer fingerprints, and session tokens issued through a phishing relay show anomalous issuance velocity compared to genuine logins.
ITID-12612.response: Force sign-out and reset credentials plus MFA re-enrollment for the targeted user immediately on confirmation; hunt for reuse of any session token or code captured during the phishing window; block the phishing infrastructure at the email/web gateway.
metrics: Count of MFA phishing attempts detected per month
Median time from click to credential reset
Percentage of targeted users on phishing-resistant MFA
ITID-12612.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by the specific factor targeted (typed TOTP code) rather than push, hardware token, or biometric.

playbook.name: Response: TOTP/Authenticator App Code Phishing
playbook.description: For an attack where the user was tricked into entering a time-based one-time passcode from an authenticator app into an attacker-controlled relay page (real-time credential/OTP relay, typically AiTM).

steps.title: Confirm the code was entered on an attacker-controlled page
steps.desc: Interview the user and review the phishing page URL to confirm a TOTP code was submitted, not just viewed.
steps.guidance: Because TOTP codes expire in ~30-60 seconds, a relay attack requires the attacker to use the code almost immediately — this narrows the window to check.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether a valid TOTP code was submitted to the phishing page.
steps.abort: If the user only opened the link and did not submit a code, downgrade to a near-miss.

steps.title: Force password reset and revoke all sessions/tokens
steps.desc: Reset the account password and invalidate all active sessions, refresh tokens, and app passwords immediately.
steps.guidance: An AiTM relay typically steals the session cookie as well as the credential and code — revoking sessions is essential, not optional.
steps.outcome: Password rotated and all sessions terminated.

steps.title: Audit for attacker persistence
steps.desc: Check the account for new MFA methods, forwarding rules, OAuth app grants, or privilege changes made after the incident.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of persistence mechanisms.

steps.title: Restore access and consider phishing-resistant MFA
steps.desc: Restore the user's access and, if available, migrate them to a phishing-resistant method (FIDO2/passkey) instead of TOTP.
steps.guidance: TOTP is inherently phishable via relay; a hardware-bound method closes this specific gap going forward.
steps.outcome: User restored to access; stronger MFA method recommended or applied.

steps.title: Document the AiTM technique and recommend mitigations
steps.desc: Record the relay technique observed and recommend conditional access hardening (e.g., token-binding, device compliance checks) or MFA method migration.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a concrete follow-up action.

steps.title: Check for a near-simultaneous attacker authentication
steps.desc: Search identity provider logs for a successful login on the account within minutes of the code submission, from an unfamiliar IP/device.
steps.guidance: A relayed TOTP code is typically used within seconds, so correlate timestamps tightly.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the relayed code resulted in attacker access.

steps.title: Invalidate the TOTP seed and re-enroll the authenticator
steps.desc: Remove and re-register the TOTP authenticator app entry for the account.
steps.guidance: If the phishing page harvested the raw code only (not the seed), re-enrollment isn't strictly required, but do it anyway as a precaution given the seed's exposure risk is hard to rule out.
steps.outcome: New TOTP enrollment in place; old code no longer valid.

steps.title: Remove confirmed persistence
steps.desc: Delete any rogue MFA method, rule, or grant identified.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access mechanism remains.

steps.title: Block the relay/phishing infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the phishing domain at the web proxy and mail gateway, and purge the message from other mailboxes.
steps.outcome: Infrastructure blocked; message purged org-wide.

ITID-12613.def: An adversary uses a phishing lure (email, chat, or fake portal) to convince a victim to approve a single push-notification MFA request triggered by the adversary's own sign-in attempt.
ITID-12613.purpose: Captures phishing that induces a victim to approve a single, targeted push-notification MFA prompt as part of a phishing pretext, distinct from high-volume push bombing.
scopeIncludes: A single or small number of push prompts tied to a specific phishing pretext (e.g. fake IT ticket)
Phishing pages that trigger a push and instruct the victim to approve it
scopeExcludes: High-volume, repeated push bombing without a specific phishing narrative (MFA Fatigue Type, ITID-12621-12629)
Live phone-call-based real-time OTP/push relay (ITID-11218, vishing)
ITID-12613.severity: High — approval grants the adversary an authenticated session directly.
ITID-12613.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for privileged accounts.
ITID-12613.escalation: Escalate immediately once approval is confirmed; treat as an active account compromise.
indicators: Single unexplained push approval correlated with a phishing report
IdP sign-in from new device/location immediately after approval
vectors: Phishing email with a pretext for approving a single push (e.g. spoofed IT support message)
rootCauses: Users not trained to verify unsolicited push context before approving
No number-matching or context display on push prompts
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn) rollout for high-value accounts
Number-matching / context-rich push approval prompts
AiTM-aware conditional access (token binding, IP/device continuity checks)
User security awareness training on real-time credential relay phishing
ITID-12613.detection: Strong technical signal: IdP logs surface impossible-travel and new-device sign-ins immediately following a phishing click, reverse-proxy/AiTM kits leave detectable TLS and referrer fingerprints, and session tokens issued through a phishing relay show anomalous issuance velocity compared to genuine logins.
ITID-12613.response: Force sign-out and reset credentials plus MFA re-enrollment for the targeted user immediately on confirmation; hunt for reuse of any session token or code captured during the phishing window; block the phishing infrastructure at the email/web gateway.
metrics: Count of MFA phishing attempts detected per month
Median time from click to credential reset
Percentage of targeted users on phishing-resistant MFA
ITID-12613.notes: Scoped to a single, pretext-driven push tied to phishing; the volume-based repeated-prompt pattern is out of scope and lives under the MFA Fatigue Type (ITID-12621-12629).

playbook.name: Response: Push Notification Approval Phishing
playbook.description: For a single, deceptively-framed push authentication prompt (e.g., disguised as an IT/helpdesk request) that tricked a user into approving one attacker-initiated login, distinct from high-volume push-bombing.

steps.title: Confirm the user approved a push they did not initiate
steps.desc: Interview the user to confirm they approved a push notification while not actively signing in, and capture what pretext (e.g., fake IT call) was used.
steps.guidance: Distinguish this from MFA fatigue/push-bombing: here it is typically one or two deceptively-framed prompts with a social-engineering pretext, not a flood.
steps.outcome: Confirmed circumstances of the approval and the pretext used.

steps.title: Force password reset and revoke sessions
steps.desc: Reset the account password and terminate all active sessions and tokens.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated and prior sessions killed.

steps.title: Audit for attacker persistence
steps.desc: Check for new MFA enrollments, forwarding rules, or OAuth grants added during the attacker's session.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of persistence.

steps.title: Restore access and re-enroll MFA
steps.desc: Restore user access with a fresh password and re-enrolled MFA method.
steps.outcome: User has clean, verified access restored.

steps.title: Reinforce the 'never approve a prompt you didn't initiate' message and tune push policy
steps.desc: Document the pretext used and issue a targeted reminder to the affected team; evaluate number-matching or context-aware push approval if not already enabled.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness or policy follow-up initiated.

steps.title: Correlate the approval with the resulting login
steps.desc: Check identity provider logs for the login event tied to the approved push, including source IP, device, and location.
steps.outcome: Confirmed attacker login details established.

steps.title: Block the source IP/infrastructure used for the approval request
steps.desc: Block or flag the IP address and any associated infrastructure that generated the fraudulent push.
steps.outcome: Source infrastructure blocked at the firewall/identity provider risk policy.

steps.title: Remove confirmed persistence
steps.desc: Delete any rogue MFA method, rule, or grant found.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access mechanism remains.

ITID-12614.def: An adversary phishes a victim for the numeric code displayed on, or the challenge-response generated by, a hardware OTP token, then relays it to the legitimate service before expiry.
ITID-12614.purpose: Captures phishing attempts to capture the numeric or challenge-response output of a hardware OTP token (not phishing-resistant FIDO2/WebAuthn keys).
scopeIncludes: Phishing pages requesting a hardware-token-generated numeric code
Social engineering to read out a hardware token's display over chat/phone in support of a phishing flow
scopeExcludes: Phishing-resistant FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys, which are not phishable by design and out of scope for this leaf
Software authenticator-app TOTP phishing (ITID-12612)
ITID-12614.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for privileged accounts.
ITID-12614.escalation: Escalate immediately if the token response was relayed and used.
indicators: Phishing page requesting a hardware-token code
Sign-in event immediately following code submission from an unrecognized device
vectors: Fake login/support page prompting for a hardware token's displayed code
rootCauses: Legacy hardware OTP tokens still deployed without a phishing-resistant migration path
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn) rollout for high-value accounts
Number-matching / context-rich push approval prompts
AiTM-aware conditional access (token binding, IP/device continuity checks)
User security awareness training on real-time credential relay phishing
ITID-12614.detection: Strong technical signal: IdP logs surface impossible-travel and new-device sign-ins immediately following a phishing click, reverse-proxy/AiTM kits leave detectable TLS and referrer fingerprints, and session tokens issued through a phishing relay show anomalous issuance velocity compared to genuine logins.
ITID-12614.response: Force sign-out and reset credentials plus MFA re-enrollment for the targeted user immediately on confirmation; hunt for reuse of any session token or code captured during the phishing window; block the phishing infrastructure at the email/web gateway.
metrics: Count of MFA phishing attempts detected per month
Median time from click to credential reset
Percentage of targeted users on phishing-resistant MFA
ITID-12614.notes: Explicitly excludes FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware security keys, whose challenge-response is bound to origin and not phishable; this leaf covers legacy OTP-generating hardware tokens only.

playbook.name: Response: Hardware Token/Security Key Response Phishing
playbook.description: For an attack where a user was phished into reading out or relaying the numeric response from a hardware OTP token (e.g., RSA SecurID-style device) to an attacker-controlled site or caller.

steps.title: Confirm what was disclosed and to whom
steps.desc: Interview the user to determine whether they read a hardware token code to a caller, entered it on a phishing page, or both.
steps.guidance: Hardware OTP tokens generate short-lived codes, so timing of the disclosure versus any resulting login is critical.
steps.outcome: Confirmed disclosure method and timing.

steps.title: Force password reset and revoke sessions
steps.desc: Reset the account password and terminate active sessions and VPN connections tied to the account.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated and sessions terminated.

steps.title: Audit for attacker persistence
steps.desc: Review the account and any systems accessed via VPN/remote access for new accounts, rules, or lateral movement.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any further attacker action.

steps.title: Reissue token and restore access
steps.desc: Provision the user with a new or reseeded token and restore normal access.
steps.outcome: User has functioning, verified-clean token access restored.

steps.title: Document the vishing/phishing pretext and reinforce token-handling policy
steps.desc: Record how the disclosure was elicited and reinforce that hardware token codes should never be read to a caller or entered outside the legitimate login prompt.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; targeted awareness reminder issued.

steps.title: Check for a correlated attacker authentication
steps.desc: Search identity/VPN logs for a successful authentication using the account within the token code's validity window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the token response was actually used by an attacker.

steps.title: Suspend or re-seed the hardware token
steps.desc: Work with the token administrator to suspend the affected token and, if the seed itself may be compromised, request a reseed or replacement device.
steps.guidance: A single disclosed code does not compromise the seed, but repeated social-engineering against the same user may indicate seed-level compromise — assess accordingly.
steps.outcome: Token suspended or reseeded; account cannot authenticate with the old token state.
steps.tool: Token management system (e.g., RSA Authentication Manager)
