steps.desc: Enumerate all accounts using this phone number for SMS MFA, voice verification, or recovery.
steps.outcome: Complete list of at-risk accounts.

ITID-12645.def: An adversary requests or triggers activation of a new eSIM profile for the victim's number, causing the carrier to deactivate the victim's existing SIM/eSIM and route service to the adversary's device.
ITID-12645.purpose: Captures the eSIM-specific variant of number hijacking, where an adversary triggers a new eSIM QR/profile activation that silently deactivates the victim's physical or existing eSIM profile.

scopeExcludes: Physical SIM card swap/cloning with no eSIM involvement (ITID-12647)

ITID-12645.escalation: Escalate immediately; carrier eSIM reprovisioning is often near-instantaneous and requires urgent carrier fraud escalation.
indicators: eSIM activation event on the victim's line with no corresponding legitimate device-change request
Instantaneous loss of service without a physical SIM removal
vectors: Fraudulent eSIM QR-based reprovisioning requests via carrier app or support channel
rootCauses: eSIM reprovisioning flows with weaker identity verification than physical SIM replacement
controls: Migration away from SMS/voice as an MFA factor for high-value accounts toward app-based or hardware MFA
Carrier account PIN/passcode and port-freeze enrollment

Real-time carrier port/SIM-change notification monitoring where available

playbook.name: Response: eSIM Reprovisioning Attack
playbook.description: For an attack where an adversary fraudulently generated a new eSIM QR code/activation profile for the victim's number and activated it on attacker-controlled hardware, bypassing the need for physical SIM possession.

steps.title: Confirm the eSIM reprovisioning and obtain the activation record
steps.desc: Contact the carrier to confirm a new eSIM profile was generated/activated for the number, and obtain the activation timestamp, channel (app/web/store), and device it was activated on.
steps.outcome: Confirmed reprovisioning event with activation details.

steps.title: Deactivate the fraudulent eSIM profile and restore the legitimate one
steps.desc: Work with the carrier to deactivate the attacker's eSIM profile and reprovision the number to the user's legitimate device.
steps.outcome: Number restored to the legitimate device; fraudulent profile deactivated.

steps.title: Audit each at-risk account for compromise
steps.desc: Review each account for evidence of attacker access during the reprovisioning window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any account compromise.

steps.title: Add carrier account protections and restore service
steps.desc: Add a carrier PIN and port/eSIM-change lock, and confirm the user's phone service is fully restored.
steps.outcome: Phone service restored with hardened carrier account controls.

steps.title: Document the eSIM reprovisioning gap and push for carrier-side hardening
steps.desc: Record the authorization gap identified and, if it reflects a broader carrier weakness, formally raise it with the carrier and recommend additional identity verification for eSIM changes.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; carrier notified of the gap.

steps.title: Determine how the reprovisioning was authorized
steps.desc: Establish whether the eSIM profile generation required only account-level authentication (making it equivalent to an online portal swap) or additional identity verification that was bypassed.
steps.outcome: Understood authorization gap that allowed the reprovisioning.

steps.title: Force password reset and revoke sessions on every account tied to the number
steps.desc: Reset passwords and terminate sessions on all identified at-risk accounts.
steps.outcome: Credentials rotated and sessions terminated across all at-risk accounts.

steps.title: Remove confirmed persistence and migrate off SMS-based MFA
steps.desc: Remove any rogue access mechanism found, and move affected accounts to app-based or hardware MFA.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access remains; accounts hardened.

steps.title: Identify all accounts tied to the phone number
steps.desc: Enumerate all accounts using this phone number for SMS MFA, voice verification, or recovery.
steps.outcome: Complete list of at-risk accounts.

ITID-12646.def: An adversary submits a fraudulent number-port request to move the victim's phone number to a new carrier and a device under the adversary's control, severing the number from the original carrier entirely.
ITID-12646.purpose: Captures number porting to an entirely different carrier (rather than a same-carrier SIM swap), which fully removes the number from the original carrier's fraud-monitoring visibility.
scopeIncludes: Cross-carrier port-out fraud using a stolen account number/PIN or forged authorization
scopeExcludes: Same-carrier SIM/eSIM swaps that do not change carrier (ITID-12642, ITID-12644, ITID-12645)
ITID-12646.severity: Critical — cross-carrier porting is harder to reverse quickly and removes the original carrier's ability to intervene directly.
ITID-12646.escalation: Escalate immediately; coordinate with both the losing and gaining carrier, which typically requires longer resolution than an in-carrier swap.
indicators: Port-out confirmation notice from the original carrier that the subscriber did not initiate
Number now active on a different carrier's network
vectors: Fraudulent port-out request using a stolen account PIN or forged letter of authorization
rootCauses: Weak cross-carrier port-authorization verification (e.g. NPAC porting-fraud gaps)
controls: Migration away from SMS/voice as an MFA factor for high-value accounts toward app-based or hardware MFA
Carrier account PIN/passcode and port-freeze enrollment
Step-up verification for any SIM-swap-adjacent event (new device sign-in shortly after a carrier change)
Real-time carrier port/SIM-change notification monitoring where available

ITID-12646.response: On any indicator, immediately disable SMS/voice as an MFA factor for the affected account, force a credential reset, and coordinate with the user to re-secure the carrier account.

Mean time to disable SMS MFA after a suspected swap

New-device sign-in shortly after phone-number-based MFA reset

playbook.name: Response: Port-Out (Number Porting) Attack
playbook.description: For an attack where the victim's phone number was fraudulently ported to an entirely different carrier under attacker control, rather than swapped to a new SIM on the same carrier.

steps.title: Confirm the port-out and identify the receiving carrier
steps.desc: Contact the losing (original) carrier to confirm the port-out, and identify the receiving carrier the number was ported to.
steps.guidance: A port-out to a different carrier requires cross-carrier coordination to reverse, unlike a same-carrier SIM swap.
steps.outcome: Confirmed port-out with receiving carrier identified.

steps.title: File a port-out dispute and initiate cross-carrier reversal
steps.desc: File a fraudulent-port dispute with both the losing and receiving carriers to initiate reversal of the port.
steps.guidance: This can take longer than a same-carrier SIM swap reversal — set expectations accordingly and pursue urgently.
steps.outcome: Dispute filed with both carriers; reversal process underway.

steps.title: Audit each at-risk account for compromise
steps.desc: Review each account for evidence of attacker access during the window the number was ported away.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any account compromise.

steps.title: Confirm the number is restored and add a port freeze
steps.desc: Confirm the number has been returned to the original carrier and device, and request a port freeze/lock to prevent future unauthorized ports.
steps.outcome: Number restored; port freeze applied.

steps.title: Document the port authorization gap and consider a regulatory complaint
steps.desc: Record how the port authorization was bypassed, and if the carrier's process was clearly deficient, consider filing a complaint with the relevant telecom regulator.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; external complaint filed where warranted.

steps.title: Determine what authorization was used for the port
steps.desc: Obtain from the losing carrier what information/authorization code was presented to approve the port.
steps.guidance: Ports typically require an account PIN or the last bill amount — determine how the attacker obtained it.
steps.outcome: Understood authorization gap that allowed the port.

steps.title: Force password reset and revoke sessions on every account tied to the number
steps.desc: Reset passwords and terminate sessions on all identified at-risk accounts without waiting for the port reversal to complete.
steps.outcome: Credentials rotated and sessions terminated across all at-risk accounts.

steps.title: Remove confirmed persistence and migrate off SMS-based MFA
steps.desc: Remove any rogue access mechanism found, and move affected accounts to app-based or hardware MFA.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access remains; accounts hardened.

steps.title: Identify all accounts tied to the phone number
steps.desc: Enumerate all accounts using this phone number for SMS MFA, voice verification, or recovery.
steps.outcome: Complete list of at-risk accounts.

ITID-12647.def: An adversary obtains physical possession of, or clones the identifiers from, the victim's physical SIM card to receive SMS/voice-based MFA intended for the victim.
ITID-12647.purpose: Captures physical theft or cloning of the victim's actual SIM card, requiring physical access rather than remote social engineering or portal abuse.

SIM cloning using extracted Ki/authentication key material from physical access to the card
scopeExcludes: Remote carrier social engineering or self-service portal abuse (other leaves in this Type)

indicators: Reported physical theft of a device/SIM correlated with subsequent account access anomalies
Two SIMs with identical identifiers active on the network (cloning)
vectors: Physical theft
SIM-cloning hardware used against a physically accessed card
rootCauses: Older SIM technology vulnerable to key extraction
No device/SIM PIN lock
controls: Migration away from SMS/voice as an MFA factor for high-value accounts toward app-based or hardware MFA
Carrier account PIN/passcode and port-freeze enrollment
Step-up verification for any SIM-swap-adjacent event (new device sign-in shortly after a carrier change)
Real-time carrier port/SIM-change notification monitoring where available

metrics: Count of SIM-swap-related incidents per quarter
Percentage of high-value accounts still using SMS/voice as an MFA factor
Mean time to disable SMS MFA after a suspected swap
detections: SMS-based MFA reset correlated with reported service loss
New-device sign-in shortly after phone-number-based MFA reset
ITID-12647.notes: Differentiating axis: requires physical access to the SIM itself, the only leaf in this group with a physical-custody element.

playbook.name: Response: Physical SIM Card Theft/Cloning
playbook.description: For an incident where an attacker gained physical possession of a victim's SIM card, or cloned it using specialized hardware, to intercept calls/SMS without any carrier-side account change.

steps.title: Confirm whether the SIM was physically stolen or cloned in place
steps.desc: Determine whether the user's physical SIM/device is missing (theft) or still in their possession while service anomalies persist (cloning).
steps.guidance: Cloning without theft is technically harder and rarer, but leaves the legitimate SIM operative alongside the clone, which is a distinguishing sign.
steps.outcome: Confirmed theft vs. cloning scenario.

steps.title: Deactivate the physical SIM and issue a replacement
steps.desc: Have the carrier deactivate the stolen/cloned SIM entirely and issue a fresh SIM with a new ICCID to the legitimate user.
steps.outcome: Old SIM deactivated; legitimate user has a new, uncloned SIM.

steps.title: Audit each at-risk account for compromise
steps.desc: Review each account for evidence of attacker access during the period the SIM was compromised.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any account compromise.

steps.title: Confirm restored service on the new SIM
steps.desc: Confirm the user's phone service is fully functional on the new, uncompromised SIM.
steps.outcome: Phone service restored on a verified-clean SIM.

steps.title: Document the theft/cloning method and consider a police report
steps.desc: Record how the physical SIM was obtained or cloned, and if theft was involved, advise the user to file a police report for identity-theft protection purposes.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; user advised on external reporting.

steps.title: Check for concurrent/duplicate registration on the carrier network
steps.desc: Ask the carrier to check for simultaneous or overlapping network registrations for the SIM, which indicates cloning.
steps.outcome: Confirmed or ruled-out concurrent registration.

steps.title: Force password reset and revoke sessions on every account tied to the number
steps.desc: Reset passwords and terminate sessions on all identified at-risk accounts.
steps.outcome: Credentials rotated and sessions terminated across all at-risk accounts.

steps.title: Remove confirmed persistence and migrate off SMS-based MFA
steps.desc: Remove any rogue access mechanism found, and move affected accounts to app-based or hardware MFA.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access remains; accounts hardened.

steps.title: Identify all accounts tied to the phone number
steps.desc: Enumerate all accounts using this phone number for SMS MFA, voice verification, or recovery.
steps.outcome: Complete list of at-risk accounts.

scopeIncludes: SIM swaps where the enabling PII/credentials are traced to a specific prior breach or leak
scopeExcludes: SIM swaps with no identifiable prior-leak dependency (ITID-12642)

indicators: Carrier verification answers matching data known to be exposed in a specific prior breach

rootCauses: Carrier identity verification relying on static, breach-exposable PII (SSN, DOB, address)

Carrier account PIN/passcode and port-freeze enrollment

Percentage of high-value accounts still using SMS/voice as an MFA factor
Mean time to disable SMS MFA after a suspected swap
detections: SMS-based MFA reset correlated with reported service loss
New-device sign-in shortly after phone-number-based MFA reset

playbook.name: Response: SIM Swap Enabled by Prior Credential/PII Leak
playbook.description: For a SIM swap traced back to a specific prior data breach or leak that gave the attacker the PII needed to pass carrier identity verification (e.g., a leaked account PIN, SSN, or billing history).

steps.title: Confirm the swap and identify the specific leaked data used
steps.desc: Contact the carrier to confirm the swap and identify exactly which PII/authorization data was presented, then trace it to the specific prior breach or leak.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference against known breach-monitoring alerts already on file for the user or organization.
steps.outcome: Confirmed swap with the leaked-data source identified.
steps.tool: Carrier fraud team / breach monitoring service

steps.title: Reverse the swap and change the compromised carrier verification data
steps.desc: Work with the carrier to restore the number and change the specific PIN/verification data that was leaked and used.
steps.outcome: Number restored; leaked verification data rotated.

steps.title: Audit each at-risk account for compromise
steps.desc: Review each account for evidence of attacker access using either the number or the leaked data.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of any account compromise.

steps.title: Restore service and place a fraud/credit alert if identity data was involved
steps.desc: Confirm restored phone service, and if SSN or similar identity data was part of the leak, recommend the user place a fraud alert or credit freeze with credit bureaus.
steps.outcome: Phone service restored; broader identity-theft protections advised.

steps.title: Document the breach linkage and recommend eliminating knowledge-based verification
steps.desc: Record which breach enabled the attack and recommend the carrier/organization stop relying on static, potentially-leaked PII (SSN, DOB) as sole identity verification.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a concrete control recommendation.

steps.title: Assess what else that same leaked data set exposes
steps.desc: Determine what other accounts or systems are protected by the same leaked PII/credential, since the same data may enable further attacks beyond this SIM swap.
steps.outcome: Full understanding of the breach's exposure beyond this single incident.

steps.title: Force password reset and revoke sessions on every account tied to the number and the leaked data
steps.desc: Reset passwords and terminate sessions on all accounts identified as at risk from either the number or the underlying leaked data.
steps.outcome: Credentials rotated and sessions terminated across all at-risk accounts.

steps.title: Remove confirmed persistence and migrate off SMS-based MFA
steps.desc: Remove any rogue access mechanism found, and move affected accounts to app-based or hardware MFA.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access remains; accounts hardened.

steps.desc: Enumerate all accounts using this phone number for SMS MFA, voice verification, or recovery.
steps.outcome: Complete list of at-risk accounts.

playbook.name: Response: Successful SIM Swap with Confirmed Downstream Account Takeover
playbook.description: For a confirmed case where a SIM swap (of any method) was used to successfully take over one or more downstream accounts protected by SMS-based verification — the high-severity, post-compromise variant requiring full account-takeover response across every affected account.

steps.title: Confirm the swap and establish the full timeline of attacker control over the number
steps.desc: Establish, from carrier records, exactly when the number was under attacker control.
steps.outcome: Confirmed timeline of attacker control over the number.

steps.title: Restore the phone number and lock the carrier account
steps.desc: Work with the carrier to restore the number to the legitimate device and apply a port/SIM-change lock.
steps.outcome: Number restored; carrier account locked.

steps.title: Remove attacker persistence across every compromised account
steps.desc: Remove rogue MFA enrollments, forwarding rules, OAuth grants, or new payees/recipients added by the attacker on every affected account.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access mechanism remains on any account.

steps.title: Restore access to every affected account and validate with the user
steps.desc: Restore access to all affected accounts and confirm with the user that data and account state look correct.
steps.outcome: Verified-clean access restored across all affected accounts.

steps.title: Conduct a formal post-incident review and report to relevant authorities
steps.desc: Document root cause, full timeline, blast radius, and required control changes; report to relevant stakeholders and, given confirmed financial/identity impact, consider a law-enforcement report.
steps.outcome: Formal after-action report completed with assigned remediation owners.

steps.title: Enumerate every downstream account compromised via the number
steps.desc: Review every account that uses this number for SMS MFA/recovery and determine which were actually accessed or reset by the attacker during the window.
steps.guidance: Pay particular attention to financial, email, and cloud identity accounts, which are the highest-value common SIM-swap targets.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of every account actually compromised.
steps.tool: SIEM / account activity logs across affected platforms

steps.title: Force password reset and revoke sessions/tokens on every compromised account
steps.desc: Reset credentials and terminate all sessions and tokens on every account confirmed compromised.
steps.outcome: All compromised accounts have rotated credentials and terminated sessions.
steps.tool: Identity provider / IAM consoles across platforms

steps.title: Migrate every affected account off SMS-based verification
steps.desc: Move every affected account to app-based or hardware MFA, removing the phone number as a factor wherever possible.
steps.outcome: No affected account remains dependent on SMS verification.

steps.title: Extended monitoring across all affected accounts and the carrier account
steps.desc: Place all affected accounts and the carrier account under elevated monitoring for at least 30 days.
steps.outcome: No further anomalous activity observed during the window.

steps.title: Determine the full extent of attacker activity on each compromised account
steps.desc: For each compromised account, review data accessed, funds moved, emails sent, or configuration changes made.
steps.outcome: Complete activity timeline for every compromised account.

steps.title: Contain financial impact if funds were moved
steps.desc: If any financial account was accessed, contact the financial institution immediately to freeze transactions and attempt recall of any transferred funds.
steps.outcome: Financial institution engaged; transaction freeze/recall attempted.

ITID-12711.def: An incident of forged Kerberos ticket-granting-ticket (TGT) use based on a compromised krbtgt account hash, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type.
ITID-12711.purpose: Catch-all for golden ticket reports not yet matching a more specific mechanism or objective.
scopeIncludes: Reports of suspected golden ticket use where the extraction method, ticket properties, or objective are not yet determined
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID once details are known
Forged service tickets only (Pass-the-Ticket Type covers reuse of legitimate/forged service tickets more broadly, ITID-12731-12739)
ITID-12711.severity: Critical by default — any suspected krbtgt compromise is treated as domain-wide until ruled out.
ITID-12711.escalation: Escalate immediately to AD/identity team regardless of confirmation status.
indicators: Alert of unclear specific golden-ticket indicator (anomalous ticket, DCSync, unexplained domain admin action)
vectors: Activity of unclear specific krbtgt-compromise vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
mitreTechniques: T1558.001 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket
controls: krbtgt account password rotated twice in succession per Microsoft guidance after any suspected compromise
Tiered administration model (no domain admin credentials on lower-tier hosts) to limit krbtgt exposure
Monitoring/alerting on Kerberos ticket lifetime and encryption-type anomalies
Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) restricting where domain controller credential material can be touched
ITID-12711.detection: One of the best-instrumented techniques in this domain: Kerberos ticket lifetime far exceeding domain policy, encryption downgrade (RC4 where AES is enforced), TGS requests with no corresponding AS-REQ, and DCSync-pattern replication requests from non-DC hosts are all reliably observable in Windows Security and domain-controller logs.
ITID-12711.response: Treat any confirmed golden ticket as full domain compromise: reset the krbtgt password twice with an interval, invalidate all existing Kerberos tickets domain-wide, and conduct a full compromise-scope investigation before considering the domain trustworthy again.
metrics: Count of golden ticket incidents/attempts per year
Time from krbtgt compromise to double password reset
Percentage of domain controllers with tiered-admin enforcement
ITID-12711.notes: Intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one; treated as critical-by-default given blast radius even before full confirmation.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Golden Ticket Attack
playbook.description: General-purpose checklist for a suspected Golden Ticket attack before the specific vector/scope has been confirmed. Golden Ticket attacks are domain-critical and warrant immediate escalation regardless of sub-type.

steps.title: Confirm indicators are consistent with a forged TGT
steps.desc: Review the alert (e.g. anomalous ticket lifetime, TGT for a nonexistent/disabled account, PAC anomaly) against known Golden Ticket detection signatures.
steps.guidance: Escalate to the AD/domain team immediately given the severity even while confirming — do not wait for full confirmation before notifying.
steps.outcome: Confirmed indicators consistent with a forged Kerberos TGT.
steps.abort: If explained by a legitimate ticket renewal or clock skew, close as false positive.

steps.title: Engage the domain/AD team and prepare for krbtgt remediation
steps.desc: Escalate to Active Directory administrators to prepare for the krbtgt password reset procedure required to invalidate forged tickets.
steps.outcome: AD team engaged and briefed on the domain-wide implications.

steps.title: Hand off to the matching specific Golden Ticket playbook
steps.desc: Once the vector is confirmed, escalate to and follow the specific playbook (DCSync-obtained hash, direct DC extraction, long-lived ticket, forged group membership, cross-domain trust abuse, anomalous lifetime, or post-single-reset reuse) for the krbtgt remediation procedure.
steps.outcome: Incident reassigned with all evidence carried forward.

steps.title: Confirm no forged tickets remain valid
steps.desc: Monitor domain authentication for a defined window to confirm no further forged-ticket activity following remediation.
steps.outcome: No further Golden Ticket activity observed.

steps.title: Full incident report and leadership briefing
steps.desc: Document root cause, scope, and response; brief leadership given the domain-wide severity of any confirmed Golden Ticket attack.
steps.outcome: Full report completed.

steps.title: Determine the specific Golden Ticket vector
steps.desc: Establish how the krbtgt hash was likely obtained (DCSync, direct DC extraction) and any distinguishing characteristics (forged group membership, cross-domain trust abuse, anomalous lifetime).
steps.guidance: This determines which specific playbook to hand off to.
steps.outcome: Vector identified or narrowed to a short list.

steps.title: Isolate any system with confirmed malicious activity using the forged ticket
steps.desc: Network-isolate any endpoint or server where the forged ticket was used for access.
steps.outcome: Confirmed-affected systems isolated.

steps.title: Assume domain-wide compromise pending scoping
steps.desc: Treat every domain-joined system and account as potentially at risk until the investigation proves otherwise — a Golden Ticket implies the krbtgt account hash is already compromised.
steps.outcome: Incident scoped as domain-wide by default; stakeholders and leadership notified.

ITID-12712.def: An adversary with directory-replication rights (or rights obtained through privilege escalation) issues a DCSync request to a domain controller to extract the krbtgt account's password hash, then uses it to forge golden tickets.
ITID-12712.purpose: Captures golden ticket forgery where the krbtgt hash was obtained via a DCSync replication request rather than direct disk/memory access to a domain controller.

scopeExcludes: Direct extraction from a domain controller's NTDS.dit or LSASS memory (ITID-12713)
ITID-12712.escalation: Escalate immediately; the account/host used to issue DCSync must also be investigated for how it obtained replication rights.
indicators: DRS GetNCChanges request originating from a workstation/server rather than a domain controller
Replication request for the krbtgt object specifically outside normal DC-to-DC replication
vectors: Abuse of an account granted (or escalated to) Replicating Directory Changes/Replicating Directory Changes All rights
rootCauses: Over-permissioned service or admin accounts holding directory-replication rights unnecessarily
mitreTechniques: T1558.001 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket

Tiered administration model (no domain admin credentials on lower-tier hosts) to limit krbtgt exposure
Monitoring/alerting on Kerberos ticket lifetime and encryption-type anomalies
Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) restricting where domain controller credential material can be touched
ITID-12712.detection: One of the best-instrumented techniques in this domain: Kerberos ticket lifetime far exceeding domain policy, encryption downgrade (RC4 where AES is enforced), TGS requests with no corresponding AS-REQ, and DCSync-pattern replication requests from non-DC hosts are all reliably observable in Windows Security and domain-controller logs.
ITID-12712.response: Treat any confirmed golden ticket as full domain compromise: reset the krbtgt password twice with an interval, invalidate all existing Kerberos tickets domain-wide, and conduct a full compromise-scope investigation before considering the domain trustworthy again.
metrics: Count of golden ticket incidents/attempts per year
Time from krbtgt compromise to double password reset
Percentage of domain controllers with tiered-admin enforcement
ITID-12712.notes: Differentiating axis: extraction source is a remote DCSync replication call rather than direct DC compromise.

playbook.name: Response: Golden Ticket via DCSync-Obtained krbtgt Hash
playbook.description: For a Golden Ticket attack where the attacker obtained the krbtgt account hash by abusing directory replication permissions (DCSync) rather than direct access to a domain controller.

steps.title: Confirm DCSync activity in the authentication logs
steps.desc: Review domain controller security logs (Event ID 4662 with replication GUIDs, or EDR/SIEM DCSync detections) to confirm a DCSync-style replication request occurred from a non-DC source.
steps.outcome: Confirmed DCSync event with source account/host identified.

steps.title: Disable or contain the account that performed the DCSync request
steps.desc: Disable the compromised account used for DCSync and revoke its unwarranted replication permissions.
steps.outcome: Source account disabled; replication permissions removed.

steps.title: Perform the double krbtgt password reset with the required replication wait
steps.desc: Reset the krbtgt account password twice, waiting for full AD replication convergence between resets (and allowing existing legitimate ticket lifetimes to lapse), per Microsoft's documented procedure.
steps.guidance: A single reset is insufficient — krbtgt maintains two password versions, so the first reset alone does not invalidate tickets forged with the previous hash. This is the single most critical step for this ITID.
steps.outcome: Both krbtgt password versions rotated and confirmed replicated to all domain controllers.

steps.title: Rebuild trust: re-issue affected credentials and monitor domain-wide
steps.desc: Reset passwords for privileged accounts active during the compromise window and apply elevated monitoring domain-wide for a defined observation period.
steps.outcome: No further forged-ticket or DCSync activity observed.

steps.title: Full incident report and leadership briefing on domain-wide compromise
steps.desc: Document the complete attack chain from initial access through DCSync to Golden Ticket use; brief leadership and assess breach notification obligations.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Identify the account used to perform DCSync and how it obtained replication rights
steps.desc: Determine which account executed the DCSync request and how it acquired Replicating Directory Changes / Replicating Directory Changes All permissions — misconfigured delegation, compromised privileged account, or GPO/ACL abuse.
steps.outcome: Source account and privilege-acquisition path identified.

steps.title: Isolate systems showing forged-ticket-based access
steps.desc: Network-isolate any system accessed using tickets forged with the stolen krbtgt hash.
steps.outcome: Affected systems isolated.

steps.title: Audit and remediate every account/group with directory replication permissions
steps.desc: Review all accounts holding Replicating Directory Changes/All rights domain-wide and remove any unwarranted grants beyond built-in DC accounts and legitimate directory-sync service accounts.
steps.guidance: This closes the root cause — otherwise the attacker can simply DCSync again with a different or the same account.
steps.outcome: Replication permissions confirmed minimal and appropriate domain-wide.

steps.title: Confirm subsequent Golden Ticket use following the DCSync event
steps.desc: Correlate the DCSync timestamp with subsequent anomalous TGT/ticket activity to confirm the stolen hash was used to forge tickets.
steps.outcome: Confirmed forged-ticket activity tied to the DCSync event.

steps.title: Investigate how the DCSync-capable account was itself compromised
steps.desc: Trace back to the initial access or privilege-escalation path that gave the attacker control of the account used for DCSync.
steps.outcome: Initial access vector identified and closed.

ITID-12713.def: An adversary with direct administrative or physical access to a domain controller extracts the krbtgt password hash from LSASS memory or the NTDS.dit database, then uses it to forge golden tickets.
ITID-12713.purpose: Captures golden ticket forgery where the krbtgt hash was extracted directly from a compromised domain controller's memory or NTDS.dit database.

Offline extraction from a copied/exfiltrated NTDS.dit file
scopeExcludes: Remote extraction via DCSync replication request (ITID-12712)

indicators: LSASS access alert (e.g. credential-dumping tool signature) on a domain controller
NTDS.dit file access/copy activity outside normal backup processes
vectors: Credential-dumping tooling (e.g. Mimikatz) run directly on a compromised DC
Volume Shadow Copy abuse to extract NTDS.dit

ITID-12713.response: Treat any confirmed golden ticket as full domain compromise: reset the krbtgt password twice with an interval, invalidate all existing Kerberos tickets domain-wide, and conduct a full compromise-scope investigation before considering the domain trustworthy again.

Time from krbtgt compromise to double password reset
Percentage of domain controllers with tiered-admin enforcement

playbook.name: Response: Golden Ticket via Direct Domain Controller Extraction
playbook.description: For a Golden Ticket attack where the attacker obtained the krbtgt hash through direct compromise of a domain controller (e.g. NTDS.dit extraction, LSASS dump on the DC), implying the DC itself was breached.

steps.title: Confirm direct compromise of a domain controller
steps.desc: Review EDR/security logs on all domain controllers for evidence of NTDS.dit access/copy, LSASS memory dumping, volume shadow copy abuse, or unauthorized admin logon.
steps.guidance: This is more severe than DCSync — it implies the attacker had interactive or remote administrative access to a DC.
steps.outcome: Confirmed which DC(s) were directly compromised and the extraction method.

steps.title: Isolate the compromised domain controller(s)
steps.desc: Network-isolate the affected DC(s) while maintaining domain functionality via remaining healthy DCs.
steps.guidance: Coordinate carefully with AD team to avoid domain-wide authentication outage.
steps.outcome: Compromised DC(s) isolated; domain services continue via healthy DCs.

steps.title: Perform the double krbtgt password reset with replication wait
steps.desc: Reset the krbtgt account password twice with a full replication-convergence wait between resets, per documented procedure.
steps.guidance: Required regardless of extraction method — this is the only way to invalidate tickets already forged with the stolen hash.
steps.outcome: Both krbtgt password versions rotated and confirmed replicated.

steps.title: Phased domain-wide recovery with elevated monitoring
steps.desc: Bring rebuilt DCs and reset accounts back into normal operation in phases with heightened logging and monitoring active throughout.
steps.outcome: Domain services fully restored with no signs of recurring compromise.

steps.title: Full incident report, root-cause analysis, and regulatory notification assessment
steps.desc: Document the complete attack chain, full scope of exposure (entire AD database), response, and assess breach notification obligations given the severity.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Determine how the attacker gained administrative access to the DC
steps.desc: Trace the access path — compromised Domain Admin credential, unpatched vulnerability, lateral movement from another privileged system.
steps.outcome: Initial access/privilege-escalation path identified.

steps.title: Disable the compromised administrative account(s) used for access
steps.desc: Disable any Domain Admin or privileged account confirmed used to access the DC.
steps.outcome: Compromised privileged accounts disabled.

steps.title: Reset ALL domain account credentials given full database exposure
steps.desc: Given direct DC/NTDS.dit access implies the entire account hash database was likely exposed, plan and execute an organization-wide credential reset, prioritizing privileged and service accounts first.
steps.guidance: This is a large undertaking — coordinate timing and communications carefully, but it is warranted given the exposure scope.
steps.outcome: All domain credentials rotated, prioritized by sensitivity.

steps.title: Assess what else was accessed on the compromised DC
steps.desc: Given direct DC access, assume the attacker could have exfiltrated the full AD database (all account hashes, not just krbtgt) — confirm scope.
steps.guidance: Treat this as a full domain database compromise, not just a krbtgt theft.
steps.outcome: Full scope of data accessed on the DC established.

steps.title: Rebuild the compromised domain controller(s) from a known-clean state
steps.desc: Given the depth of compromise, rebuild affected DCs from verified-clean installation media rather than in-place remediation.
steps.outcome: Compromised DC(s) rebuilt and verified clean.

ITID-12714.def: An adversary forges a golden ticket with an extended or effectively unlimited lifetime value, bypassing the default Kerberos ticket-renewal window to maintain long-term domain access without needing to re-forge tickets.
ITID-12714.purpose: Captures golden tickets forged with an unusually long or unlimited validity/lifetime field, intended for extended, low-visibility persistence.
scopeIncludes: Golden tickets with a lifetime field set well beyond the domain's default (commonly configured up to 10 years in known toolkits)
scopeExcludes: Golden tickets with default/standard lifetime values used for short-term objectives (ITID-12711)
ITID-12714.severity: Critical — extended lifetime is a strong persistence indicator warranting the highest scrutiny.
ITID-12714.escalation: Escalate immediately; the extended validity strongly suggests a long-dwell compromise requiring extensive historical log review.
indicators: Kerberos ticket lifetime field far exceeding domain Group Policy-configured maximum
vectors: Golden ticket forged with a deliberately extended lifetime parameter
rootCauses: No automated alerting on ticket-lifetime values exceeding policy

Tiered administration model (no domain admin credentials on lower-tier hosts) to limit krbtgt exposure
Monitoring/alerting on Kerberos ticket lifetime and encryption-type anomalies
Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) restricting where domain controller credential material can be touched

ITID-12714.response: Treat any confirmed golden ticket as full domain compromise: reset the krbtgt password twice with an interval, invalidate all existing Kerberos tickets domain-wide, and conduct a full compromise-scope investigation before considering the domain trustworthy again.
metrics: Count of golden ticket incidents/attempts per year
Time from krbtgt compromise to double password reset
Percentage of domain controllers with tiered-admin enforcement
ITID-12714.notes: Differentiating axis: the specific forged-ticket property (extended lifetime) rather than the extraction method used to obtain krbtgt.

playbook.name: Response: Long-Lived/Extended-Validity Golden Ticket
playbook.description: For a Golden Ticket forged with an abnormally long or effectively unlimited validity period, granting the attacker persistent domain access far beyond a normal ticket's 10-hour default lifetime.

steps.title: Confirm the anomalous ticket lifetime
steps.desc: Review the forged ticket's lifetime value against the domain's default Kerberos policy (typically 10 hours) to confirm it was set to an extended or maximum value.
steps.outcome: Confirmed anomalous lifetime value with supporting evidence.

steps.title: Isolate all systems accessed during the extended exposure window
steps.desc: Network-isolate every system identified in the access catalogue, given the likely broader footprint from extended persistence.
steps.outcome: All identified systems isolated.

steps.title: Perform the double krbtgt password reset with replication wait
steps.desc: Reset the krbtgt account password twice with a full replication-convergence wait between resets.
steps.outcome: Both krbtgt password versions rotated and confirmed replicated.

steps.title: Extended monitoring given confirmed long-dwell persistence
steps.desc: Apply an extended elevated-monitoring period, longer than the standard window, given the confirmed extended dwell time of this incident.
steps.outcome: No further anomalous activity observed during the extended window.

steps.title: Full incident report with dwell-time analysis and leadership briefing
steps.desc: Document the complete attack chain, extended dwell time, full access catalogue, and response; brief leadership and assess notification obligations.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Determine the full active window the ticket has already covered
steps.desc: Given the extended lifetime, establish how far back the ticket may have been in use and correlate with all authentication activity during that entire window, not just recent activity.
steps.guidance: A long-lived ticket may have been used intermittently over days or weeks — the investigation window must extend back to the ticket's likely creation time.
steps.outcome: Full historical exposure window established.

steps.title: Engage AD team for immediate krbtgt remediation
steps.desc: Escalate for the double krbtgt password reset given active, extended-duration attacker persistence.
steps.outcome: AD team engaged with urgency appropriate to active persistence.

steps.title: Hunt for persistence established during the extended access window
steps.desc: Given the extended dwell time, thoroughly hunt for additional persistence mechanisms (backdoor accounts, scheduled tasks, GPO changes, additional forged tickets) the attacker may have set up.
steps.guidance: An attacker with days or weeks of domain access typically does not rely on the Golden Ticket alone — assume additional footholds exist.
steps.outcome: Additional persistence identified and removed, or confirmed absent via thorough hunt.

steps.title: Catalogue all access performed using the long-lived ticket
steps.desc: Build a complete list of systems and data accessed across the entire exposure window.
steps.outcome: Complete access catalogue for the exposure window.

steps.title: Investigate initial access and krbtgt hash theft vector
steps.desc: Determine how the krbtgt hash was originally obtained and remediate that root cause.
steps.outcome: Initial access vector identified and closed.

ITID-12715.def: An adversary forges a golden ticket embedding privileged group SIDs (such as Domain Admins or Enterprise Admins) into the ticket's PAC, granting privileges the referenced account was never actually assigned.

scopeExcludes: Golden tickets impersonating an account's real, legitimately-held privileges with no SID forgery

indicators: PAC validation failure or SID-history anomaly on a ticket-bearing session (Microsoft's PAC validation/'Golden SAML' detections)
Actions performed under privileges inconsistent with the account's real group membership in the directory
vectors: SID-history injection into a forged ticket's PAC
rootCauses: PAC validation not enforced/monitored on resource servers

T1134.005 Access Token Manipulation: SID-History Injection

Time from krbtgt compromise to double password reset
Percentage of domain controllers with tiered-admin enforcement

playbook.name: Response: Golden Ticket with Forged Group Membership
playbook.description: For a Golden Ticket forged to include fabricated privileged group memberships (e.g. Domain Admins SID, SID History injection) beyond what the account legitimately holds, granting escalated privilege via the ticket itself.

steps.title: Identify the specific forged group memberships/SIDs in the ticket
steps.desc: Analyze the ticket's PAC (Privilege Attribute Certificate) or correlate with unexpected privileged-group-scoped access to determine exactly which group SIDs/SID History entries were fabricated.
steps.guidance: Compare the account's actual AD group membership against what the ticket claimed to identify the discrepancy precisely.
steps.outcome: Specific forged SIDs/group claims identified.

steps.title: Isolate systems accessed via the forged-privilege ticket
steps.desc: Network-isolate every system where privileged access was exercised using the forged group membership.
steps.outcome: Affected systems isolated.

steps.title: Perform the double krbtgt password reset with replication wait
steps.desc: Reset the krbtgt account password twice with a full replication-convergence wait between resets.
steps.outcome: Both krbtgt password versions rotated and confirmed replicated.

steps.title: Verify privileged group memberships domain-wide match expected baseline
steps.desc: Audit membership of Domain Admins and other privileged groups against the last known-good baseline to confirm no unauthorized additions remain.
steps.outcome: Privileged group membership confirmed to match baseline.

steps.title: Full incident report and leadership briefing
steps.desc: Document the complete attack chain including the specific forged privilege claim, response, and assess notification obligations.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Determine what privileged actions were taken using the forged membership
steps.desc: Since the ticket granted privilege the underlying account does not legitimately have, identify every privileged action taken that relied on the forged group claim.
steps.outcome: Full list of privileged actions taken via the forged membership.

steps.title: Audit and reverse any privileged changes made via the forged access
steps.desc: Given the ticket granted privileged-group-level access, review AD, GPO, and privileged system configurations for any unauthorized changes made during the exposure window and reverse them.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized privileged changes identified and reversed.

steps.title: Audit domain-wide for SID History abuse and clean up any injected SID History
steps.desc: Since forged group membership attacks often leverage SID History, audit all accounts domain-wide for illegitimate SID History entries and remove any found (beyond legitimate migration-related history).
steps.guidance: SID History is a common historical migration artifact — verify each entry's legitimacy rather than removing all.
steps.outcome: Domain confirmed free of illegitimate SID History entries.

steps.title: Identify the underlying account the ticket was forged for
steps.desc: Determine the (likely low-privilege or even fictitious) account the ticket was created for, since a Golden Ticket can be forged for any username.
steps.outcome: Underlying account identity established.

steps.title: Investigate initial access and krbtgt hash theft vector
steps.desc: Determine how the krbtgt hash was originally obtained and remediate that root cause.
steps.outcome: Initial access vector identified and closed.

ITID-12716.def: An adversary uses a golden ticket forged in one domain, together with inter-realm trust material, to obtain access in a trusting domain or forest, extending the compromise across a trust boundary.
ITID-12716.purpose: Captures golden tickets used to pivot across a domain/forest trust boundary, extending the compromise beyond the originally-compromised domain.
scopeIncludes: Use of a golden ticket combined with inter-realm TGT/trust-key abuse to access resources in a separate trusting domain or forest
scopeExcludes: Golden ticket use confined to the originally compromised domain (other leaves in this Type)
ITID-12716.severity: Critical — cross-forest compromise represents the maximum blast radius for this technique.
ITID-12716.escalation: Escalate immediately to all affected domains/forests; requires coordinated multi-domain krbtgt and trust-key rotation.
indicators: Inter-realm TGT use inconsistent with legitimate cross-domain access patterns
Privileged activity in a trusting domain with no corresponding legitimate authentication chain
vectors: Compromise of the inter-realm trust key alongside krbtgt to cross a forest trust
rootCauses: Overly permissive forest/domain trust relationships (e.g. bidirectional trusts where one-way would suffice)

playbook.name: Response: Golden Ticket Used for Cross-Domain/Forest Trust Abuse
playbook.description: For a Golden Ticket leveraged to abuse an inter-domain or cross-forest trust relationship (e.g. forged inter-realm TGT, SID History across a trust) to extend access beyond the originally compromised domain.

steps.title: Confirm cross-domain/forest access via the forged ticket
steps.desc: Review authentication logs in the trusting domain/forest for access using an inter-realm ticket originating from the compromised domain, confirming the trust boundary was actually crossed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed cross-domain/forest access with supporting evidence.

steps.title: Disable or restrict the abused trust relationship as an emergency measure
steps.desc: Coordinate with both domain/forest owners to temporarily disable or tightly restrict the trust to stop further cross-boundary abuse.
steps.guidance: This will impact legitimate cross-domain operations — coordinate business impact communication before/during execution.
steps.outcome: Trust relationship disabled or restricted; further cross-boundary abuse blocked.

steps.title: Perform the double krbtgt password reset in the originally compromised domain
steps.desc: Reset the krbtgt account password twice with a full replication-convergence wait in the domain where the Golden Ticket was originally forged.
steps.outcome: Both krbtgt password versions rotated in the source domain.

steps.title: Coordinated phased restoration of the trust relationship
steps.desc: Restore the trust relationship in a controlled, monitored fashion once both domains are confirmed clean and hardened.
steps.outcome: Trust restored with SID filtering and monitoring in place.

steps.title: Full multi-domain incident report and leadership briefing
steps.desc: Document the complete cross-domain attack chain, impact in both domains/forests, response, and assess notification obligations given the multi-domain blast radius.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Map the trust relationship and its configured scope
steps.desc: Document the specific trust used (direction, transitivity, SID filtering status) to understand exactly how far the attacker's reach extends.
steps.guidance: Check whether SID filtering is enabled on the trust — its absence is often what makes this attack possible.
steps.outcome: Trust relationship and its abuse path fully mapped.

steps.title: Isolate systems accessed in the trusting domain/forest
steps.desc: Network-isolate every system identified as accessed via the abused trust.
steps.outcome: Affected systems in the second domain/forest isolated.

steps.title: Reset the inter-domain trust password
steps.desc: Reset the trust account password shared between the two domains to invalidate any trust-key material the attacker may have captured.
steps.outcome: Trust password rotated on both sides.

steps.title: Catalogue access gained in the second domain/forest
steps.desc: Identify every system and account accessed in the trusting domain/forest via the abused trust.
steps.outcome: Full access catalogue in the secondary domain/forest.

steps.title: Enable SID filtering on the trust if not already present
steps.desc: Enable SID filter quarantining on the trust relationship to prevent SID History-based privilege escalation across it going forward, unless a documented business need requires it disabled.
steps.outcome: SID filtering enabled or a documented exception recorded.

steps.title: Audit and reverse unauthorized changes made in the trusting domain
steps.desc: Review the trusting domain for any unauthorized changes made during the attacker's cross-domain access and reverse them.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized changes in the trusting domain identified and reversed.

playbook.name: Response: Golden Ticket Detected via Anomalous Ticket Lifetime
playbook.description: For a Golden Ticket where the primary and defining detection signal was an anomalous ticket lifetime value flagged by automated detection (SIEM correlation rule / UEBA), before broader attacker activity has necessarily been confirmed — an early-detection scenario.

steps.title: Validate the detection rule's finding against raw ticket data
steps.desc: Pull the raw Kerberos event and confirm the flagged ticket's lifetime genuinely deviates from domain policy, ruling out a detection-rule false positive (e.g. a legitimate long-lifetime service account policy).
steps.guidance: Check whether any legitimate accounts are intentionally configured with extended ticket lifetimes before treating as malicious.
steps.outcome: Confirmed genuine anomaly, or closed as tuning/false-positive.
steps.abort: If a legitimate policy explains the lifetime, close as false positive and tune the detection rule.
steps.tool: SIEM correlation rule output / DC logs

steps.title: Isolate any system where the ticket was confirmed used
steps.desc: Network-isolate any system where the forged ticket was used for authentication, if any use was confirmed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed-used systems isolated, or none required if no use occurred.

steps.title: Perform the double krbtgt password reset with replication wait
steps.desc: Reset the krbtgt account password twice with a full replication-convergence wait between resets, even if no confirmed malicious use has occurred yet.
steps.guidance: The compromised hash itself is the threat, independent of observed use — do not skip this because damage appears limited.
steps.outcome: Both krbtgt password versions rotated and confirmed replicated.

steps.title: Confirm detection rule performance and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Verify the detection rule that caught this event continues to function correctly, and monitor for any further anomalous-lifetime tickets.
steps.outcome: No further anomalous-lifetime tickets observed; detection confirmed effective.

steps.title: Document the early-detection success and reinforce the detection rule
steps.desc: Record what worked in catching this early and ensure the detection rule/threshold is preserved or improved for future coverage.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; detection rule reviewed and confirmed or improved.

steps.title: Determine whether the ticket has been used yet
steps.desc: Given early detection, check whether the forged ticket has actually been used for authentication anywhere, or was caught before use.
steps.guidance: Early detection may mean the attacker has not yet acted — this changes urgency but not the required krbtgt remediation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any use has occurred.

steps.title: Engage AD team immediately for krbtgt remediation
steps.desc: Given the fundamental nature of a Golden Ticket — the krbtgt hash is compromised regardless of how much the attacker has used it — escalate for immediate remediation.
steps.guidance: Early detection is an opportunity to remediate before significant damage; treat with urgency.
steps.outcome: AD team engaged and remediation scheduled urgently.

steps.title: Investigate and close the krbtgt hash theft vector
steps.desc: Determine how the hash was obtained (DCSync, direct DC extraction, or other) and remediate the specific root cause.
steps.outcome: Hash theft vector identified and closed.

steps.title: Identify the account the ticket was forged for and trace hash-theft indicators
steps.desc: Determine the target account and look for related DCSync or DC-access indicators around the same timeframe that would explain how the krbtgt hash was obtained.
steps.outcome: Forged account identity and likely hash-theft vector identified where possible.

ITID-12718.def: An adversary continues to use a previously-forged golden ticket successfully after the organization has reset the krbtgt password only once, exploiting the fact that a single reset does not immediately invalidate tickets encrypted with the prior password's second-to-last hash history entry under some configurations.
ITID-12718.purpose: Captures the specific and well-known failure mode where a golden ticket forged before a krbtgt password reset remains valid after only a single reset, because Microsoft's guidance requires two resets to fully invalidate old tickets.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed golden ticket use after a single krbtgt password reset was believed to have remediated the compromise
scopeExcludes: Golden ticket use prior to any remediation attempt (other leaves in this Type)
ITID-12718.severity: Critical — indicates a failed remediation and requires immediate correction (a second krbtgt reset).
ITID-12718.escalation: Escalate immediately; perform the second krbtgt password reset without delay and re-verify all forged-ticket indicators are gone.
indicators: Golden-ticket-consistent activity observed after a krbtgt reset event was logged
Only one krbtgt reset present in the password-change history around the incident window
vectors: Continued use of a pre-existing forged ticket exploiting incomplete remediation
rootCauses: Incident responders unaware that a single krbtgt reset is insufficient to fully invalidate golden tickets
mitreTechniques: T1558.001 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket
controls: krbtgt account password rotated twice in succession per Microsoft guidance after any suspected compromise
Tiered administration model (no domain admin credentials on lower-tier hosts) to limit krbtgt exposure
Monitoring/alerting on Kerberos ticket lifetime and encryption-type anomalies
Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) restricting where domain controller credential material can be touched

metrics: Count of golden ticket incidents/attempts per year
Time from krbtgt compromise to double password reset
Percentage of domain controllers with tiered-admin enforcement

playbook.name: Response: Golden Ticket Used After Single krbtgt Password Reset
playbook.description: For a case where a Golden Ticket remained valid and was used by an attacker despite the organization having already performed a krbtgt password reset — because only a single reset was performed instead of the required double reset, leaving the previous password version still valid.

steps.title: Confirm the ticket is using the pre-reset krbtgt password version
steps.desc: Analyze the forged ticket to confirm it validates against the krbtgt account's N-1 (previous) password version rather than the current one, confirming the single-reset gap.
steps.guidance: AD retains both current and previous krbtgt password versions as valid for ticket validation — a single reset does not close this gap.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the previous-version password is still being accepted.

steps.title: Isolate all systems accessed during the gap period
steps.desc: Network-isolate every system identified in the access catalogue from the gap period.
steps.outcome: Affected systems isolated.

steps.title: Perform the second krbtgt password reset with replication wait
steps.desc: Complete the double-reset procedure by performing the second krbtgt password reset and confirming full replication convergence across all domain controllers before considering the account remediated.
steps.guidance: Confirm replication convergence explicitly this time — do not close the loop until every DC has the new password version.
steps.outcome: Both krbtgt password versions now fully rotated and confirmed replicated.

steps.title: Verify no ticket forged with either krbtgt password version remains valid
steps.desc: Confirm through testing or monitoring that tickets forged with both the old and older krbtgt password versions are now rejected.
steps.outcome: Confirmed both password versions rotated and enforced.

steps.title: Process failure review and leadership briefing
steps.desc: Document how the incomplete remediation occurred as a process failure (not just a technical incident), the extended exposure it caused, and corrective action taken; brief leadership given the repeat nature of the incident.
steps.outcome: Full report completed including process failure analysis; notification obligations reassessed given extended exposure.

steps.title: Review the prior incident's remediation record for the reset gap
steps.desc: Pull the prior incident's documentation to confirm only a single krbtgt reset was performed and identify why the second reset was missed or delayed.
steps.outcome: Root cause of the incomplete remediation identified.

steps.title: Escalate urgently for the second (completing) krbtgt reset
steps.desc: Escalate to the AD team to immediately perform the second krbtgt password reset that was missed in the original response.
steps.outcome: Second reset scheduled with high urgency.

steps.title: Hunt for persistence established during the extended gap window
steps.desc: Given the attacker retained usable Golden Ticket access through the gap period, thoroughly hunt for additional persistence mechanisms established during that time.
steps.outcome: Additional persistence identified and removed, or confirmed absent.

steps.title: Catalogue all access performed since the original (incomplete) remediation
steps.desc: Build a complete list of systems and data accessed using tickets forged with the still-valid previous krbtgt hash since the original incident's partial remediation.
steps.outcome: Complete access catalogue for the gap period.

steps.title: Update the krbtgt reset runbook/procedure to prevent recurrence
steps.desc: Revise the internal krbtgt remediation procedure/runbook to explicitly require and verify both resets and replication confirmation as mandatory, non-optional steps.
steps.outcome: Runbook updated with an explicit verification checkpoint for both resets.

playbook.name: Response: Successful Golden Ticket Attack with Confirmed Domain-Wide Access
playbook.description: For a confirmed case where a Golden Ticket attack resulted in demonstrated domain-wide unauthorized access — the most severe confirmed outcome in this category, treated as a full domain compromise.

steps.title: Confirm and scope domain-wide access
steps.desc: Establish concrete evidence that the attacker accessed multiple systems/accounts across the domain using forged tickets, confirming this is not confined to a single system.
steps.outcome: Domain-wide access confirmed with specific evidence and scope.

steps.title: Isolate all confirmed-affected systems domain-wide
steps.desc: Network-isolate every system confirmed accessed by the attacker.
steps.outcome: All affected systems isolated.

steps.title: Perform the double krbtgt password reset with replication wait
steps.desc: Reset the krbtgt account password twice with a full replication-convergence wait between resets.
steps.outcome: Both krbtgt password versions rotated and confirmed replicated.

steps.title: Phased domain-wide recovery with extended elevated monitoring
steps.desc: Restore domain services and access in phases with extended heightened monitoring given the confirmed severity.
steps.outcome: Domain services fully restored with no signs of recurring compromise over an extended observation period.

steps.title: Full incident report, executive briefing, and regulatory notification
steps.desc: Document the complete attack chain, full domain-wide impact, and response; brief executive leadership and complete any required regulatory/contractual breach notifications.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; all applicable notification obligations actioned.

steps.title: Build the complete attack timeline and impact catalogue
steps.desc: Reconstruct the full attack chain from initial krbtgt hash theft through every subsequent access, action, and any data exfiltrated or systems modified.
steps.outcome: Complete attack timeline and impact catalogue.

steps.title: Disable all confirmed-compromised accounts
steps.desc: Disable every account confirmed used or created by the attacker during the compromise.
steps.outcome: All compromised accounts disabled.

steps.title: Reset all domain account credentials given confirmed domain-wide compromise
steps.desc: Execute an organization-wide credential reset given confirmed domain-wide access, prioritizing privileged and service accounts first.
steps.outcome: All domain credentials rotated.

steps.title: Identify all persistence mechanisms established domain-wide
steps.desc: Hunt across the domain for backdoor accounts, scheduled tasks, GPO modifications, additional forged tickets, or other footholds established during the compromise.
steps.outcome: All persistence mechanisms identified.

steps.title: Remove every identified persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Remove all backdoor accounts, scheduled tasks, GPO modifications, and other attacker-established footholds identified during the hunt.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled persistence remains anywhere in the domain.

steps.title: Consider rebuild of critical infrastructure given depth of compromise
steps.desc: For domain controllers or other critical systems with deep/uncertain compromise, rebuild from known-clean sources rather than attempting in-place remediation.
steps.outcome: Critical infrastructure rebuilt or confirmed clean via thorough forensic review.

ITID-12721.def: An incident of NTLM hash reuse to authenticate without cracking the underlying password, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type.
ITID-12721.purpose: Catch-all for pass-the-hash reports not yet matching a more specific extraction source or target.
scopeIncludes: Reports of suspected pass-the-hash activity where extraction source and target are not yet determined
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID once details are known

Pass-the-hash tracked as a step within a broader network-intrusion lateral-movement incident (ITID-42241) or a dedicated lateral-movement-context incident (ITID-33331), which remain separate ITIDs for those contexts
ITID-12721.severity: High by default; reassess once extraction source and target are confirmed.
ITID-12721.priority: P2 pending reclassification, P1 if a domain controller or privileged account is involved.
ITID-12721.escalation: Escalate once the specific extraction source/target is clarified, sooner if privileged systems are implicated.
indicators: Alert of unclear specific NTLM-hash-reuse indicator
vectors: Activity of unclear specific hash-extraction vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
mitreTechniques: T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
controls: Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) to eliminate shared local admin hash reuse
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block hash extraction from memory
Restricted Admin / tiered administration to prevent privileged hash exposure on lower-tier hosts
SMB signing and NTLM restriction/blocking where Kerberos is available
ITID-12721.detection: Strong technical signal: Windows Security event 4624 logon-type anomalies (Type 3 network logons using NTLM where Kerberos is expected), EDR alerts on LSASS memory access, and abnormal lateral authentication patterns from a single host to many targets are all reliable, well-documented detections for this technique.
ITID-12721.response: Reset the compromised account's password (invalidating the hash) and, for privileged/shared accounts, rotate all related local admin passwords; isolate the source host and hunt for further lateral movement.
metrics: Count of pass-the-hash incidents per quarter
Percentage of endpoints with LAPS deployed
Mean time to isolate a host after a PtH alert
ITID-12721.notes: Intake/catch-all classification for this Type, not a terminal one. Scope decision: this branch (under Attacks Against the Human / Credential-Based Attacks) covers pass-the-hash as an identity/credential-exploitation technique; the technical lateral-movement execution of PtH within a broader network intrusion is tracked separately at ITID-33331 and ITID-42241 to avoid duplicating those incident narratives.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Pass-the-Hash Attack
playbook.description: General-purpose checklist for a suspected Pass-the-Hash attack before the specific source/target has been confirmed.

steps.title: Confirm indicators consistent with PtH (NTLM logon without interactive password entry)
steps.desc: Review the alert against NTLM logon type patterns (Type 3/9 network logons without prior interactive session) to confirm PtH-consistent behavior.
steps.outcome: Confirmed indicators consistent with a hash-based authentication rather than password entry.
steps.abort: If explained by legitimate service account NTLM use, close as false positive.

steps.title: Isolate the source system where the hash was extracted
steps.desc: Network-isolate the endpoint where the credential material was captured.
steps.outcome: Source system isolated.

steps.title: Hand off to the matching specific Pass-the-Hash playbook
steps.desc: Once the source/target is confirmed, escalate to and follow the specific playbook for detailed eradication steps.
steps.outcome: Incident reassigned with all evidence carried forward.

steps.title: Confirm no further hash-based logons observed
steps.desc: Monitor for continued use of the stolen hash to confirm containment held.
steps.outcome: No successful hash reuse observed post-reset.

steps.title: Document findings and recommend a control improvement
steps.desc: Record the mechanism once confirmed and recommend a control such as LSASS protection, Credential Guard, or local admin password randomization.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; improvement ticket opened where applicable.

steps.title: Determine the hash source and target
steps.desc: Establish where the hash was extracted from (LSASS, SAM database, network capture) and what it was used against (workstation, domain controller).
steps.guidance: This determines which specific playbook to hand off to.
steps.outcome: Hash source and target identified.

steps.title: Reset the affected account's password
steps.desc: Rotate the password for every account whose hash was stolen — this invalidates the stolen hash.
steps.outcome: Stolen hash invalidated.

steps.title: Establish scope of affected accounts and systems
steps.desc: Identify every account and system touched using the stolen hash.
steps.outcome: Affected accounts/systems enumerated.

ITID-12722.def: An adversary dumps NTLM password hashes from the LSASS process memory of a compromised endpoint, then replays a hash to authenticate to other systems without knowing the plaintext password.
ITID-12722.purpose: Captures pass-the-hash attacks where the NTLM hash was extracted directly from LSASS process memory on the source endpoint.
scopeIncludes: Credential-dumping tooling (e.g. Mimikatz sekurlsa) targeting LSASS memory on an endpoint
scopeExcludes: Extraction from the local SAM database rather than live LSASS memory (ITID-12723)
ITID-12722.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for privileged account hashes.
ITID-12722.escalation: Escalate immediately; isolate the source endpoint and reset every account whose hash may have been cached there.
indicators: EDR alert on LSASS memory access by an untrusted process
Credential-dumping tool signature detected on the endpoint
vectors: Credential-dumping malware/tooling run with local admin rights on the endpoint
rootCauses: LSASS not protected (Credential Guard/PPL not enabled)
Local admin rights held by standard users enabling dumping tools to run
mitreTechniques: T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
controls: Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) to eliminate shared local admin hash reuse
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block hash extraction from memory
Restricted Admin / tiered administration to prevent privileged hash exposure on lower-tier hosts
SMB signing and NTLM restriction/blocking where Kerberos is available
ITID-12722.detection: Strong technical signal: Windows Security event 4624 logon-type anomalies (Type 3 network logons using NTLM where Kerberos is expected), EDR alerts on LSASS memory access, and abnormal lateral authentication patterns from a single host to many targets are all reliable, well-documented detections for this technique.
ITID-12722.response: Reset the compromised account's password (invalidating the hash) and, for privileged/shared accounts, rotate all related local admin passwords; isolate the source host and hunt for further lateral movement.
metrics: Count of pass-the-hash incidents per quarter
Percentage of endpoints with LAPS deployed
Mean time to isolate a host after a PtH alert
ITID-12722.notes: Differentiating axis: extraction source is live process memory (LSASS) on the endpoint.

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Hash via LSASS Memory Extraction
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Hash attack where the NTLM hash was obtained by dumping LSASS process memory on an endpoint (e.g. Mimikatz-style tooling).

steps.title: Confirm LSASS access/dump on the source endpoint
steps.desc: Review EDR alerts for LSASS process access by an unauthorized process, memory dump creation, or known credential-dumping tool signatures.
steps.outcome: Confirmed LSASS dump event with process and endpoint identified.

steps.title: Isolate the source endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the endpoint where LSASS was dumped to stop further credential harvesting.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated.

steps.title: Remove the credential-dumping tool and rebuild the endpoint
steps.desc: Reimage the affected endpoint rather than in-place cleanup, given the likely presence of additional attacker tooling.
steps.outcome: Endpoint reimaged from a known-clean source.

steps.title: Verify LSASS protection is active on the rebuilt endpoint before return to service
steps.desc: Confirm Credential Guard/PPL is enabled and functioning before returning the endpoint to the user.
steps.outcome: Protection confirmed active.

steps.title: Document and audit fleet-wide LSASS protection coverage
steps.desc: Record the finding and confirm what percentage of the fleet has LSASS protection enabled, ticketing gaps.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; coverage gap addressed or ticketed.

steps.title: Identify which account hashes were resident in LSASS at dump time
steps.desc: Determine which accounts had cached credentials in LSASS on the endpoint — typically the logged-in user and any accounts that authenticated interactively or via RDP to that host.
steps.outcome: List of exposed account hashes.

steps.title: Reset passwords for all exposed accounts
steps.desc: Rotate the password for every account whose hash was resident in the dumped LSASS memory.
steps.outcome: All exposed credentials invalidated.

steps.title: Enable LSASS protection (Credential Guard / PPL) domain-wide
steps.desc: Deploy Windows Defender Credential Guard and/or LSASS Protected Process Light on managed endpoints to prevent future memory-dump-based hash theft.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive systemic fix — reimaging one endpoint does not prevent recurrence elsewhere.
steps.outcome: LSASS protection enabled fleet-wide or rollout ticketed.

steps.title: Confirm subsequent use of the stolen hash(es)
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for NTLM logons using the exposed accounts shortly after the dump, from systems inconsistent with normal use.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the hash was actually reused.

ITID-12723.def: An adversary extracts NTLM hashes from a system's local SAM database (offline or via registry hive dump), then replays a hash to authenticate as a local account elsewhere on the network.
ITID-12723.purpose: Captures pass-the-hash attacks where the NTLM hash was extracted from the local Security Account Manager (SAM) database rather than live memory.
scopeIncludes: Registry hive dumping (SAM/SYSTEM) and offline SAM database extraction
scopeExcludes: Live LSASS memory extraction (ITID-12722)
ITID-12723.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the extracted account is shared across many hosts.
ITID-12723.escalation: Escalate immediately; treat all hosts sharing the extracted local account's password as compromised.
indicators: Registry hive save/export activity (reg save SAM/SYSTEM) on an endpoint
Local account authentication from an unexpected source host
vectors: Offline registry hive extraction followed by hash-cracking or direct replay
rootCauses: Local SAM database accessible to a compromised local admin account with no LAPS-style password uniqueness
mitreTechniques: T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
controls: Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) to eliminate shared local admin hash reuse
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block hash extraction from memory
