playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Hash via SAM Database Extraction
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Hash attack where local account hashes were obtained by extracting the SAM (Security Account Manager) database from an endpoint or server.

steps.title: Confirm SAM database extraction on the source system
steps.desc: Review EDR/security logs for SAM registry hive access, volume shadow copy creation followed by SAM/SYSTEM hive copy, or known SAM-dumping tool signatures.
steps.outcome: Confirmed SAM extraction event with system identified.

steps.title: Isolate the source system
steps.desc: Network-isolate the system where the SAM database was extracted.
steps.outcome: Source system isolated.

steps.title: Deploy LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) if not already in place
steps.desc: Implement or verify LAPS is deployed to enforce unique, randomized local administrator passwords per system, eliminating the shared-credential risk.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive systemic fix for this attack class.
steps.outcome: LAPS deployed fleet-wide or rollout ticketed.

steps.title: Verify unique local admin passwords are enforced across the fleet
steps.desc: Confirm via LAPS reporting that local admin passwords are now unique per system.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unique passwords fleet-wide.

steps.title: Document and confirm LAPS coverage gap closure
steps.desc: Record the finding and confirm LAPS deployment reaches 100% of applicable systems, ticketing any remaining gap.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; coverage confirmed or ticketed.

steps.title: Identify which local accounts were exposed
steps.desc: Determine every local account present in the extracted SAM database, with particular attention to the built-in local Administrator account.
steps.outcome: List of exposed local accounts.

steps.title: Reset all exposed local account passwords, including any shared local admin credential across all affected systems
steps.desc: Rotate the local Administrator and other exposed local account passwords on the source system and every other system found sharing the same credential.
steps.outcome: All exposed local credentials rotated across every affected system.

steps.title: Rebuild the source system if broader compromise is suspected
steps.desc: If the system shows signs of compromise beyond the SAM extraction itself, reimage rather than clean in place.
steps.outcome: System confirmed clean or rebuilt.
steps.abort: If SAM extraction appears to be an isolated event with no other compromise indicators, in-place remediation with credential reset may suffice.

steps.title: Check whether the exposed local Administrator hash is shared across other systems
steps.desc: Determine whether the same local admin password/hash is reused on other systems in the environment (a common historical practice).
steps.guidance: This is the critical scoping question — if the local admin credential is shared, every system using it is now at risk from this single extraction.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of credential reuse across systems.

scopeExcludes: Pass-the-hash targeting a domain controller specifically (ITID-12725)
ITID-12724.escalation: Escalate immediately; deploy LAPS if not already present to break the shared-hash chain.
indicators: Sequential local-admin authentications across multiple workstations from a single origin point in a short window
vectors: Replay of a shared local administrator hash across the workstation fleet
rootCauses: Identical local administrator password (and therefore hash) deployed across many workstations

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Hash for Workstation-to-Workstation Lateral Movement
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Hash attack used specifically to move laterally between workstations (peer-to-peer), typically leveraging a shared local administrator credential.

steps.title: Confirm the lateral movement path between workstations
steps.desc: Trace the sequence of NTLM authentication events across workstations to build the lateral movement chain (source workstation, hash origin, subsequent target workstations).
steps.outcome: Full lateral movement chain mapped across affected workstations.

steps.title: Isolate every workstation in the lateral movement chain
steps.desc: Network-isolate all workstations identified as touched by the attacker.
steps.outcome: All affected workstations isolated.

steps.title: Deploy LAPS and remove unnecessary local admin rights across workstations
steps.desc: Implement LAPS for unique local admin passwords and review/reduce standing local administrator group membership across the workstation fleet.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive fix that prevents a single hash from unlocking multiple workstations.
steps.outcome: LAPS deployed and local admin rights minimized, or rollout ticketed.

steps.title: Rebuild or verify each affected workstation before returning to service
steps.desc: Confirm each affected workstation is clean (reimage if compromise depth is uncertain) before returning to normal use.
steps.outcome: All affected workstations confirmed clean.

steps.title: Document the lateral movement chain and reinforce workstation hardening
steps.desc: Record the full attack chain and confirm LAPS/segmentation controls are applied fleet-wide, not just to affected systems.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; fleet-wide hardening confirmed or ticketed.

steps.title: Identify the credential enabling the movement
steps.desc: Determine whether movement relied on a shared local admin account, a domain account with local admin rights on multiple workstations, or another mechanism.
steps.outcome: Enabling credential/mechanism identified.

steps.title: Reset the enabling credential(s) everywhere they are valid
steps.desc: Rotate the shared/reused credential across every workstation where it grants access, not just the originally affected ones.
steps.outcome: Enabling credential invalidated fleet-wide.

steps.title: Segment workstation-to-workstation traffic where feasible
steps.desc: Apply host-based firewall rules or network segmentation to restrict unnecessary SMB/RPC traffic between workstations, limiting future lateral movement paths.
steps.outcome: Workstation-to-workstation traffic restricted per policy.

steps.title: Determine the full set of workstations reached
steps.desc: Build the complete list of every workstation the attacker accessed during the lateral movement chain.
steps.outcome: Complete list of affected workstations.

ITID-12725.escalation: Escalate immediately to AD/identity team; treat as a potential precursor to golden ticket/DCSync activity and hunt accordingly.

SMB signing and NTLM restriction/blocking where Kerberos is available

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Hash Against Domain Controller
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Hash attack where the stolen hash was used to authenticate directly against a domain controller — a high-severity escalation given the DC's central role.

steps.title: Confirm the PtH-based authentication against the domain controller
steps.desc: Review DC security logs for an NTLM logon (rather than Kerberos, which is normally used domain-internally) using a privileged or unexpected account.
steps.guidance: NTLM authentication against a DC using a privileged account is itself anomalous and worth flagging even before confirming PtH specifically.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hash-based authentication event against the DC with account and source identified.

steps.title: Isolate the domain controller if further compromise is confirmed, or restrict the account otherwise
steps.desc: If the DC shows signs of deeper compromise (credential extraction, tampering), isolate it while maintaining domain functionality via other DCs; otherwise disable the compromised account immediately.
steps.guidance: Coordinate carefully with AD team given production impact of DC isolation.
steps.outcome: DC isolated if warranted, or compromised account disabled.

steps.title: If krbtgt or NTDS.dit access is confirmed, execute the double krbtgt password reset
steps.desc: If the DC-level access enabled krbtgt hash theft, perform the double krbtgt password reset with full replication wait as the priority remediation step.
steps.outcome: krbtgt rotated if applicable, or confirmed not accessed.
steps.abort: If no evidence of krbtgt/NTDS.dit access exists, this step is not required — document the determination.

steps.title: Verify DC integrity and confirm no residual compromise
steps.desc: Confirm through integrity checks and monitoring that the DC and domain remain clean before closing.
steps.outcome: DC and domain confirmed clean.

steps.title: Full incident report and leadership briefing given DC involvement
steps.desc: Document the complete attack chain, DC-level impact, and response; brief leadership given the severity of any DC-targeting attack.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Determine the privilege level of the account used and what was accessed on the DC
steps.desc: Establish whether the account used had privileged (e.g. Domain Admin) rights and what actions were taken once authenticated to the DC.
steps.outcome: Account privilege level and actions on the DC documented.

steps.title: Reset the password for every account confirmed used against the DC
steps.desc: Rotate the password for every account whose stolen hash was used to authenticate to the DC.
steps.outcome: All confirmed-used credentials invalidated.

steps.title: Investigate and close the original hash-theft vector
steps.desc: Determine where the original NTLM hash was stolen from (workstation LSASS/SAM dump, network capture) and remediate that endpoint/vector.
steps.outcome: Original hash-theft vector identified and closed.

steps.title: Assess whether the DC compromise enabled further hash/credential theft
steps.desc: Given DC access, determine whether the attacker used this foothold to extract additional credentials (e.g. NTDS.dit, krbtgt hash) — this may escalate to a Golden Ticket scenario.
steps.guidance: If evidence of krbtgt or NTDS.dit access is found, escalate immediately to the Golden Ticket playbook in parallel.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether further credential theft occurred from the DC.

steps.title: Enable Protected Users group / Credential Guard for privileged accounts
steps.desc: Add privileged accounts to the Protected Users security group and ensure Credential Guard is enforced on systems they log into, preventing NTLM hash caching for those accounts.
steps.outcome: Privileged accounts hardened against future PtH.

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Hash via Network Traffic Capture
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Hash attack where the NTLM hash/challenge-response was obtained by capturing authentication traffic on the network rather than extracting it from a host.

steps.title: Confirm the network capture vector
steps.desc: Determine how the traffic was captured — a compromised network tap/span port, a relay/poisoning tool (LLMNR/NBT-NS), or a compromised network device.
steps.guidance: If poisoning-based, this overlaps with the rogue KDC/LLMNR playbook — cross-reference and avoid duplicate remediation.
steps.outcome: Capture mechanism and location identified.

steps.title: Isolate the capture point
steps.desc: Disconnect or disable the device/host performing the network capture or poisoning.
steps.outcome: Capture point neutralized.

steps.title: Enable SMB signing and disable NTLM where feasible
steps.desc: Enforce SMB signing domain-wide and, where compatible, disable or restrict NTLM authentication in favor of Kerberos to remove the underlying weakness.
steps.guidance: This closes the protocol-level gap that made capture-and-reuse possible.
steps.outcome: SMB signing enforced; NTLM usage reduced/restricted domain-wide.

steps.title: Verify SMB signing enforcement and confirm no further capture activity
steps.desc: Confirm SMB signing is active and monitor the network for further capture/poisoning attempts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed enforcement and no recurrence.

steps.title: Document and confirm NTLM/SMB hardening is domain-wide
steps.desc: Record the finding and confirm SMB signing/NTLM restriction is consistently applied beyond just the affected segment.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; hardening confirmed domain-wide.

steps.title: Identify the account(s) whose authentication traffic was captured
steps.desc: Determine which account(s) authentication was captured and correlate with subsequent PtH activity.
steps.outcome: Affected account(s) identified.

steps.title: Reset passwords for all accounts whose hash was captured
steps.desc: Rotate the password for every affected account to invalidate the captured hash.
steps.outcome: Captured credentials invalidated.

steps.title: Remediate the specific capture mechanism (poisoning tool, rogue device)
steps.desc: If the capture used LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning, follow the corresponding remediation (disable LLMNR/NBT-NS); if a rogue device, remove/investigate it.
steps.outcome: Capture mechanism eliminated.

steps.title: Confirm subsequent use of the captured hash
steps.desc: Check authentication logs for use of the captured credential against a target system following the capture.
steps.outcome: Confirmed reuse and target(s) identified.

ITID-12727.def: An adversary leverages the fact that a local administrator account's password (and therefore NTLM hash) is identical across many hosts in the environment, allowing one captured hash to authenticate broadly.

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Hash Using a Shared Local Administrator Hash
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Hash attack that succeeded specifically because the same local Administrator account password/hash is reused across many systems in the environment.

steps.title: Confirm the shared local admin credential and its scope of reuse
steps.desc: Determine exactly which systems share the same local Administrator password/hash used in the attack.
steps.outcome: Complete list of systems sharing the exposed credential.

steps.title: Isolate all actually-accessed systems
steps.desc: Network-isolate every system confirmed accessed by the attacker.
steps.outcome: Accessed systems isolated.

steps.title: Deploy LAPS across the entire affected population
steps.desc: Roll out LAPS (or equivalent) to enforce unique, randomized local administrator passwords on every system, eliminating the shared-credential model entirely.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive fix for this specific ITID — the incident exists because this control was missing.
steps.outcome: LAPS deployed to 100% of the previously shared-credential population, or rollout plan/timeline ticketed with executive visibility given the scale.

steps.title: Verify unique passwords are enforced and no system reverted to the shared value
steps.desc: Audit via LAPS reporting that every system now has a unique local admin password with no exceptions.
steps.outcome: Confirmed 100% unique-password compliance.

steps.title: Document the systemic exposure and its remediation as a control-maturity finding
steps.desc: Record this as a broader control gap (not just a single incident) and confirm LAPS deployment and password-rotation policy are now embedded in standard build processes.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; standard build process updated to prevent recurrence of shared local credentials.

steps.title: Determine which systems were actually accessed using the shared hash
steps.desc: Distinguish between systems merely sharing the vulnerable credential and systems the attacker actually authenticated to.
steps.outcome: List of actually-accessed systems separate from the broader at-risk population.

steps.title: Reset the shared local admin password across every system that uses it
steps.desc: Rotate the local Administrator password on every system in the identified shared-credential population, not just the ones actually accessed.
steps.guidance: This is urgent and broad by nature of this specific incident type — leaving any system on the old shared password leaves it exposed.
steps.outcome: Shared credential invalidated across the entire population.

steps.title: Assess impact on each actually-accessed system
steps.desc: Determine what the attacker did on each system it actually reached.
steps.outcome: Impact documented per accessed system.

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Hash Detected via Anomalous Logon Type
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Hash attack where the primary detection signal was an anomalous Windows logon type/event pattern (e.g. NTLM Type 3 logon for an account that normally only uses Kerberos, or a logon without a corresponding interactive session) flagged by automated detection.

steps.title: Validate the detection rule's finding against raw event data
steps.desc: Pull the raw Windows security event (Event ID 4624 with LogonType and AuthenticationPackageName fields) to confirm the anomaly is genuine and not a detection-rule false positive.
steps.guidance: Check whether a legitimate scenario (e.g. a service account correctly using NTLM) explains the pattern before treating as malicious.
steps.outcome: Confirmed genuine anomaly, or closed as tuning/false-positive.
steps.abort: If explained by legitimate NTLM-dependent service behavior, close as false positive and tune the detection rule.
steps.tool: SIEM correlation rule output / Windows security logs

steps.title: Isolate the target system accessed via the anomalous logon
steps.desc: Network-isolate the system that was authenticated to using the anomalous logon.
steps.outcome: Target system isolated.

steps.title: Remediate the identified hash-theft source
steps.desc: If a source system with credential-dumping activity was identified, follow the appropriate specific playbook (LSASS/SAM extraction) to remediate it.
steps.outcome: Hash-theft source remediated.
steps.abort: If no clear source was identified, document as an investigative gap and monitor for recurrence.

steps.title: Confirm no further anomalous logons for the affected account
steps.desc: Monitor authentication activity for the account to confirm normal logon-type patterns resumed post-remediation.
steps.outcome: No further anomalous logon activity observed.

steps.title: Document the detection success and reinforce logon-type monitoring
steps.desc: Record what worked in catching this via logon-type anomaly detection and consider expanding similar detection coverage.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; detection coverage reviewed.

steps.title: Determine the account and source/target of the anomalous logon
steps.desc: Identify the account used, the source system the logon originated from, and the target system accessed.
steps.outcome: Account and source/target systems identified.

steps.title: Reset the affected account's password
steps.desc: Rotate the password for the account involved in the anomalous logon.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated.

steps.title: Tune and preserve the detection rule that caught this event
steps.desc: Review the detection logic that flagged the anomalous logon type and confirm it remains sensitive to this pattern for future detections.
steps.outcome: Detection rule confirmed effective and preserved.

steps.title: Trace back to the likely hash-theft source
steps.desc: Investigate the source system for evidence of LSASS/SAM access or other credential-dumping activity that would explain how the hash was obtained.
steps.outcome: Likely hash-theft source and method identified where possible.

playbook.name: Response: Successful Pass-the-Hash Attack with Confirmed Lateral Movement
playbook.description: For a confirmed case where a Pass-the-Hash attack resulted in demonstrated lateral movement across multiple systems — the most severe confirmed outcome in this category.

steps.title: Confirm and map the full lateral movement chain
steps.desc: Build the complete chain of systems accessed via PtH, from the initial hash-theft source through every subsequent hop.
steps.outcome: Complete lateral movement chain mapped.

steps.title: Isolate every system in the lateral movement chain
steps.desc: Network-isolate all systems identified as accessed during the attack.
steps.outcome: All affected systems isolated.

steps.title: Remove persistence established at each hop
steps.desc: Identify and remove any backdoor account, scheduled task, or other persistence mechanism the attacker established at any point in the chain.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled persistence remains anywhere in the chain.

steps.title: Rebuild or verify integrity of every affected system before return to service
steps.desc: Confirm each system in the chain is clean — reimage where compromise depth is uncertain.
steps.outcome: All affected systems confirmed clean.

steps.title: Full incident report with lateral movement analysis and leadership briefing
steps.desc: Document the complete attack chain, impact, and response; brief leadership and assess breach notification obligations given confirmed multi-system compromise.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Catalogue all actions and impact across every accessed system
steps.desc: Document what the attacker accessed, modified, or exfiltrated at each hop in the chain.
steps.outcome: Full impact catalogue across all affected systems.

steps.title: Reset credentials for every account used across the chain
steps.desc: Rotate passwords for every account whose hash was captured or used at any point in the lateral movement.
steps.outcome: All affected credentials rotated.

steps.title: Deploy LAPS and Credential Guard/Protected Users across the affected population
steps.desc: Roll out unique local admin passwords and credential-protection controls across all systems in the affected population to prevent recurrence of the underlying weakness.
steps.outcome: Systemic controls deployed or rollout ticketed.

steps.title: Extended monitoring across the entire affected population
steps.desc: Apply elevated monitoring across all systems and accounts in the lateral movement chain for an extended period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed during the monitoring window.

steps.title: Identify the highest-value system/account reached
steps.desc: Determine the most sensitive system or most privileged account the attacker accessed during the lateral movement, to prioritize response.
steps.outcome: Highest-value compromised asset identified.

ITID-12731.def: An incident of exported/stolen Kerberos ticket reuse, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type.
ITID-12731.purpose: Catch-all for pass-the-ticket reports not yet matching a more specific ticket type or mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Reports of suspected pass-the-ticket activity where the ticket type or extraction mechanism is not yet determined
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID once details are known
Forged golden tickets, tracked under the Golden Ticket Attack Type (ITID-12711-12719)
ITID-12731.severity: High by default; reassess once ticket type and target are confirmed.
ITID-12731.priority: P2 pending reclassification, P1 if a domain controller or privileged account is involved.
ITID-12731.escalation: Escalate once the specific ticket type/mechanism is clarified.
indicators: Alert of unclear specific Kerberos ticket-reuse indicator
vectors: Activity of unclear specific ticket-export vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
mitreTechniques: T1550.003 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
controls: Kerberos ticket lifetime and renewal policy hardening
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block ticket cache extraction
Privileged Access Workstations restricting where high-value tickets can be cached
Conditional access / re-authentication requirements resistant to stale ticket reuse
ITID-12731.detection: Strong technical signal: ticket reuse from an inconsistent source IP/host, renewal requests outside policy-defined windows, and correlation between exported-ticket tooling signatures (e.g. Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets, Rubeus) and subsequent authentication are all reliably observable in Kerberos and EDR telemetry.
ITID-12731.response: Invalidate the specific compromised ticket(s) where possible, reset the underlying account's credentials, and isolate the host from which the ticket was exported; hunt for reuse across other systems in the same window.
metrics: Count of pass-the-ticket incidents per quarter
Mean time to detect a ticket-reuse anomaly
Percentage of privileged sessions on Credential Guard-protected hosts
ITID-12731.notes: Intake/catch-all classification for this Type, not a terminal one. Scope decision: a fully forged ticket built from a compromised krbtgt hash is a golden ticket and belongs to ITID-12711-12719; this Type covers reuse of genuinely-issued tickets that were exported/stolen.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Pass-the-Ticket Attack
playbook.description: General-purpose checklist for a suspected Pass-the-Ticket attack before the specific source/mechanism has been confirmed.

steps.title: Confirm indicators consistent with ticket reuse across sessions/hosts
steps.desc: Review the alert for a Kerberos ticket used from a host or session inconsistent with where it was originally issued.
steps.outcome: Confirmed indicators consistent with ticket export/reuse rather than normal Kerberos flow.
steps.abort: If explained by legitimate roaming profile or RDP behavior, close as false positive.

steps.title: Isolate the source system where the ticket was extracted
steps.desc: Network-isolate the endpoint where the ticket material was captured.
steps.outcome: Source system isolated.

steps.title: Hand off to the matching specific Pass-the-Ticket playbook
steps.desc: Once the source/mechanism is confirmed, escalate to and follow the specific playbook for detailed eradication steps.
steps.outcome: Incident reassigned with all evidence carried forward.

steps.title: Confirm no further ticket reuse observed
steps.desc: Monitor for continued use of the stolen ticket material to confirm containment held.
steps.outcome: No successful ticket reuse observed post-reset.

steps.title: Document findings and recommend a control improvement
steps.desc: Record the mechanism once confirmed and recommend a control such as Credential Guard or reduced ticket lifetime.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; improvement ticket opened where applicable.

steps.title: Determine the ticket source and type (TGT vs. service ticket)
steps.desc: Establish whether a TGT or a specific service ticket was stolen/exported, and from where (LSASS cache, exported file).
steps.guidance: This determines which specific playbook to hand off to.
steps.outcome: Ticket type and source identified.

steps.title: Reset the affected account's password to invalidate outstanding tickets
steps.desc: Rotate the password for every account whose ticket was stolen.
steps.outcome: Outstanding tickets invalidated.

steps.title: Establish scope of affected accounts and systems
steps.desc: Identify every account and system touched using the stolen ticket.
steps.outcome: Affected accounts/systems enumerated.

ITID-12732.def: An adversary exports a victim's legitimately-issued TGT from the source host's memory and imports it into a session on adversary-controlled infrastructure to request service tickets as the victim without knowing their password.
ITID-12732.purpose: Captures pass-the-ticket attacks using an exported, genuinely-issued Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT).
scopeIncludes: Export and reuse of a genuine TGT obtained from the victim's authenticated session
scopeExcludes: Export and reuse of a single service ticket rather than the TGT (ITID-12733)
ITID-12732.severity: Critical — a stolen TGT allows the adversary to request service tickets for any resource the victim can access.
ITID-12732.escalation: Escalate immediately; the victim's account should be treated as fully compromised until the TGT's remaining lifetime expires or is revoked.
indicators: TGT reuse from a host/IP inconsistent with the original issuance
Multiple service-ticket requests immediately following an imported-TGT indicator
vectors: Ticket-export tooling (e.g. Mimikatz, Rubeus) run against a compromised session's memory
rootCauses: LSASS/ticket cache not protected against extraction on the source host
mitreTechniques: T1550.003 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
controls: Kerberos ticket lifetime and renewal policy hardening
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block ticket cache extraction
Privileged Access Workstations restricting where high-value tickets can be cached
Conditional access / re-authentication requirements resistant to stale ticket reuse
ITID-12732.detection: Strong technical signal: ticket reuse from an inconsistent source IP/host, renewal requests outside policy-defined windows, and correlation between exported-ticket tooling signatures (e.g. Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets, Rubeus) and subsequent authentication are all reliably observable in Kerberos and EDR telemetry.
ITID-12732.response: Invalidate the specific compromised ticket(s) where possible, reset the underlying account's credentials, and isolate the host from which the ticket was exported; hunt for reuse across other systems in the same window.
metrics: Count of pass-the-ticket incidents per quarter
Mean time to detect a ticket-reuse anomaly
Percentage of privileged sessions on Credential Guard-protected hosts
ITID-12732.notes: Differentiating axis: the specific ticket type exported is the TGT itself, the broadest-scope ticket in this Type.

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Ticket via Exported TGT
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Ticket attack where a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) was exported from an endpoint and replayed elsewhere to impersonate the account for any service the account can access.

steps.title: Confirm TGT export from the source endpoint
steps.desc: Review EDR alerts for LSASS access/ticket export tool signatures (e.g. Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets, Rubeus) on the source endpoint.
steps.outcome: Confirmed TGT export event with endpoint and account identified.

steps.title: Isolate the source endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the endpoint where the TGT was exported.
steps.outcome: Source endpoint isolated.

steps.title: Rebuild the source endpoint and remove ticket-extraction tooling
steps.desc: Reimage the source endpoint given the presence of credential-extraction tooling.
steps.outcome: Endpoint reimaged from a known-clean source.

steps.title: Verify Credential Guard is active on the rebuilt endpoint before return to service
steps.desc: Confirm protection is enabled and functioning before returning the endpoint to the user.
steps.outcome: Protection confirmed active.

steps.title: Document and audit fleet-wide Credential Guard coverage
steps.desc: Record the finding and confirm what percentage of the fleet has Credential Guard enabled, ticketing gaps.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; coverage gap addressed or ticketed.

steps.title: Identify every service the account can access using the stolen TGT
steps.desc: Since a TGT can be used to request service tickets for any resource the account is authorized for, enumerate the account's full access scope.
steps.guidance: A stolen TGT is broader in impact than a stolen service ticket — treat the account's entire access scope as at risk.
steps.outcome: Full access scope of the compromised account documented.

steps.title: Reset the account's password to invalidate the TGT
steps.desc: Rotate the account's password, which invalidates all outstanding TGTs issued to it.
steps.outcome: Stolen TGT invalidated.

steps.title: Enable Credential Guard and reduce TGT lifetime for sensitive accounts
steps.desc: Deploy Credential Guard on managed endpoints and consider reducing the maximum ticket lifetime for privileged accounts to shrink the window an exported TGT remains useful.
steps.outcome: Credential Guard enabled fleet-wide or ticketed; ticket lifetime policy reviewed.

steps.title: Determine what was actually accessed using the stolen TGT
steps.desc: Review service ticket requests made using the stolen TGT to determine actual (not just potential) access.
steps.outcome: Actual access catalogue documented.

steps.title: Isolate any system accessed using service tickets derived from the stolen TGT
steps.desc: Network-isolate every system actually accessed per the identification-phase access catalogue.
steps.outcome: All actually-accessed systems isolated.

ITID-12733.def: An adversary exports a victim's legitimately-issued service ticket (TGS) for a specific resource and reuses it to access that single resource without needing the victim's TGT or password.
ITID-12733.purpose: Captures pass-the-ticket attacks using an exported service ticket (TGS) scoped to a single resource, narrower than a full TGT.
scopeIncludes: Export and reuse of a single service ticket scoped to one target resource/service
scopeExcludes: Export and reuse of the broader TGT (ITID-12732)
ITID-12733.severity: High — impact is scoped to the single resource the ticket was issued for.
ITID-12733.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the target resource is highly privileged.
ITID-12733.escalation: Escalate immediately; scope containment to the specific resource while investigating for broader compromise.
indicators: Service ticket reuse against a single resource from an inconsistent source host
vectors: Ticket-export tooling targeting a specific cached service ticket
rootCauses: Service ticket cache not protected against extraction on the source host
mitreTechniques: T1550.003 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
controls: Kerberos ticket lifetime and renewal policy hardening
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block ticket cache extraction
Privileged Access Workstations restricting where high-value tickets can be cached
Conditional access / re-authentication requirements resistant to stale ticket reuse
ITID-12733.detection: Strong technical signal: ticket reuse from an inconsistent source IP/host, renewal requests outside policy-defined windows, and correlation between exported-ticket tooling signatures (e.g. Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets, Rubeus) and subsequent authentication are all reliably observable in Kerberos and EDR telemetry.
ITID-12733.response: Invalidate the specific compromised ticket(s) where possible, reset the underlying account's credentials, and isolate the host from which the ticket was exported; hunt for reuse across other systems in the same window.
metrics: Count of pass-the-ticket incidents per quarter
Mean time to detect a ticket-reuse anomaly
Percentage of privileged sessions on Credential Guard-protected hosts
ITID-12733.notes: Differentiating axis: scope is a single service ticket rather than the account-wide TGT.

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Ticket via Exported Service Ticket
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Ticket attack where a specific service ticket (rather than a TGT) was exported and replayed to access a single specific service/resource.

steps.title: Confirm service ticket export from the source endpoint
steps.desc: Review EDR alerts for ticket export tool signatures targeting a specific service ticket rather than the full ticket cache.
steps.outcome: Confirmed service ticket export event with endpoint, account, and target service identified.

steps.title: Isolate the source endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the endpoint where the service ticket was exported.
steps.outcome: Source endpoint isolated.

steps.title: Rebuild the source endpoint and remove ticket-extraction tooling
steps.desc: Reimage the source endpoint given the presence of credential-extraction tooling.
steps.outcome: Endpoint reimaged from a known-clean source.

steps.title: Verify the source endpoint is clean before return to service
steps.desc: Confirm the rebuilt endpoint is clean before returning it to the user.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean.

steps.title: Document and reinforce endpoint credential protection
steps.desc: Record the finding and confirm LSASS/Credential Guard protections are in place on the source endpoint's peer population.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; protection coverage confirmed or ticketed.

steps.title: Identify the specific service/resource the ticket grants access to
steps.desc: Determine exactly which service (file share, SQL server, web application via Kerberos auth) the exported ticket is scoped to.
steps.guidance: Unlike a TGT, a service ticket's impact is bounded to the specific service it was issued for — scope the investigation accordingly, but confirm this bound rather than assuming it.
steps.outcome: Specific target service identified and access scope confirmed bounded.

steps.title: Reset the account's password to invalidate the ticket
steps.desc: Rotate the account's password, invalidating the stolen service ticket.
steps.outcome: Stolen ticket invalidated.

steps.title: Reverse any unauthorized changes on the target service
steps.desc: Work with the target service owner to identify and reverse any unauthorized changes made using the replayed ticket.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized changes reversed.

steps.title: Determine what was accessed on the target service
steps.desc: Review the target service's own logs for the actions taken using the replayed ticket.
steps.outcome: Actions on the target service documented.

steps.title: Review and, if needed, restrict access to the specific target service
steps.desc: If the target service shows signs of unauthorized changes/data access, restrict access pending investigation.
steps.outcome: Target service secured pending investigation.

ITID-12734.def: An adversary uses credential-dumping tooling to extract cached Kerberos tickets directly from LSASS process memory, then replays one or more of them on adversary-controlled infrastructure.
ITID-12734.purpose: Captures pass-the-ticket attacks where the ticket was extracted specifically from LSASS's Kerberos ticket cache using credential-dumping tooling.
scopeIncludes: LSASS ticket-cache extraction via tooling such as Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets
scopeExcludes: Ticket theft via cross-session reuse without direct LSASS extraction (ITID-12735)
ITID-12734.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for privileged account tickets.
ITID-12734.escalation: Escalate immediately; isolate the source endpoint and treat it as compromised.
indicators: EDR alert on LSASS memory access consistent with ticket-cache extraction
Credential-dumping tool signature on the endpoint
vectors: Credential-dumping tooling run with local admin rights on the endpoint
rootCauses: LSASS not protected (Credential Guard/PPL not enabled)
mitreTechniques: T1550.003 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
controls: Kerberos ticket lifetime and renewal policy hardening
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block ticket cache extraction
Privileged Access Workstations restricting where high-value tickets can be cached
Conditional access / re-authentication requirements resistant to stale ticket reuse
ITID-12734.detection: Strong technical signal: ticket reuse from an inconsistent source IP/host, renewal requests outside policy-defined windows, and correlation between exported-ticket tooling signatures (e.g. Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets, Rubeus) and subsequent authentication are all reliably observable in Kerberos and EDR telemetry.
ITID-12734.response: Invalidate the specific compromised ticket(s) where possible, reset the underlying account's credentials, and isolate the host from which the ticket was exported; hunt for reuse across other systems in the same window.
metrics: Count of pass-the-ticket incidents per quarter
Mean time to detect a ticket-reuse anomaly
Percentage of privileged sessions on Credential Guard-protected hosts
ITID-12734.notes: Differentiating axis: extraction mechanism is direct LSASS memory access, the most tooling-dependent variant in this Type.

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Ticket via LSASS Ticket Cache Extraction
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Ticket attack where the full Kerberos ticket cache was dumped from LSASS memory, exposing multiple tickets (potentially for multiple accounts on a shared/jump host) at once.

steps.title: Confirm LSASS ticket cache dump on the source endpoint
steps.desc: Review EDR alerts for LSASS memory access consistent with ticket cache dumping (distinct from a targeted single-ticket export).
steps.outcome: Confirmed ticket cache dump event with endpoint identified.

steps.title: Isolate the source endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the endpoint where the ticket cache was dumped.
steps.outcome: Source endpoint isolated.

steps.title: Rebuild the source endpoint given multi-account exposure
steps.desc: Reimage the endpoint rather than clean in place, given the scale of credential exposure typical of this ITID.
steps.outcome: Endpoint reimaged from a known-clean source.

steps.title: Verify all exposed accounts confirmed clean before restoring normal access
steps.desc: Confirm no residual unauthorized access remains for any of the exposed accounts before closing.
steps.outcome: All exposed accounts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Document the multi-account exposure and shared-host risk finding
steps.desc: Record the finding, the number of accounts affected, and the architectural recommendation regarding shared/jump host hardening.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; architecture review ticket opened.

steps.title: Identify every account with cached tickets on the endpoint at dump time
steps.desc: Given this is a full cache dump, determine every account that had authenticated to or through this endpoint recently — especially relevant if this is a shared jump host or RDP gateway with multiple users' cached tickets.
steps.guidance: A shared/jump host can expose far more accounts than a single-user workstation — treat this as a potentially multi-account incident from the start.
steps.outcome: Complete list of accounts with exposed cached tickets.

steps.title: Reset passwords for every account with exposed cached tickets
steps.desc: Rotate the password for every account identified in the exposed-account list, not just those confirmed reused.
steps.guidance: Given the multi-account nature of this ITID, err toward broader containment.
steps.outcome: All exposed accounts' outstanding tickets invalidated.

steps.title: Review the necessity and hardening of shared/jump hosts
steps.desc: If the source was a shared jump host or RDP gateway, review whether privileged access workstations (PAWs) or a bastion host model with stricter isolation should replace it.
steps.guidance: Shared hosts that accumulate many users' cached credentials are a recurring high-value target — this incident is an opportunity to address the architectural root cause.
steps.outcome: Jump host architecture reviewed; hardening recommendation made.

steps.title: Determine which exposed tickets were actually reused
steps.desc: Check DC/service logs for use of each exposed account's tickets following the dump.
steps.outcome: Confirmed reuse per exposed account.

steps.title: Enable Credential Guard fleet-wide, prioritizing shared/jump hosts
steps.desc: Deploy Credential Guard with priority on shared and jump-host systems where ticket cache exposure has outsized impact.
steps.outcome: Credential Guard enabled on priority systems or rollout ticketed.

ITID-12735.def: An adversary reuses a Kerberos ticket in a session context different from where it was originally issued (e.g. via shared credential caches, remote session artifacts, or ticket copy between sessions), extending its validity beyond its intended session boundary.
ITID-12735.purpose: Captures reuse of a valid Kerberos ticket across a different session or host than the one it was originally issued to, without necessarily involving direct memory extraction.
scopeIncludes: Cross-session or cross-host reuse of a Kerberos ticket where the extraction method itself is secondary to the cross-session reuse pattern
scopeExcludes: Ticket extraction via direct LSASS memory dumping as the primary technique (ITID-12734)

General web session-token/cookie hijacking with no Kerberos ticket involved (Session Hijacking Type, ITID-12921-12929) and standalone credential replay of non-Kerberos session artifacts (Credential Replay Attack Type, ITID-12931-12939)
ITID-12735.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for privileged accounts.
ITID-12735.escalation: Escalate immediately; identify every session/host where the ticket was reused.
indicators: The same Kerberos ticket instance observed used from two or more distinct sessions/hosts
vectors: Shared credential-cache locations or session-artifact copying enabling cross-session ticket reuse
rootCauses: Ticket/session artifacts persisted in locations accessible across sessions or hosts
mitreTechniques: T1550.003 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
controls: Kerberos ticket lifetime and renewal policy hardening
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block ticket cache extraction
Privileged Access Workstations restricting where high-value tickets can be cached
Conditional access / re-authentication requirements resistant to stale ticket reuse
ITID-12735.detection: Strong technical signal: ticket reuse from an inconsistent source IP/host, renewal requests outside policy-defined windows, and correlation between exported-ticket tooling signatures (e.g. Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets, Rubeus) and subsequent authentication are all reliably observable in Kerberos and EDR telemetry.
ITID-12735.response: Invalidate the specific compromised ticket(s) where possible, reset the underlying account's credentials, and isolate the host from which the ticket was exported; hunt for reuse across other systems in the same window.
metrics: Count of pass-the-ticket incidents per quarter
Mean time to detect a ticket-reuse anomaly
Percentage of privileged sessions on Credential Guard-protected hosts
ITID-12735.notes: Scope decision: this leaf is specifically for Kerberos ticket reuse across sessions; general web session-cookie hijacking is tracked separately under the Session Hijacking Type (ITID-12921-12929), and non-Kerberos credential-material replay is tracked under the Credential Replay Attack Type (ITID-12931-12939), to avoid duplicating those incident narratives.

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Ticket for Cross-Session Reuse
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Ticket attack where a ticket issued in one user session was injected into and reused within a different session (same or different host), enabling access without the attacker knowing the account's actual credential.

steps.title: Confirm the ticket was injected into a different session than it was issued in
steps.desc: Correlate the ticket's original issuance session/logon ID with its subsequent use under a different logon session ID.
steps.outcome: Confirmed cross-session ticket injection with both session IDs documented.

steps.title: Isolate both the source and destination hosts/sessions
steps.desc: Network-isolate the system where the ticket originated and the system/session where it was injected and used, if different.
steps.outcome: Both source and destination systems isolated.

steps.title: Rebuild affected endpoints and remove ticket-injection tooling
steps.desc: Reimage the source and, if compromised, destination endpoints.
steps.outcome: Endpoints reimaged from a known-clean source.

steps.title: Verify affected endpoints are clean before return to service
steps.desc: Confirm rebuilt endpoints are clean before returning to normal use.
steps.outcome: Endpoints confirmed clean.

steps.title: Document and reinforce endpoint ticket-cache protection
steps.desc: Record the finding and confirm Credential Guard coverage across the endpoint population.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; coverage confirmed or ticketed.

steps.title: Identify the session the ticket was injected into and who/what controls it
steps.desc: Determine whether the destination session belongs to the attacker's own process, a different compromised user's session, or a service account context.
steps.outcome: Destination session context identified.

steps.title: Reset the affected account's password
steps.desc: Rotate the password for the account whose ticket was reused.
steps.outcome: Ticket invalidated.

steps.title: Enable Credential Guard to block ticket injection into the LSASS cache
steps.desc: Deploy Credential Guard, which prevents user-mode processes (including ticket-injection tools) from writing directly into the protected ticket cache.
steps.outcome: Credential Guard enabled or rollout ticketed.

steps.title: Determine what was accessed using the injected ticket
steps.desc: Review logs for actions taken using the ticket once injected into the new session.
steps.outcome: Actions documented.

ITID-12736.def: An adversary presents a stolen ticket at a point where the application/service required re-authentication (e.g. a step-up MFA prompt or session-timeout re-login), and the ticket satisfies the check without triggering the intended re-authentication challenge.
ITID-12736.purpose: Captures pass-the-ticket used specifically to bypass a re-authentication or step-up authentication prompt that should have interrupted the adversary's access.
scopeIncludes: Ticket reuse that specifically defeats a re-authentication/step-up checkpoint
scopeExcludes: Ticket reuse where no re-authentication checkpoint was involved (other leaves in this Type)
ITID-12736.severity: Critical — defeating a deliberately-placed re-authentication control indicates a significant control gap.
ITID-12736.escalation: Escalate immediately; review why the re-authentication checkpoint accepted a stale/replayed ticket.
indicators: A step-up/re-authentication event logged as satisfied without a corresponding fresh interactive logon
vectors: Ticket replay timed to coincide with a session's re-authentication requirement
rootCauses: Re-authentication checkpoints validating ticket presence rather than requiring fresh interactive authentication
mitreTechniques: T1550.003 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
controls: Kerberos ticket lifetime and renewal policy hardening
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block ticket cache extraction
Privileged Access Workstations restricting where high-value tickets can be cached
Conditional access / re-authentication requirements resistant to stale ticket reuse
ITID-12736.detection: Strong technical signal: ticket reuse from an inconsistent source IP/host, renewal requests outside policy-defined windows, and correlation between exported-ticket tooling signatures (e.g. Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets, Rubeus) and subsequent authentication are all reliably observable in Kerberos and EDR telemetry.
ITID-12736.response: Invalidate the specific compromised ticket(s) where possible, reset the underlying account's credentials, and isolate the host from which the ticket was exported; hunt for reuse across other systems in the same window.
metrics: Count of pass-the-ticket incidents per quarter
Mean time to detect a ticket-reuse anomaly
Percentage of privileged sessions on Credential Guard-protected hosts
ITID-12736.notes: Differentiating axis: defined by the specific control defeated (a re-authentication checkpoint) rather than the ticket type or extraction method.

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Ticket Used to Bypass Re-Authentication
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Ticket attack specifically used to bypass a step-up or re-authentication control (e.g. a sensitive operation normally requiring fresh credential entry) by presenting a previously issued ticket instead.

steps.title: Confirm the re-authentication control was bypassed via ticket reuse
steps.desc: Review the sensitive operation's access logs to confirm a stale/replayed ticket was accepted in place of the expected fresh re-authentication.
steps.outcome: Confirmed bypass with supporting evidence.
steps.abort: If the re-authentication control functioned correctly and this is a different bypass mechanism, reclassify accordingly.

steps.title: Reverse or freeze the sensitive action taken via the bypass
steps.desc: Work with the affected system/business owner to reverse or freeze any change/transaction made using the bypassed re-authentication.
steps.guidance: Time-sensitive given the sensitivity of the operation this control was meant to protect.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized sensitive action reversed or frozen.

steps.title: Fix the re-authentication control to require fresh, non-replayable proof
steps.desc: Work with the application/security engineering team to ensure the sensitive operation requires a genuinely fresh authentication factor (e.g. a fresh password/MFA prompt bound to a short-lived, single-use challenge) rather than accepting any valid-looking ticket regardless of age.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive fix — the control exists specifically to prevent this scenario and must be corrected.
steps.outcome: Re-authentication control confirmed to reject replayed tickets.

steps.title: Verify the re-authentication fix in testing before closing
steps.desc: Confirm a replayed ticket is now rejected by the sensitive operation's re-authentication check.
steps.outcome: Fix verified.

steps.title: Document and audit other sensitive operations for the same re-authentication gap
steps.desc: Record the finding and check whether other step-up-protected operations share the same replay weakness.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; sweep completed or ticketed.

steps.title: Identify the sensitive operation/system the bypass enabled
steps.desc: Determine exactly what sensitive action (privileged configuration change, financial transaction, data export) was performed using the bypassed re-authentication.
steps.outcome: Sensitive operation identified.

steps.title: Reset the affected account's password and revoke the ticket
steps.desc: Rotate the account's password to invalidate the replayed ticket.
steps.outcome: Ticket invalidated.

steps.title: Investigate and remediate how the ticket was originally captured
steps.desc: Address the underlying ticket-theft vector per the relevant specific playbook.
steps.outcome: Ticket-theft vector remediated.

steps.title: Determine the ticket's origin and how it was captured/replayed
steps.desc: Trace back to where the replayed ticket was originally issued and how the attacker obtained it.
steps.outcome: Ticket origin and capture method identified.

ITID-12737.def: An adversary uses a stolen NTLM hash to request a legitimate TGT from the KDC (overpass-the-hash / 'pass-the-key'), converting hash-based access into a genuine Kerberos ticket, then passes that ticket to another session.
ITID-12737.purpose: Captures pass-the-ticket as the final step of an overpass-the-hash chain, where a stolen NTLM hash is first used to request a genuine TGT, which is then passed.
scopeIncludes: The overpass-the-hash chain: NTLM hash used to obtain a genuine TGT via Kerberos pre-authentication, followed by reuse of that TGT elsewhere
scopeExcludes: Direct export/reuse of an already-issued ticket with no preceding hash-to-ticket conversion step (other leaves in this Type)
Pure pass-the-hash with no ticket ever requested (Pass-the-Hash Type, ITID-12721-12729)
ITID-12737.severity: Critical — this chain converts a hash into a fully legitimate Kerberos ticket, often evading NTLM-specific detections.
ITID-12737.escalation: Escalate immediately; treat both the source hash and the resulting ticket as compromised credential material.
indicators: Kerberos AS-REQ using RC4 pre-authentication encrypted with a hash rather than a password-derived key (Rubeus asktgt-style pattern)
TGT issuance immediately followed by cross-host reuse
vectors: Overpass-the-hash tooling (e.g. Rubeus asktgt /rc4)
rootCauses: RC4 Kerberos pre-authentication still permitted where AES-only would block this technique
mitreTechniques: T1550.003 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
controls: Kerberos ticket lifetime and renewal policy hardening
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block ticket cache extraction
Privileged Access Workstations restricting where high-value tickets can be cached
Conditional access / re-authentication requirements resistant to stale ticket reuse
ITID-12737.detection: Strong technical signal: ticket reuse from an inconsistent source IP/host, renewal requests outside policy-defined windows, and correlation between exported-ticket tooling signatures (e.g. Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets, Rubeus) and subsequent authentication are all reliably observable in Kerberos and EDR telemetry.
ITID-12737.response: Invalidate the specific compromised ticket(s) where possible, reset the underlying account's credentials, and isolate the host from which the ticket was exported; hunt for reuse across other systems in the same window.
metrics: Count of pass-the-ticket incidents per quarter
Mean time to detect a ticket-reuse anomaly
Percentage of privileged sessions on Credential Guard-protected hosts
ITID-12737.notes: Differentiating axis: this leaf specifically captures the hash-to-ticket conversion chain, bridging the Pass-the-Hash and Pass-the-Ticket Types without duplicating either.

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Ticket via Overpass-the-Hash Chain
playbook.description: For an attack chain where a stolen NTLM hash was first used to request a legitimate Kerberos ticket (Overpass-the-Hash), which was then passed/reused elsewhere — combining both PtH and PtT techniques.

steps.title: Confirm the two-stage chain: hash theft followed by Kerberos ticket request
steps.desc: Correlate an initial NTLM hash theft indicator (LSASS access) with a subsequent unusual Kerberos AS-REQ using that account's hash rather than its actual password.
steps.guidance: Overpass-the-Hash is distinguishable from standard PtH by the resulting Kerberos ticket issuance rather than direct NTLM authentication.
steps.outcome: Confirmed two-stage chain with both events correlated.

steps.title: Isolate every system in the full attack chain
steps.desc: Network-isolate the original hash-theft source and every subsequent system reached via the resulting ticket.
steps.outcome: All systems in the chain isolated.

steps.title: Rebuild the original source endpoint
steps.desc: Reimage the endpoint where the original hash theft occurred.
steps.outcome: Source endpoint reimaged.

steps.title: Verify all systems in the chain are confirmed clean before restoring access
steps.desc: Confirm no residual unauthorized access remains anywhere in the attack chain before closing.
steps.outcome: All systems confirmed clean.

steps.title: Full incident report documenting the combined attack chain
steps.desc: Document the full two-stage attack chain from hash theft through ticket reuse, and the priority given to Credential Guard as a chain-disrupting control.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed if required.

steps.title: Identify the resulting ticket's use across subsequent systems
steps.desc: Trace how the Kerberos ticket obtained via Overpass-the-Hash was subsequently passed to and used on other systems.
steps.outcome: Full chain of subsequent ticket use mapped.

steps.title: Reset the affected account's password to invalidate both the hash and derived tickets
steps.desc: Rotate the account's password, which invalidates the stolen NTLM hash and all tickets derived from it.
steps.outcome: Both the stolen hash and derived tickets invalidated.

steps.title: Enable Credential Guard to disrupt the full chain
steps.desc: Deploy Credential Guard, which addresses both the initial hash theft (LSASS protection) and subsequent ticket injection stages of this attack chain.
steps.guidance: This single control disrupts both stages of the chain, making it a high-priority remediation.
steps.outcome: Credential Guard enabled fleet-wide or rollout ticketed with priority.

steps.title: Identify the original hash-theft source
steps.desc: Trace back to the endpoint where the original NTLM hash was extracted, starting this entire attack chain.
steps.outcome: Original source endpoint identified.

ITID-12738.def: An incident where pass-the-ticket activity was identified specifically through detection of an anomalous ticket-renewal pattern (e.g. a renewal request from a host inconsistent with original issuance, or renewal beyond expected policy).
ITID-12738.purpose: Captures pass-the-ticket use first identified through anomalous ticket-renewal detection logic, representing the primary technical detection pathway for this technique.
scopeIncludes: Cases where the detection trigger itself was a ticket-renewal anomaly rule
scopeExcludes: Pass-the-ticket incidents detected through other means (e.g. EDR ticket-export tooling alert as the primary trigger) with no renewal anomaly involved
ITID-12738.priority: P2, escalating to P1 for privileged accounts.
ITID-12738.escalation: Escalate promptly upon detection; correlate with the source host for extraction-method evidence.
indicators: SIEM alert specifically keyed on Kerberos ticket-renewal requests from an inconsistent source or outside policy window
vectors: Any pass-the-ticket extraction technique that happens to trip the renewal anomaly detector
rootCauses: Detection logic tuned to the environment's expected ticket-renewal baseline
mitreTechniques: T1550.003 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
controls: Kerberos ticket lifetime and renewal policy hardening
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block ticket cache extraction
Privileged Access Workstations restricting where high-value tickets can be cached
Conditional access / re-authentication requirements resistant to stale ticket reuse
ITID-12738.detection: Strong technical signal: ticket reuse from an inconsistent source IP/host, renewal requests outside policy-defined windows, and correlation between exported-ticket tooling signatures (e.g. Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets, Rubeus) and subsequent authentication are all reliably observable in Kerberos and EDR telemetry.
ITID-12738.response: Invalidate the specific compromised ticket(s) where possible, reset the underlying account's credentials, and isolate the host from which the ticket was exported; hunt for reuse across other systems in the same window.
metrics: Count of pass-the-ticket incidents per quarter
Mean time to detect a ticket-reuse anomaly
Percentage of privileged sessions on Credential Guard-protected hosts
ITID-12738.notes: Differentiating axis: classified by detection pathway (renewal anomaly) rather than by ticket type or extraction source.

playbook.name: Response: Pass-the-Ticket Detected via Ticket Renewal Anomaly
playbook.description: For a Pass-the-Ticket attack where the primary detection signal was an anomalous ticket renewal pattern (e.g. renewal from a different source IP/host than issuance, or renewal beyond expected frequency) flagged by automated detection.

steps.title: Validate the detection rule's finding against raw renewal event data
steps.desc: Pull the raw Kerberos renewal event (Event ID 4770) and compare the renewal source against the original issuance source to confirm a genuine anomaly.
steps.outcome: Confirmed genuine renewal anomaly, or closed as tuning/false-positive.
steps.abort: If explained by legitimate roaming/VPN IP changes, close as false positive and tune the detection rule.
steps.tool: SIEM correlation rule output / DC security logs

steps.title: Isolate the anomalous renewal source system
steps.desc: Network-isolate the system from which the anomalous renewal originated.
steps.outcome: Renewal source system isolated.

steps.title: Trace back to and remediate the original theft source
steps.desc: Identify where the ticket was originally stolen from (the legitimate issuance host, if compromised) and remediate that endpoint.
steps.outcome: Original theft source remediated where identified.

steps.title: Confirm no further anomalous renewals for the affected account
steps.desc: Monitor renewal activity for the account to confirm normal patterns resumed.
steps.outcome: No further anomalous renewal activity observed.

steps.title: Document the detection success and reinforce renewal-pattern monitoring
steps.desc: Record what worked in catching this via renewal-anomaly detection and consider expanding similar detection coverage.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; detection coverage reviewed.

steps.title: Identify the account and the original vs. renewal source
steps.desc: Determine the account involved and document both the original issuance source and the anomalous renewal source.
steps.outcome: Account and both sources identified.

steps.title: Reset the affected account's password
steps.desc: Rotate the account's password to invalidate the ticket.
steps.outcome: Ticket invalidated.

steps.title: Tune and preserve the detection rule that caught this event
steps.desc: Review the detection logic for ticket renewal anomalies and confirm it remains sensitive for future detections.
steps.outcome: Detection rule confirmed effective and preserved.

steps.title: Determine what access occurred using the renewed ticket
steps.desc: Review logs for actions taken using the ticket following the anomalous renewal.
steps.outcome: Actions documented.

ITID-12739.def: A confirmed instance of pass-the-ticket (any ticket type or mechanism) in which the adversary is verified to have successfully authenticated to and accessed resources using the replayed ticket.
ITID-12739.purpose: Escalation leaf for confirmed pass-the-ticket attacks where the adversary is verified to have gained access using the replayed ticket.
scopeIncludes: Any sibling pass-the-ticket leaf in this Type where confirmed access is verified
scopeExcludes: Pass-the-ticket attempts with no confirmed successful access (respective attempt-stage sibling leaves)
ITID-12739.severity: Critical — confirmed unauthorized access, markedly higher than the attempt-stage siblings.
ITID-12739.escalation: Immediate incident response: invalidate the ticket where possible, reset the underlying account's credentials, and scope the full access chain.
indicators: Confirmed unauthorized authentication and post-authentication activity using the replayed ticket
vectors: Any pass-the-ticket vector in this Type that reached confirmed access
rootCauses: Ticket cache exposure combined with insufficient re-authentication controls enabling successful reuse
mitreTechniques: T1550.003 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
controls: Kerberos ticket lifetime and renewal policy hardening
Credential Guard / LSASS protection to block ticket cache extraction
Privileged Access Workstations restricting where high-value tickets can be cached
Conditional access / re-authentication requirements resistant to stale ticket reuse
ITID-12739.detection: Strong technical signal: ticket reuse from an inconsistent source IP/host, renewal requests outside policy-defined windows, and correlation between exported-ticket tooling signatures (e.g. Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets, Rubeus) and subsequent authentication are all reliably observable in Kerberos and EDR telemetry.
ITID-12739.response: Invalidate the specific compromised ticket(s) where possible, reset the underlying account's credentials, and isolate the host from which the ticket was exported; hunt for reuse across other systems in the same window.
metrics: Count of pass-the-ticket incidents per quarter
Mean time to detect a ticket-reuse anomaly
Percentage of privileged sessions on Credential Guard-protected hosts
ITID-12739.notes: This is the confirmed-outcome escalation of the pass-the-ticket leaves above it.

playbook.name: Response: Successful Pass-the-Ticket Attack with Confirmed Access
playbook.description: For a confirmed case where a Pass-the-Ticket attack (any mechanism) resulted in demonstrated unauthorized access and use.

steps.title: Confirm and catalogue every action taken using the stolen ticket
steps.desc: Build a complete, timestamped list of every action the attacker performed using the stolen/replayed ticket.
steps.guidance: Treat this as an active intrusion investigation.
steps.outcome: Complete action log documented.

steps.title: Terminate attacker access immediately
steps.desc: Invalidate the stolen ticket and disable any account or access the attacker established from it.
steps.outcome: Attacker no longer has active access.
steps.tool: Active Directory / target system admin console

steps.title: Remediate the specific mechanism per the matching specific playbook
steps.desc: Follow the applicable specific Pass-the-Ticket playbook to close the underlying vulnerability that enabled the attack.
steps.outcome: Underlying mechanism eradicated.

steps.title: Validate system/data integrity before closing
steps.desc: Confirm affected data and systems have been restored/verified.
steps.outcome: Integrity confirmed.

steps.title: Full incident report with impact and notification assessment
steps.desc: Document the complete attack chain, impact, and response; assess breach notification obligations given confirmed unauthorized access.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Determine the specific Pass-the-Ticket mechanism used
steps.desc: Establish the specific vector (exported TGT, exported service ticket, LSASS cache dump, cross-session reuse, re-authentication bypass, overpass-the-hash chain) to identify the matching specific playbook.
steps.outcome: Mechanism identified.

steps.title: Reset credentials for all affected accounts
steps.desc: Rotate credentials for the original account plus any account reached via lateral movement.
steps.outcome: All affected credentials rotated.

steps.title: Remove any persistence the attacker established
steps.desc: Identify and remove any backdoor account, scheduled task, or other persistence mechanism.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled persistence remains.

steps.title: Assess data/system impact and lateral movement
steps.desc: Determine what data was accessed/exfiltrated and whether the attacker pivoted to other accounts or systems.
steps.outcome: Full impact scope established.

steps.title: Isolate all confirmed-affected systems
steps.desc: Network-isolate every system the attacker accessed.
steps.outcome: All affected systems isolated.

ITID-12741.def: An incident of an adversary stealing or duplicating a Windows access token to act with another user/process's privileges, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type.
ITID-12741.purpose: Catch-all for token impersonation reports not yet matching a more specific technique or objective.
scopeIncludes: Reports of suspected token impersonation where the specific technique is not yet determined
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID once the technique is known
ITID-12741.severity: High by default; reassess once technique and target privilege level are confirmed.
ITID-12741.priority: P2 pending reclassification, P1 if SYSTEM/domain-privileged.
ITID-12741.escalation: Escalate once the specific technique is clarified, sooner if SYSTEM-level access is suspected.
indicators: EDR alert of unclear specific token-manipulation indicator
vectors: Activity of unclear specific token-theft vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Least-privilege assignment of SeImpersonatePrivilege/SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege to only the accounts/services that require it
EDR behavioral detection for token-duplication and impersonation API call chains
Windows Defender Attack Surface Reduction rules limiting credential-theft/token-abuse tooling
Service-account hardening (no interactive logon, restricted token scope)
ITID-12741.detection: Well-instrumented via EDR: token-manipulation API calls (DuplicateToken/ImpersonateLoggedOnUser-style sequences), anomalous parent-child process token lineage (a low-privilege process spawning a SYSTEM-token child), and named-pipe creation immediately followed by privilege escalation are all reliable detection points on modern endpoint telemetry.
ITID-12741.response: Isolate the affected host immediately, terminate the impersonating process, and audit for any actions taken under the impersonated token's identity before remediation.
metrics: Count of token-impersonation incidents per quarter
Percentage of hosts with EDR token-manipulation detection enabled
Mean time to isolate a host after a token-impersonation alert
ITID-12741.notes: Intake/catch-all classification for this Type, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Token Impersonation Attack
playbook.description: General-purpose checklist for a suspected Windows access token impersonation attack before the specific mechanism has been confirmed.

steps.title: Confirm indicators consistent with token impersonation
steps.desc: Review the alert for a process operating with a token/privilege level inconsistent with its parent process or the launching user.
steps.outcome: Confirmed indicators consistent with token theft/impersonation.
steps.abort: If explained by a legitimate service/admin tool behavior, close as false positive.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the endpoint where the impersonation occurred.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated.

steps.title: Hand off to the matching specific token-impersonation playbook
steps.desc: Once the mechanism is confirmed, escalate to and follow the specific playbook for detailed eradication steps.
steps.outcome: Incident reassigned with all evidence carried forward.

steps.title: Confirm no further impersonation activity observed
steps.desc: Monitor the endpoint/environment for a defined window to confirm no recurrence.
steps.outcome: No further impersonation activity observed.

steps.title: Document findings and recommend a control improvement
steps.desc: Record the mechanism once confirmed and recommend a control such as privilege restriction or application allowlisting.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; improvement ticket opened where applicable.

steps.title: Determine the specific impersonation mechanism
steps.desc: Establish how the token was obtained/used — named pipe impersonation, process injection, rogue service, SeImpersonatePrivilege abuse.
steps.guidance: This determines which specific playbook to hand off to.
steps.outcome: Mechanism identified or narrowed to a short list.

steps.title: Terminate the malicious process and any resulting elevated sessions
steps.desc: Kill the process performing impersonation and any child processes/sessions it spawned with elevated privilege.
steps.outcome: Malicious process and derived access terminated.

steps.title: Determine the privilege level gained
steps.desc: Establish what privilege level (e.g. SYSTEM) the attacker's process obtained via the impersonated token.
steps.outcome: Resulting privilege level documented.

ITID-12742.def: An adversary creates a named pipe and induces a higher-privileged process (often SYSTEM) to connect to it, then calls ImpersonateNamedPipeClient to assume that process's security token.
ITID-12742.purpose: Captures token impersonation carried out via named-pipe impersonation, where an adversary tricks a privileged process into connecting to an attacker-controlled named pipe.
scopeIncludes: Named-pipe creation and impersonation call chains used to capture a higher-privileged token
scopeExcludes: Token theft via process injection with no named-pipe component (ITID-12743)
ITID-12742.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if SYSTEM privileges are obtained.
ITID-12742.escalation: Escalate immediately; isolate the host and determine what actions were taken under the captured token.
indicators: Named pipe created by a low-privilege process immediately followed by a privileged process connection and token change
vectors: Named-pipe impersonation exploit tooling (e.g. common in local privilege-escalation exploit chains)
rootCauses: Overly permissive named-pipe ACLs allowing a low-privilege process to create pipes that a privileged service will connect to
controls: Least-privilege assignment of SeImpersonatePrivilege/SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege to only the accounts/services that require it
EDR behavioral detection for token-duplication and impersonation API call chains
Windows Defender Attack Surface Reduction rules limiting credential-theft/token-abuse tooling
Service-account hardening (no interactive logon, restricted token scope)
ITID-12742.detection: Well-instrumented via EDR: token-manipulation API calls (DuplicateToken/ImpersonateLoggedOnUser-style sequences), anomalous parent-child process token lineage (a low-privilege process spawning a SYSTEM-token child), and named-pipe creation immediately followed by privilege escalation are all reliable detection points on modern endpoint telemetry.
ITID-12742.response: Isolate the affected host immediately, terminate the impersonating process, and audit for any actions taken under the impersonated token's identity before remediation.
metrics: Count of token-impersonation incidents per quarter
Percentage of hosts with EDR token-manipulation detection enabled
Mean time to isolate a host after a token-impersonation alert
ITID-12742.notes: Differentiating axis: the specific technique is named-pipe impersonation, distinct from process injection or service creation.

playbook.name: Response: Token Impersonation via Named Pipe Impersonation
playbook.description: For a token impersonation attack where the attacker created a named pipe and tricked or forced a higher-privileged process/service to connect to it, then called ImpersonateNamedPipeClient to capture its token.

steps.title: Confirm named pipe creation and impersonation API usage
steps.desc: Review EDR telemetry for creation of an unusual named pipe followed by an ImpersonateNamedPipeClient call from a lower-privileged process.
steps.outcome: Confirmed named pipe impersonation sequence with process and pipe identified.

steps.title: Isolate the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the endpoint where the attack occurred.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated.

steps.title: Rebuild the endpoint given SYSTEM-level compromise
steps.desc: Reimage the endpoint, since named pipe impersonation typically yields SYSTEM privilege, implying deep compromise potential.
steps.outcome: Endpoint reimaged from a known-clean source.

steps.title: Verify the rebuilt endpoint is clean before return to service
steps.desc: Confirm the endpoint is clean before returning it to the user.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed clean.

steps.title: Document the technique and reinforce EDR detection coverage
steps.desc: Record the finding and confirm EDR behavioral detection for named pipe impersonation techniques is tuned and effective.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; detection coverage reviewed.

steps.title: Identify the higher-privileged process/service tricked into connecting
steps.desc: Determine which privileged service or process connected to the malicious named pipe, providing the token that was captured.
steps.outcome: Source of the captured privileged token identified.

steps.title: Terminate the malicious process and any spawned elevated processes
steps.desc: Kill the attacking process and any process it spawned using the impersonated token.
steps.outcome: Malicious activity terminated.

steps.title: Investigate initial access and how the attacker gained the low-privilege foothold
steps.desc: Determine how the attacker initially got code execution on the endpoint to attempt this privilege escalation technique.
steps.outcome: Initial access vector identified.
