scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (ITID-12912 through ITID-12919)
Session hijacking of an already-established session (ITID-12921 and siblings) rather than capture at the point of authentication
ITID-12911.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Medium pending triage.
ITID-12911.priority: P3 by default, escalating once the specific vector is identified.
ITID-12911.escalation: Reclassify to the specific rogue-infrastructure leaf once the vector is confirmed; escalate immediately if credential capture is confirmed successful.
indicators: User report of an unusual or unexpected login prompt
Alert of unclear specific rogue-authentication pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector, pending investigation
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: General security awareness training on verifying authentication prompts
ITID-12911.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-12911.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once the rogue infrastructure type is confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-12911.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Rogue Authentication System
playbook.description: General-purpose checklist for a suspected rogue authentication system (any type) discovered before it has been classified into a specific sub-type. Use to triage and stabilize, then hand off to the matching specific playbook once the mechanism is known.

steps.title: Confirm the system is not sanctioned
steps.desc: Check the reported authentication endpoint, AP, or portal against the asset inventory and change records to rule out a legitimate but unannounced deployment.
steps.guidance: Contact IT/network team directly rather than relying on inventory alone — inventories lag real deployments.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the system is unauthorized, or the alert is closed as a false positive.
steps.abort: If confirmed sanctioned, close as false positive and document the inventory gap.

steps.title: Isolate or disable the rogue system
steps.desc: Take the rogue device or service offline — physically disconnect, deauthenticate, block at switch/firewall, or null-route as appropriate to the mechanism.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with network team; avoid tipping off an on-site attacker before physical response if applicable.
steps.outcome: Rogue system no longer reachable by users.

steps.title: Hand off to the matching specific rogue-authentication playbook
steps.desc: Once the mechanism is confirmed, escalate to and follow the specific playbook (Evil Twin, rogue DNS/DHCP, rogue KDC, rogue SAML/OAuth IdP, rogue VPN gateway, or rogue captive portal) for detailed eradication steps.
steps.outcome: Incident reassigned to the correct specific playbook with all identification/containment evidence carried forward.

steps.title: Confirm normal authentication service restored
steps.desc: Verify users can authenticate through only the legitimate system and no rogue infrastructure remains reachable.
steps.outcome: No further rogue-system sightings after a defined monitoring window.

steps.title: Document detection gap and recommend control improvement
steps.desc: Record how the rogue system was discovered, how long it was active, and what detection/prevention control would catch it sooner.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; improvement ticket opened where applicable.

steps.title: Determine the rogue system's mechanism and vector
steps.desc: Establish what the rogue system is impersonating (Wi-Fi, VPN, SSO/IdP, DNS/DHCP redirect, KDC, captive portal) and how users are being steered to it.
steps.guidance: This determines which specific playbook to hand off to; capture MAC/IP, SSID, hostname, or URL evidence.
steps.outcome: Rogue mechanism identified and logged.

steps.title: Force credential reset for potentially affected accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke active sessions for any account that may have authenticated against the rogue system.
steps.guidance: Prioritize privileged and VIP accounts if scope is still being confirmed.
steps.outcome: Affected accounts' credentials rotated and sessions invalidated.

steps.title: Identify potentially affected users and systems
steps.desc: Determine which users, devices, or network segments could have reached or interacted with the rogue system.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference DHCP leases, association logs, or DNS query logs within the exposure window.
steps.outcome: Preliminary list of potentially exposed accounts/devices.

ITID-12912.def: An adversary stands up a rogue wireless access point using the same or a confusingly similar SSID as a legitimate network so that a victim's device connects to it, allowing the adversary to capture credentials entered on a spoofed captive/login page or to intercept authentication traffic.
ITID-12912.purpose: Captures a human being tricked into authenticating against an attacker-operated Wi-Fi access point impersonating a legitimate network.
scopeIncludes: A rogue AP broadcasting a legitimate-looking SSID (evil twin) that a victim connects to
Credential or MFA-token capture occurring after connection to the rogue AP
scopeExcludes: Rogue captive portals encountered on genuine public Wi-Fi infrastructure that has itself been compromised (ITID-12917)
DNS/DHCP redirection on a legitimate, uncompromised network (ITID-12913)
ITID-12912.severity: High if corporate credentials or MFA material were entered; Medium if only connection occurred with no entry confirmed.
ITID-12912.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if credential entry is confirmed.
ITID-12912.escalation: Escalate to SOC and network security immediately upon confirmed rogue AP detection near a facility; escalate to IR if credentials were entered.
indicators: Duplicate/confusable SSID detected via wireless scanning
User report of an unexpected re-authentication prompt on a familiar network
Device connection logs showing an unrecognized BSSID for a known SSID
vectors: Evil-twin access point with a stronger signal than the legitimate AP
Deauthentication attack forcing reconnection to the rogue AP
rootCauses: Devices configured to auto-connect to known SSIDs without certificate validation
Lack of wireless intrusion detection coverage in the affected area
controls: Wireless intrusion detection/prevention system (WIDS/WIPS)
Certificate-based Wi-Fi authentication (EAP-TLS) instead of PSK
ITID-12912.detection: Wireless scanning and WIDS/WIPS provide a genuine technical detection surface for rogue APs.
ITID-12912.response: Force credential reset and re-issue MFA for any user confirmed connected during the window; locate and report the rogue AP for physical takedown.
metrics: Count of rogue APs detected per quarter
Mean time to takedown after detection
ITID-12912.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the spoofed infrastructure is Wi-Fi/wireless-layer.

playbook.name: Response: Rogue Wi-Fi Access Point (Evil Twin) Authentication Capture
playbook.description: For a rogue wireless access point impersonating a legitimate SSID to capture Wi-Fi or captive-portal credentials from associating clients.

steps.title: Locate and characterize the rogue AP
steps.desc: Use wireless IDS/spectrum analysis to identify the rogue AP's SSID, BSSID/MAC, channel, and approximate physical location.
steps.guidance: Compare BSSID and signal characteristics against the authorized AP inventory to confirm it is not a legitimate AP with a misconfiguration.
steps.outcome: Rogue AP identified with BSSID and location.

steps.title: Locate and physically remove/disable the rogue AP
steps.desc: Use signal triangulation to physically locate and power down or confiscate the rogue hardware.
steps.guidance: If the AP cannot be located immediately, suppress it via WIPS containment (deauth) as an interim measure.
steps.outcome: Rogue AP powered off or contained; no longer broadcasting.

steps.title: Sweep for repeat/duplicate rogue APs
steps.desc: Run an extended WIPS sweep to check for additional rogue APs using the same or similar SSID pattern nearby.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no other rogue APs remain active.

steps.title: Verify affected devices are clean before rejoining sensitive systems
steps.desc: Confirm affected devices have no unexpected profiles, certificates, or config pushed while connected to the rogue AP.
steps.outcome: Devices confirmed clean and reconnected normally.

steps.title: Document location, dwell time, and recommend WIPS coverage improvement
steps.desc: Record where and how long the rogue AP was active and whether WIPS coverage or alerting needs improvement for that area.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; WIPS coverage ticket opened if a blind spot is identified.

steps.title: Determine how many clients associated
steps.desc: Pull association/deauth logs from the WIPS or wireless controller to list every client device that connected to the rogue AP.
steps.outcome: List of affected client devices/MAC addresses.

steps.title: Force affected clients to reconnect to the legitimate network
steps.desc: Push a deauthentication/reconnect notice or MDM policy nudging affected devices back onto the corporate SSID.
steps.outcome: Affected devices confirmed reconnected to the legitimate network.

steps.title: Determine what credentials the rogue AP could have captured
steps.desc: Assess whether the rogue AP presented a fake captive portal, WPA2-Enterprise auth prompt, or was open (no credential prompt), which changes exposure severity.
steps.outcome: Confirmed credential exposure type (none, network credentials, or corporate SSO if chained to a fake portal).
steps.abort: If the AP was open with no credential prompt, downgrade to a network-eavesdropping concern rather than credential compromise.

steps.title: Reset credentials for any account entered on the rogue portal
steps.desc: Rotate Wi-Fi/802.1X credentials or SSO passwords for any user confirmed to have submitted credentials.
steps.outcome: Exposed credentials invalidated.

ITID-12913.def: An adversary manipulates DNS resolution or issues rogue DHCP responses on a network the victim already trusts, redirecting the victim's browser or client to an attacker-controlled fake authentication page.
ITID-12913.purpose: Captures a human redirected to a fake authentication portal via manipulated DNS or DHCP responses on an otherwise trusted network.
scopeIncludes: Rogue DHCP server issuing a malicious DNS server or gateway to victims
DNS cache poisoning or hijacked resolution redirecting a login URL to a spoofed page
scopeExcludes: The victim connecting to an entirely rogue wireless network rather than a manipulated legitimate one (ITID-12912)
Local-segment name-resolution poisoning specifically via LLMNR/NBT-NS used to relay credentials (ITID-12914)
ITID-12913.severity: High, given the network-wide blast radius of a rogue DHCP/DNS server.
ITID-12913.priority: P1 while the rogue DHCP/DNS service remains active on the network.
ITID-12913.escalation: Escalate to network engineering immediately to identify and disable the rogue DHCP/DNS source; escalate to IR if credentials were captured.
indicators: Multiple clients receiving DHCP leases from an unauthorized server
Unexpected DNS resolution for authentication domains
TLS certificate warnings on a normally trusted login page
vectors: Rogue DHCP server on a shared network segment
ARP or DNS cache poisoning redirecting resolution
rootCauses: No DHCP snooping/port security on access switches
Lack of DNSSEC or DNS monitoring
controls: DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection on switches
DNS monitoring and DNSSEC validation
ITID-12913.detection: Network telemetry (DHCP snooping logs, DNS query monitoring) provides a strong technical detection surface.
ITID-12913.response: Disable the rogue DHCP/DNS source, force affected clients to renew leases, and reset credentials entered on the spoofed portal.
metrics: Count of rogue DHCP/DNS events detected per quarter
Time to disable rogue service
ITID-12913.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the network itself is trusted, but its DNS/DHCP resolution has been subverted.

playbook.name: Response: Rogue DNS/DHCP Redirect to Fake Authentication Portal
playbook.description: For an attacker who has compromised or spoofed DNS/DHCP on the local network to redirect users to a fake authentication portal.

steps.title: Confirm rogue DNS/DHCP server is present on the segment
steps.desc: Compare DHCP lease records and DNS resolver responses against the authorized server list to identify the rogue server's IP/MAC.
steps.guidance: Look for unexpected DHCP OFFER responses racing the legitimate server, or DNS responses resolving internal hostnames to unexpected IPs.
steps.outcome: Rogue DHCP/DNS server identified by IP and switch port/MAC.

steps.title: Block the rogue server at the switch port
steps.desc: Disable the switch port the rogue DHCP/DNS server is connected to, or enable DHCP snooping/port security to drop its responses.
steps.outcome: Rogue server can no longer respond to DHCP/DNS requests on the segment.

steps.title: Identify and remove the rogue device or compromised host running the service
steps.desc: Physically locate the rogue device, or if it is a compromised legitimate host, remove the malicious DHCP/DNS service and investigate the host for compromise.
steps.outcome: Rogue service permanently removed from the network.

steps.title: Confirm network services returned to normal
steps.desc: Verify DHCP and DNS resolution across the affected segment are functioning solely through legitimate servers.
steps.outcome: No rogue responses observed over a monitoring window.

steps.title: Document root cause and control gap
steps.desc: Record how the rogue server gained network access and whether port security/DHCP snooping would have prevented it.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; network hardening ticket opened.

steps.title: Identify the fake portal and what it captured
steps.desc: Examine the redirect target to determine what it mimics (SSO login, VPN portal, webmail) and what fields it collects.
steps.guidance: Do not enter real credentials while investigating; use a sandboxed/isolated analysis system.
steps.outcome: Fake portal characterized; credential fields identified.

steps.title: Force affected clients to renew DHCP and flush DNS
steps.desc: Push a script/GPO or instruct users to release/renew their IP lease and flush DNS cache so they pick up legitimate settings.
steps.outcome: Affected clients confirmed using legitimate DHCP/DNS again.

steps.title: Enable DHCP snooping/DNS security controls network-wide
steps.desc: Where not already enabled, deploy DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection on affected switches to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Preventive controls active on the affected segment.

steps.title: Determine which clients received the rogue redirect
steps.desc: Pull DHCP lease logs to identify all clients that received an address or DNS setting from the rogue server during the exposure window.
steps.outcome: List of affected client IPs/hostnames.

steps.title: Reset credentials submitted to the fake portal
steps.desc: Rotate passwords for any user who confirms entering credentials on the redirect target.
steps.outcome: Exposed credentials invalidated.

ITID-12914.def: An adversary responds to broadcast name-resolution requests (LLMNR/NBT-NS) or otherwise poses as a local authentication relay point, capturing or relaying credential material (e.g. NTLM hashes) offered by a victim's client during automatic authentication attempts.
ITID-12914.purpose: Captures a human's authentication attempt intercepted or relayed via LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or a rogue KDC-style relay on the local network segment.
scopeIncludes: LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning capturing NTLM authentication attempts
Relay of captured authentication material to another system to gain access
scopeExcludes: Rogue DHCP/DNS redirection to a fake web-based login portal (ITID-12913)
Use of already-captured credentials to authenticate elsewhere, tracked as a downstream/lateral-movement incident rather than the capture event itself
ITID-12914.severity: High, since relayed NTLM authentication can lead directly to unauthorized access.
ITID-12914.priority: P1 while poisoning/relay activity is active on the network.
ITID-12914.escalation: Escalate to SOC and IR immediately; treat as an active on-path attack requiring urgent network isolation.
indicators: Unusual volume of LLMNR/NBT-NS responses from a single host
NTLM authentication attempts relayed to unexpected destination systems
Responder-style tool signatures in network traffic
vectors: LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning tool (e.g. Responder) run from a compromised or rogue host
NTLM relay to a service with signing disabled
rootCauses: LLMNR/NBT-NS not disabled on endpoints
SMB/LDAP signing not enforced, permitting relay
mitreTechniques: T1557.001 Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay
controls: Disable LLMNR/NBT-NS via group policy
Enforce SMB and LDAP signing
ITID-12914.detection: Network and endpoint telemetry provide a strong technical detection surface for poisoning and relay activity.
ITID-12914.response: Isolate the poisoning host, reset any relayed credentials, and confirm whether the relay resulted in unauthorized access.
metrics: Count of poisoning/relay events detected per quarter
Time to isolate poisoning host
ITID-12914.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: exploitation of local broadcast name-resolution protocols rather than DNS/DHCP or a fake web portal.

playbook.name: Response: Rogue KDC / LLMNR-NBT-NS Poisoning Relay
playbook.description: For an attacker on the local network using LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS poisoning (e.g. Responder-style tooling) or a rogue Kerberos KDC to capture or relay authentication attempts.

steps.title: Confirm poisoning/relay activity on the segment
steps.desc: Review SIEM/NIDS alerts for LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS name resolution responses from an unexpected host, or Kerberos traffic directed at a non-domain-controller IP.
steps.guidance: Look for a single host answering broadcast name-resolution queries for many different hostnames — a strong Responder-style indicator.
steps.outcome: Source host of the poisoning/relay identified.

steps.title: Isolate the offending host
steps.desc: Disconnect or network-isolate the host running the poisoning/relay tool.
steps.outcome: Host no longer able to respond to broadcast name-resolution traffic.

steps.title: Disable LLMNR/NBT-NS and enable SMB/LDAP signing network-wide
steps.desc: Push GPO to disable LLMNR and NetBIOS name resolution and require SMB signing and LDAP channel binding to prevent recurrence.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive fix — removing the offending host alone does not close the underlying weakness other hosts on the segment share.
steps.outcome: LLMNR/NBT-NS disabled and signing enforced across the domain.

steps.title: Confirm no further poisoning responses observed
steps.desc: Monitor the segment for a defined window to confirm no further LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or relay activity.
steps.outcome: Clean monitoring window with no recurrence.

steps.title: Document exposure and confirm hardening is domain-wide
steps.desc: Record which accounts/systems were exposed and confirm LLMNR/NBT-NS disablement and signing enforcement were rolled out beyond just the affected segment.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; hardening confirmed organization-wide.

steps.title: Identify what was relayed or captured
steps.desc: Determine whether the tool captured NTLM hashes/challenge-responses for offline cracking, or actively relayed authentication to another service (SMB relay, LDAP relay).
steps.guidance: Relay activity is far more urgent — it can yield immediate authenticated access rather than just a crackable hash.
steps.outcome: Confirmed capture-only vs. active-relay scenario.

steps.title: Reset credentials for accounts whose authentication was captured or relayed
steps.desc: Rotate passwords for every affected account, prioritizing any with relayed access to a sensitive system.
steps.outcome: Affected credentials invalidated.

steps.title: Investigate the offending host for how it gained network access
steps.desc: Determine whether the host running the tool is a compromised legitimate endpoint or unauthorized device, and remediate accordingly.
steps.outcome: Root presence of the offending host explained and resolved.

steps.title: Identify affected accounts and target systems
steps.desc: Determine which accounts' authentication attempts were captured/relayed and what downstream systems (if any) were accessed via relay.
steps.outcome: List of affected accounts and any systems accessed via relay.

steps.title: Terminate any sessions established via relay
steps.desc: If relay resulted in an authenticated session or new object (e.g. a new AD computer account, added group membership), identify and terminate/revert it.
steps.outcome: No lingering access from the relay attack.

ITID-12915.def: An adversary stands up a fraudulent SAML or OAuth identity provider (or a forged federation/consent flow) that mimics a trusted IdP, tricking the victim into entering credentials or granting consent that the adversary then captures or exploits.
ITID-12915.purpose: Captures a human being redirected to authenticate against an attacker-controlled identity provider impersonating a trusted SAML or OAuth IdP.
scopeIncludes: A spoofed SSO login page mimicking the organization's real IdP
A malicious OAuth application consent screen tricking a user into granting token access
scopeExcludes: A genuinely compromised, legitimate IdP being misused rather than impersonated (ITID-12918)
Reuse of an already-stolen session cookie against a legitimate site (ITID-12921 and siblings)
ITID-12915.severity: High, given federated IdPs typically grant access across many downstream applications.
ITID-12915.priority: P1, given the blast radius of a compromised federation trust.
ITID-12915.escalation: Escalate to identity/IAM team and IR immediately; revoke any OAuth consent grants issued during the window.
indicators: Login page hosted on a domain that mimics but does not match the real IdP
Unexpected OAuth consent prompt requesting broad scopes
Federation/token-issuance logs showing an untrusted issuer
vectors: Phishing link to a rogue SSO login page
Malicious OAuth application registered to request delegated access
rootCauses: Users not trained to verify IdP domain/certificate before entering credentials
No conditional access policy restricting third-party OAuth app consent
mitreTechniques: T1606.002 Forge Web Credentials: SAML Tokens
T1550.001 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token
controls: Conditional access restricting third-party OAuth app consent
IdP domain/certificate pinning guidance for users
ITID-12915.detection: Federation and token-issuance logs provide a genuine technical detection surface, alongside user reporting.
ITID-12915.response: Revoke forged tokens/consent grants, reset affected credentials, and audit downstream applications for unauthorized access.
metrics: Count of rogue IdP/OAuth consent incidents per quarter
Time to revoke fraudulent tokens/grants
sops: Identity and Access Management Incident SOP
ITID-12915.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the spoofed infrastructure is a federated identity/SSO trust relationship.

playbook.name: Response: Rogue SAML/OAuth Identity Provider
playbook.description: For an attacker-operated identity provider or OAuth authorization endpoint impersonating the organization's legitimate SSO to harvest credentials or consent tokens.

steps.title: Confirm the rogue IdP/OAuth endpoint and how it was delivered
steps.desc: Identify the rogue login/consent URL and the delivery vector (phishing email, malicious app registration, typosquatted domain).
steps.guidance: Capture the full URL, hosting infrastructure, and any spoofed branding for takedown and threat intel purposes.
steps.outcome: Rogue IdP/OAuth endpoint and delivery vector documented.

steps.title: Revoke any malicious OAuth app registrations and consent grants
steps.desc: Identify and remove any rogue application registered in the tenant, and revoke all user consent grants to it.
steps.guidance: Check the tenant's enterprise application list for anything unrecognized created around the incident window.
steps.outcome: Malicious app removed; all consent grants revoked.
steps.tool: IdP admin console (Entra ID / Okta / etc.)

steps.title: Audit affected accounts for persistence set up via the stolen access
steps.desc: Review affected accounts for new MFA methods, forwarding rules, or app grants added after the compromise window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of attacker persistence.

steps.title: Restore access and re-enroll MFA from a known-clean device
steps.desc: Have affected users set new passwords and re-enroll MFA.
steps.outcome: Users have confirmed-clean access restored.

steps.title: Document the spoofing technique and improve IdP phishing resistance
steps.desc: Record how the rogue IdP mimicked the real branding/domain and recommend a control improvement (e.g. phishing-resistant MFA, conditional access, brand-protection monitoring).
steps.outcome: Finding logged; control improvement ticket opened.

steps.title: Determine what was captured — password, MFA, or an OAuth token/consent grant
steps.desc: Establish whether users entered a password, completed MFA on the fake page, or granted OAuth consent to a malicious app that legitimately proxied to the real IdP.
steps.guidance: A malicious OAuth consent grant against the real IdP is especially dangerous — the resulting token bypasses password reset entirely and must be revoked separately.
steps.outcome: Confirmed capture type per affected user.

steps.title: Force password reset and session/token revocation for affected accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke all active sessions and refresh tokens for every affected user.
steps.outcome: All affected accounts require full re-authentication.

steps.title: Remove any confirmed persistence
steps.desc: Delete any malicious MFA enrollment, forwarding rule, or app grant identified in the prior step.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access mechanism remains.

steps.title: Identify the full list of affected users
steps.desc: Search email/proxy logs for everyone who received the phishing link or visited the rogue endpoint.
steps.outcome: Complete affected-user list.

steps.title: Take down or block the rogue endpoint
steps.desc: Submit a takedown request to the hosting provider/registrar and add the domain to web/email blocklists.
steps.outcome: Rogue endpoint blocked org-wide and takedown request submitted.
steps.tool: Web proxy / mail gateway / registrar abuse contact

ITID-12916.def: An adversary stands up a fake VPN or remote-access gateway login portal (or spoofs the legitimate one via DNS/typosquatting) so that a victim enters remote-access credentials, which the adversary then captures.
ITID-12916.purpose: Captures a human being tricked into authenticating against a fraudulent VPN or remote-access gateway impersonating the organization's legitimate remote-access infrastructure.
scopeIncludes: A cloned VPN login portal hosted on a lookalike domain
Credential capture via a fraudulent remote-access client update prompt
scopeExcludes: Redirection via manipulated DNS/DHCP to a generic fake portal not specifically impersonating the VPN gateway (ITID-12913)
A genuinely compromised, legitimate VPN gateway (ITID-12918)
ITID-12916.severity: High, since VPN credentials typically grant broad internal network access.
ITID-12916.priority: P1, given the direct path to internal network access.
ITID-12916.escalation: Escalate to network security and IR immediately; force reset of any VPN credentials entered during the window.
indicators: Lookalike/typosquatted domain hosting a VPN login page
User report of an unfamiliar VPN client update prompt
Login attempts against the real VPN gateway using credentials just entered elsewhere
vectors: Typosquatted VPN portal domain sent via phishing
Fraudulent remote-access client installer prompting for credentials
rootCauses: No MFA required on VPN authentication
Lack of brand/domain monitoring for lookalike VPN portal domains
controls: MFA enforced on all VPN/remote-access authentication
Domain/brand monitoring for lookalike VPN portals
ITID-12916.detection: VPN authentication logs and domain monitoring provide a real technical detection surface.
ITID-12916.response: Reset affected VPN credentials, enforce MFA re-enrollment, and take down or report the fraudulent portal.
metrics: Count of rogue VPN portal incidents per quarter
Time to reset affected credentials
ITID-12916.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the spoofed infrastructure is the organization's remote-access/VPN gateway specifically.

playbook.name: Response: Rogue VPN/Remote Access Gateway
playbook.description: For an attacker-operated VPN or remote access gateway impersonating the organization's legitimate remote access service to harvest credentials.

steps.title: Confirm the rogue gateway and its delivery vector
steps.desc: Identify the rogue VPN/remote-access endpoint's URL/IP and how users were directed to it (phishing, typosquat domain, DNS manipulation).
steps.outcome: Rogue gateway and delivery vector documented.

steps.title: Force password reset and MFA re-enrollment for affected accounts
steps.desc: Reset VPN/domain passwords and invalidate existing MFA tokens for all affected users.
steps.outcome: Affected credentials and MFA state rotated.

steps.title: Audit internal network access gained via any successful rogue-credential login
steps.desc: If any exposed credential was confirmed used against the real gateway, review what internal systems that session accessed.
steps.outcome: Scope of any internal access via the rogue credential confirmed.
steps.abort: If no real-gateway login occurred with exposed credentials, this step can be marked not applicable.

steps.title: Restore VPN access with new credentials and MFA
steps.desc: Issue new credentials and re-enroll MFA for affected users before restoring VPN access.
steps.outcome: Users have confirmed-clean VPN access restored.

steps.title: Document the spoofing method and recommend a detection/prevention improvement
steps.desc: Record how the rogue gateway was made to look legitimate and recommend controls such as client-certificate-based VPN auth or brand-monitoring.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; improvement ticket opened.

steps.title: Determine what credentials/tokens the gateway could capture
steps.desc: Assess whether the fake gateway harvested username/password only, or also prompted for and captured an MFA/OTP code or client certificate.
steps.guidance: Capturing a one-time MFA code is time-limited but still enables immediate hijack if used quickly by the attacker — treat as urgent regardless.
steps.outcome: Confirmed capture scope.

steps.title: Terminate any active VPN sessions established with exposed credentials
steps.desc: Identify and forcibly disconnect any VPN session tied to an affected account, especially any originating from an unrecognized IP/geo.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled VPN session remains active.

steps.title: Identify affected users and check for real logins immediately following exposure
steps.desc: Cross-reference the affected-user list against real VPN gateway logs for suspicious logins shortly after their exposure.
steps.outcome: Identified whether any captured credential was actually used against the real gateway.

steps.title: Take down or block the rogue gateway
steps.desc: Submit a takedown request and block the rogue domain/IP at the web proxy and email gateway.
steps.outcome: Rogue gateway blocked org-wide; takedown submitted.

ITID-12917.def: An adversary presents a fake captive portal on public wireless infrastructure that mimics a legitimate network's sign-in page, or clones the legitimate captive portal itself, in order to capture credentials the victim reflexively enters.
ITID-12917.purpose: Captures a human being tricked into entering corporate credentials into a fraudulent captive portal encountered on public Wi-Fi (e.g. airport, hotel, cafe).
scopeIncludes: A cloned captive portal on public Wi-Fi requesting corporate SSO credentials
A fake captive portal used to harvest credentials from a traveling employee
scopeExcludes: An evil-twin access point operated by the attacker at a private/corporate location (ITID-12912)
A legitimate public Wi-Fi provider's own captive portal that has itself been compromised (ITID-12918)
ITID-12917.severity: Medium-High, depending on whether corporate SSO credentials were entered.
ITID-12917.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if corporate credentials were confirmed entered.
ITID-12917.escalation: Escalate to SOC once credential entry is confirmed; advise affected traveling users to disconnect immediately.
indicators: User report of a captive portal unexpectedly requesting corporate credentials
Corporate SSO login attempt originating from an unmanaged public network context
vectors: Cloned public-Wi-Fi captive portal requesting SSO credentials
Man-in-the-middle captive portal injection on shared public networks
rootCauses: Employees not trained to avoid entering corporate credentials on public Wi-Fi captive portals
No mandated VPN/always-on tunnel for travel use
controls: Mandatory always-on VPN for travel/public-network use
Security awareness training on public Wi-Fi captive portal risk
ITID-12917.detection: Limited technical detection surface; relies heavily on user reporting and anomalous SSO login context.
ITID-12917.response: Reset any credentials entered, review SSO login context for anomalies, and remind the user of safe public-Wi-Fi practices.
metrics: Count of public-Wi-Fi captive-portal credential-capture reports per quarter
ITID-12917.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the setting is public Wi-Fi infrastructure a traveling employee does not control or fully trust to begin with.

playbook.name: Response: Rogue Captive Portal (Public Wi-Fi Context)
playbook.description: For a report of an employee/user encountering or falling for a fake captive portal on public Wi-Fi (airport, hotel, cafe) that harvested corporate or personal credentials.

steps.title: Interview the user and capture portal details
steps.desc: Get the location, network name, portal appearance, and exactly what was entered from the reporting user.
steps.guidance: Since this occurred off-network, the organization's own telemetry will show nothing — the user interview is the primary evidence source.
steps.outcome: Documented account of the incident and what credential(s) were entered.

steps.title: Reset the exposed corporate credential and revoke sessions
steps.desc: Rotate the affected corporate password and revoke active sessions/tokens.
steps.outcome: Exposed credential invalidated.

steps.title: Remove any rogue profile/certificate found on the device
steps.desc: Wipe or remediate any malicious configuration identified in the prior step; reimage the device if compromise is suspected beyond the profile.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed free of attacker-installed configuration.

steps.title: Restore access with new credential and confirm device health
steps.desc: Issue the user a new password/MFA enrollment and confirm the device passes a compliance/health check before regaining full network access.
steps.outcome: User and device restored to a known-good state.

steps.title: Document and reinforce public Wi-Fi guidance
steps.desc: Log the incident and remind the affected team (or org-wide, if pattern suggests it) of VPN-on-public-Wi-Fi policy and how to recognize captive portal risk.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; awareness reminder issued where appropriate.

steps.title: Determine whether corporate credentials or a corporate device were involved
steps.desc: Confirm whether the credential entered was a corporate account/SSO password, and whether a corporate-managed device connected to the rogue portal.
steps.outcome: Confirmed corporate exposure scope (credential-only, device-only, or both).
steps.abort: If only a personal account/device was involved with no corporate credential entered, log as informational and close.

steps.title: Check the corporate device for rogue certificates or configuration profiles
steps.desc: If a managed device connected to the rogue portal, check for any unexpected certificate, VPN profile, or proxy setting pushed during the session.
steps.guidance: Malicious captive portals sometimes push a CA certificate to enable ongoing traffic interception.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean or remediated.

ITID-12918.def: An adversary gains control of or modifies the organization's actual authentication infrastructure (e.g. by compromising the IdP server, injecting malicious code into a real login page, or modifying its authentication logic) so that legitimate users authenticating through the real system have their credentials captured or their sessions manipulated.
ITID-12918.purpose: Captures cases where a genuine, legitimate authentication system (the organization's real IdP, VPN gateway, or captive portal) has itself been compromised and is being misused to capture credentials, rather than an attacker standing up separate rogue infrastructure.
scopeIncludes: Malicious code injected into the organization's genuine login page to log entered credentials
A compromised, legitimate IdP configured by the adversary to export authentication material
scopeExcludes: Attacker-stood-up rogue/impersonating infrastructure that is separate from the real system (ITID-12912, ITID-12913, ITID-12914, ITID-12915, ITID-12916, ITID-12917)
Confirmed successful use of captured credentials to take further action, tracked separately (ITID-12919)
ITID-12918.severity: Critical, since the trusted system itself is compromised and every user authenticating through it is at risk.
ITID-12918.escalation: Escalate to IR and executive security leadership immediately; consider taking the authentication system offline pending remediation.
indicators: Unexpected modification to authentication system code or configuration
Unauthorized administrative access to the IdP/authentication server
Discrepancy between expected and actual login page source
vectors: Web shell or malicious code injected into the login page
Compromise of IdP server via unpatched vulnerability or stolen admin credentials
rootCauses: Unpatched vulnerabilities on authentication infrastructure
Insufficient integrity monitoring on authentication system code/configuration
controls: File integrity monitoring on authentication system code and configuration
Privileged access management for authentication system administration
ITID-12918.detection: Integrity monitoring and admin-access auditing provide a strong technical detection surface.
ITID-12918.response: Contain and rebuild the compromised authentication system from a known-good state; force organization-wide credential reset.
metrics: Time to detect authentication system compromise
Time to full remediation
detections: File integrity monitoring alerting on authentication systems
ITID-12918.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the infrastructure is genuinely the organization's own, not an impersonation, but has been subverted.

playbook.name: Response: Compromised Legitimate Authentication System
playbook.description: For confirmation that the organization's own legitimate authentication system (IdP, RADIUS server, AD, VPN gateway) has itself been compromised, rather than a rogue impersonator — the system attackers control IS the real one.

steps.title: Confirm compromise of the legitimate authentication system
steps.desc: Establish concrete evidence that the real authentication system's configuration, code, or infrastructure has been tampered with (e.g. malicious auth module, backdoor account, altered login flow).
steps.guidance: Distinguish this from a rogue impersonator — this is the trusted system itself under attacker control, which is far higher severity.
steps.outcome: Compromise confirmed with specific evidence of tampering.
steps.abort: If no tampering evidence is found and behavior is explained by misconfiguration, reclassify accordingly.

steps.title: Take the authentication system offline or fail over to a clean instance
steps.desc: Isolate the compromised authentication service and, if available, fail over authentication to a verified-clean redundant instance.
steps.guidance: Coordinate carefully — taking the sole authentication system offline can itself cause an outage; have a fallback plan ready before cutting over.
steps.outcome: Authentication no longer flows through the compromised system.

steps.title: Rebuild the authentication system from a known-clean source
steps.desc: Rebuild the compromised system from verified-clean installation media/images and configuration baselines rather than attempting to clean in place.
steps.guidance: An authentication system compromise warrants a full rebuild — do not trust the existing binaries or configuration.
steps.outcome: Authentication system rebuilt and verified against a known-clean baseline.

steps.title: Phased restoration of authentication service with enhanced monitoring
steps.desc: Bring the rebuilt authentication system back online in phases, with elevated logging/monitoring active throughout.
steps.outcome: Authentication service fully restored with no signs of recurring compromise.

steps.title: Conduct full incident review and report to leadership
steps.desc: Document root cause, scope, response timeline, and control improvements; given the severity, brief leadership and determine any regulatory/breach notification obligations.
steps.outcome: Full incident report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Determine scope: how long compromised and what was captured
steps.desc: Establish the compromise window and whether the attacker was capturing all authentication attempts, a subset, or had additionally created backdoor access.
steps.guidance: Assume every authentication event within the compromise window is potentially exposed until proven otherwise.
steps.outcome: Compromise window and exposure scope established.

steps.title: Force organization-wide credential reset and session revocation
steps.desc: Reset passwords and revoke all active sessions/tokens for every account that authenticated during the compromise window.
steps.guidance: Coordinate timing and communications carefully given the scale — this is a mass password reset event.
steps.outcome: All potentially exposed credentials rotated and sessions invalidated.

steps.title: Investigate and close the initial access vector
steps.desc: Determine how the attacker initially compromised the authentication system (e.g. vulnerable software, stolen admin credential, supply-chain) and remediate that vector.
steps.outcome: Initial access vector identified and closed.

steps.title: Extended monitoring window for reused/leaked credentials
steps.desc: Monitor for authentication attempts using pre-reset credentials or anomalous access patterns for an extended period post-recovery.
steps.outcome: No anomalous activity observed during the extended window.

steps.title: Identify all accounts that authenticated during the compromise window
steps.desc: Pull the full authentication log for the compromise window to build the affected-account list.
steps.guidance: This is likely to include a large percentage of the user base — treat as an organization-wide credential compromise.
steps.outcome: Complete list of potentially exposed accounts.

steps.title: Identify and disable any backdoor accounts or access created by the attacker
steps.desc: Audit the authentication system and downstream directory for accounts, service principals, or trust relationships created or modified during the compromise window.
steps.outcome: Any attacker-created access confirmed and disabled.

ITID-12919.def: A rogue authentication system incident (of any of the sibling vector types) where it has been confirmed that the adversary obtained working credentials or authentication material and successfully used it to authenticate to a real system or take further unauthorized action, distinct from the capture attempt itself.
ITID-12919.purpose: Captures the confirmed-successful outcome where a rogue authentication system captured valid credentials or session material and the adversary actually used it to authenticate or take action.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed adversary login to a real system using credentials captured via a rogue authentication vector
Confirmed downstream unauthorized action taken using captured credentials/tokens
scopeExcludes: The rogue-infrastructure capture event itself with no confirmed successful use (ITID-12912 through ITID-12918)
Session hijacking of an already-authenticated session not originating from a rogue authentication capture (ITID-12921 and siblings)
ITID-12919.severity: Critical, given confirmed unauthorized access or action.
ITID-12919.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response as an active compromise; treat as a full account-takeover incident.
indicators: Successful login using credentials known to have been captured via a rogue authentication vector
Unauthorized actions performed under the victim's identity following capture
vectors: Direct reuse of captured credentials against the real authentication system
Reuse of captured MFA/session tokens to bypass step-up authentication
rootCauses: No anomaly detection on login velocity/geolocation following credential capture
Lack of rapid credential-reset workflow following a confirmed capture event
controls: Impossible-travel/anomalous-login detection
Automated credential-reset workflow tied to confirmed capture events
ITID-12919.detection: Authentication and identity logs provide strong confirmation once cross-referenced with the originating capture event.
ITID-12919.response: Treat as full incident response: contain, reset all affected credentials/tokens, and investigate scope of unauthorized actions taken.
metrics: Count of confirmed successful captures per quarter
Time from capture to detection of unauthorized use
ITID-12919.notes: This leaf and ITID-12929 are the confirmed-impact outcome leaves for their respective Tier-4 groups; use only once successful post-capture use is confirmed, not merely suspected.

playbook.name: Response: Successful Rogue Authentication System Capture with Confirmed Credential Use
playbook.description: For a confirmed case where a rogue authentication system (of any type — AP, DNS/DHCP, KDC, IdP, VPN, captive portal) not only captured credentials but the attacker has demonstrably used them for unauthorized access.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized use of the captured credential
steps.desc: Establish concrete evidence that a captured credential was used to authenticate to a real system by the attacker — anomalous source IP/geo, impossible travel, or activity inconsistent with the legitimate user.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized use with supporting evidence.

steps.title: Disable compromised accounts and terminate all active attacker sessions
steps.desc: Immediately disable every confirmed-compromised account and forcibly terminate any active session tied to the attacker's activity.
steps.outcome: Attacker no longer has active access through any identified account.

steps.title: Remove attacker-established persistence across all affected systems
steps.desc: Identify and remove any backdoor account, scheduled task, forwarding rule, OAuth grant, or malware the attacker installed while they had access.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled persistence mechanism remains anywhere in scope.

steps.title: Restore affected systems from verified-clean state
steps.desc: Restore or rebuild any affected system from a known-clean backup/image, validating integrity before returning to production.
steps.outcome: Affected systems restored and verified clean.

steps.title: Full incident report with breach-notification assessment
steps.desc: Document the complete attack chain, impact, and response, and assess whether any regulatory or contractual breach-notification obligation was triggered.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Determine the full scope of access gained
steps.desc: Trace everything the attacker accessed, modified, exfiltrated, or created using the compromised credential(s).
steps.guidance: Treat this as an active intrusion investigation, not just a credential-exposure cleanup.
steps.outcome: Full scope of attacker activity documented.

steps.title: Contain the rogue authentication system itself
steps.desc: Take down, isolate, or block the rogue system per its specific mechanism (see the matching specific rogue-authentication playbook).
steps.outcome: Rogue system no longer capturing additional credentials.

steps.title: Reset credentials for every compromised account and rotate any exposed secrets
steps.desc: Rotate passwords, API keys, and certificates for every account or system the attacker touched.
steps.outcome: All exposed credentials/secrets invalidated.

steps.title: Elevated monitoring across all affected accounts and systems
steps.desc: Apply heightened logging/alerting on all affected accounts and systems for an extended observation period.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed during the monitoring window.

steps.title: Identify any additional accounts or systems compromised via lateral movement
steps.desc: Check whether the attacker used the initial foothold to pivot to other accounts or systems.
steps.outcome: Full list of compromised accounts/systems.

steps.title: Isolate any affected systems the attacker reached
steps.desc: Network-isolate any endpoint or server the attacker accessed using the compromised credential to prevent further lateral movement or data loss.
steps.outcome: Attacker's foothold systems isolated.

ITID-12921.def: An incident involving the hijacking of an already-established, human-initiated authenticated session, not yet matched to a more specific leaf (e.g. network sniffing, session fixation, predictable tokens, malware-resident theft, cross-device, compromised proxy, physical device access, or confirmed successful outcome).
ITID-12921.purpose: Catch-all for cases that do not fit the more specific Session Hijacking leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to identify how the session was obtained or exploited
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (ITID-12922 through ITID-12929)

ITID-33511 Unclassified/General Cookie Theft (Session Hijacking Context), ITID-33521 Unclassified/General Session Replay Attack, and ITID-33531 Unclassified/General MITM Session Hijacking, which live under a separate Tier-1 domain focused on pure technical/protocol exploitation rather than the human/credential-attack-surface framing used here
ITID-12921.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Medium pending triage.
ITID-12921.priority: P3 by default, escalating once the specific mechanism is identified.
ITID-12921.escalation: Reclassify once the specific session-hijacking pattern is clarified; escalate immediately if confirmed unauthorized actions are found.
indicators: Alert of unclear specific session-hijacking pattern
User report of unexpected activity on an authenticated session
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector, pending investigation
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: General session-management hygiene controls (idle timeout, re-authentication for sensitive actions)
ITID-12921.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-12921.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once the hijacking mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-12921.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one. This branch is the human/credential-attack-surface framing of session hijacking; the protocol-exploitation framing lives separately at ITID-33511/33521/33531.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Session Hijacking
playbook.description: General-purpose checklist for a suspected session hijacking incident (any mechanism) before the specific technique has been confirmed. Use to triage and stabilize, then hand off to the matching specific playbook.

steps.title: Confirm the session anomaly is not a benign explanation
steps.desc: Rule out VPN/proxy IP changes, shared device use, or legitimate multi-device login before treating as hijacking.
steps.guidance: Check with the user directly where possible before committing response resources.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the activity is not explained by legitimate use.
steps.abort: If explained by legitimate behavior, close as false positive.

steps.title: Invalidate the affected session(s)
steps.desc: Force-expire the suspect session token(s) at the application/identity provider.
steps.outcome: Suspect session tokens no longer valid.

steps.title: Hand off to the matching specific session-hijacking playbook
steps.desc: Once the mechanism is confirmed, escalate to and follow the specific playbook for detailed eradication steps.
steps.outcome: Incident reassigned with all evidence carried forward.

steps.title: Confirm account access restored to the legitimate user only
steps.desc: Verify the account is fully back under the legitimate user's control with no lingering attacker session.
steps.outcome: No anomalous sessions observed post-recovery.

steps.title: Document findings and recommend a control improvement
steps.desc: Record the mechanism once confirmed and recommend a session-security improvement (e.g. shorter token lifetime, device binding).
steps.outcome: Finding logged; improvement ticket opened where applicable.

steps.title: Determine the hijacking mechanism
steps.desc: Establish how the session was likely captured — network sniffing, fixation, predictable token, malware token theft, cross-device reuse, proxy compromise, or physical access.
steps.guidance: This determines which specific playbook to hand off to.
steps.outcome: Hijacking mechanism identified or narrowed to a short list.

steps.title: Reset the affected account's credentials
steps.desc: Rotate the account password and any long-lived tokens as a precaution.
steps.outcome: Credentials rotated.

steps.title: Establish scope of affected session(s) and account(s)
steps.desc: Identify every session token, account, and application affected by the suspected hijack.
steps.outcome: Affected sessions/accounts enumerated.

ITID-12922.def: An adversary positioned on the network path (e.g. shared Wi-Fi, compromised switch port, on-path interception) captures a victim's session token or cookie in transit because the session was transmitted without adequate transport protection, then reuses it to impersonate the victim.
ITID-12922.purpose: Captures session hijacking where an adversary passively or actively sniffed unencrypted or weakly protected network traffic to obtain a victim's session token or cookie.
scopeIncludes: Session token/cookie captured over unencrypted HTTP or a misconfigured TLS session on a shared network
On-path packet capture of session material during transmission
scopeExcludes: ITID-33531 Unclassified/General MITM Session Hijacking, which covers pure protocol-level MITM interception under the technical-exploitation Tier-1 domain rather than the human-network-exposure framing here
Token theft performed by resident malware on the victim's device rather than in-transit network capture (ITID-12925)
ITID-12922.severity: High if the captured session grants access to sensitive systems; Medium otherwise.
ITID-12922.priority: P1 while the sniffing capability remains active on the network.
ITID-12922.escalation: Escalate to SOC immediately upon detection of active network sniffing; invalidate the affected session(s) without delay.
indicators: Session used from a network location inconsistent with the legitimate user's activity
Detection of packet-capture tooling or promiscuous-mode NICs on the network segment
Unencrypted session traffic observed on a shared network
vectors: Packet sniffing on shared/unencrypted Wi-Fi
ARP spoofing enabling traffic interception on a local segment
rootCauses: Session cookies not marked Secure/transmitted without TLS enforcement
Lack of network segmentation isolating untrusted shared network segments
controls: Enforce HTTPS/Secure and HttpOnly cookie attributes
Network segmentation and encrypted transport for session traffic
ITID-12922.detection: Network traffic monitoring provides a genuine technical detection surface for sniffing activity.
ITID-12922.response: Invalidate the hijacked session, force re-authentication, and investigate the network segment for ongoing sniffing capability.
metrics: Count of network-sniffing-based hijacking events per quarter
ITID-12922.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the session was obtained via in-transit network capture rather than device compromise, fixation, prediction, or physical access.

playbook.name: Response: Network-Level Session Sniffing
playbook.description: For a session hijacked by capturing session cookies/tokens in cleartext or weakly-protected network traffic.

steps.title: Confirm the capture vector — unencrypted traffic or weak TLS
steps.desc: Determine whether the session token traveled over plain HTTP, a downgraded/stripped TLS connection, or an unencrypted internal protocol.
steps.guidance: Check for missing HSTS, mixed content, or a captive-portal/proxy stripping TLS as likely causes.
steps.outcome: Confirmed transport weakness that allowed sniffing.

steps.title: Invalidate the sniffed session token
steps.desc: Force-expire the affected session at the application.
steps.outcome: Session token no longer usable.

steps.title: Enforce HTTPS/HSTS and secure cookie flags on the affected application
steps.desc: Configure the application to require TLS, enable HSTS, and set Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite flags on session cookies.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive fix — without it, the next session over the same network path is equally exposed.
steps.outcome: Application no longer transmits session tokens in cleartext.

steps.title: Verify the application enforces TLS for all sessions going forward
steps.desc: Test that HTTP requests are redirected/rejected and session cookies carry secure flags.
steps.outcome: Confirmed enforcement in production.

steps.title: Document the exposure and audit other applications for the same gap
steps.desc: Record the finding and check whether other internal applications share the same missing-TLS/cookie-flag weakness.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; sweep of other applications completed or ticketed.

steps.title: Identify the network segment and potential sniffing point
steps.desc: Determine where on the network path the capture likely occurred (shared Wi-Fi, compromised switch, malicious proxy).
steps.outcome: Likely sniffing location identified.

steps.title: Reset the account credential as a precaution
steps.desc: Rotate the account password in case additional credential material was exposed on the same unencrypted channel.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated.

steps.title: Investigate and remediate the sniffing point if internal
steps.desc: If the capture occurred on an internal network segment (compromised switch, rogue tap), investigate and remediate that infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Sniffing capability removed from the network path.
steps.abort: If the capture occurred on external/public infrastructure outside organizational control, document and move to user guidance instead.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized use of the captured session
steps.desc: Check application logs for session activity from an IP/device inconsistent with the legitimate user around the capture time.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the sniffed session was actually reused by an attacker.

ITID-12923.def: An adversary sets or supplies a known session identifier to the victim (e.g. via a crafted link or a vulnerable application that accepts pre-set session IDs) before the victim authenticates, then uses that same session identifier after authentication to impersonate the victim.
ITID-12923.purpose: Captures session hijacking where an adversary forced or tricked a victim into using a session identifier already known to the adversary, then hijacked the session once the victim authenticated.
scopeIncludes: A crafted link containing a pre-set session ID that the victim unknowingly authenticates under
An application accepting an externally supplied session identifier without regenerating it at login
scopeExcludes: A session token stolen after it was legitimately issued and randomly generated (ITID-12922, ITID-12925)
Exploitation of a predictable/guessable token-generation algorithm rather than a fixation technique (ITID-12924)
ITID-12923.severity: Medium-High, depending on the sensitivity of the fixated session.
ITID-12923.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if confirmed unauthorized actions occurred.
ITID-12923.escalation: Escalate to the application owner and SOC upon confirmation; require session ID regeneration on authentication as an immediate mitigation.
indicators: Victim's session ID observed matching a value distributed prior to login
Application logs showing session ID reuse across the pre- and post-authentication boundary
vectors: Phishing link embedding a pre-set session identifier
Cross-site scripting used to set a known session cookie on the victim's browser
rootCauses: Application fails to regenerate the session identifier upon successful authentication
Session identifiers accepted from URL parameters or client-supplied cookies without validation
mitreTechniques: T1550.004 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
controls: Session ID regeneration on authentication
Reject client-supplied session identifiers not issued by the server
ITID-12923.detection: Application session-management logs provide a real, if narrow, technical detection surface.
ITID-12923.response: Invalidate the fixated session, require the application to regenerate session IDs on login, and notify the affected user.
metrics: Count of confirmed session fixation incidents per quarter
detections: Session ID continuity monitoring across authentication boundary
ITID-12923.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the adversary supplies or pre-establishes the session identifier before the victim authenticates, rather than stealing one already in use.

playbook.name: Response: Session Fixation Attack
playbook.description: For an attacker who pre-set a known session identifier on a victim and then hijacked the session once the victim authenticated under that identifier.

steps.title: Confirm the application does not regenerate session IDs at authentication
steps.desc: Test or review the affected application's login flow to confirm whether the session ID stays the same before and after authentication.
steps.guidance: This is the root vulnerability enabling fixation — confirming it is central to scoping the fix.
steps.outcome: Confirmed vulnerable behavior (session ID unchanged across authentication) or ruled out.
steps.abort: If the application correctly regenerates session IDs at login, reconsider the classification — this may be a different hijacking mechanism.

steps.title: Invalidate the fixed session and all sessions for the account
steps.desc: Force-expire the specific fixed session ID and, as a precaution, all other active sessions for the affected account.
steps.outcome: All sessions for the account terminated.

steps.title: Fix the application to regenerate session IDs on authentication
steps.desc: Work with the application owner/development team to ensure a new session ID is issued immediately upon successful login, invalidating any pre-authentication ID.
steps.guidance: This is the only durable fix for session fixation; document as a required code change, not just a config toggle.
steps.outcome: Application confirmed to issue a fresh session ID at every successful authentication.

steps.title: Verify the fix in a test environment before closing
steps.desc: Confirm the session-regeneration fix is deployed and working as expected.
steps.outcome: Fix verified in production.

steps.title: Document and add session-regeneration check to the secure development checklist
steps.desc: Record the finding and recommend this check be added to the organization's secure coding/AppSec review checklist for future applications.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; AppSec checklist updated.

steps.title: Identify how the fixed session ID was delivered to the victim
steps.desc: Determine the delivery vector — a crafted link with the session ID embedded, a shared/public terminal, or a cross-site scripting flaw setting the cookie.
steps.outcome: Delivery vector identified.

steps.title: Reset the account credential
steps.desc: Rotate the affected account's password.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated.

steps.title: Remove any malicious link/campaign delivering the fixed session ID
steps.desc: If delivered via phishing or a public posting, take down the link/campaign and block associated infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Delivery vector no longer active.

steps.title: Confirm the attacker actually accessed the account post-authentication
steps.desc: Check application logs for activity under the fixed session ID from an IP/device inconsistent with the victim.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized access via the fixed session.

ITID-12924.def: An adversary analyzes a sequence of issued session tokens or the application's token-generation algorithm, determines a predictable pattern, and computes or guesses a valid token for another user's session without ever intercepting or stealing an actual issued token.
ITID-12924.purpose: Captures session hijacking where an adversary derived or guessed a valid session token because the application's token-generation scheme was weak or predictable.
scopeIncludes: Sequential or low-entropy session tokens allowing an adversary to guess a valid value
Reverse-engineering a weak token-generation algorithm to compute another user's token
scopeExcludes: A cryptographically strong token stolen via network capture, malware, or physical access (ITID-12922, ITID-12925, ITID-12928)
Replaying a previously captured token verbatim rather than deriving/guessing a new one (ITID-33521, under the separate protocol-exploitation Tier-1 domain)
ITID-12924.severity: High, since a predictable-token weakness typically affects many sessions, not just one.
ITID-12924.priority: P1, given the likely scope across the user base.
ITID-12924.escalation: Escalate to the application owner and SOC immediately; treat as a systemic application weakness requiring urgent remediation.
indicators: Successful authentication using a token that was never legitimately issued to that requester
Application security review flagging low-entropy or sequential token generation
Multiple unrelated accounts hijacked in a short window with no phishing or malware indicators
vectors: Brute-force or pattern analysis of sequential session identifiers
Statistical analysis of a weak pseudo-random token generator
rootCauses: Session tokens generated with insufficient entropy or a predictable algorithm
No rate limiting on token-guessing attempts
mitreTechniques: T1550.004 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
controls: Cryptographically secure random session token generation
Rate limiting and anomaly detection on token-validation attempts
ITID-12924.detection: Application-layer logs and dedicated security testing (not routine monitoring) are the primary way this is identified.
ITID-12924.response: Force immediate remediation of the token-generation weakness and invalidate all outstanding sessions from the affected scheme.
metrics: Count of predictable-token incidents per quarter
Time to remediate token-generation weakness
ITID-12924.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the token was mathematically derived or guessed, not stolen from an in-transit, stored, or physically accessed source.

playbook.name: Response: Predictable Session Token Exploitation
playbook.description: For an attacker who guessed or brute-forced a valid session token due to weak/predictable token generation.

steps.title: Confirm the token generation weakness
steps.desc: Analyze the affected application's session token format to confirm it is sequential, time-based, or otherwise insufficiently random.
steps.guidance: Compare a sample of issued tokens to check for a discernible pattern.
steps.outcome: Confirmed weak token generation, with example evidence.
steps.abort: If tokens appear cryptographically random, reconsider the classification.

steps.title: Invalidate all active sessions on the affected application
steps.desc: Force-expire all currently issued session tokens application-wide as a precaution, since the weakness may affect any session.
steps.outcome: All existing tokens invalidated; users must re-authenticate.

steps.title: Fix the token generation to use a cryptographically secure random source
steps.desc: Work with the development team to replace the weak token generator with one using a CSPRNG and sufficient entropy/length.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive fix; treat as a required code change.
steps.outcome: New tokens confirmed to be cryptographically random and sufficiently long.

steps.title: Verify new tokens resist pattern analysis before closing
steps.desc: Sample a batch of newly issued tokens and confirm no discernible pattern remains.
steps.outcome: Fix verified.

steps.title: Document and audit other applications for the same weakness
steps.desc: Record the finding and check other internally developed applications for similarly weak token generation.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; sweep of other applications completed or ticketed.

steps.title: Identify evidence of scanning/guessing activity
steps.desc: Review web server logs for a high volume of session-token variations attempted from a single source, indicating brute-force guessing.
steps.outcome: Source of guessing activity identified where present.

steps.title: Block the source of the guessing/scanning activity
steps.desc: Block the offending IP(s) at the WAF/firewall and rate-limit session-related endpoints.
steps.outcome: Guessing activity blocked.

steps.title: Add rate limiting and lockout on session/token-related endpoints
steps.desc: Implement rate limiting to slow or block brute-force token-guessing attempts going forward.
steps.outcome: Rate limiting active and verified.

steps.title: Determine which accounts had tokens successfully guessed
steps.desc: Correlate successful authenticated actions against sessions not matching the legitimate user's normal pattern.
steps.outcome: List of affected accounts.

ITID-12925.def: Malware running on a victim's endpoint (e.g. an infostealer or browser-targeting trojan) reads session tokens or cookies from browser storage/memory and exfiltrates them so the adversary can hijack the victim's active authenticated session.
ITID-12925.purpose: Captures session hijacking where malware resident on the victim's device extracted a live session token or cookie specifically to hijack an active session.
scopeIncludes: Infostealer malware harvesting browser session cookies for session-hijacking purposes
Malware reading in-memory session tokens from a running browser process
scopeExcludes: ITID-12135 Cached Authentication Token/Cookie Extraction Malware, the general cataloguing of token-extraction malware capability and prevalence across the environment; this leaf covers only the session-hijacking-specific incident where an extracted token was used to hijack a session
ITID-33511 Unclassified/General Cookie Theft (Session Hijacking Context), the protocol-exploitation framing under a separate Tier-1 domain
Session material obtained via physical, hands-on-keyboard device access rather than malware (ITID-12928)
ITID-12925.severity: High, given malware presence combined with confirmed session compromise.
ITID-12925.escalation: Escalate to SOC and endpoint security immediately; treat as an active malware incident requiring device isolation, not merely a session issue.
indicators: Endpoint detection alert for known infostealer/session-token-harvesting malware
Session activity from a device/location inconsistent with the legitimate user immediately following a malware alert
Exfiltration traffic containing browser cookie-store data
vectors: Infostealer malware delivered via phishing attachment or malicious download
Malicious browser extension harvesting session cookies
rootCauses: Endpoint protection failing to detect the infostealer variant
Session cookies not bound to device/browser fingerprint, allowing reuse elsewhere
mitreTechniques: T1555.003 Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
controls: Endpoint detection and response (EDR) with infostealer signatures
Device/browser-bound session tokens
ITID-12925.detection: EDR and exfiltration monitoring provide a strong technical detection surface.
ITID-12925.response: Isolate the infected endpoint, invalidate all sessions active on that device, and perform full malware remediation before restoring access.
metrics: Count of malware-driven session-hijacking incidents per quarter
Time from malware detection to session invalidation
ITID-12925.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the session token was extracted by resident malware on the victim's own device, distinct from the general token-extraction-malware cataloguing at ITID-12135.

playbook.name: Response: Session Hijacking via Malware-Resident Token Theft
playbook.description: For a session hijacked because malware (infostealer, browser-token-dumping tool) resident on the victim's endpoint extracted a live session token/cookie.

steps.title: Confirm malware presence on the source endpoint
steps.desc: Run EDR/AV scan and review alerts on the endpoint associated with the affected account to confirm infostealer or token-theft malware presence.
steps.guidance: Look specifically for browser-cookie-database access or known infostealer families.
steps.outcome: Malware confirmed present, or ruled out in favor of another vector.
steps.abort: If no malware evidence is found on the endpoint, reconsider classification (e.g. network sniffing or phishing-based token theft).

steps.title: Isolate the infected endpoint
steps.desc: Network-isolate the endpoint via EDR to stop further exfiltration and prevent the malware from harvesting new tokens.
steps.outcome: Endpoint isolated from the network.

steps.title: Remove the malware and rebuild the endpoint
steps.desc: Reimage the infected endpoint rather than attempting in-place cleanup, given infostealers commonly persist via multiple mechanisms.
steps.outcome: Endpoint reimaged from a known-clean source.

steps.title: Restore user access on the rebuilt, verified-clean endpoint
steps.desc: Return the endpoint to the user only after confirming it is clean and all credentials have been rotated.
steps.outcome: User restored to normal operation on a clean device.

steps.title: Document the infection vector and reinforce endpoint protection coverage
steps.desc: Record how the malware was delivered and confirm EDR/AV coverage and web-filtering controls are adequate to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; control gap addressed or ticketed.

steps.title: Determine what else the malware exfiltrated
steps.desc: Review EDR telemetry for what the malware collected beyond the session token — saved passwords, other application cookies, crypto wallets, etc.
steps.guidance: Infostealers typically harvest broadly, not just one session — assume all credential material on the device is compromised.
steps.outcome: Full list of data potentially exfiltrated by the malware.

steps.title: Invalidate the hijacked session and reset the account credential
steps.desc: Force-expire the stolen session and rotate the affected account's password.
steps.outcome: Session invalidated; credential rotated.

steps.title: Investigate initial infection vector
steps.desc: Determine how the malware was delivered (malicious download, drive-by, phishing attachment) and remediate that vector.
steps.outcome: Initial infection vector identified and addressed.

steps.title: Confirm the stolen session was actually reused by the attacker
steps.desc: Check application logs for session activity from an IP/device inconsistent with the victim.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized session reuse.

steps.title: Reset credentials for every other account/service the malware may have harvested
steps.desc: Based on the exfiltration scope from identification, rotate every credential the malware could have stolen from that endpoint (all browser-saved passwords, not just the one hijacked session).
steps.outcome: All potentially exposed credentials on the device rotated.

ITID-12926.def: An adversary transfers or replicates a victim's valid session token/cookie onto a different device (theirs) — for example via a trusted-device sync mechanism, a malicious browser-sync exploit, or manual token export — and continues the session from that device without the victim's involvement.
ITID-12926.purpose: Captures session hijacking where a session token or cookie was moved from the victim's legitimate device to an adversary-controlled device and used there to impersonate the victim.
scopeIncludes: Session cookie exported from a trusted device and imported into an adversary's browser on a different device
Abuse of a device-trust/session-sync mechanism to extend a session to an unauthorized device
scopeExcludes: ITID-12637 Trusted-Device Cookie/Token Theft, the sibling Tier-3 branch covering theft of cookies/tokens from a trusted device generally; this leaf covers only the session-hijacking-specific incident where such material was used to continue the session on another device

ITID-12836 Session/Cookie Injection, which covers the technical injection mechanism itself; this leaf focuses on the cross-device transfer and reuse pathway rather than cataloguing the injection technique
Malware on the original device extracting the token, tracked at the point of extraction (ITID-12925)
ITID-12926.severity: High, since the session continues to operate under a device the legitimate user does not control.
ITID-12926.priority: P1, given active unauthorized device access to a live session.
ITID-12926.escalation: Escalate to SOC immediately upon detection of session activity from an unrecognized device; invalidate the session across all devices.
indicators: Session activity from a new, previously unseen device fingerprint mid-session
Device/browser attributes inconsistent with the originating authentication event
User report of session activity they did not perform on an unfamiliar device
vectors: Export/import of session cookies between devices via manual copy or malicious tooling
Abuse of a legitimate cross-device session-continuity feature
rootCauses: Sessions not bound to a specific device/browser fingerprint
No re-authentication challenge when a session's device fingerprint changes mid-session
mitreTechniques: T1550.004 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
controls: Device/browser-bound session tokens
Step-up re-authentication on device fingerprint change mid-session
