ITID-12926.detection: Device fingerprinting and session-continuity monitoring provide a genuine technical detection surface.
ITID-12926.response: Invalidate the session across all devices, require re-authentication with MFA, and investigate how the token reached the unauthorized device.
metrics: Count of cross-device session-hijacking incidents per quarter
sops: Identity and Access Management Incident SOP
ITID-12926.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the defining event is the session's continuation on a second, unauthorized device rather than how the token was originally obtained.

playbook.name: Response: Cross-Device Session Hijacking
playbook.description: For a session token or authentication state improperly transferred or reused across a different, unauthorized device from the one it was originally issued to.

steps.title: Confirm the session is genuinely active on an unrecognized device
steps.desc: Compare device fingerprint, user agent, and device-binding metadata between the original and the suspect session.
steps.guidance: Rule out legitimate multi-device use (new phone, browser sync) via user confirmation before treating as hijacking.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized cross-device session, or ruled out as legitimate.
steps.abort: If the user confirms the new device is their own, close as false positive.

steps.title: Invalidate the session on the unauthorized device
steps.desc: Force-expire the specific session tied to the unrecognized device without necessarily logging out the legitimate device, if the application supports per-device session management.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized device's session terminated.

steps.title: Address the root cause of the cross-device transfer
steps.desc: If caused by an application flaw (e.g. missing device binding on session tokens), work with the development team on a fix; if caused by malware or social engineering, follow the relevant specific playbook for that vector.
steps.outcome: Root cause addressed or handed off to the appropriate specific playbook.

steps.title: Confirm only the legitimate device retains access
steps.desc: Verify the account's active sessions/devices list shows only devices the user recognizes.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean device list.

steps.title: Document the transfer mechanism and recommend device-binding improvement
steps.desc: Record how session material crossed devices and recommend a control such as device binding or step-up authentication on new-device sign-in.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; improvement ticket opened.

steps.title: Determine how the session material crossed devices
steps.desc: Establish the mechanism — synced browser profile, shared cloud backup, session token copied via malware/social engineering, or a device-binding bypass flaw in the application.
steps.outcome: Cross-device transfer mechanism identified.

steps.title: Reset the account credential and re-establish device trust
steps.desc: Rotate the password and, if applicable, reset device-trust/registration so only the legitimate device is trusted going forward.
steps.outcome: Credential rotated; device trust reset to the legitimate device only.

steps.title: Assess what actions were taken from the unauthorized device
steps.desc: Review the application/audit log for actions performed during the unauthorized device's session.
steps.outcome: Full list of actions taken by the attacker documented.

ITID-12927.def: An adversary gains control of or implants malicious logic into a reverse proxy or load balancer that legitimately handles user traffic to an application, using that position to capture session tokens/cookies in transit or to inject/redirect sessions for multiple victims simultaneously.
ITID-12927.purpose: Captures session hijacking enabled by an adversary compromising a reverse proxy or load balancer sitting in the path between users and an application, allowing session material to be intercepted or manipulated at that chokepoint.
scopeIncludes: A compromised reverse proxy logging or exfiltrating session cookies passing through it
Malicious configuration change to a load balancer redirecting session traffic through an interception point
scopeExcludes: ITID-33531 Unclassified/General MITM Session Hijacking, the protocol-exploitation framing of on-path interception under a separate Tier-1 domain; this leaf covers the human-attack-surface angle where a specific trusted infrastructure component was compromised
An adversary sniffing traffic without having compromised the proxy/load-balancer infrastructure itself (ITID-12922)
ITID-12927.severity: Critical, since a compromised proxy/load balancer can expose sessions for many users simultaneously.
ITID-12927.escalation: Escalate to infrastructure/network engineering and IR immediately; consider taking the affected proxy/load balancer out of service pending remediation.
indicators: Unauthorized configuration change on a reverse proxy or load balancer
Multiple, unrelated users' sessions hijacked in a short window pointing to a shared infrastructure chokepoint
Unexpected outbound traffic from proxy/load-balancer infrastructure
vectors: Exploitation of an unpatched vulnerability in reverse proxy/load balancer software
Compromised administrative credentials used to reconfigure the proxy/load balancer
rootCauses: Unpatched reverse proxy/load balancer software
Insufficient privileged access controls on infrastructure administration
controls: Patch management for reverse proxy/load balancer software
Privileged access management and change monitoring for infrastructure components
ITID-12927.detection: Infrastructure change monitoring and traffic anomaly detection provide a genuine technical detection surface.
ITID-12927.response: Take the compromised infrastructure out of service, rebuild from a known-good configuration, and invalidate all sessions that passed through it during the compromise window.
metrics: Time to detect proxy/load-balancer compromise
Count of sessions invalidated following compromise
ITID-12927.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the compromise occurs at a shared infrastructure chokepoint, giving it a much wider blast radius than a single-victim vector.

playbook.name: Response: Session Hijacking via Compromised Reverse Proxy/Load Balancer
playbook.description: For a session hijacked because an attacker gained control of a reverse proxy or load balancer sitting in front of the application, enabling capture or injection of session tokens for many users at once.

steps.title: Confirm compromise of the proxy/load balancer
steps.desc: Review the device/service's configuration, logs, and integrity against known-good baselines to confirm unauthorized modification (altered routing rules, injected header logic, unexpected admin access).
steps.guidance: Given this sits in the path of many users, verify carefully but move quickly — this is a potential mass-compromise vector.
steps.outcome: Compromise confirmed with specific evidence.
steps.abort: If no tampering is found, reconsider the classification.

steps.title: Take the compromised proxy/load balancer out of service
steps.desc: Remove the compromised instance from the traffic path and fail over to a verified-clean redundant instance if available.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with infrastructure/network teams given the likely production impact.
steps.outcome: Traffic no longer flows through the compromised device.

steps.title: Rebuild the proxy/load balancer from a known-clean configuration
steps.desc: Rebuild the device/service from verified-clean images and configuration baselines rather than cleaning in place.
steps.outcome: Proxy/load balancer rebuilt and verified against a known-clean baseline.

steps.title: Phased return to production with elevated monitoring
steps.desc: Bring the rebuilt proxy back into the traffic path in phases with heightened logging active throughout.
steps.outcome: Service fully restored with no signs of recurring compromise.

steps.title: Full incident review and leadership briefing given scale of exposure
steps.desc: Document root cause, scope, and response; brief leadership and assess regulatory/breach notification obligations given the likely broad user impact.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Determine scope: how many sessions/users potentially affected
steps.desc: Estimate the number of users whose traffic passed through the compromised proxy during the compromise window.
steps.guidance: Given the shared-infrastructure nature, this is likely to affect a large percentage of the application's user base.
steps.outcome: Estimated affected-user population and compromise window established.

steps.title: Invalidate all sessions established during the compromise window
steps.desc: Force-expire all sessions that passed through the compromised proxy during the identified window.
steps.outcome: All potentially affected sessions terminated.

steps.title: Investigate and close the initial access vector
steps.desc: Determine how the attacker gained access to the proxy/load balancer (stolen admin credential, unpatched vulnerability, supply-chain) and remediate.
steps.outcome: Initial access vector identified and closed.

steps.title: Determine attacker capability — passive capture vs. active session injection
steps.desc: Establish whether the attacker only captured tokens passing through, or actively injected/modified traffic to hijack sessions in real time.
steps.guidance: Active injection is far more severe and implies the attacker may have taken direct action as users.
steps.outcome: Confirmed attacker capability and any evidence of active abuse.

steps.title: Reset credentials for any account with confirmed unauthorized activity
steps.desc: Rotate passwords for accounts where the audit log shows activity inconsistent with the legitimate user during the compromise window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed-affected credentials rotated.

ITID-12928.def: An adversary with physical access to a victim's unlocked or improperly secured device directly uses an already-authenticated session (e.g. an open browser tab, unlocked mobile app, or extracted local session storage) to impersonate the victim, without needing to intercept network traffic or deploy malware.
ITID-12928.purpose: Captures session hijacking where an adversary obtained a live authenticated session by gaining physical, hands-on access to the victim's unlocked device.
scopeIncludes: Direct use of an already-open authenticated session on an unattended, unlocked device
Extraction of session tokens from local storage on a physically accessed device
scopeExcludes: Malware-based extraction of session tokens without physical hands-on access (ITID-12925)
Loss/theft of a device followed by offline forensic extraction outside the scope of an active session (tracked as a lost/stolen device incident rather than session hijacking)
ITID-12928.severity: High, since physical access typically bypasses most technical controls entirely.
ITID-12928.priority: P1 once confirmed; treat as an active insider-adjacent or opportunistic access incident.
ITID-12928.escalation: Escalate to SOC and physical/facility security immediately; invalidate all sessions on the accessed device.
indicators: Unattended, unlocked device observed or reported in a shared/public space
Session activity performed at a time/location inconsistent with the legitimate user's known whereabouts
Facility access logs placing an unauthorized individual near the device at the relevant time
vectors: Opportunistic use of an unlocked, unattended workstation or mobile device
Deliberate targeting of a device left unlocked in a shared or public space
rootCauses: No automatic screen lock/idle timeout enforced on endpoints
Lack of physical security awareness training
mitreTechniques: T1555.003 Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
controls: Enforced automatic screen lock/idle timeout
Physical security awareness training
ITID-12928.detection: Limited technical detection surface; relies on session-activity anomalies and physical-access correlation rather than direct instrumentation.
ITID-12928.response: Invalidate all sessions on the affected device, require re-authentication, and review physical access controls in the area.
metrics: Count of physical-access session-hijacking incidents per quarter
detections: Session activity/location anomaly detection correlated with physical access logs
ITID-12928.notes: Differentiator within this sibling group: the session was accessed through direct, hands-on physical possession of the victim's own device rather than any remote or malware-based mechanism.

playbook.name: Response: Session Hijacking via Physical Device Access
playbook.description: For a session hijacked because an attacker obtained physical access to an unlocked or unattended device with an active authenticated session.

steps.title: Confirm physical access occurred and establish the window
steps.desc: Interview the user and review physical access logs/CCTV where available to confirm the device was unattended/unlocked and establish the exposure window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed physical access window and circumstances.

steps.title: Lock/remote-wipe the device if still missing, or secure it if recovered
steps.desc: If the device remains out of the user's control, trigger a remote lock or wipe via MDM; if recovered, ensure it is secured and not reconnected until cleared.
steps.outcome: Device secured or wiped as appropriate.

steps.title: Check the device for any tampering, malware, or added persistence
steps.desc: If the device was out of positive control for any meaningful period, inspect it for unauthorized software, added accounts, or hardware tampering before returning to service.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed clean or remediated.

steps.title: Restore user access with new credentials on a verified device
steps.desc: Return the device (or a replacement) to the user with new credentials and confirmed-clean status.
steps.outcome: User restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Reinforce screen-lock policy and device physical security awareness
steps.desc: Log the incident and, where relevant, reinforce auto-lock timeout policy and physical security awareness with the affected user/team.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; policy reminder issued where appropriate.

steps.title: Identify what sessions/applications were active and accessible
steps.desc: Determine which applications had active authenticated sessions on the device during the exposure window.
steps.outcome: List of exposed active sessions/applications.

steps.title: Invalidate active sessions and reset credentials for exposed accounts
steps.desc: Force-expire all sessions that were active during the exposure window and rotate the affected account credentials.
steps.outcome: Sessions terminated; credentials rotated.

steps.title: Check for evidence of actual misuse during the window
steps.desc: Review application/system logs for any action taken during the exposure window that the legitimate user does not recognize.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether misuse occurred, and if so what.
steps.abort: If no misuse is found and the device was recovered quickly, this may be downgraded to a near-miss after credential rotation.

ITID-12929.def: A session-hijacking incident (of any of the sibling vector types) where it has been confirmed that the adversary not only obtained the session but actually used it to perform unauthorized actions (e.g. data access, financial transactions, further account changes), warranting escalation as a confirmed compromise rather than a hijacking attempt.
ITID-12929.purpose: Captures the confirmed-successful outcome where a hijacked session was used by the adversary to take actual unauthorized action, distinct from the hijacking mechanism itself.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed unauthorized data access, exfiltration, or transaction performed via a hijacked session
Confirmed account or security-setting changes made by the adversary via a hijacked session
scopeExcludes: The hijacking event itself with no confirmed unauthorized action taken (ITID-12922 through ITID-12928)

ITID-12735 Pass-the-Ticket for Cross-Session Reuse, the Kerberos-ticket-specific sibling Tier-3 branch for cross-session credential-material reuse, which is tracked separately from this human-session-hijacking outcome leaf
ITID-12929.severity: Critical, given confirmed unauthorized action taken under the victim's identity.
ITID-12929.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response as a confirmed account-takeover-equivalent incident.
indicators: Confirmed unauthorized transaction, data access, or configuration change traced to a hijacked session
Victim reports actions they did not perform appearing in their account activity log
vectors: Continued use of a hijacked session to browse, transact, or modify account settings as the victim
rootCauses: No step-up re-authentication required for sensitive actions within an existing session
Lack of real-time behavioral anomaly detection within authenticated sessions
mitreTechniques: T1550.004 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
controls: Step-up re-authentication for sensitive in-session actions
Real-time behavioral anomaly detection within authenticated sessions
ITID-12929.detection: Application audit logs and behavioral analytics provide strong confirmation once cross-referenced with the originating hijacking event.
ITID-12929.response: Treat as full incident response: contain, invalidate all sessions, reverse unauthorized actions where possible, and notify affected parties per policy.
metrics: Count of confirmed successful session-hijacking incidents per quarter
Time from hijacking to detection of unauthorized action
ITID-12929.notes: This leaf and ITID-12919 are the confirmed-impact outcome leaves for their respective Tier-4 groups; use only once unauthorized action is confirmed, not merely suspected. Distinct from ITID-12735, which tracks Kerberos ticket-reuse specifically.

playbook.name: Response: Successful Session Hijacking with Confirmed Unauthorized Actions
playbook.description: For a confirmed case where a hijacked session (via any mechanism) was used by an attacker to take specific unauthorized actions — data access, changes, transactions, or further compromise.

steps.title: Confirm and catalogue every unauthorized action taken
steps.desc: Build a complete, timestamped list of every action the attacker performed using the hijacked session.
steps.guidance: Treat this as an active intrusion investigation — the hijack itself is now secondary to understanding impact.
steps.outcome: Complete action log for the attacker's session.

steps.title: Terminate the attacker's session and any resulting access immediately
steps.desc: Force-expire the hijacked session and disable any account or access the attacker established from it.
steps.outcome: Attacker no longer has active access.

steps.title: Remediate the hijacking mechanism per the relevant specific playbook
steps.desc: Follow the applicable specific session-hijacking playbook to close the underlying vulnerability that enabled the hijack.
steps.outcome: Underlying hijacking mechanism eradicated.

steps.title: Validate business data/system integrity before closing
steps.desc: Confirm affected data and systems have been restored/verified and that reversed transactions settled correctly.
steps.outcome: Data/system integrity confirmed.

steps.title: Full incident report with impact and notification assessment
steps.desc: Document the complete attack chain, business impact, and response; assess breach notification obligations given confirmed unauthorized actions.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Determine data or system impact
steps.desc: Assess whether the attacker viewed, modified, deleted, or exfiltrated sensitive data, or made changes with downstream business impact (e.g. fraudulent transaction, config change).
steps.outcome: Impact assessment completed.

steps.title: Reverse or freeze unauthorized changes/transactions where possible
steps.desc: Work with the affected system/application owner to reverse fraudulent transactions or freeze pending ones initiated by the attacker.
steps.guidance: Time-sensitive — coordinate with finance/business owners immediately, especially for financial transactions.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized changes reversed or frozen.

steps.title: Remove any persistence the attacker established
steps.desc: Identify and remove any backdoor account, forwarding rule, or scheduled task created during the attacker's access.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled persistence remains.

steps.title: Check for lateral movement or additional compromised accounts
steps.desc: Determine whether the attacker used the hijacked session to pivot to other accounts or systems.
steps.outcome: Full scope of compromise beyond the original account established.

steps.title: Reset credentials and revoke sessions for all affected accounts
steps.desc: Rotate credentials and revoke sessions for the original account plus any account reached via lateral movement.
steps.outcome: All affected credentials rotated.

ITID-12931.def: An incident involving replay of a captured authentication credential or artifact, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under Credential Replay.
ITID-12931.purpose: Catch-all for cases that do not fit the more specific credential-replay leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to identify which artifact/protocol was replayed
Confirmed credential-replay activity where the capture vector and artifact type remain unknown
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (e.g. Kerberos Ticket Replay, API Request Replay)

ITID-33521 'Unclassified / General Session Replay Attack', which sits under a different Tier-1 domain framed as pure technical/protocol session-token exploitation, not a human-facing credential attack; ITID-12931 covers replay of authentication credentials/artifacts specifically, framed as a credential-based attack against a human-facing auth flow
ITID-12931.severity: Reassess once more detail is available.
ITID-12931.priority: P3 by default, escalating once the specific replay pattern is confirmed.
ITID-12931.escalation: Reclassify to the specific replay leaf once the captured artifact type and vector are clarified.
indicators: Authentication alert of unclear specific artifact type
Duplicate authentication attempt flagged with insufficient triage detail
vectors: Credential-replay activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
Triage performed before full log context was available
controls: Kerberos ticket lifetime and replay-cache enforcement
Network traffic analysis for repeated authentication token reuse
Multi-factor authentication on sensitive systems to invalidate replayed credentials
ITID-12931.detection: Same general authentication telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-12931.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once the artifact type and vector are confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-12931.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one. Distinct from ITID-33521, which belongs to a separate technical/protocol-exploitation domain rather than the human-facing credential-attack framing used here.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Credential Replay Attack
playbook.description: General-purpose checklist for a suspected credential replay attack (any mechanism) before the specific technique has been confirmed.

steps.title: Confirm replay activity is not a benign retry/duplicate request
steps.desc: Rule out legitimate client retries, load-balancer duplication, or clock-skew artifacts before treating as a replay attack.
steps.outcome: Confirmed genuine replay of previously captured authentication material.
steps.abort: If explained by a benign cause, close as false positive.

steps.title: Invalidate the replayed credential/session material
steps.desc: Force-expire the affected session/ticket/token and block further acceptance of the captured material.
steps.outcome: Replayed material no longer usable.

steps.title: Hand off to the matching specific replay-attack playbook
steps.desc: Once the mechanism is confirmed, escalate to and follow the specific playbook for detailed eradication steps.
steps.outcome: Incident reassigned with all evidence carried forward.

steps.title: Confirm no further replay attempts succeed
steps.desc: Monitor for continued replay attempts using the same captured material to confirm containment held.
steps.outcome: No successful replay observed during a monitoring window.

steps.title: Document findings and recommend a control improvement
steps.desc: Record the mechanism once confirmed and recommend a control such as nonce/timestamp validation or mutual TLS.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; improvement ticket opened where applicable.

steps.title: Determine the replayed material and mechanism
steps.desc: Establish what was replayed (handshake, nonce-protected request, API request, Kerberos ticket, biometric template, hardware token response) and how it was likely captured.
steps.guidance: This determines which specific playbook to hand off to.
steps.outcome: Replay mechanism identified or narrowed to a short list.

steps.title: Reset the affected account's credentials
steps.desc: Rotate the account password/secret as a precaution.
steps.outcome: Credentials rotated.

steps.title: Establish scope of affected accounts/systems
steps.desc: Identify every account or system where replayed authentication material was accepted.
steps.outcome: Affected accounts/systems enumerated.

ITID-12932.def: An adversary captures a valid network-level authentication handshake exchange and resubmits or relays it to a service to complete authentication.
ITID-12932.purpose: Captures replay of a captured network authentication handshake (e.g. NTLM, EAP) to authenticate without knowing the underlying secret.
scopeIncludes: Captured NTLM challenge/response resubmitted to authenticate to a service
Captured EAP or 802.1X handshake exchange replayed against an authenticator
scopeExcludes: Replay where the capture position itself was an on-path attacker (ITID-12938, Man-in-the-Middle Capture)
Kerberos ticket replay specifically (ITID-12935)
App-layer request replay stemming from missing/weak nonce validation (ITID-12933)
ITID-12932.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the replayed handshake succeeds in authenticating.
ITID-12932.escalation: Escalate to IR if the handshake is confirmed accepted by the authenticator; otherwise track as a blocked attempt.
indicators: Duplicate NTLM challenge/response observed from a different source
Authentication log showing an out-of-sequence or reused handshake nonce/timestamp
vectors: Network capture of an authentication handshake in transit
SMB/NTLM relay of a captured handshake to a second host
rootCauses: Legacy authentication protocols without mutual/session binding (e.g. NTLM)
SMB signing or channel binding not enforced
controls: SMB signing enforcement
Disabling NTLM in favor of Kerberos where possible
Extended Protection for Authentication / channel binding
ITID-12932.detection: Authentication server logs can show duplicate or replayed handshake artifacts, giving a real technical signal.
ITID-12932.response: Contain the source and target hosts, force credential rotation for affected accounts, and verify no follow-on access occurred.
metrics: Count of detected handshake replay attempts per quarter
Mean time to contain confirmed handshake replay
ITID-12932.notes: Distinguished from sibling leaves by the specific artifact being a network authentication handshake, not a ticket, token, or biometric signal.

playbook.name: Response: Network Authentication Handshake Replay
playbook.description: For an attacker who captured and replayed a network authentication handshake (e.g. WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake, NTLM challenge-response) to gain unauthorized access.

steps.title: Confirm the handshake capture and replay
steps.desc: Review wireless/NIDS logs and packet captures to confirm a handshake was captured and subsequently replayed successfully.
steps.outcome: Confirmed capture and replay with supporting packet evidence.

steps.title: Force re-authentication and rotate the pre-shared key/credential
steps.desc: Change the affected Wi-Fi PSK or account password/credential so the captured handshake material is no longer valid.
steps.outcome: Captured handshake material invalidated.

steps.title: Move to a replay-resistant authentication protocol where possible
steps.desc: Where the captured protocol lacks replay protection (e.g. WPA2-PSK), migrate to WPA3-SAE or 802.1X with per-session keys.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive fix — a rotated key alone does not close the underlying protocol weakness for future captures.
steps.outcome: Replay-resistant protocol deployed or migration ticketed.

steps.title: Verify the network requires the new credential and rejects old handshake material
steps.desc: Test that devices using the old PSK/credential can no longer authenticate.
steps.outcome: Confirmed enforcement.

steps.title: Document and assess other networks/services for the same weak protocol
steps.desc: Record the finding and check for other deployments using the same replay-vulnerable protocol.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; sweep completed or ticketed.

steps.title: Identify the network/service targeted and accounts affected
steps.desc: Determine which network (Wi-Fi/VPN) or authentication service accepted the replayed handshake and which account(s) were used.
steps.outcome: Affected network/service and accounts identified.

steps.title: Terminate any session established via the replayed handshake
steps.desc: Identify and disconnect any active connection resulting from the replay.
steps.outcome: Attacker session terminated.

steps.title: Assess what access the attacker gained via the replay
steps.desc: Determine what the attacker did once authenticated using the replayed handshake.
steps.outcome: Scope of resulting access documented.

ITID-12933.def: An adversary resubmits a previously captured authentication request to an application that fails to enforce a unique, single-use nonce or timestamp check, allowing the request to be accepted again.
ITID-12933.purpose: Captures replay of an application-layer authentication request enabled by missing or weak nonce/anti-replay validation.
scopeIncludes: Resubmission of a captured login POST request against an endpoint with no nonce/anti-replay check
Reuse of a one-time authentication token beyond its intended single use due to weak server-side validation
scopeExcludes: Signed API request replay against an otherwise well-formed anti-replay design (ITID-12934, API Request Replay)
Network handshake replay (ITID-12932)
Replay enabled specifically by an on-path MITM capture position (ITID-12938)
ITID-12933.escalation: Escalate to application security and IR if the replayed request results in a successful authentication event.
indicators: Identical authentication request body observed more than once
Application logs showing acceptance of a request with a stale or reused nonce/timestamp
vectors: Capture and resubmission of a login/authentication HTTP request
Browser/proxy replay tooling used against a vulnerable login form
rootCauses: Application does not implement or enforce a single-use nonce
Missing or overly permissive timestamp window on authentication requests
controls: Mandatory single-use nonce validation on authentication endpoints
Timestamp/expiry enforcement with server-side replay cache
ITID-12933.detection: Application logs can reveal duplicate request bodies or reused nonces, providing a real technical signal when logging is sufficiently granular.
ITID-12933.response: Confirm whether the replayed request was accepted, disable the affected account/session, and flag the endpoint for remediation.
metrics: Count of confirmed nonce-validation replay incidents per quarter
Number of endpoints remediated for anti-replay gaps
ITID-12933.notes: Differentiated from API Request Replay (ITID-12934) by root cause: this leaf is specifically about the target's missing/weak anti-replay design, not a well-formed signed request being resubmitted.

playbook.name: Response: Replay Attack Against Missing/Weak Nonce Validation
playbook.description: For an attacker who successfully replayed a request because the target application failed to validate or properly scope a nonce/anti-replay token.

steps.title: Confirm the nonce validation weakness
steps.desc: Analyze the affected application/API to confirm whether nonces are missing, reused, predictable, or not checked against a server-side seen-list.
steps.outcome: Confirmed nonce validation weakness with example evidence.
steps.abort: If nonce validation is functioning correctly, reconsider the classification.

steps.title: Block the source and rate-limit the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Block the offending source at the WAF/API gateway and apply rate limiting to the affected endpoint as an interim mitigation.
steps.outcome: Further replay attempts blocked.

steps.title: Fix nonce generation and server-side validation
steps.desc: Work with the development team to generate cryptographically random, single-use nonces and enforce a server-side seen-list/expiry check.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive fix; treat as a required code change.
steps.outcome: Nonce validation confirmed correct — repeated requests with the same nonce are rejected.

steps.title: Verify the fix rejects a captured-and-replayed request in testing
steps.desc: Attempt to replay a previously valid request against the patched endpoint and confirm it is rejected.
steps.outcome: Replay confirmed blocked by the fix.

steps.title: Document and add anti-replay check to the secure development checklist
steps.desc: Record the finding and recommend this check be added to the AppSec review checklist for future APIs/endpoints.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; AppSec checklist updated.

steps.title: Identify the specific request(s) replayed and their effect
steps.desc: Determine exactly what request was replayed (login, transaction, state-changing API call) and what effect the replay had.
steps.outcome: Replayed request and effect documented.

steps.title: Reverse or freeze any unauthorized effect caused by the replayed request
steps.desc: If the replayed request caused a state change (duplicate transaction, unintended action), work with the application owner to reverse or freeze it.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized effect reversed or frozen.

steps.title: Determine the source of the replay and scope of impact
steps.desc: Identify the source IP/actor and how many times the request was successfully replayed, and what accounts/data were affected.
steps.outcome: Scope of impact established.

ITID-12934.def: An adversary captures a previously issued, signed API authentication request (e.g. an OAuth token exchange, HMAC-signed call) and resubmits it to the same or a different endpoint to authenticate or act on behalf of the legitimate caller.
ITID-12934.purpose: Captures replay of a captured, signed API request to obtain unauthorized access or perform an action without the underlying credential.
scopeIncludes: Resubmission of a captured signed API call to the same endpoint within its validity window
Replay of a captured OAuth token-exchange or client-assertion request
scopeExcludes: Replay resulting from missing/weak nonce validation on a non-API authentication form (ITID-12933)
Hardware token OTP/challenge-response output replay (ITID-12937)
Kerberos ticket replay (ITID-12935)
ITID-12934.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the replayed API call results in a state-changing action.
ITID-12934.escalation: Escalate to API/platform owners and IR when a replayed call is confirmed accepted by the API gateway.
indicators: Duplicate API request signature or token observed from a different source IP
API gateway logs showing acceptance of a request outside its expected single-use window
vectors: Interception of an API call via a compromised client, proxy, or logging pipeline
Reuse of a leaked signed request captured from application logs or browser storage
rootCauses: API does not bind signed requests to a single use or short validity window
Overly long-lived signed tokens without replay protection
controls: Short-lived, single-use API tokens
Request signing with mandatory nonce and timestamp binding at the gateway
ITID-12934.detection: API gateway and access logs can show duplicate signed requests, giving a real technical signal.
ITID-12934.response: Revoke the affected token/credential, review actions taken via the replayed call, and confirm scope of exposure.
metrics: Count of confirmed API replay incidents per quarter
Number of tokens revoked in response
ITID-12934.notes: Differentiated from ITID-12933 by scope: this leaf covers a well-formed, signed API request being resubmitted, not a form suffering from missing anti-replay design.

playbook.name: Response: API Request Replay
playbook.description: For an attacker who captured a valid API request (including its authentication header/signature) and replayed it to repeat an action or gain unauthorized access.

steps.title: Confirm the replayed API request and its authentication method
steps.desc: Identify the specific API call replayed and whether authentication was via API key, bearer token, or a signed request.
steps.outcome: Replayed request and auth method identified.

steps.title: Revoke the affected API key/token
steps.desc: Immediately revoke the credential associated with the replayed request and issue a new one to the legitimate consumer.
steps.outcome: Captured credential invalidated.

steps.title: Require request signing with timestamp and single-use nonce
steps.desc: Work with the API development team to require a signed request including a timestamp window and single-use nonce, rejecting replayed calls outside the window or already seen.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive fix for API replay.
steps.outcome: API confirmed to reject replayed requests.

steps.title: Verify the fix and confirm legitimate API consumers still function
steps.desc: Test that a replayed request is rejected and legitimate traffic is unaffected.
steps.outcome: Fix verified; no legitimate-traffic regression.

steps.title: Document and audit other APIs for the same weakness
steps.desc: Record the finding and check other internal/external APIs for missing request-signing/anti-replay protection.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; sweep completed or ticketed.

steps.title: Determine the effect and volume of replayed calls
steps.desc: Establish how many times the request was replayed and what effect resulted (duplicate records, repeated charges, data access).
steps.outcome: Impact and volume documented.

steps.title: Block the source and rate-limit the endpoint
steps.desc: Block the offending source at the API gateway/WAF and apply rate limiting as an interim mitigation.
steps.outcome: Further replay attempts blocked.

steps.title: Identify the source of the replay
steps.desc: Determine the source IP/actor issuing the replayed calls.
steps.outcome: Source identified where possible.

steps.title: Reverse duplicate effects caused by the replayed calls
steps.desc: Work with the application/business owner to identify and reverse duplicate records, charges, or actions caused by the replay.
steps.outcome: Duplicate effects reversed.

ITID-12935.def: An adversary captures a valid Kerberos ticket (TGT or service ticket) and resubmits it to authenticate, logged as a discrete replay event rather than subsequent lateral-movement activity.
ITID-12935.purpose: Captures the initial capture-and-replay of a Kerberos authentication ticket as a discrete credential-replay event.
scopeIncludes: Extraction of a Kerberos ticket from memory/disk and its initial reuse to authenticate to a service
Detection of a Kerberos ticket presented from a host or IP inconsistent with its original issuance
scopeExcludes: ITID-12735 'Pass-the-Ticket for Cross-Session Reuse', which classifies the subsequent lateral-movement use pattern once a ticket is established as being reused across sessions/hosts; ITID-12935 is scoped to the initial ticket-capture-and-replay authentication event, while ongoing lateral movement built on that ticket is classified at ITID-12735 instead
Network handshake replay not involving Kerberos (ITID-12932)
ITID-12935.escalation: Escalate immediately to IR; a confirmed ticket replay indicates likely credential material has already been extracted from a host.
indicators: Kerberos ticket used from a source inconsistent with its issuing host
Ticket-granting-service request with anomalous ticket lifetime or renewal pattern
vectors: Extraction of tickets from LSASS memory
Golden/silver ticket forgery leveraged for initial replay
rootCauses: Insufficient endpoint protection against credential-dumping tools
Ticket lifetimes configured longer than operationally necessary
mitreTechniques: T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
controls: LSASS protection (Credential Guard)
Kerberos ticket lifetime hardening
Privileged Access Workstation isolation for ticket-issuing accounts
ITID-12935.detection: Domain controller and Kerberos event logs provide a real technical signal for anomalous ticket issuance and reuse.
ITID-12935.response: Force krbtgt/account credential reset as appropriate, isolate the source host, and hand off to ITID-12735 workflow if cross-session lateral movement is confirmed.
metrics: Count of confirmed initial ticket-replay events per quarter
Time to credential reset after confirmation
ITID-12935.notes: Scoping rule versus ITID-12735: ITID-12935 = the initial ticket-capture-and-replay authentication event; ITID-12735 = the subsequent cross-session lateral-movement use pattern built on that ticket.

playbook.name: Response: Kerberos Ticket Replay
playbook.description: For an attacker who captured and replayed a Kerberos authenticator/ticket outside its normal validity window or replay-cache protection, distinct from Pass-the-Ticket in that the focus is on the replay-protection failure itself.

steps.title: Confirm replay-cache/clock-skew failure allowed the replay
steps.desc: Review Kerberos event logs (Event ID 4649 replay detected, or lack thereof) and domain controller replay-cache configuration to confirm why the replay was accepted.
steps.guidance: A properly functioning replay cache should reject a duplicate authenticator — determine why it did not (cache disabled, excessive clock skew tolerance, or ticket lifetime misconfiguration).
steps.outcome: Confirmed cause of replay-protection failure.

steps.title: Reset the affected account's password to invalidate outstanding tickets
steps.desc: Force a password reset for the affected account, which invalidates its Kerberos tickets.
steps.outcome: Outstanding tickets for the account invalidated.

steps.title: Correct replay-cache and clock-skew configuration domain-wide
steps.desc: Verify Kerberos replay-cache is enabled on all relevant services and clock-skew tolerance is set to the recommended default (typically 5 minutes), correcting any misconfiguration found.
steps.outcome: Replay-cache confirmed enforced and clock-skew tolerance corrected domain-wide.

steps.title: Verify replay protection is functioning before closing
steps.desc: Confirm via test or configuration review that a duplicate authenticator is now rejected.
steps.outcome: Replay protection confirmed functioning.

steps.title: Document and audit domain-wide Kerberos hardening
steps.desc: Record the finding and confirm Kerberos hardening (signing, replay-cache, clock sync) is consistent across the domain.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; hardening confirmed domain-wide.

steps.title: Identify the account and service ticket replayed
steps.desc: Determine which account's ticket was captured and which service accepted the replayed authenticator.
steps.outcome: Affected account and service identified.

steps.title: Terminate any session established via the replayed ticket
steps.desc: Identify and terminate any active session/access resulting from the replay.
steps.outcome: Attacker session terminated.

steps.title: Investigate how the ticket/authenticator was captured
steps.desc: Determine the capture vector (network sniffing, compromised host, malicious proxy) and remediate it — see the related network-sniffing or pass-the-ticket playbooks if applicable.
steps.outcome: Capture vector identified and closed.

steps.title: Assess what access the attacker gained
steps.desc: Determine what the attacker accessed or did using the replayed ticket.
steps.outcome: Scope of resulting access documented.

ITID-12936.def: An adversary resubmits a captured or reconstructed biometric authentication artifact (e.g. a stored fingerprint template, recorded voiceprint, or replayed facial-recognition image/video) to authenticate as the legitimate user.
ITID-12936.purpose: Captures replay of a previously captured biometric template or signal to bypass biometric authentication.
scopeIncludes: Presentation of a captured fingerprint template or lifted print to a biometric reader
Playback of a recorded voice or facial-recognition capture against a liveness-checked system
scopeExcludes: Hardware token OTP/challenge-response replay (ITID-12937)
Network handshake or API request replay not involving a biometric factor (ITID-12932, ITID-12934)
ITID-12936.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the biometric system accepted the replayed artifact.
ITID-12936.escalation: Escalate to identity/physical-access security teams when a biometric system logs a successful match under suspicious replay conditions.
indicators: Biometric match confirmed with no corresponding live presence indicator
Repeated identical biometric capture signatures across distinct authentication attempts
vectors: Lifted fingerprint used to fabricate a physical spoof
Recorded video/audio played back against a liveness-detection sensor
rootCauses: Biometric sensor lacks robust liveness detection
Biometric templates stored or transmitted without adequate protection
controls: Liveness detection on biometric sensors
Encrypted, non-exportable storage of biometric templates
ITID-12936.detection: Biometric system logs and liveness-detection telemetry provide a real, if sensor-dependent, technical signal.
ITID-12936.response: Suspend the affected biometric enrollment, investigate the capture vector, and require a secondary authentication factor pending review.
metrics: Count of confirmed biometric replay attempts per quarter
Liveness-detection false-accept rate reviewed post-incident
ITID-12936.notes: The only sibling leaf where the replayed artifact is a physiological/behavioral template rather than a digital token, ticket, or handshake.

playbook.name: Response: Biometric Authentication Replay
playbook.description: For an attacker who captured a biometric authentication response/template transmission and replayed it to bypass biometric verification, rather than spoofing the biometric itself.

steps.title: Confirm this is a replay of captured biometric response data, not live spoofing
steps.desc: Distinguish between a captured-and-replayed authentication response (this incident type) and a live presentation attack (fake fingerprint/face) — review the authentication system's liveness/replay-detection logs.
steps.outcome: Confirmed replay of captured biometric response data.
steps.abort: If this is a live spoofing/presentation attack rather than a data replay, reclassify accordingly.

steps.title: Disable biometric authentication for the affected user as an interim measure
steps.desc: Temporarily fall back the affected user to an alternate strong authentication method while the biometric channel is investigated.
steps.outcome: Replayed biometric data no longer accepted for that user.

steps.title: Enable or repair liveness detection and challenge-response protections
steps.desc: Work with the biometric system vendor/owner to ensure liveness detection is active and that the response transmission is bound to a fresh, single-use challenge that cannot be replayed.
steps.guidance: This is the definitive fix — the root cause is a missing or bypassed liveness/anti-replay control.
steps.outcome: Liveness detection and replay protection confirmed active.

steps.title: Re-enroll the affected user's biometric and restore access
steps.desc: Re-enroll the user's biometric template and restore biometric authentication once protections are confirmed fixed.
steps.outcome: User restored to normal biometric authentication with protections verified.

steps.title: Document and audit other biometric-protected systems for the same gap
steps.desc: Record the finding and check whether other systems using the same biometric platform share the missing liveness/replay protection.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; sweep completed or ticketed.

steps.title: Identify the affected user and system
steps.desc: Determine whose biometric authentication response was captured and which system accepted the replay.
steps.outcome: Affected user and system identified.

steps.title: Terminate any access gained via the replay
steps.desc: Revoke any session or physical/logical access obtained through the replayed authentication.
steps.outcome: Attacker access terminated.

steps.title: Assess what access the attacker gained
steps.desc: Determine what the attacker accessed using the replayed biometric authentication.
steps.outcome: Scope of resulting access documented.

ITID-12937.def: An adversary captures the output of a hardware authentication token (OTP or challenge-response) and resubmits it before it expires or before the legitimate user completes authentication.
ITID-12937.purpose: Captures replay of a captured hardware token's one-time-passcode or challenge-response output.
scopeIncludes: Interception of an OTP displayed on or generated by a hardware token and use of it before expiry
Capture and resubmission of a challenge-response token output via a real-time phishing relay
scopeExcludes: Biometric template/signal replay (ITID-12936)
Signed API request replay (ITID-12934)
Replay where the capture vector is specifically an on-path MITM position (ITID-12938)
ITID-12937.priority: P1, given the narrow validity window typically indicates active, time-sensitive attacker involvement.
ITID-12937.escalation: Escalate immediately to IR; a successful OTP/challenge-response replay typically indicates a real-time phishing or relay operation in progress.
indicators: Same OTP value used in two authentication attempts from different sources
Authentication succeeding just after a token generation event with an implausible relay delay
vectors: Real-time phishing (adversary-in-the-middle) relay of a token prompt
Shoulder-surfing or camera capture of a hardware token display
rootCauses: OTP validity window longer than necessary
No binding of the OTP to a specific session/device context
controls: Session/device-bound OTP validation
Phishing-resistant authentication (FIDO2/WebAuthn) as a replacement for OTP tokens
ITID-12937.detection: Authentication logs showing OTP reuse or implausible timing provide a real technical signal.
ITID-12937.response: Invalidate the token/session, notify the affected user, and review for signs of a broader real-time phishing campaign.
metrics: Count of confirmed OTP/challenge-response replay incidents per quarter
Adoption rate of phishing-resistant MFA as a mitigating trend
ITID-12937.notes: Differentiated from Man-in-the-Middle Capture (ITID-12938) by focus: this leaf is about the captured token output itself, regardless of whether the specific capture mechanism was an on-path relay.

playbook.name: Response: Hardware Token Response Replay
playbook.description: For an attacker who captured a hardware token's one-time response (e.g. OTP, challenge-response) and replayed it before it expired or despite it being single-use.

steps.title: Confirm the token response was replayed rather than independently generated
steps.desc: Review authentication logs to confirm the same OTP/response value was accepted twice, or was accepted outside its intended validity window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed replay of a captured token response.
steps.abort: If the value differs each time and was independently correct, reconsider — this may indicate token seed compromise instead.

steps.title: Invalidate the account's session and force re-authentication
steps.desc: Force-expire any session established via the replayed response and require full re-authentication.
steps.outcome: Attacker session terminated.

steps.title: Fix the server-side replay window/single-use enforcement
steps.desc: If a server-side flaw allowed the same OTP to be accepted more than once or outside its window, work with the application/IAM team to enforce strict single-use and time-window validation.
steps.guidance: If the capture was via an AiTM phishing relay rather than a server flaw, prioritize migrating the affected users to phishing-resistant MFA (e.g. FIDO2) instead.
steps.outcome: Replay confirmed blocked by server-side enforcement, or phishing-resistant MFA migration initiated.

steps.title: Verify the fix and restore normal token use
steps.desc: Confirm the same OTP/response can no longer be accepted twice, then restore normal use.
steps.outcome: Fix verified.

steps.title: Document and evaluate migration to phishing-resistant MFA
steps.desc: Record the finding and evaluate whether the affected population should migrate from OTP/hardware-token response to a phishing-resistant method.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; MFA strategy recommendation made.

steps.title: Identify how the response was captured
steps.desc: Determine the capture vector — phishing (real-time relay/AiTM), shoulder-surfing, compromised endpoint, or a server-side replay-window flaw.
steps.outcome: Capture vector identified.

steps.title: Reset the account password and re-provision the hardware token if compromised
steps.desc: Rotate the password and, if the token seed itself may be compromised (rather than just one response captured), re-provision a new hardware token.
steps.outcome: Credential and token material rotated as needed.

steps.title: Assess what access the attacker gained
steps.desc: Determine what the attacker accessed using the replayed token response.
steps.outcome: Scope of resulting access documented.

ITID-12938.def: An adversary positioned on-path between a user and an authentication service (e.g. via a rogue access point, proxy, or DNS manipulation) captures an authentication artifact in transit and replays it, independent of the specific artifact type captured.
ITID-12938.purpose: Captures credential replay where the defining feature is an on-path adversary-in-the-middle position used to capture the authentication artifact.
scopeIncludes: Rogue Wi-Fi access point or transparent proxy used to capture and replay an authentication exchange
DNS or ARP-spoofing-facilitated interception of an authentication artifact later resubmitted
scopeExcludes: Replay attributed to a specific artifact-type leaf where the capture vector was not an on-path MITM position (e.g. ITID-12932, ITID-12934, ITID-12936, ITID-12937)
Passive network sniffing without an active on-path relay/injection capability (out of scope for this leaf)
ITID-12938.escalation: Escalate immediately to IR and network security; an active on-path position may still be present on the network.
indicators: Unrecognized access point or certificate/proxy anomaly on the authentication path
ARP or DNS anomalies correlated with a captured authentication exchange
vectors: Rogue access point positioned near a target network
Transparent proxy or ARP/DNS spoofing inserted into the authentication path
rootCauses: Lack of mutual TLS or certificate pinning on authentication channels
Unmonitored/unsegmented wireless or local network segments
controls: Certificate pinning / mutual TLS on authentication channels
Wireless intrusion detection for rogue access points
Network segmentation limiting ARP/DNS spoofing blast radius
ITID-12938.detection: Network and wireless monitoring can reveal the on-path position itself, providing a real technical signal distinct from the artifact-specific leaves.
ITID-12938.response: Locate and remove the on-path device/position, rotate any credentials transiting the affected path, and audit for further exposure.
metrics: Count of confirmed on-path capture incidents per quarter
Mean time to remove a confirmed rogue on-path device
ITID-12938.notes: This leaf is organized by capture vector (an active on-path position) rather than by the artifact type replayed, which is why it can overlap in artifact type with other leaves but is classified here whenever the on-path position is the defining feature of the incident.

playbook.name: Response: Replay Attack via Man-in-the-Middle Capture
playbook.description: For a credential replay attack where an attacker positioned themselves as a man-in-the-middle to capture authentication material in real time (e.g. adversary-in-the-middle phishing proxy) for subsequent or immediate replay.

steps.title: Confirm MitM/AiTM positioning and what was captured
steps.desc: Determine the MitM mechanism (malicious proxy, ARP spoofing, rogue certificate, AiTM phishing kit) and what authentication material it captured — password, session cookie, MFA response.
steps.guidance: AiTM phishing kits typically capture the full post-MFA session cookie, which is more dangerous than a password alone since it bypasses MFA entirely.
steps.outcome: MitM mechanism and captured material identified.

steps.title: Revoke sessions and tokens for all affected accounts
steps.desc: Force-expire all sessions and refresh tokens for every affected account — a password reset alone does not kill an already-established session cookie.
steps.outcome: All affected sessions/tokens invalidated.

steps.title: Audit affected accounts for persistence established via the stolen session
steps.desc: Review affected accounts for new MFA methods, forwarding rules, or app grants added after the compromise window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of attacker persistence.

steps.title: Restore access with new credentials and re-enrolled MFA
steps.desc: Have affected users set new passwords and re-enroll MFA from a known-clean device.
steps.outcome: Users have confirmed-clean access restored.

steps.title: Document root cause and recommend conditional access hardening
steps.desc: Record the AiTM/MitM technique used and recommend controls such as conditional access token binding, phishing-resistant MFA, or DNS/proxy filtering.
steps.outcome: Finding logged; control improvement ticket opened.

steps.title: Identify affected users and confirm real-system login using captured material
steps.desc: Determine everyone exposed to the MitM and check real authentication logs for logins using the captured material shortly after capture.
steps.outcome: Affected users identified; confirmed use of captured material where it occurred.

steps.title: Force password reset and MFA re-enrollment
steps.desc: Reset passwords and require MFA re-enrollment for all affected accounts.
steps.outcome: Credentials and MFA state rotated.

steps.title: Remove any confirmed persistence and migrate to phishing-resistant MFA
steps.desc: Remove any attacker-added persistence, and migrate affected/high-risk users to phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn) which is not susceptible to AiTM session-cookie theft.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled access remains; phishing-resistant MFA rollout initiated for the affected population.

steps.title: Assess what access the attacker gained
steps.desc: Determine what the attacker accessed or did using the replayed credential/session.
steps.outcome: Scope of resulting access documented.

steps.title: Take down the MitM/AiTM infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the malicious proxy domain/IP and submit a takedown request; remediate any local network MitM positioning (ARP spoofing, rogue cert).
steps.outcome: MitM infrastructure blocked/removed.

ITID-12939.def: A confirmed outcome-based classification for any credential-replay attempt (regardless of artifact type or capture vector) where the adversary successfully authenticated or acted using the replayed artifact.
ITID-12939.purpose: Captures a credential replay attack confirmed to have successfully bypassed authentication, resulting in attacker access or action.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed unauthorized login or session establishment resulting from a replayed credential artifact
Confirmed post-authentication action (data access, privilege use, lateral movement) taken using a successfully replayed artifact
scopeExcludes: Attempted or blocked replay that did not result in successful authentication (classified under the relevant process-oriented sibling leaf instead)
Subsequent lateral-movement activity classified separately under ITID-12735 once pass-the-ticket reuse is established across sessions
ITID-12939.priority: P1, treated as an active incident.
ITID-12939.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response for containment, scoping, and forensic preservation; do not wait for full triage before initiating IR engagement.
indicators: Confirmed successful authentication using a previously flagged replayed artifact
Post-authentication activity inconsistent with the legitimate account owner's behavior
vectors: Any of the artifact-specific replay vectors above (handshake, ticket, token, biometric, hardware token, on-path capture) that succeeded
rootCauses: Underlying replay vulnerability was not detected or mitigated in time
Absence of secondary verification (step-up authentication, anomaly detection) at the point of use
controls: Step-up/adaptive authentication on anomalous sign-ins
Automated session revocation on confirmed replay detection
ITID-12939.detection: Confirmed by correlating authentication success logs with prior replay indicators; the strongest and least ambiguous technical signal in this ITID group.
ITID-12939.response: Immediately revoke the compromised session/credential, contain affected systems, and conduct full forensic review of attacker actions taken during the session.
metrics: Count of confirmed successful replay bypasses per quarter
Mean time to detect and mean time to contain a confirmed bypass
ITID-12939.notes: This leaf is outcome-based rather than vector-based: any of the sibling leaves above escalate here once the replay is confirmed successful, at which point severity, priority, and IR engagement all increase accordingly.

playbook.name: Response: Successful Credential Replay Attack with Confirmed Bypass
playbook.description: For a confirmed case where a credential replay attack (any mechanism) successfully bypassed authentication and the attacker gained and used unauthorized access.

steps.title: Confirm and catalogue the attacker's actions post-bypass
steps.desc: Build a complete, timestamped list of every action the attacker performed after successfully replaying the captured authentication material.
steps.guidance: Treat this as an active intrusion investigation.
steps.outcome: Complete action log for the attacker's access.

steps.title: Terminate attacker access immediately
steps.desc: Force-expire the session/ticket/token used and disable any account or access the attacker established from it.
steps.outcome: Attacker no longer has active access.

steps.title: Remediate the specific replay mechanism per the matching specific playbook
steps.desc: Follow the applicable specific replay playbook to close the underlying protocol/validation weakness that enabled the bypass.
steps.outcome: Underlying replay mechanism eradicated.

steps.title: Validate system/data integrity before closing
steps.desc: Confirm affected data and systems have been restored/verified and that reversed transactions settled correctly.
steps.outcome: Integrity confirmed.

steps.title: Full incident report with impact and notification assessment
steps.desc: Document the complete attack chain, business impact, and response; assess breach notification obligations given confirmed unauthorized access.
steps.outcome: Full report completed; notification obligations assessed and actioned if required.

steps.title: Determine the replay mechanism and how material was captured
steps.desc: Establish the specific replay mechanism (handshake, nonce failure, API, Kerberos, biometric, hardware token, MitM) to identify the matching specific playbook.
steps.outcome: Replay mechanism identified.

steps.title: Reset credentials and revoke sessions for all affected accounts
steps.desc: Rotate credentials for the original account plus any account reached via lateral movement.
steps.outcome: All affected credentials rotated.

steps.title: Remove any persistence the attacker established
steps.desc: Identify and remove any backdoor account, forwarding rule, or scheduled task created during the attacker's access.
steps.outcome: No attacker-controlled persistence remains.

steps.title: Assess data/system impact and lateral movement
steps.desc: Determine what data was accessed/exfiltrated and whether the attacker pivoted to other accounts or systems.
steps.outcome: Full impact scope established.

steps.title: Reverse or freeze any unauthorized changes/transactions
steps.desc: Work with the affected system/application owner to reverse fraudulent transactions or freeze pending ones.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized changes reversed or frozen.

ITID-13111.def: A trusted insider's deliberate, unauthorized copying or removal of customer PII or financial records for personal gain, sale, or harm to the organization.
ITID-13111.purpose: Captures a malicious insider stealing customer personally identifiable information (PII) or financial records, distinguishing this specific data class for breach-notification and regulatory-reporting purposes.
scopeIncludes: Bulk export of customer records to a personal device or external service
Unauthorized queries against a customer database outside normal job function
Screenshotting or photographing customer financial data for later use
scopeExcludes: Theft of proprietary source code or trade secrets (ITID-13112)
Theft of employee/HR records (ITID-13113)
Sabotage of IT systems or facilities (ITID-13121, ITID-13122) — a destructive act, not a data-theft one
Negligent/accidental exposure with no theft intent (ITID-13211)
ITID-13111.severity: High — customer PII/financial theft carries real breach-notification and regulatory exposure (e.g. state breach laws, PCI-DSS, GDPR where applicable).
ITID-13111.escalation: Escalate immediately to legal/privacy and, once confirmed, initiate breach-notification assessment; involve HR for personnel action.
indicators: Anomalous bulk export or query volume against customer data by a single user
Access to customer records outside the user's normal role/team scope
Data access shortly before resignation or termination
vectors: Direct database query/export using legitimate access
Copying data to personal cloud storage or removable media
Emailing records to a personal account
rootCauses: Overly broad data access not scoped to job function
No DLP or export-volume monitoring on customer data stores
No user-and-entity behavior analytics (UEBA) baseline for normal access patterns
controls: Data loss prevention (DLP) on customer data stores
Least-privilege access scoping
UEBA/anomalous-access-volume alerting
ITID-13111.detection: DLP export alerts, database audit logs, and UEBA anomalous-access-volume detection provide real technical signal here.
ITID-13111.response: Preserve access/export logs, suspend the insider's access pending investigation, and coordinate with legal on breach-notification obligations.
metrics: Count of confirmed insider PII/financial data theft incidents per year
Mean time from anomalous access to detection
ITID-13111.notes: Scoped specifically to customer PII/financial data — the regulatory and notification obligations differ materially from theft of internal-only data (source code, HR records), which is why this is its own leaf rather than folded into a general insider data-theft leaf.

playbook.name: Response: Insider Theft of Customer PII/Financial Records
playbook.description: For a confirmed or strongly suspected case of an insider deliberately exfiltrating customer PII or financial records, e.g. before resignation or for external sale.

steps.title: Confirm the scope of data accessed and exported
steps.desc: Review DLP, database access logs, and file-server audit logs for the individual's account to determine exactly what records were accessed and exported.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with legal before broadly reviewing an employee's activity — this may need to follow the org's formal insider-investigation process, not ad hoc SOC review.
steps.outcome: A documented, timestamped record of what data was accessed and where it went (USB, personal cloud, personal email, etc.).

steps.title: Preserve evidence with proper chain of custody
steps.desc: Image the employee's device and preserve relevant logs before any account action that could alert them or lose volatile data.
steps.guidance: Follow this org's formal evidence-handling procedure — this may later support disciplinary action or law enforcement referral.
steps.outcome: Forensically sound evidence preserved.

steps.title: Determine if exfiltrated data is recoverable/revocable
steps.desc: Assess whether the destination (personal cloud, USB, email) can be remotely wiped or access revoked (e.g. shared-link revocation, MDM wipe of a corporate-owned personal device).
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any remote remediation of the exfiltrated copy is possible.
steps.abort: If the data left on a personal, non-company-managed device or account, remote remediation typically isn't possible — proceed to Legal for external options (cease-and-desist, etc.).

steps.title: Assess and notify affected customers if required
steps.desc: Work with Legal/Privacy to determine breach-notification obligations for the affected customer records.
steps.outcome: Notification obligations determined and, if applicable, executed on the required timeline.

steps.title: Document the case and review access-control gaps
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and assess whether tighter DLP rules, access reviews, or offboarding timing would have prevented or caught this sooner.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with HR/Legal sign-off; control improvement recommended if a real gap is identified.

steps.title: Loop in HR and Legal before proceeding further
steps.desc: Notify HR and Legal that a suspected insider data-theft investigation is underway.
steps.guidance: This is a personnel matter with potential legal/disciplinary consequences — SOC should not act unilaterally beyond initial evidence preservation.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal aware and providing direction on next steps (including whether/when to confront the employee).

steps.title: Restrict account access per HR/Legal direction
steps.desc: Suspend or restrict the account's access to sensitive systems, timed and worded per HR/Legal guidance.
steps.guidance: Timing matters — acting before evidence preservation is complete can tip off the individual.
steps.outcome: Further data access prevented.

ITID-13112.def: A trusted insider's deliberate, unauthorized copying or removal of proprietary source code, algorithms, designs, or trade secrets for personal gain, use at a competitor, or harm to the organization.
ITID-13112.purpose: Captures a malicious insider stealing proprietary source code or trade secrets, distinguishing intellectual-property theft from customer-data or HR-record theft for impact-assessment purposes.
scopeIncludes: Copying source code repositories to personal storage before resignation
Exfiltrating proprietary designs, formulas, or algorithms
Taking trade secrets to a competing employer
scopeExcludes: Theft of customer PII/financial records (ITID-13111)
Theft of employee/HR records (ITID-13113)
Insider espionage on behalf of a foreign government or organized threat actor (ITID-13141) — this leaf covers self-motivated IP theft, not directed espionage
ITID-13112.severity: High — proprietary IP theft can cause lasting competitive harm independent of any regulatory notification obligation.
ITID-13112.escalation: Escalate to legal (IP/trade-secret counsel) and executive leadership immediately upon confirmation; consider civil/criminal referral.
indicators: Bulk repository clone or download shortly before resignation
Access to code/design repositories outside the user's project scope
Departure to a known competitor shortly after anomalous access
vectors: Git clone or bulk repository download to a personal device
Copying design files to external/cloud storage
Printing or photographing sensitive documents
rootCauses: No repository access review tied to project relevance
No offboarding checklist step for revoking repository access immediately
No DLP coverage on source-code/design repositories
mitreTechniques: T1213.003 Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories
controls: Repository access scoped to active project need
DLP on source-code repositories
Immediate access revocation on resignation notice
ITID-13112.detection: Version-control audit logs and DLP bulk-download alerting provide real technical signal here.
ITID-13112.response: Preserve repository/access logs, revoke access immediately, and engage legal on trade-secret protection options.
metrics: Count of confirmed IP theft incidents per year
Time from resignation notice to access revocation
ITID-13112.notes: Distinguished from ITID-13141 (Espionage) by motive/sponsor: this leaf is self-motivated theft (personal gain, new employer), while Espionage implies a directed external sponsor.

playbook.name: Response: Insider Theft of Proprietary Source Code or Trade Secrets
playbook.description: For a confirmed or strongly suspected case of an insider deliberately exfiltrating source code, product designs, or other trade secrets, e.g. for a competitor or a new venture.

steps.title: Confirm the scope of repositories/systems accessed and exported
steps.desc: Review version control audit logs, DLP, and file-share logs for the individual's account to determine which repositories or trade-secret materials were accessed, cloned, or exported.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with Legal before broadly reviewing an employee's activity.
steps.outcome: Documented, timestamped record of what was accessed and where it went.

steps.title: Preserve evidence with proper chain of custody
steps.desc: Image the employee's device(s) and preserve relevant repository/access logs before any account action.
steps.outcome: Forensically sound evidence preserved.

steps.title: Assess whether the exfiltrated material can be recovered or its use restricted
steps.desc: Evaluate remote-wipe options for company-managed devices, and whether the destination (new employer, personal repo) can be reached via legal cease-and-desist.
steps.outcome: Remediation options identified.

steps.title: Engage Legal on external enforcement options
steps.desc: If the individual moved to a competitor or is using the material externally, Legal may pursue a cease-and-desist, injunction, or litigation.
steps.outcome: Legal strategy determined and executed.

steps.title: Document the case and review repository access controls
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and assess whether tighter code-repository access controls, DLP on source code, or offboarding practices would have caught this sooner.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with HR/Legal sign-off; control improvement recommended if a gap is identified.

steps.title: Loop in HR and Legal before proceeding further
steps.desc: Notify HR and Legal — trade-secret theft often precedes departure to a competitor and carries significant legal weight (e.g., trade-secret litigation).
steps.guidance: Legal may want to preserve options like an injunction, which depends on how the investigation is conducted.
steps.outcome: HR/Legal aware and directing next steps.

steps.title: Restrict access to source code and trade-secret repositories
steps.desc: Suspend or restrict the individual's access, timed per HR/Legal guidance, and consider rotating any credentials/keys they held.
steps.outcome: Further access and exfiltration prevented.

ITID-13113.def: A trusted insider's deliberate, unauthorized copying or removal of employee personnel files, compensation data, or other HR records.
ITID-13113.purpose: Captures a malicious insider stealing internal employee or HR records, distinguishing workforce-data theft from customer-data or IP theft for notification and impact purposes.
scopeIncludes: Unauthorized export of payroll or compensation data
Copying personnel files outside HR's normal access scope
Accessing colleagues' HR records out of curiosity or malice and removing the data
scopeExcludes: Theft of customer PII/financial records (ITID-13111)
Theft of proprietary source code or trade secrets (ITID-13112)
ITID-13113.severity: High — employee data theft carries internal trust and, depending on jurisdiction, notification implications.
ITID-13113.escalation: Escalate to HR leadership and legal immediately upon confirmation; assess notification obligations to affected employees.
indicators: HR-system access or export outside the user's job function
Bulk export of payroll/compensation data
Access to specific colleagues' records with no legitimate business reason
vectors: Direct HRIS query/export using legitimate access
Copying files to personal storage
rootCauses: Overly broad HRIS access not scoped to role
No audit logging/alerting on HR-system bulk exports
controls: HRIS access scoped to role
Audit logging and export alerting on HR systems
ITID-13113.detection: HRIS audit logs and export-volume alerting provide real technical signal here.
ITID-13113.response: Preserve access logs, suspend access, and coordinate with HR/legal on employee notification if warranted.
metrics: Count of confirmed HR-data theft incidents per year
ITID-13113.notes: Kept as its own leaf rather than folded into the general customer-data leaf because the affected population (employees) and notification path (HR-led) differ materially.

playbook.name: Response: Insider Theft of Employee/HR Records
playbook.description: For a confirmed or strongly suspected case of an insider (often HR/IT staff with legitimate access) deliberately exfiltrating employee/HR records.

steps.title: Confirm the scope of records accessed and exported
steps.desc: Review HRIS audit logs, DLP, and file access logs for the individual's account to determine which employee records were accessed and where data went.
steps.guidance: Coordinate closely with HR and Legal from the outset — this involves other employees' personal data and the suspect may hold legitimate elevated HR-system access.
steps.outcome: Documented, timestamped record of what data was accessed and exported.

steps.title: Preserve evidence with proper chain of custody
steps.desc: Image the employee's device and preserve relevant HRIS/access logs before any account action.
steps.outcome: Forensically sound evidence preserved.

steps.title: Determine if exfiltrated data is recoverable/revocable
steps.desc: Assess whether the destination can be remotely wiped or access revoked.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether remote remediation is possible.
